Term / Figure / Concept / Era / Language / Literature / Port / Art & Culture Description & Key Details
FIGURES
Lopamudra One of the earliest known female Vedic sages (Brahmavadini); wife of Rishi Agastya; composer of hymns in the Rigveda (e.g., 1.179 – dialogue on marital duties and spiritual pursuit); symbol of intellectual partnership in Vedic tradition.
Gargi Vachaknavi Prominent female philosopher in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad; engaged Yajnavalkya in a profound debate on the nature of Brahman and the ultimate reality at King Janaka’s court; represents women’s participation in Vedic philosophical discourse.
Leelavati (Lilavati) Traditionally described as the daughter of Bhaskara II; his famous mathematical treatise Lilavati (part of Siddhanta Shiromani) is named after her; written in verse form with engaging problems on arithmetic, geometry, and algebra; used as a textbook for centuries.
Savitri Legendary figure in the Mahabharata (Vana Parva); daughter of King Ashwapati; wife of Satyavan; through wit and devotion, persuaded Yama (god of death) to restore her husband’s life; source of the famous “Savitri-Satyavan” narrative symbolising moral resolve and marital devotion.
Saumilla Figure mentioned in some ancient literary references; identity and contributions remain obscure and debated in canonical sources.
Shaunaka Ancient Vedic scholar; head of the Naimisha Forest assembly; associated with the classification of the Atharvaveda; traditionally associated with Rigveda Pratisakhya (phonetics); narrator frame for the Mahabharata (recited by Sauti Ugrashravas).
Vasumitra Buddhist scholar associated with the Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka (c. 100 CE); key figure of the Sarvastivada school; linked with compilation of the Mahavibhasha Shastra, a major Abhidharma text.
Bhavabhuti 8th-century Sanskrit dramatist; court poet of Yashovarman of Kannauj; author of Mahaviracharita, Malatimadhava, and Uttararamacharita; known for depth of emotion (karuna rasa) and lyrical beauty; regarded as second only to Kalidasa.
Hastimalla Jain scholar and poet (traditionally dated to c. 13th–14th century); author of Shantinatha Charita and other works in Apabhramsha and Sanskrit; belonged to the Kharatara Gaccha sect; known for historical and religious narratives.
Kshemeshwara Poorly documented medieval author mentioned in limited regional sources; not firmly established in canonical Sanskrit literary traditions.
Aryadeva 3rd-century CE Madhyamaka philosopher; chief disciple of Nagarjuna; author of Chatushatika (400 Verses) and Shata Shastra; influential Mahayana thinker within the Madhyamaka tradition.
Sanghabhuti Early Buddhist monk; according to Sri Lankan chronicles (Dipavamsa), one of the missionaries sent by Ashoka to propagate Buddhism in Vanavasa (location debated); contributed to the spread of Theravada traditions.
Dignaga (Dinnaga) 5th-century CE Buddhist logician; founder of Buddhist epistemology (Pramana school); authored Pramanasamuccaya; systematised theories of valid cognition through perception (pratyaksha) and inference (anumana); influenced later Nyaya and Buddhist logic.
Nathamuni 10th-century Vaishnava saint and philosopher; compiler of the Divya Prabandham (4000 Tamil verses of Alvars); early systematiser and reviver of the Srivaishnava tradition; integrated yoga and devotional practices.
Family Members of Buddha & Mahavira Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama):
  • Father: King Suddhodana (Shakya clan leader)
  • Mother: Queen Maya Devi (Koliya princess; died 7 days after birth)
  • Step-mother/Aunt: Mahaprajapati Gotami (first Buddhist nun)
  • Wife: Yashodhara
  • Son: Rahula (later became a monk)
  • Other names: Shakyamuni, Tathagata, Bhagavat, Arhat; sometimes referred to as Jina in comparative traditions
Mahavira (Vardhamana):
  • Father: King Siddhartha (Kshatriya, Jnatrika clan)
  • Mother: Trishala (sister of Chetaka, Lichchhavi chief)
  • Wife: Yashoda
  • Daughter: Priyadarshana (Anovrati)
  • Brother: Nandivardhana
  • Other names: Nayaputta (“son of Natas”), Jina, Arhata
ERAS
Vikrama Era Started in 57 BCE; traditionally linked to King Vikramaditya; widely used in North India for calendars, inscriptions, and dating; still used in traditional Hindu panchangs.
Saka Era Began in 78 CE; origin debated (often linked to Kanishka or Western Kshatrapas); official era of the Government of India; used in inscriptions and Jain texts.
Gupta Era Started in 319–320 CE by Chandragupta I; used in Gupta inscriptions; marks the beginning of the Gupta Golden Age.
Kali Era (Kali Yuga) Began in 3102 BCE (traditional date of Mahabharata war & Krishna’s departure); used in Puranas and astronomical texts; current year (2025 CE) ≈ 5127 Kali Yuga.
LANGUAGES & SCRIPTS
Sauraseni Middle Indo-Aryan Prakrit spoken in the Mathura region; used in Jain and early literary traditions; language of classical Sanskrit dramas (used by female and lower-class characters); contributed to the development of Western Hindi.
Kharosthi Ancient script written right-to-left; used in Gandhara (NW India and Afghanistan) from 3rd c. BCE to 3rd c. CE; appears in north-western Ashokan edicts and Kushan inscriptions; derived from Aramaic.
Nandnagari Medieval script derived from Devanagari; used in Maharashtra and Karnataka (9th–19th c.) for Sanskrit manuscripts, especially in temple and scholastic traditions.
Brahmi Ancient script (3rd c. BCE onward); ancestor of most Indian scripts; used in Ashokan edicts; left-to-right; gave rise to Gupta and regional script forms.
Sharada Script used in Kashmir and north-western India (8th–12th c.); evolved from Gupta script; used for Sanskrit Buddhist and Shaiva texts; influenced scripts such as Takri.
CONCEPTS
Core Jain Philosophical Principles Ahimsa (non-violence), Anekantavada (multiplicity of viewpoints), Syadvada (conditional predication); form the ethical and epistemological foundation of Jainism.
Pavarana Buddhist monastic ceremony held at the end of the rainy season retreat (Vassa); monks invite criticism from peers to confess faults and purify conduct.
Dharma and Rita Rita: Vedic concept of cosmic order and truth; Dharma: evolved moral and social duty in later texts; Dharma develops conceptually from Rita in Upanishads and Dharmashastras.
Sautrantika and Sammitiya Early Buddhist schools: Sautrantika relied primarily on sutras and inference; Sammitiya (Pudgalavada) accepted a “person” (pudgala) beyond the skandhas.
Sarvastivadin Buddhist school holding that past, present, and future dharmas exist; dominant in Kashmir and Gandhara; associated with Mahavibhasha; influential during Kushan rule.
Lokottaravadin Mahayana offshoot of Mahasanghika; regarded Buddha as supramundane (lokottara); texts such as Mahavastu reflect this doctrine.
LITERATURE
Manava Dharma Shastra Also known as Manusmriti; Dharmashastra text dealing with social, legal, and ethical norms; compiled approximately between 200 BCE and 200 CE.
Acarangasutra Oldest Jain Agama; part of the 12 Angas; focuses on monastic conduct, non-violence, and ascetic discipline; composed in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit.
Sukra Nitisara Later political text attributed to Shukracharya (likely a medieval compilation); discusses governance, administration, and ethics; often compared with Arthashastra.
Dipavamsa Earliest Pali chronicle of Sri Lanka (4th–5th c. CE); records Buddhist missions, kings, and early councils.
Mahaparinibbana Sutta Digha Nikaya 16; describes the final days and parinirvana of the Buddha at Kushinagar; foundational Theravada text, also respected in Mahayana traditions.
Baudhayan Sulva Sutras Part of Baudhayana Shrauta Sutra (~800–600 BCE); among the earliest texts on geometry; instructions for altar construction; contains an early statement of the Pythagorean theorem.
TERMS
Eripatti Land assignment or revenue allocation for the maintenance of irrigation tanks in Chola administration; often tax-free and recorded in inscriptions.
ART & CULTURE
Chausath Yogini Temple 9th–10th century temples (e.g., Bhedaghat, Mitaoli); circular, open-air structures with 64 (or 81) Yogini shrines; associated with Tantric traditions; sometimes cited in discussions on circular architectural symbolism.
- Basic timeline (validated) -
Period Timeframe Key Features
Prehistoric Period Paleolithic Age (~2.5 million BCE – 10,000 BCE) Hunter-gatherer societies, use of chipped stone tools, cave and open-air sites
Mesolithic Age (10,000 BCE – 8000 BCE) Microlithic tools, hunting-gathering economy, early human adaptation; limited and regional beginnings of animal domestication
Neolithic Age (c. 7000 BCE – 2500 BCE) Agriculture, pottery, permanent settlements; early farming sites such as Mehrgarh
Chalcolithic Age (c. 2500 BCE – 1500 BCE) Use of copper along with stone tools; rural settlements and regional cultures (e.g., Jorwe, Ahar)
Indus Valley Civilization Early Harappan (3300 BCE – 2600 BCE) Regional cultures, village settlements, growth of trade networks
Mature Harappan (2600 BCE – 1900 BCE) Urban centres (Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro), planned cities, drainage system, script
Late Harappan (1900 BCE – 1300 BCE) Decline of urbanism, regionalisation, continuation of rural settlements
Vedic Period Early Vedic Age (c. 1500 BCE – 1000 BCE) Rigvedic culture, pastoral economy, tribal polity, worship of nature deities
Later Vedic Age (c. 1000 BCE – 600 BCE) Territorial states (Janapadas), varna system, agrarian expansion, Upanishadic thought
Mahajanapada & Second Urbanization Mahajanapada Phase (600 BCE – 400 BCE) Sixteen Mahajanapadas; rise of Magadha as dominant power
Rise of Buddhism & Jainism (6th century BCE) Teachings of Gautama Buddha and Mahavira; challenge to Vedic ritualism
Persian & Greek Contacts/Invasions (c. 520 BCE – 300 BCE) Achaemenid control of north-western regions; Alexander’s invasion (326 BCE)
Maurya Empire Chandragupta Maurya (321 BCE – 297 BCE) Founded Maurya Empire; defeated Seleucus Nicator; centralized administration
Bindusara (297 BCE – 273 BCE) Territorial expansion of the empire
Ashoka (c. 268 BCE – 232 BCE) Kalinga War, policy of Dhamma, spread of Buddhism through missions
Decline of Mauryas (185 BCE) Assassination of Brihadratha; end of centralised Mauryan rule
Post-Mauryan Period Shunga Dynasty (185 BCE – 73 BCE) Revival of Brahmanical traditions; patronage of art and learning
Kanva Dynasty (73 BCE – 28 BCE) Short-lived dynasty replacing the Shungas
Indo-Greeks (2nd century BCE – 1st century CE) Hellenistic cultural influence; bilingual and gold coinage
Shakas (Western Kshatrapas) (1st century BCE – 4th century CE) Rule in western India; centres such as Ujjain
Kushana Empire (1st century CE – 3rd century CE) Kanishka; patronage of Mahayana Buddhism; Silk Route trade
Gupta Empire Chandragupta I (c. 320 CE – 335 CE) Foundation of Gupta rule
Samudragupta (c. 335 CE – 375 CE) Military campaigns; Allahabad Pillar Inscription
Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) (c. 375 CE – 415 CE) Cultural florescence; foreign trade; Iron Pillar inscription
Decline of Guptas (mid-6th century CE) Hun invasions and administrative fragmentation
Post-Gupta & Early Medieval Period Harsha Empire (606 CE – 647 CE) Harshavardhana; patronage of learning and Buddhism
Chalukyas (6th – 8th century CE) Deccan power; Pulakesin II; Aihole and Badami
Pallavas (6th – 9th century CE) Kanchipuram; rock-cut and structural temples
Pala Empire (8th – 12th century CE) Bengal and Bihar; patronage of Buddhist institutions like Nalanda
Rashtrakutas (8th – 10th century CE) Deccan empire; Kailasanatha Temple at Ellora
Chola Dynasty (9th – 13th century CE) Imperial Cholas; maritime power; Brihadeshwara Temple under Rajaraja I
- Indus Valley Civilization (IVC) towns (validated) -
Site Location Key Features
INDUS RIVER BASIN (PAKISTAN)
Harappa Punjab, Pakistan Granaries, fortified citadel, terracotta figurines, cemeteries (H and R-37)
Mohenjo-Daro Sindh, Pakistan Great Bath, granary structures, Dancing Girl, Pashupati seal, advanced drainage
Chanhudaro Sindh, Pakistan Bead-making centre, shell and bangle industry; absence of a citadel
Kot Diji Sindh, Pakistan Pre-Harappan culture, early fortifications, distinctive pottery
Amri Sindh, Pakistan Pre-Harappan settlement, early ceramic traditions
Ganweriwala Punjab, Pakistan Large urban centre in Cholistan Desert; size comparable to major Harappan cities
Balakot Balochistan, Pakistan Coastal Harappan site; shell-working industry
GUJARAT & KACHCHH REGION
Dholavira Kachchh, Gujarat Sophisticated water-management system, three-part city layout, large open spaces
Lothal Ahmedabad district, Gujarat Dockyard-like structure (interpretation debated), bead-making, evidence of rice husk
Surkotada Kachchh, Gujarat Small fortified settlement; remains of equids (horse identification debated)
Kuntasi Gujarat Craft and industrial activities; evidence of copper and stone tool production
Desalpur Gujarat Fortified Harappan settlement; structural remains and ritual features (interpretation debated)
Prabhas (Prabhas Patan) Gujarat Late Harappan phase; associated with Prabhas ware cultural tradition
Daimabad Maharashtra Southernmost Harappan site; famous bronze sculptures; Late Harappan phase
SARASVATI–GHAGGAR–HAKRA BASIN (HARYANA & RAJASTHAN)
Rakhigarhi Haryana Largest Harappan site in India; planned layout, drainage system, burials
Banawali Haryana Fortified settlement; evidence of agriculture (barley) and terracotta objects
Jognakhera Haryana Early Harappan site; evidence of bead-making and ritual activity
Bhirrana Haryana Early Hakra phase site; among the earliest settlements in the Sarasvati basin
Mitathal Haryana Early Harappan settlement with fortification remains
Kalibangan Rajasthan Ploughed agricultural field, fire altars, mud-brick houses
Ropar (Rupar) Punjab, India Late Harappan site; human and dog burials, terracotta artefacts
EASTERN & LATE HARAPPAN SITES (UTTAR PRADESH)
Alamgirpur Uttar Pradesh Easternmost Harappan site; pottery, tools, Late Harappan phase
Hulas Uttar Pradesh Late Harappan rural settlement; mud-brick houses
Sanauli Uttar Pradesh Late Harappan / OCP-associated site; copper artefacts and burial practices (cultural attribution debated)

Nanda Empire (~345–321 BCE)
Nanda Empire Nanda Dynasty Mahapadma Nanda ~345–329 BCE Pataliputra Ekarat, Sarvakshatrantaka Subjugated most Mahajanapadas; established Magadha as the paramount power in North India Highly centralized bureaucracy; enormous revenue through systematic taxation Succeeded by his sons; administrative unpopularity grew
Dhana Nanda ~329–321 BCE Pataliputra Agrammes (Greek sources) Maintained a massive standing army; reputation of strength discouraged Alexander’s advance Oppressive taxation and autocratic rule led to widespread discontent Overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya with Chanakya’s support
Maurya Empire (~322–185 BCE)
Maurya Empire Maurya Dynasty Chandragupta Maurya ~322–298 BCE Pataliputra Founder of Maurya Empire Defeated Nanda dynasty; defeated Seleucus Nicator (305 BCE); unified North India; extended empire to Afghanistan Arthashastra-based centralized administration; Jainism patronage Abdicated throne; became Jain monk; died at Shravanabelagola
Bindusara ~298–273 BCE Pataliputra Amitraghata (“Slayer of enemies”) Consolidated Mauryan rule; extended control to Deccan (except Kalinga); maintained diplomatic relations with Hellenistic kingdoms Continued Mauryan bureaucracy; patronized Ajivika sect Natural death; succession struggle followed
Ashoka the Great ~268–232 BCE Pataliputra Devanampiya, Piyadassi Conquest of Kalinga; issuance of Major & Minor Rock Edicts; spread of Buddhism to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia Dhamma policy; religious tolerance; hospitals, roads, rest houses; Third Buddhist Council Natural death; administrative overstretch weakened empire
Kunala c. 232 BCE (traditional accounts) Taxila (as Viceroy) Prince; mentioned in Buddhist traditions (status as emperor disputed) Governorship of Taxila mentioned in later Buddhist sources Buddhist leanings (traditional accounts) Not firmly attested as emperor; succession unclear
Dasharatha ~232–224 BCE Pataliputra Grandson of Ashoka Issued cave inscriptions; dedicated Barabar caves to Ajivikas Continued Ashokan religious tolerance; Ajivika patronage Loss of western provinces; authority declined
Samprati ~224–215 BCE (traditional Jain chronology) Ujjain / Pataliputra Called “Jain Ashoka” in Jain traditions (not epigraphically attested) Jain missionary activity mentioned in later Jain texts; construction of Jain temples (traditional accounts) Patronage of Jainism; religious tolerance Historicity and reign details debated among historians
Brihadratha ~187–185 BCE Pataliputra Last Mauryan ruler Ruled a diminished empire; no major territorial control Weak central authority Assassinated by Pushyamitra Shunga; Maurya dynasty ended
Post-Maurya / Pre-Gupta Period (~2nd Century BCE–3rd Century CE)
Indo-Greek Kingdom Euthydemid Dynasty Demetrius I ~200–180 BCE Bactra → Taxila Founder of Indo-Greek rule in India Invaded north-west India after Mauryan decline; occupied Gandhara and Punjab Introduced Hellenistic political control; issued bilingual coins (Greek legends) Empire expanded but fragmented under successors
Euthydemid Dynasty Apollodotus I ~180–160 BCE Taxila / Western Punjab First Indo-Greek ruler to issue coins with Indian symbols Consolidated Indo-Greek rule in India; coins in Greek and Prakrit (Kharosthi) Strengthened Indo-Greek administration in Punjab Succeeded by Menander I
Euthydemid Dynasty Menander I (Milinda) ~165–130 BCE Sagala (Sialkot) Most famous Indo-Greek ruler Expanded deep into Punjab; associated with *Milinda Panha* dialogue with Nagasena Patronized Buddhism; bilingual coins (Greek–Prakrit); Buddhist tradition regards him as convert Kingdom fragmented after his death
Later Indo-Greek Antialcidas ~115–95 BCE Taxila Known from Heliodorus Pillar Sent Heliodorus as ambassador to Shunga ruler Bhagabhadra Evidence of Indo-Greek–Indian diplomatic relations; Heliodorus pillar shows early Vaishnavism Indo-Greek power confined to NW India
Later Indo-Greek (Fragmented Phase) Strato I ~125–110 BCE Punjab / Mathura Ruled easternmost Indo-Greek territories Issued coins showing Greek and Indian deities; evidence of cultural syncretism Continued Hellenistic traditions with Indian elements Gradual displacement by Indo-Scythians (Shakas)
Shunga Empire Shunga Dynasty Pushyamitra Shunga ~185–149 BCE Pataliputra / Vidisha Senapati (Mauryan army commander) Assassinated Mauryan ruler Brihadratha; established Shunga rule; defended north India against Indo-Greek incursions Brahmanical revival; Ashvamedha sacrifices (as per Puranic tradition); Buddhist structures like Bharhut and Sanchi continued (patronage debated) Natural death; dynasty continued under successors
Agnimitra ~149–141 BCE Vidisha Known from Kalidasa’s *Malavikagnimitram* Consolidated Shunga authority in central India; defended against Indo-Greeks Patronage of Sanskrit drama; support to Brahmanical rituals Succeeded by Vasujyeshtha
Vasujyeshtha ~141–131 BCE Vidisha — Maintained territorial control; limited historical records Continued Brahmanical patronage Succeeded by Vasumitra
Bhagabhadra ~110 BCE Vidisha Known from Heliodorus Pillar inscription Hosted Indo-Greek ambassador Heliodorus; evidence of diplomatic relations Vaishnava patronage; Heliodorus pillar dedicated to Vasudeva Followed by later Shunga rulers
Devabhuti ~83–73 BCE Vidisha Last Shunga ruler (Puranic sources) Ruled a weakened empire; court intrigue and decline Brahmanical orientation; limited political control Assassinated by minister Vasudeva Kanva; Shunga dynasty ended
Kanva Dynasty Kanva Dynasty Vasudeva Kanva ~73–66 BCE Pataliputra Brahmin minister of Shungas Assassinated last Shunga ruler Devabhuti; established Kanva rule over Magadha Brahmanical orientation; continued Shunga administrative structure Succeeded by Bhumimitra
Bhumimitra ~66–52 BCE Pataliputra — Exercised limited authority over Magadha; Kanva power confined to core Gangetic region Brahmanical traditions; no major cultural or political initiatives Succeeded by Narayana
Narayana ~52–40 BCE Pataliputra — Ruled a declining polity; faced pressure from Satavahanas and regional powers Continued Brahmanical practices; weak central control Succeeded by Susarman
Susarman ~40–28 BCE Pataliputra Last Kanva ruler Nominal authority; Kanva rule largely symbolic by this stage No significant patronage recorded Kanva dynasty ended; Magadha absorbed into Satavahana sphere (indirect control)
Satavahana Empire Satavahana Dynasty Simuka ~100–70 BCE Pratishthana (Paithan) Founder Established Satavahana rule in Deccan; ended Kanva authority in Magadha indirectly; controlled western Deccan trade routes Issued lead and copper coins; supported Brahmanical traditions Succeeded by Kanha (Krishna)
Kanha (Krishna) ~70–60 BCE Pratishthana — Consolidated Deccan territories; extended control into central India Continued trade links with western ports; patronized Brahmanical institutions Succeeded by Satakarni I
Satakarni I ~60–37 BCE Pratishthana Husband of Naganika Performed Ashvamedha and Rajasuya; expanded influence to Malwa and western India Strong Brahmanical patronage; Naneghat inscription records sacrifices Died early; regency of Queen Naganika
Gautamiputra Satakarni ~106–130 CE Pratishthana Saka-Yavana-Pahlava-nisudana Defeated Western Kshatrapa ruler Nahapana; restored Satavahana supremacy over Deccan Patronized both Brahmanism and Buddhism; reissued Nahapana’s silver coins Succeeded by Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
Vasishthiputra Pulumavi ~130–160 CE Pratishthana Son of Gautamiputra Maintained Deccan control; faced renewed pressure from Western Kshatrapas Issued coins with ship motifs; continued trade with Roman world Gradual decline; Satavahana power fragmented by 3rd century CE
Indo-Parthian Kingdom Gondopharid Dynasty Gondophares I ~19–46 CE Taxila / Seistan (regional centers) Founder of Indo-Parthian rule in NW India Extended control over Arachosia, Sindh, Punjab; associated with St. Thomas in Christian tradition (not historical certainty) Issued bilingual Greek–Prakrit coins; Parthian (Zoroastrian-influenced) background with religious tolerance Succeeded by successors; authority weakened over time
Abdagases ~46–60 CE Taxila / Seistan Nephew and successor of Gondophares Controlled eastern Indo-Parthian territories; known mainly from silver drachms Maintained Parthian-style administration; continued Indo-Roman trade links Gradually displaced by expanding Kushans
Orthagnes / Sases ~60–80 CE Gandhara region Later Indo-Parthian rulers Represent last phase of Indo-Parthian authority in NW India Continued Parthian-style coinage; declining political control Absorbed into Kushan Empire under Kujula Kadphises
Śakas (Western Satraps) Kardamaka Dynasty Chastana ~78–130 CE Ujjain Founder of Kardamaka line of Western Satraps Contemporary of Satavahana ruler Gautamiputra Satakarni Established power in Malwa & Kathiawar His dynasty ruled for ~300 years
Kardamaka Dynasty Rudradaman I ~130–150 CE Ujjain Mahakshatrapa Junagadh inscription (in Sanskrit); defeated Satavahanas Repaired Sudarshana lake; promoted Sanskrit literature Powerful ruler; stabilized kingdom
Kardamaka Dynasty Rudrasimha I ~175–197 CE Ujjain Mahakshatrapa Continued expansion & consolidation Maintained trade networks with Roman Empire Weakened gradually after his reign
Kardamaka Dynasty Rudrasimha III ~388–415 CE Ujjain Last Western Satrap ruler Defeated by Gupta emperor Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) End of Śaka power in western India Western Satraps absorbed into Gupta Empire
Kushan Empire Kushan Dynasty Kujula Kadphises ~30–80 CE Purushapura Yabgu Unified Yuezhi tribes, conquered Gandhara Promoted Silk Route trade, issued early Kushan coins Succeeded by Vima Takto
Vima Takto ~80–105 CE Purushapura/Mathura Soter Megas Expanded into Northwest India, established Mathura as a center Standardized coinage, supported mixed religions Succeeded by Vima Kadphises
Vima Kadphises ~105–127 CE Purushapura/Mathura Maharajadhiraja Introduced gold coinage, expanded trade with Rome Patronized Shaivism, promoted trade networks Succeeded by Kanishka I
Kanishka I ~127–151 CE Purushapura/Mathura Shaonanoshao Hosted 4th Buddhist Council, developed Gandhara and Mathura art Mahayana Buddhism, Sanskrit literature, Greco-Buddhist art Empire fragmented after successors
Gupta Empire (~240–550 CE)
Gupta Empire Gupta Dynasty Sri Gupta ~240–280 CE — Maharaja Founder of the Gupta lineage; ruled a small territory in Magadha region Early local governance; beginnings of Gupta political authority Succeeded by Ghatotkacha
Ghatotkacha ~280–319 CE — Maharaja Strengthened Gupta position prior to imperial expansion Prepared ground for rise of Chandragupta I Succeeded by Chandragupta I
Chandragupta I ~319–335 CE Pataliputra Maharajadhiraja Marriage with Lichchhavi princess; Gupta Era (319–320 CE) Issued gold coins; centralized monarchy Natural death; empire expanded
Samudragupta ~335–380 CE Pataliputra Kaviraja, Parakramanka Allahabad Pillar inscription; Dakshinapatha campaign; Ashvamedha Religious tolerance; patron of arts, music, Brahmanism Natural death; empire at peak
Chandragupta II ~380–415 CE Pataliputra / Ujjain Vikramaditya, Sakari Defeated Western Kshatrapas; access to Arabian Sea trade Navaratnas (Kalidasa); Vaishnavism; cultural florescence Natural death; Golden Age continued
Kumaragupta I ~415–455 CE Pataliputra Mahendraditya Patron of Nalanda; repelled Pushyamitras Diverse coinage; promotion of education Natural death; Huna pressure emerged
Skandagupta ~455–467 CE Pataliputra — Successfully resisted Huna invasions; repaired Sudarshana lake Preserved Gupta administration under severe economic strain Natural death; empire weakened
Narasimhagupta (Baladitya) ~467–473 CE Pataliputra — Associated with resistance to Hunas (as per some sources); Nalanda patronage Buddhist support; temporary stabilization Succeeded by Kumaragupta II
Kumaragupta II ~473–476 CE Pataliputra Kramaditya Maintained limited eastern control Weak central authority; declining revenues Succeeded by Buddhagupta
Buddhagupta ~477–495 CE Pataliputra — Issued inscriptions; ruled fragmented territories Administrative decline amid Huna pressure Gupta authority further weakened
Vishnugupta ~540–550 CE Pataliputra (nominal) — Last recognized Gupta ruler with nominal authority Minimal political control; symbolic rule End of Gupta imperial power
Contemporary / Post-Gupta Dynasties (~3rd–7th Century CE)
Vakataka Dynasty Vakataka Dynasty Vindhyashakti ~250–270 CE — (Vidarbha region) Founder Laid foundations of Vakataka power in Vidarbha Brahmanical traditions; early consolidation Succeeded by Pravarasena I
Pravarasena I ~270–330 CE Nandivardhana (probable) Samrat Performed four Ashvamedhas; expanded Vakataka authority Strong Brahmanical patronage; Prakrit inscriptions Empire divided into Nandivardhana & Vatsagulma branches
Rudrasena II ~400–410 CE Nandivardhana — Marriage with Prabhavatigupta (Gupta alliance) Vaishnava patronage; strong Gupta political influence Died early; regency of Prabhavatigupta
Prithvisena I ~410–430 CE Nandivardhana — Stabilized kingdom after regency period Continued Vaishnava orientation; regional governance Dynasty weakened in later decades
Kadamba Dynasty Kadamba Dynasty Mayurasharma ~345–365 CE Banavasi Founder Established first native dynasty of Karnataka after conflict with Pallavas Brahmanical traditions; early Kannada & Sanskrit inscriptions (Talagunda) Dynasty consolidated under successors
Kakusthavarman ~435–455 CE Banavasi — Expanded kingdom; maintained diplomatic ties with Guptas & Vakatakas Vaishnava patronage; matrimonial alliances with major dynasties Peak of Kadamba political influence
Ravivarman ~485–519 CE Banavasi Assumed imperial titles Issued gold coins; asserted independent sovereignty in northern Karnataka Shaiva & Vaishnava patronage; temple grants Declined under rising Chalukya power
Maitraka Dynasty Maitraka Bhatarka ~500–524 CE Valabhi Senapati (Gupta vassal) Founded Maitraka rule in Saurashtra as a Gupta military governor Shaiva in royal titles; patronized Buddhist institutions Initially subordinate to Guptas
Dhruvasena I ~524–544 CE Valabhi Maharaja (later phase) Issued land grants; strengthened Valabhi as an educational center Buddhist learning alongside Brahmanical traditions Succeeded by later Maitraka rulers
Dharasena II ~600–620 CE Valabhi — Consolidated Maitraka political power in western India Continued patronage of Buddhist & Sanskrit learning Valabhi at its political peak
Maukhari Dynasty Maukhari Ishvaravarman ~550–570 CE Kannauj Maharajadhiraja Asserted Maukhari independence; checked Later Gupta authority in the Ganga valley Primarily Shaiva; limited Buddhist patronage Established Kannauj as a major political center
Grahavarman ~590–610 CE Kannauj Last effective Maukhari ruler Married Rajyashri (Harsha’s sister); alliance with Pushyabhutis Shaiva patronage; maintained religious tolerance Killed by Devagupta of Malwa; Maukhari power collapsed
Western Ganga Dynasty Ganga Dynasty Kongunivarma Madhava ~350–370 CE Kolar region (later Talakadu) Founder; Dharmamaharaja Established Western Ganga rule in southern Karnataka after decline of Satavahanas Strong patronage of Jainism; support to Brahmanical traditions Maintained early independence
Durvinita ~529–579 CE Talakadu Scholar-king Asserted Ganga autonomy against Pallavas; renowned Sanskrit and Kannada scholar Major patron of Jainism; promoted Kannada literature and Sanskrit learning Dynasty continued; later became Chalukya vassals
Later Guptas Later Gupta Krishnagupta ~490–505 CE Magadha — Early ruler of the Later Gupta line in post-imperial Magadha; limited political authority Brahmanical (Vaishnava) orientation with religious tolerance Restricted to regional control
Adityasena ~670–690 CE Magadha — Performed Ashvamedha to revive Gupta imperial prestige; known from Deo-Baranark inscription Strong Vaishnava patronage; use of imperial Gupta titles Decline due to Maukhari–Harsha ascendancy and political fragmentation
Kalabhra Interregnum — — (Obscure rulers) ~300–600 CE Tamilakam (South India) — Displaced early Chera, Chola, and Pandya rulers; period of political disruption in South India Patronized Buddhism and Jainism; challenged Brahmanical dominance Overthrown by Pallavas, revived Pandyas, and Chalukyas
Early Cholas (Sangam Cholas) Chola Dynasty (Early Phase) Early Chola Polity ~3rd Century BCE – 3rd Century CE Kaveri Delta (Tamilakam)
  • Mentioned in Ashokan inscriptions
  • One of the Three Crowned Kings (Muvendars)
  • Controlled fertile Kaveri basin
  • Early agrarian state with clan-based monarchy
  • Participated in Indo-Roman maritime trade
  • Trade via ports like Kaveripattinam (Puhar)
  • Early Tamil polity before Sangam peak
 Declined later during Kalabhra interregnum
Ellalan (Elara) ~2nd Century BCE Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka)
  • Tamil Chola ruler who ruled Sri Lanka
  • Administered Sri Lanka with justice (Mahavamsa)
  • Represents early overseas political expansion
  • Known for impartial justice and rule of law
 Defeated by Dutugemunu of Sri Lanka
Karikala Chola ~1st–2nd Century CE Uraiyur; port at Kaveripattinam (Puhar)
  • Great Sangam Chola ruler
  • Associated with Pattinappalai
  • Defeated Cheras and Pandyas (Battle of Venni)
  • Strengthened Chola political dominance
  • Early construction of Kaveri embankments (Kallanai tradition)
  • Patron of Sangam literature
  • Promoted irrigation, agriculture, and overseas trade
 Chola power declined after Sangam age
Chera Dynasty (Early Cheras) Chera Dynasty Uthiyan Cheralathan ~1st Century BCE – 1st Century CE Karur (Vanji) — Associated with Sangam age; controlled western trade routes and ports like Muziris Patronized Sangam poets; active Indo-Roman trade (pepper, spices) Succession disputes and decline during Kalabhra interregnum
Nedunjeral Adan ~2nd Century CE Karur (Vanji) — Fought Cholas and Pandyas; celebrated for naval and military exploits in Sangam poems Patronage to Tamil literature; sustained maritime trade with Roman world Weakened prior to Kalabhra domination
Pandya Dynasty (Early Medieval Revival) Pandya Kadungon ~590–620 CE Madurai — Ended Kalabhra rule; restored Pandya authority in Tamilakam Shaiva revival; revival of Tamil literary and temple traditions Foundation laid for Later Pandya resurgence
Pallava Dynasty Pallava Dynasty Sivaskandavarman ~3rd century CE Kanchipuram – Issued grants (Hirehadagalli Copper Plate), earliest known Pallava ruler Performed Ashvamedha, patronized Brahmanism Early expansion and state formation
Simhavarman II ~4th century CE Kanchipuram – Consolidated Pallava power in Tamil and Telugu regions Hindu patronage Predecessor to later imperial Pallavas
Simhavishnu ~575–600 CE Kanchipuram Avanisimha Defeated Kalabhras, revived Pallava power Vaishnava patronage, early Dravidian temples Established dominance, succeeded by Mahendravarman I
Mahendravarman I ~600–630 CE Kanchipuram Vichitrachitta Initiated rock-cut temples, authored *Mattavilasa Prahasana* Shaivism, music, painting patronage Succeeded by Narasimhavarman I
Narasimhavarman I ~630–668 CE Kanchipuram Mamalla, Vatapikonda Sacked Badami (defeated Pulakesin II), built Mahabalipuram monuments Shaiva patronage, Dravidian architecture Peak of Pallava power, natural death
Paramesvaravarman I ~670–695 CE Kanchipuram – Faced Chalukya invasions, defended Kanchi Shaivism Stability maintained despite wars
Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) ~695–722 CE Kanchipuram Rajasimha Built Kailasanatha Temple (Kanchi), expansion of art and architecture Shaiva patronage, refined Dravidian style High cultural zenith
Nandivarman II (Pallavamalla) ~731–796 CE Kanchipuram Pallavamalla Restored dynasty after internal strife, faced Rashtrakutas and Pandyas Shaivism and Vaishnavism co-patronage Later consolidation phase
Dantivarman ~796–846 CE Kanchipuram – Decline phase; faced Rashtrakutas and Pandyas Hindu patronage Weak political control
Nandivarman III ~846–869 CE Kanchipuram – Temporary revival of power; alliances with Gangas Shaivism Brief stability before decline
Aparajitavarman ~880–897 CE Kanchipuram – Last ruler; defeated by Aditya I (Chola) – End of Pallava rule; absorbed into Chola Empire
Chalukyas of Badami Chalukya Dynasty Pulakeshin I ~543–566 CE Badami (Vatapi) Founder, Satyashraya Founded the Chalukya dynasty; established Vatapi as capital Early consolidation of power; Vaishnava leanings Foundation of Chalukya rule
Kirtivarman I ~566–597 CE Badami — Conquered Kadambas, Mauryas of Konkan; expanded kingdom Early patronage of rock-cut architecture Succeeded by Mangalesha
Mangalesha ~597–609 CE Badami — Regent for nephew Pulakeshin II; patronized cave temples Vaishnava and Jain patronage Overthrown by Pulakeshin II
Pulakeshin II ~609–642 CE Badami Satyashraya, Parameshwara Defeated Harsha on Narmada; checked Pallavas; received Persian embassy Aihole inscription; Xuanzang visit; peak of Chalukya power Killed after Pallava invasion led by Narasimhavarman I
Vikramaditya I ~655–680 CE Badami Rajamalla Restored Chalukya power after Pallava invasion; reasserted control Temple patronage; revival phase Natural death
Vinayaditya ~680–696 CE Badami — Conducted successful military expeditions in Deccan and western India Maintained imperial stability; military administration Natural death
Vijayaditya ~696–733 CE Badami — Long and stable reign; consolidation of administration Temple building and cultural patronage Natural death
Vikramaditya II ~733–746 CE Badami — Defeated Pallavas; sacked Kanchipuram; asserted Chalukya supremacy Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal; architectural zenith Succeeded by Kirtivarman II
Kirtivarman II ~746–753 CE Badami Last Chalukya ruler Faced Rashtrakuta challenge under Dantidurga Weak administration Defeated by Rashtrakuta Dantidurga; end of Badami Chalukyas
Vardhana Dynasty Pushyabhuti / Vardhana Prabhakaravardhana ~580–605 CE Thanesar Founder of political power Established Thanesar as a strong regional kingdom; repelled Hunas Shaiva and Surya worship; strong military organization Succeeded by Rajyavardhana
Rajyavardhana ~605–606 CE Thanesar — Defeated Malwa ruler Devagupta; allied with Maukhari dynasty Military consolidation of north India Killed by Shashanka of Gauda
Harshavardhana ~606–647 CE Thanesar → Kannauj Shiladitya (Xuanzang) Unified large parts of North India; shifted capital to Kannauj Patron of Buddhism; Kannauj & Prayag assemblies; Nalanda support Died heirless; empire disintegrated
Naravardhana Pre-6th century CE Thanesar (lineage) Ancestor Early Pushyabhuti lineage ruler (mentioned in inscriptions) Dynastic continuity (not political founder) Pre-imperial phase

  • Aryabhatiya (Arithmetic, algebra, trigonometry, astronomy; value of π, sine tables, explanation of eclipses, Earth’s rotation)
  • Arya-siddhanta (Lost work, known through later references)
 Gupta Period (Buddha Gupta / early 6th century context)
Bhartrihari ~5th Century CE Uncertain (possibly Ujjain) Books (Grammar/Philosophy):
  • Vakyapadiya (Linguistic philosophy; Sphota theory)
Books (Poetry):
  • Shatakatraya (Niti, Shringara, Vairagya – attribution debated)

Varahamihira ~Early 6th Century CE (c. 505–587 CE) Ujjain (Avanti) Books (Astronomy/Astrology/Encyclopedic):
  • Panchasiddhantika (Synthesis of five astronomical traditions)
  • Brihat Samhita (Encyclopedic work on astronomy, architecture, meteorology, omens)
  • Brihat Jataka
  • Laghu Jataka
 Post-Gupta / Aulikara-era Malwa (probable)
Banabhatta 7th Century CE Kannauj (Harsha's court) & Pritikuta (birthplace) Books (Prose Romance/Biography):
  • Harshacharita (Biography of Emperor Harshavardhana; ornate Sanskrit prose and historical narrative)
  • Kadambari (Elaborate prose romance; completed by his son Bhushanabhatta)
Plays: (Parvatiparinaya – attribution debated)
Devotional Hymn: (Chandikashtaka – traditional attribution) 		Harshavardhana (Pushyabhuti Dynasty)
Harshavardhana (Emperor Harsha) Reigned c. 606–647 CE Kannauj (Capital), Thanesar (Original Seat) Plays (Attributed):
  • Ratnavali (Court romance centered on King Udayana)
  • Priyadarsika (Romantic drama involving Princess Aranyaka)
  • Nagananda (Buddhist-themed play on the self-sacrifice of Jimutavahana)
Accomplished patron of learning; authorship traditionally attributed. 		Harshavardhana (Self)
Brahmagupta Born 598 CE; major work composed 628 CE Bhillamala (Bhinmal, Rajasthan?) / Ujjain? Books (Mathematics & Astronomy):
  • Brahmasphutasiddhanta (Rules for zero and negative numbers, algebraic equations, cyclic quadrilateral geometry, astronomy)
  • Khandakhadyaka (Practical astronomical manual)
Mentions attraction (gurutva) in a non-Newtonian sense. 		Early medieval western India (political patronage debated)
Kumarila Bhatta ~7th–8th Century CE Uncertain (possibly Prayaga or eastern India) Books (Philosophy – Purva Mimamsa):
  • Shlokavartika, Tantravartika, Tuptika
  • Defended Vedic authority; major critic of Buddhist epistemology
 Post-Harsha intellectual period
Dandin ~7th–8th Century CE Kanchipuram? (Pallava sphere) Books (Literature/Poetics):
  • Dashakumaracharita (Prose romance depicting social life)
  • Kavyadarsha (Foundational treatise on Sanskrit poetics)
  • Avantisundari Katha (Attribution debated)
 Pallava cultural milieu (probable)
Bhavabhuti ~Early 8th Century CE Padmapura (Vidarbha), later Kannauj? Plays (Nataka):
  • Mahaviracharita
  • Uttararamacharita (Noted for karuna rasa)
  • Malatimadhava
Renowned for emotional depth; second only to Kalidasa in dramatic pathos. 		Yashovarman of Kannauj? / Post-Harsha
Shankaracharya (Adi Shankara) ~Early 8th Century CE (Traditional dates 788–820 CE; earlier dates also proposed) Born Kaladi (Kerala); travelled extensively across India; death place traditionally associated with Kedarnath Books (Philosophy/Commentary – Advaita Vedanta):
  • Major Bhashyas on principal Upanishads, Brahma Sutras, and Bhagavad Gita (systematizing non-dualistic philosophy).
  • Independent treatises (Prakarana texts) such as Upadesasahasri, Atmabodha, Vivekachudamani (authorship of some texts debated).
  • Numerous devotional hymns (Stotras).
  • Traditionally credited with organizing the Dashanami monastic order and establishing four major Mathas.
 Post-Harsha period; early medieval regional polities
Vijnaneshwara ~Late 11th / Early 12th Century CE Kalyani (Western Chalukya capital?) Laws (Dharmashastra Commentary):
  • Mitakshara (Authoritative commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti; foundation of the Mitakshara school of Hindu law, especially inheritance by birth in joint families).
 Vikramaditya VI (Western Chalukya Empire)
Bilhana 11th Century CE Kashmir (origin); later at Kalyani (Western Chalukya court) Poetry / Biography:
  • Vikramankadeva-Charita (Eulogistic biography of King Vikramaditya VI).
  • Chaurapanchasika (Fifty Stanzas of the Thief – lyrical poem on secret love; possibly autobiographical).

  • Rajatarangini (Chronicle of Kashmiri kings; notable for citing sources, chronology, and critical historical method).

Bhaskara II (Bhaskaracharya) Born 1114 CE Vijjadavidda (possibly Bijapur region) / Ujjain (astronomical tradition) Books (Mathematics & Astronomy):
  • Siddhanta Shiromani (1150 CE), comprising:
    • Lilavati (Arithmetic and geometry)
    • Bijaganita (Advanced algebra)
    • Grahaganita (Planetary calculations)
    • Goladhyaya (Spherical astronomy and trigonometry)
  • Karanakutuhala (Astronomical handbook).
  • Contains proto-calculus ideas (instantaneous motion) and philosophical treatment of division by zero.
 Late Western Chalukya / Kalachuri / Yadava period
- Important literature (validated) -
Text/Work Time (Approx.) Language/Region Description & Key Details Category/Subcategory
Vedic Literature (~1500–500 BCE)
Rigveda ~1500–1200 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North-West Indian subcontinent (Sapta Sindhu region) Composed by various Rishis such as Vishvamitra, Vamadeva, and Atri. Contains 1028 hymns dedicated to deities like Indra (warrior god), Agni (fire god), and Soma (ritual drink). Oldest Indo-Aryan text and foundational to Vedic religion, reflecting the socio-religious life of early Indo-Aryans. Vedic Literature / Samhitas
Samaveda ~1200–1000 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Composed by various Rishis. A collection of melodies and chants, largely derived from the Rigveda, used primarily in Soma sacrifices. Closely associated with the Udgatri priest and forms the musical foundation of Vedic ritual tradition. Vedic Literature / Samhitas
Yajurveda ~1200–1000 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Sacrificial manual consisting of prose and verse formulas used by the Adhvaryu priest. Closely associated with ritual performance including Ashvamedha. Exists in two major recensions: Krishna (Black) Yajurveda and Shukla (White) Yajurveda, the latter traditionally linked to the Vajasneyi tradition. Vedic Literature / Samhitas
Atharvaveda ~1200–1000 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Traditionally associated with sages Atharvan and Angiras. Contains hymns, spells, and charms dealing with healing, protection, domestic life, and social practices. Relatively less focused on sacrificial ritual compared to other Vedas and provides insight into popular beliefs. Vedic Literature / Samhitas
Brahmanas ~1000–700 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Prose texts composed by various sages, attached to individual Vedas. Important works include Shatapatha Brahmana (Yajurveda) and Aitareya Brahmana (Rigveda). Provide detailed explanations of rituals such as Rajasuya and their symbolic meanings. Vedic Literature / Brahmanas
Aranyakas ~1000–700 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Texts associated with forest-dwelling ascetics and advanced ritual practitioners. Emphasize meditative and symbolic interpretations of rituals and serve as a transitional layer between Brahmanas and Upanishads. Vedic Literature / Aranyakas
Kathā Upanishad ~800–400 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Features the philosophical dialogue between Nachiketa, son of Vajasravasa, and Yama, the god of death. Explores themes of Atman, death, self-knowledge, and liberation, making it a central Upanishadic text. Vedic Literature / Upanishads
Chāndogya Upanishad ~800–400 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Associated with the Samaveda. Contains philosophical discussions on Brahman and meditation, including the teaching of Uddalaka Aruni to his son Shvetaketu expressed in the dictum “Tat Tvam Asi” (You are That). Vedic Literature / Upanishads
Aitareya Upanishad ~800–400 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Linked to the Rigveda and traditionally attributed to sage Aitareya. Discusses the creation of the universe and the emergence of consciousness, focusing on the nature of Atman. Vedic Literature / Upanishads
Mundaka Upanishad ~800–400 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Philosophical text distinguishing higher (para) and lower (apara) knowledge, emphasizing realization of Brahman for liberation. Source of the maxim “Satyameva Jayate” (Truth Alone Triumphs). Vedic Literature / Upanishads
Taittiriya Upanishad ~800–400 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Linked to the Yajurveda. Composed in three sections (Vallis): Shiksha Valli (education and ethics), Ananda or Brahmananda Valli (nature of the self and bliss), and Bhrigu Valli (experiential inquiry into Brahman). Discusses the five koshas (sheaths of existence) and teacher–student traditions. Vedic Literature / Upanishads
Isha Upanishad ~800–400 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Associated with the Shukla Yajurveda. A short Upanishad emphasizing the unity of existence and harmony between action (karma) and renunciation. Opens with the famous line “Isha vasyam idam sarvam” (All this is pervaded by the Lord). Vedic Literature / Upanishads
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad ~800–400 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Linked to the Yajurveda. One of the oldest and largest Upanishads, containing philosophical dialogues such as those between sage Yajnavalkya and King Janaka of Videha. Introduces profound concepts like “Neti Neti” (not this, not this) in the inquiry into Brahman and Atman. Vedic Literature / Upanishads
Kena Upanishad ~800–400 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Associated with the Samaveda. Explores the nature of Brahman through inquiry into the source of sensory and mental powers. Includes the allegorical episode where gods such as Agni and Vayu realize their limitations before the supreme reality. Vedic Literature / Upanishads
Prashna Upanishad ~800–400 BCE Vedic Sanskrit / North India Linked to the Atharvaveda. Structured around six questions posed by students, including Sukesha, to sage Pippalada. Focuses on prana (life-breath) as a cosmic principle, the origin of life, meditation, and the soul’s journey after death. Vedic Literature / Upanishads
Baudhāyana Sulba Sutras ~800–500 BCE Sanskrit / North India Composed by Baudhāyana. Part of the Sulba Sutras within the Kalpa Vedanga, dealing with geometric principles for altar construction. Includes early statements of the Pythagorean theorem (e.g., 3-4-5 triangle) and square-root approximations used in rituals like Agnichayana. Vedanga / Kalpa (Sulba Sutras)
Prabhākaravardhana ~6th Century CE Sanskrit / North India Not a surviving literary text. Refers to historical references concerning King Prabhakaravardhana of Thanesar, father of Harshavardhana. Information about him is derived from later sources such as Banabhatta’s Harshacharita rather than an independent authored work. Historical References (Not a Surviving Text)
Hindu Literature (~500 BCE–1200 CE)
Mahabharata ~400 BCE–400 CE Sanskrit / North India Traditionally attributed to Vyasa, but composed and expanded over centuries by multiple authors. Vast epic (~100,000 shlokas) narrating the Kurukshetra War between the Pandavas and Kauravas. Central figures include Krishna, Arjuna, Draupadi, Bhishma, and Karna. Incorporates philosophical, ethical, and social discourses, including the Bhagavad Gita; reflects the evolution of dharma in society. Hindu Literature / Epics (Itihasa)
Ramayana ~500 BCE–100 CE Sanskrit / North India Traditionally attributed to Valmiki. Epic narrating the life of Rama, his exile with Sita and Lakshmana, and the battle against Ravana of Lanka with the help of Hanuman. Exists in multiple recensions (Northern, Southern, etc.). Emphasizes ideals of dharma, kingship, devotion, and moral conduct. Hindu Literature / Epics (Itihasa)
Bhagavad Gita ~400 BCE–200 CE Sanskrit / North India Part of the Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva). Dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra. Synthesizes Karma Yoga (action), Bhakti Yoga (devotion), and Jnana Yoga (knowledge). Addresses duty, detachment, liberation, and the nature of reality. Hindu Literature / Philosophical (Smriti)
Vishnu Purana ~300–500 CE Sanskrit / India Traditionally attributed to Vyasa. One of the most systematically structured Puranas. Presents Vaishnava cosmology, genealogies of kings, cycles of creation, and the doctrine of Vishnu as the preserver. Elaborates the Dashavatara framework and devotional theology. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Shiva Purana ~400–600 CE Sanskrit / India Shaiva Purana traditionally linked to Vyasa, consisting of multiple samhitas compiled over time. Focuses on Shiva as the supreme reality, his manifestations, myths (e.g., Daksha sacrifice), and rituals. Foundational text for Shaivism. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Bhagavata Purana ~800–1000 CE Sanskrit / India Devotional Vaishnava Purana traditionally attributed to Vyasa. Centers on Krishna’s life and teachings, especially his childhood and youth in Vrindavan. Integrates intense personal devotion (bhakti) with philosophical ideas of Brahman, influencing later Bhakti movements. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Markandeya Purana ~300–600 CE Sanskrit / India Attributed in tradition to Vyasa, narrated by sage Markandeya. Notable for containing the Devi Mahatmya (Durga Saptashati), which exalts the Goddess as supreme power. Important text for Shakta traditions. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Matsya Purana ~300–600 CE Sanskrit / India One of the earlier Puranas, traditionally attributed to Vyasa. Describes the Matsya avatar saving Manu from the flood. Contains sections on temple architecture, iconography, geography, and royal genealogies, blending mythology with administrative knowledge. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Agni Purana ~700–1000 CE Sanskrit / India Encyclopedic Purana narrated by Agni to sage Vashishtha. Covers rituals, cosmology, iconography, architecture, warfare, medicine, grammar, and poetics. Functions more as a compendium/manual than a narrative Purana. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Garuda Purana ~400–1000 CE Sanskrit / India Vaishnava Purana presented as a dialogue between Vishnu and Garuda. Noted for its Preta Khanda dealing with death rites, afterlife, karma, and punishments in Naraka. Frequently consulted in funerary contexts, though it also contains cosmological and devotional sections. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Padma Purana ~400–1000 CE Sanskrit / India Traditionally attributed to Vyasa; compiled and expanded over centuries. Major Vaishnava Purana with strong emphasis on pilgrimage (tirtha-mahatmya), cosmology, creation myths, and devotion. Contains extensive sections on sacred places such as Pushkar, Varanasi, and Prayaga. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Brahma Purana ~400–1000 CE Sanskrit / India Traditionally attributed to Vyasa. Focuses on creation myths narrated by Brahma, cosmology, genealogies, and descriptions of sacred geography. Strong regional orientation, especially toward eastern India and temple traditions. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Linga Purana ~500–1000 CE Sanskrit / India Shaiva Purana traditionally attributed to Vyasa. Centers on Shiva as the supreme principle symbolized by the linga. Combines mythology, cosmology, metaphysical interpretation of the linga, and Shaiva ritual practices. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Skanda Purana ~600–1200 CE Sanskrit / India Traditionally attributed to Vyasa. Largest and most expansively developed Purana. Focuses on Skanda (Kartikeya) and extensively catalogs pilgrimage sites (tirthas) across India. Highly regionalized with numerous later accretions. Hindu Literature / Puranas
Hammira-Mahakavya ~14th Century CE Sanskrit / Rajasthan By Nayachandra Suri. Historical mahakavya narrating the life and resistance of Hammiradeva, Chauhan ruler of Ranthambore, against Alauddin Khilji. Composed under Jain patronage; valuable for reconstructing Rajput resistance and medieval polity. Hindu Literature / Historical Epic
Agamas ~700–1200 CE Sanskrit/Tamil / India Composed by various traditions. Corpus of ritual, temple-construction, iconography, and worship manuals. Includes Shaiva Agamas (e.g., Kamika), Vaishnava Agamas (Pancharatra, Vaikhanasa), and Shakta Agamas. Central to South Indian temple worship. Hindu Literature / Tantric & Bhakti Texts
Alvars’ Tamil Bhakti Poetry ~700–900 CE Tamil / South India Composed by the 12 Alvars. Vaishnava devotional hymns praising Vishnu and his avatars. Collected as the Nalayira Divya Prabandham. Andal’s Tiruppavai is especially influential. Core foundation of the South Indian Bhakti movement. Hindu Literature / Tantric & Bhakti Texts
Nayanars’ Tamil Shaiva Poetry ~700–900 CE Tamil / South India Composed by 63 Nayanars including Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar. Shaiva devotional hymns compiled mainly in the Tevaram corpus. Emphasizes personal devotion to Shiva and forms the theological base of Shaiva Siddhanta. Hindu Literature / Tantric & Bhakti Texts
Yoga Sutras ~200 BCE–400 CE Sanskrit / India Attributed to Patanjali. Systematic philosophical text outlining Ashtanga Yoga (eightfold path). Focuses on mental discipline, cessation of mental fluctuations, and liberation (kaivalya). Distinct from later Hatha and Tantric yoga traditions. Hindu Literature / Tantric & Bhakti Texts
Pratyabhijna Shastra ~850–900 CE Sanskrit / Kashmir Founded by Utpaladeva, later systematized by Abhinavagupta. Core philosophical school of Kashmir Shaivism emphasizing recognition (pratyabhijna) of the self as identical with Shiva. Metaphysical and non-dualistic, not narrative-based. Hindu Literature / Tantric & Bhakti Texts
Buddhist Literature (~500 BCE–500 CE)
Sutta Pitaka ~500–300 BCE Pali / North India Traditionally attributed to early disciples of the Buddha and preserved through oral recitation at Buddhist councils. Contains the Buddha’s discourses, including the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (first sermon) at Sarnath. Core teachings include the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path; widely propagated during and after Ashoka’s reign. Buddhist Literature / Tripitaka
Vinaya Pitaka ~500–300 BCE Pali / North India Preserved by the early Buddhist Sangha. Codifies monastic discipline for monks and nuns, including rules of conduct, procedures, and origin stories of regulations. Forms the institutional foundation of Buddhist monastic life. Buddhist Literature / Tripitaka
Sarvastivada Vinaya ~200 BCE–200 CE Sanskrit / North-West India Vinaya tradition of the Sarvastivada school, preserved primarily in Sanskrit. Details monastic rules for monks and nuns with doctrinal and disciplinary variations. Widely followed in Gandhara and Kashmir, reflecting early Buddhist sectarian developments. Buddhist Literature / Tripitaka
Abhidhamma Pitaka ~300–200 BCE Pali / North India Systematic philosophical analysis of Buddhist doctrine, traditionally preserved by early schools. Texts such as the Dhammasangani classify mental and physical phenomena. Central to Theravada scholastic tradition, focusing on psychology and metaphysics. Buddhist Literature / Tripitaka
Therigatha ~300–200 BCE Pali / North India Collection of verses attributed to early Buddhist nuns such as Patacara and Kisa Gotami. Expresses personal spiritual experiences, suffering, and liberation. One of the earliest known texts highlighting women’s voices in religious literature. Buddhist Literature / Poetry
Dhammapada ~300–100 BCE Pali / North India Anthology of ethical and philosophical verses attributed to the Buddha, preserved by the early Buddhist community. Emphasizes moral conduct, mental discipline, and wisdom. One of the most widely translated and cited Buddhist texts. Buddhist Literature / Poetry
Milinda Panha ~100 BCE–200 CE Pali / North-West India Dialogical text presenting philosophical discussions between King Milinda (Menander I, Indo-Greek ruler) and the monk Nagasena. Explores doctrines such as non-self (anatta) and impermanence, illustrating Buddhism’s engagement with Hellenistic thought. Buddhist Literature / Dialogues
Lalitavistara ~200–400 CE Sanskrit / India Mahayana hagiographical text narrating the life of the Buddha from birth to enlightenment. Rich in symbolic and devotional elements, portraying the Buddha as a transcendent being. Reflects Mahayana theological developments rather than historical biography. Buddhist Literature / Mahayana Sutras
Saddharmapundarika Sutra ~100–200 CE Sanskrit / India Central Mahayana scripture known as the Lotus Sutra. Uses parables such as the burning house to teach universal salvation and the concept of Buddhahood for all beings. Emphasizes compassion, skillful means (upaya), and spiritual equality. Buddhist Literature / Mahayana Sutras
Vimalakirti Nirdesa Sutra ~100–300 CE Sanskrit / India Composed within the Mahayana tradition. Centers on Vimalakirti, an enlightened lay follower who demonstrates profound wisdom surpassing that of renowned monks. Emphasizes non-duality and the spiritual potential of laypersons; presented through philosophical dialogue rather than historical debate. Buddhist Literature / Mahayana Sutras
Prajnaparamita Sutra ~100 BCE–200 CE Sanskrit / India Corpus of Mahayana texts including the Heart Sutra and Diamond Sutra. Develops the doctrine of prajna (perfection of wisdom) and shunyata (emptiness). Framed as doctrinal discourses involving figures such as Subhuti, serving symbolic and philosophical purposes. Buddhist Literature / Mahayana Sutras
Mulamadhyamakakarika ~150–250 CE Sanskrit / India Philosophical treatise by Nagarjuna establishing the Madhyamaka school. Argues for emptiness of inherent existence through rigorous logical analysis. Non-narrative text that deeply influenced Mahayana thought across Asia. Buddhist Literature / Philosophical Texts
Buddhacharita ~100–200 CE Sanskrit / North India Sanskrit epic poem by Ashvaghosha narrating the life of the Buddha from birth to enlightenment. Written in classical kavya style, blending biography with religious idealization. Associated with early Mahayana literary culture. Buddhist Literature / Poetic Biographies
Saundarananda ~100–200 CE Sanskrit / North India Epic poem by Ashvaghosha recounting the spiritual transformation of Nanda, the Buddha’s half-brother. Contrasts sensual life with renunciation, using refined poetic expression to convey Buddhist ethics. Buddhist Literature / Poetic Biographies
Divyavadana ~200–400 CE Sanskrit / India Collection of Buddhist legends preserved in Sanskrit. Includes hagiographical narratives such as Ashoka’s conversion and patronage of Buddhism. Combines moral instruction with legendary accounts of monks, kings, and past deeds. Buddhist Literature / Legends
Jataka Tales ~400 BCE–300 CE Pali / India Stories of the Buddha’s previous births preserved through oral tradition and later compiled. Illustrate moral virtues such as generosity, compassion, and self-sacrifice. Widely depicted in Buddhist art and storytelling traditions. Buddhist Literature / Legends
Visuddhimagga ~400–500 CE Pali / Sri Lanka Authoritative Theravada manual by Buddhaghosa systematizing meditation, ethics, and wisdom. Synthesizes earlier commentarial traditions and outlines the path of purification leading to Nirvana. Buddhist Literature / Commentary
Ashoka’s Edicts ~3rd Century BCE Prakrit (Brahmi script) / India Royal inscriptions issued by Emperor Ashoka across the Mauryan Empire. Promote ethical governance, dhamma, non-violence, and religious tolerance following the Kalinga War. Primary historical sources reflecting early state-supported Buddhism. Buddhist Literature / Edicts
Jain Literature (~400 BCE–400 CE)
Acharanga Sutra ~400–300 BCE Prakrit / North India Oldest Jain canonical text, traditionally attributed to the teachings of Mahavira and preserved by his disciples. Describes Mahavira’s ascetic practices, strict discipline, and doctrine of ahimsa. Central to the Śvetāmbara Jain Agama tradition. Jain Literature / Agamas
Sutrakritanga ~300–200 BCE Prakrit / North India Early Jain canonical text presenting ethical teachings, cosmology, and refutation of rival philosophical traditions such as Vedic ritualism. Reflects Mahavira’s doctrinal positions through preserved discourses. Jain Literature / Agamas
Uttaradhyayana Sutra ~200–100 BCE Prakrit / North India Compilation of moral and philosophical teachings intended for Jain monks. Includes narratives such as King Nami’s renunciation. Widely used in monastic instruction and ritual recitation. Jain Literature / Agamas
Brihatkalpa Sutra ~100–500 CE Prakrit / India Text on monastic discipline outlining rules, penances, and procedures for Jain monks and nuns. Likely redacted over time within the Śvetāmbara tradition; practical in nature rather than narrative. Jain Literature / Agamas
Kalpa Sutra ~400–300 BCE Prakrit / North India Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabahu. Contains biographies of Tirthankaras, especially Mahavira, including his birth to Queen Trishala. Read publicly during the Paryushana festival. Jain Literature / Agamas
Dashavaikalika Sutra ~300–400 CE Prakrit / India Manual of monastic conduct arranged in ten chapters, emphasizing ethical discipline and ascetic behavior. Based on early Jain teachings, likely compiled and systematized later. Jain Literature / Agamas
Avasyaka Sutra ~300–200 BCE Prakrit / North India Text prescribing essential daily duties for Jain practitioners, including confession, repentance, and meditation. Integral to Jain ritual life and monastic routine. Jain Literature / Agamas
Sthananga Sutra ~300–200 BCE Prakrit / North India Systematic exposition of Jain doctrine using numerical classifications. Covers cosmology, knowledge, and ethical categories; analytical rather than narrative. Jain Literature / Agamas
Bhagavati Sutra ~300–200 BCE Prakrit / North India Extensive Jain text structured as dialogues between Mahavira and his chief disciple Gautama. Addresses karma, cosmology, and liberation in question–answer format; one of the most detailed Agamas. Jain Literature / Agamas
Tattvartha Sutra ~200–400 CE Sanskrit / India By Umasvati (Umasvami). Systematic exposition of Jain philosophy outlining the seven tattvas (e.g., jiva, ajiva, asrava, bandha, samvara, nirjara, moksha). Notable as the only Jain text accepted by both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, though interpreted through different commentaries. Jain Literature / Philosophical Texts
Samayasara ~1st–3rd Century CE Prakrit / India By Kundakunda. Core Digambara philosophical text emphasizing the distinction between the true self (niscaya naya) and empirical reality (vyavahara naya). Focuses on inner purity and realization of the soul’s true nature. Jain Literature / Philosophical Texts
Niyamasara ~1st–3rd Century CE Prakrit / India By Kundakunda. Treatise on Jain ethical discipline and spiritual practices necessary for liberation. Stresses vows, meditation, and internal conduct from a Digambara philosophical standpoint. Jain Literature / Philosophical Texts
Pravachanasara ~1st–3rd Century CE Prakrit / India By Kundakunda. Philosophical work discussing the nature of knowledge, conduct, and reality as expounded in Jain teachings. Influential text within Digambara metaphysical and epistemological thought. Jain Literature / Philosophical Texts
Aptamimamsa ~200–300 CE Sanskrit / South or South-Central India (Deccan region?) By Samantabhadra. Polemical Jain philosophical text defending the authority of the omniscient being (Apta) and articulating the doctrine of Anekantavada against rival schools such as Buddhism and Vedanta. Important for Jain logical and apologetic tradition. Jain Literature / Philosophical Texts
Nitivakyamrita ~10th Century CE Sanskrit / Deccan India By Somadeva Suri. Jain ethical and political treatise offering guidance on moral conduct, kingship, and governance. Written for rulers and lay society, integrating Jain values such as ahimsa and self-restraint into practical statecraft. Jain Literature / Ethical Texts
Legal & Administrative (~600 BCE–1100 CE)
Manusmriti ~200 BCE–200 CE Sanskrit / India Attributed to Manu, the mythical lawgiver. Normative dharmashastra text outlining duties (dharma) of varnas and ashramas, with rules on marriage, inheritance, punishment, and kingship. Prescriptive rather than statutory; historically influential and widely debated. Legal & Administrative / Dharmashastras
Yajnavalkya Smriti ~200 BCE–200 CE Sanskrit / India Attributed to sage Yajnavalkya. Concise and systematically arranged law text focusing on governance, judicial procedure, property, and family law. Became the base text for later authoritative commentaries, especially Mitakshara. Legal & Administrative / Dharmashastras
Narada Smriti ~100–400 CE Sanskrit / India Attributed to sage Narada. Strongly judicial in orientation, emphasizing civil and criminal law, litigation, contracts, debts, and procedure. Notable for minimizing ritual content and focusing on practical jurisprudence. Legal & Administrative / Dharmashastras
Katyayana Smriti ~300–600 CE Sanskrit / India Attributed to Katyayana. Later dharmashastra text expanding on inheritance, women’s property, marriage, and adoption. Frequently cited by medieval jurists as a supplement to earlier Smritis. Legal & Administrative / Dharmashastras
Brihaspati Smriti ~300–500 CE Sanskrit / India Attributed to sage Brihaspati. Emphasizes judicial administration, evidence, judges, and court procedures. Reflects the increasing sophistication of legal institutions in early medieval India. Legal & Administrative / Dharmashastras
Vishnu Smriti ~300–500 CE Sanskrit / India Author unknown. Dharmashastra text with a distinct Vaishnava devotional tone, integrating legal norms with bhakti-oriented elements while retaining a full juridical framework. Legal & Administrative / Dharmashastras
Parashara Smriti ~100–500 CE Sanskrit / India Attributed to sage Parashara. Known for adapting dharma rules specifically for the Kali Yuga, allowing greater flexibility in ritual and social obligations compared to earlier Smritis. Legal & Administrative / Dharmashastras
Mitakshara ~1100 CE Sanskrit / India By Vijnaneshvara. Authoritative commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti, especially influential in inheritance law through the doctrine of birthright in joint family property. Became dominant across most of India. Legal & Administrative / Dharmashastras
Apastamba Dharmasutra ~600–300 BCE Sanskrit / South India Attributed to Apastamba. One of the earliest Dharmasutras, emphasizing householder duties, daily conduct, and ritual obligations. Reflects regional traditions of southern Vedic schools. Legal & Administrative / Dharmasutras
Gautama Dharmasutra ~600–300 BCE Sanskrit / North India Attributed to sage Gautama. Early legal text addressing ethics, penance, social duties, and judicial principles. Among the foundational sources for later Smriti literature. Legal & Administrative / Dharmasutras
Vasishtha Dharmasutra ~600–300 BCE Sanskrit / North India Traditionally attributed to sage Vasishtha. One of the early Dharmasutras outlining social norms, duties, penance, and legal principles within the Brahmanical tradition. Reflects evolving conceptions of dharma in early Vedic society. Legal & Administrative / Dharmasutras
Arthashastra ~4th Century BCE Sanskrit / India Attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya). Comprehensive treatise on statecraft, administration, economics, law, diplomacy, espionage, and military strategy. Normative and pragmatic in approach; traditionally associated with Mauryan governance and early Indian political thought. Legal & Administrative / Statecraft
Sangam Literature (~300 BCE–500 CE)
Tolkappiyam ~300 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India Attributed to Tolkappiyar. Earliest extant Tamil grammatical treatise, covering phonetics (Eluttadikaram), morphology (Solladikaram), and poetics/social themes (Poruladikaram). Foundational text for Tamil language, literature, and Sangam-era conventions. Sangam Literature / Grammar
Ettuthogai ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India Collection of eight anthologies composed by various poets such as Kapilar. Contains akam (love) and puram (war, heroism) poetry, reflecting social life, polity, and values of the Sangam age. Sangam Literature / Anthologies
Pattuppattu ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India Collection of ten long poems by various poets including Nakkirar. Themes include kingship, landscape, love, war, and patronage, offering insights into Sangam-period polity and culture. Sangam Literature / Anthologies
Tirukkural ~3rd Century BCE – 6th Century CE (Debated) Tamil / South India Attributed to Thiruvalluvar. Ethical text of 1,330 couplets organized into Virtue (Aram), Wealth (Porul), and Love (Inbam). Universally revered moral work transcending sectarian and temporal boundaries. Sangam Literature / Ethics
Silappadikaram ~200–300 CE Tamil / South India Authored by Ilango Adigal. Post-Sangam epic narrating the story of Kannagi and Kovalan, emphasizing justice, chastity, and moral retribution. Provides valuable insights into Tamil society, economy, and polity. Post-Sangam Literature / Epics
Manimekalai ~200–300 CE Tamil / South India Authored by Seethalai Sattanar. Buddhist post-Sangam epic and sequel to Silappadikaram, focusing on Manimekalai’s renunciation and Buddhist philosophy. Reflects the spread of Buddhism in South India. Post-Sangam Literature / Epics
Akananuru ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Ettuthogai anthologies. Contains 400 akam (love) poems composed by various poets, structured around the five landscapes (tinai) of Sangam poetry. Sangam Literature / Love Poetry
Purananuru ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Ettuthogai anthologies. Comprises 400 puram poems celebrating kings, warriors, generosity, ethics of war, and social values of the Sangam age. Sangam Literature / Heroic Poetry
Pathittrupathu ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India Anthology of ten decads praising Chera kings. Important historical source for early Chera polity, genealogy, and military exploits during the Sangam period. Sangam Literature / Heroic Poetry
Paripadal ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India Sangam anthology consisting of devotional and musical poems dedicated to deities such as Vishnu, Murugan, and river Vaigai. Distinct for its bhakti-oriented tone within Sangam literature. Sangam Literature / Devotional Poetry
Kuruntokai ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Ettuthogai anthologies. Collection of short akam (love) poems composed by various poets, focusing on inner emotional life and relationships, reflecting Sangam-period society. Sangam Literature / Love Poetry
Natrinai ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Ettuthogai anthologies. Collection of akam (love) poems by various poets, structured around landscapes (tinai) and emotional situations of lovers in Sangam society. Sangam Literature / Love Poetry
Kalittokai ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Ettuthogai anthologies. Akam poetry composed in the kalli metre, notable for dramatic dialogue and musical elements, reflecting Sangam cultural aesthetics. Sangam Literature / Love Poetry
Aingurunuru ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Ettuthogai anthologies. Collection of 500 short akam poems, organized according to the five landscapes (tinai), depicting diverse aspects of love and separation. Sangam Literature / Love Poetry
Nedunalvadai ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Pattuppattu poems, authored by Nakkirar. Long akam poem describing the anguish of separation and the grandeur of a king’s realm, blending love and political imagery. Sangam Literature / Love Poetry
Maduraikkanchi ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Pattuppattu poems, authored by Mangudi Maruthanar. Detailed description of the city of Madurai, its markets, people, governance, and the Pandya king, providing valuable urban history. Sangam Literature / Descriptive Poetry
Mullaippattu ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Pattuppattu poems, attributed to Nappudanar. Akam poem portraying a woman’s patient waiting during her lover’s absence, associated with the mullai (pastoral) landscape. Sangam Literature / Love Poetry
Sirupanarruppadai ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Pattuppattu poems, authored by Nallur Nattattanar. Arruppadai (guide poem) describing a bard guiding another to a generous patron, offering insights into patronage and economy. Sangam Literature / Descriptive Poetry
Perumpanarruppadai ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Pattuppattu poems, authored by Uruttirangannanar. Arruppadai poem depicting the journey of a bard to a benevolent ruler, highlighting social life and political authority. Sangam Literature / Descriptive Poetry
Porunararruppadai ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Pattuppattu poems, attributed to Mudattamakkanniyar. Arruppadai poem guiding a warrior-bard to a patron king, reflecting warfare, generosity, and Sangam values. Sangam Literature / Descriptive Poetry
Kurinjippattu ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Pattuppattu poems, authored by Kapilar. Akam poem set in the kurinji (mountain) landscape, focusing on secret love and union, rich in imagery and symbolism. Sangam Literature / Love Poetry
Malaipadukadam ~100 BCE–300 CE Tamil / South India One of the Pattuppattu poems, authored by Perungunrur Perunkkausikanar. Descriptive poem portraying a mountainous region ruled by a chieftain, blending geography, polity, and culture. Sangam Literature / Descriptive Poetry
Scientific & Secular Literature (~600 BCE–1200 CE)
Charaka Samhita ~1st Century BCE – 2nd Century CE Sanskrit / North India Attributed to Charaka, based on the earlier Agnivesha Tantra. Foundational Ayurvedic text focusing on internal medicine, diagnosis, pharmacology, and physiology, including the tridosha theory (Vata, Pitta, Kapha). Central to classical Indian medical thought. Scientific & Secular Literature / Medicine
Sushruta Samhita Core traditions ancient; text redacted ~3rd–4th Century CE Sanskrit / North India Attributed to Sushruta of Kashi. Classical Ayurvedic text emphasizing surgery, anatomy, and surgical instruments, including procedures such as rhinoplasty and cataract surgery. Foundational work in the history of surgery. Scientific & Secular Literature / Medicine
Ashtanga Hridaya ~600–700 CE Sanskrit / India Composed by Vagbhata. Concise and systematic synthesis of Charaka and Sushruta traditions, covering the eight branches of Ayurveda. Widely studied in later Ayurvedic education. Scientific & Secular Literature / Medicine
Aryabhatiya 499 CE Sanskrit / Kusumapura (Pataliputra) By Aryabhata. Astronomical and mathematical treatise covering arithmetic, algebra, trigonometry, and planetary motion. Advocated Earth’s rotation and systematized place-value notation; highly influential on later Indian and Islamic astronomy. Scientific & Secular Literature / Astronomy & Mathematics
Brahmasphutasiddhanta 628 CE Sanskrit / Ujjain By Brahmagupta. Major astronomical and mathematical work introducing formal rules for zero and negative numbers, algebraic methods, and planetary calculations. Influential across India and beyond. Scientific & Secular Literature / Astronomy & Mathematics
Surya Siddhanta Textual tradition ~4th–5th Century CE (later revisions) Sanskrit / India Classical astronomical treatise of uncertain authorship, presented as divine revelation. Discusses planetary motion, eclipses, calendrical calculations, and cosmology; foundational for later Indian astronomy. Scientific & Secular Literature / Astronomy
Lilavati ~1150 CE Sanskrit / India By Bhaskara II. Mathematical work on arithmetic and geometry, written in verse form for pedagogical clarity. According to tradition, named after the author’s daughter. Scientific & Secular Literature / Mathematics
Siddhanta Shiromani ~1150 CE Sanskrit / India By Bhaskara II. Comprehensive treatise consisting of Lilavati, Bijaganita, Grahaganita, and Goladhyaya, covering advanced mathematics and astronomy. Represents a peak of medieval Indian scientific thought. Scientific & Secular Literature / Astronomy & Mathematics
Natyashastra ~200 BCE – 200 CE (composite text) Sanskrit / India Attributed to Bharata Muni. Foundational theoretical treatise on drama, dance, music, aesthetics, and performance, introducing the rasa theory. Cornerstone of classical Indian performing arts. Scientific & Secular Literature / Drama & Poetics
Kamasutra ~200–400 CE Sanskrit / India By Vatsyayana. Systematic treatise on human relationships, social conduct, marriage, and sexuality, reflecting norms of urban elite life. Primarily a sociological and ethical text rather than an erotic manual. Scientific & Secular Literature / Poetics & Sociology
Meghaduta ~4th–5th Century CE Sanskrit / India By Kalidasa. Lyric poem in which a Yaksha sends a message to his distant wife through a cloud, blending nature imagery with intense emotion (viraha). Generally associated with the Gupta age and regarded as a masterpiece of Sanskrit kavya. Scientific & Secular Literature / Poetry
Abhijnanashakuntalam ~4th–5th Century CE Sanskrit / India By Kalidasa. Sanskrit drama narrating the love story of King Dushyanta and Shakuntala, derived from the Mahabharata. Celebrated for refined rasa expression and dramatic structure; associated with the classical (Gupta-age) tradition. Scientific & Secular Literature / Drama
Raghuvamsha ~4th–5th Century CE Sanskrit / India By Kalidasa. Mahakavya tracing the lineage of the Raghu dynasty, from Dilipa to Agnivarna, portraying ideals of kingship, dharma, and royal virtue. A major work of classical Sanskrit epic poetry. Scientific & Secular Literature / Poetry
Kumarasambhava ~4th–5th Century CE Sanskrit / India By Kalidasa. Epic poem describing the courtship and marriage of Shiva and Parvati and the birth of Kartikeya. Combines mythology with refined poetic aesthetics; a canonical kavya text. Scientific & Secular Literature / Poetry
Mrichchhakatika Date debated (c. 3rd–5th Century CE) Sanskrit / India Attributed to Shudraka. Social drama depicting the love between Charudatta, a poor Brahmin, and Vasantasena, a courtesan. Notable for its realism, humor, and portrayal of urban life; date and authorship remain debated. Scientific & Secular Literature / Drama
Mudrarakshasa ~4th–6th Century CE Sanskrit / India By Vishakhadatta. Political drama centered on Chanakya’s strategies in securing Chandragupta Maurya’s rule, featuring alliances and intrigue. Unique among Sanskrit plays for its focus on real historical figures. Scientific & Secular Literature / Drama
Madhyama-vyayoga ~2nd Century BCE – 2nd Century CE Sanskrit / India Attributed to Bhasa. One-act play based on a Mahabharata episode involving Bhima and Ghatotkacha. Generally regarded as pre-Kalidasa, reflecting early Sanskrit dramatic traditions. Scientific & Secular Literature / Drama
Svapnavasavadatta ~2nd Century BCE – 2nd Century CE Sanskrit / India Attributed to Bhasa. Romantic drama centered on King Udayana and Queen Vasavadatta, employing disguise and mistaken identity. An important example of early Sanskrit drama, predating classical conventions. Scientific & Secular Literature / Drama
