Kavyadarsha ~7th Century CE Sanskrit / India By Dandin. Influential treatise on Sanskrit poetics, classifying literary styles such as Vaidarbhi and Gaudi and setting standards for kavya composition. A foundational work in Indian literary theory. Scientific & Secular Literature / Poetics
Harshacharita ~640 CE Sanskrit / Thanesar, Kannauj By Banabhatta. Courtly prose biography of King Harshavardhana, blending historical narrative with ornate literary style. An important source for early medieval Indian political and cultural history. Scientific & Secular Literature / Historical Biography
Kadambari ~7th Century CE Sanskrit / Thanesar, Kannauj By Banabhatta, completed by Bhushanabhatta. Elaborate prose romance involving rebirth and love across lifetimes. A landmark in the development of Sanskrit prose fiction. Scientific & Secular Literature / Prose Fiction
Panchatantra ~200 BCE – 300 CE Sanskrit / India Traditionally attributed to Vishnusharman. Collection of didactic animal fables teaching ethics and political wisdom through framed narratives. Widely transmitted and translated, influencing storytelling traditions across Asia and Europe. Scientific & Secular Literature / Fables
Hitopadesha ~800–1000 CE Sanskrit / India By Narayana. Didactic collection of moral tales derived partly from the Panchatantra, emphasizing practical wisdom and ethical conduct. Intended as instructional literature rather than historical narrative. Scientific & Secular Literature / Fables
- Religions (validated) -
Religion Time Period Origin (Location) Core Principles Rise & Development Key Figures (Time, Location, Background) Literature & Architecture Highlights Major Sects/Schools Key Concepts/Figures (Salvation/Guidance) Significant Councils/Assemblies (Time, Location, Patron) Important Sites Patron Rulers/Dynasties Factors of Decline
Hinduism (Sanātana Dharma) Vedic roots ~1500 BCE–Ongoing
(Synthesis as modern Hinduism ~500 BCE–300 CE)		 Indus Valley Civilization (possible continuities) & Gangetic Plain (North India); spread across Indian subcontinent
  • Dharma: Moral, ethical, and cosmic order/duty.
  • Karma: Principle of cause and effect across lives.
  • Moksha: Liberation from samsara (cycle of rebirth).
  • Samsara: Cycle of birth, death, and reincarnation.
  • Atman: Eternal individual soul.
  • Brahman: Ultimate reality (impersonal absolute in Vedanta).
  • Henotheistic/Polytheistic elements: Multiple deities (Vishnu, Shiva, Devi, etc.) as manifestations or supreme in turn.
  • Vedic Period (~1500–500 BCE): Earliest scriptures (Vedas) and rituals.
  • Upanishadic Period (~800–400 BCE): Philosophical exploration of Brahman and Atman.
  • Epic-Puranic Period (~400 BCE–500 CE): Mahabharata, Ramayana, Puranas.
  • Classical/Gupta Period (~300–600 CE): Temple architecture, Puranic consolidation.
  • Bhakti Movement (medieval, ~7th–17th CE; south India peak 7th–9th CE): Personal devotion emphasized.
  • Vedanta Schools (medieval): Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita.
  • Vyasa: Traditional (~400 BCE–400 CE composition of epics/Puranas), mythical compiler of Vedas, author of Mahabharata.
  • Valmiki: Traditional (~500 BCE–400 CE for Ramayana), sage, first poet (Adi Kavi).
  • Patanjali: ~150–400 CE, sage, author of Yoga Sutras.
  • Adi Shankara: 788–820 CE, Kerala, Advaita Vedanta founder, four mathas.
  • Ramanuja: 1017–1137 CE, Tamil Nadu, Vishishtadvaita proponent, Vishnu bhakti.
  • Madhva: 1238–1317 CE, Karnataka, Dvaita founder.
  • Nayanars: ~6th–9th CE, Tamil Nadu, 63 Shaiva saints, Tevaram hymns.
  • Alvars: ~6th–9th CE, Tamil Nadu, 12 Vaishnava saints, Divya Prabandham.
  • Primary Texts:
    • Vedas (Rig, Sama, Yajur, Atharva)
    • Upanishads
    • Epics (Mahabharata incl. Bhagavad Gita, Ramayana)
    • Puranas (e.g., Bhagavata, Vishnu, Shiva)
    • Agamas/Tantras
    • Yoga Sutras
  • Highlights:
    • Vedic rituals/hymns
    • Epic narratives
    • Puranic myths/genealogies
    • Tamil Bhakti poetry
    • Gupta/Chola-era temples
    • Rock-cut caves (Ellora, Elephanta)
  • Vaishnavism (Vishnu)
  • Shaivism (Shiva)
  • Shaktism (Devi)
  • Smartism (five/six deities; panentheistic)
  • Vedanta Schools: Advaita (non-dual), Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dual), Dvaita (dual).
  • Vishnu avatars (e.g., Rama, Krishna)
  • Dharma as guiding ethical principle
  • Bhakti (devotion) as path to moksha
  • Kumbh Mela: Periodic mass pilgrimage.
  • Philosophical debates (e.g., Shankara's digvijaya).
  • Bhakti gatherings and festivals.
  • Dashavatara Temple (Deogarh, Uttar Pradesh, ~early 6th CE): Early Vishnu temple, Gupta style.
  • Brihadeeswara Temple (Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, ~1010 CE): Chola masterpiece, UNESCO site, Shiva.
  • Khajuraho Temples (Madhya Pradesh, ~10th CE): Chandela, intricate sculptures.
  • Varanasi (Kashi Vishwanath, Uttar Pradesh): Ancient Shiva center, Jyotirlinga.
  • Mathura (Krishna Janmabhoomi): Krishna birthplace.
  • Ayodhya (Ram Janmabhoomi): Rama birthplace.
  • Ellora Caves (Kailasa Temple, Maharashtra, ~8th CE): Rashtrakuta, multi-faith (Hindu, Buddhist, Jain).
  • Elephanta Caves (Maharashtra, ~5th–8th CE): Shiva, Trimurti.
  • Puri (Jagannath Temple, Odisha, ~12th CE): Vaishnava, Rath Yatra.
  • Dwarka (Dwarkadhish, Gujarat): Krishna site, Char Dham.
  • Mauryas (Ashoka promoted tolerance)
  • Guptas (golden age patronage)
  • Cholas (Rajaraja I)
  • Pallavas
  • Rashtrakutas, Chandelas
  • Synthesis with local traditions, Buddhism, Jainism.
  • Adaptation during Islamic rule and colonial period.
  • Revival through Bhakti and modern reforms.
Buddhism c. 6th–5th Century BCE–Ongoing (declined in India ~7th–13th CE) Gangetic Plain (Magadha region, North India); Birthplace: Lumbini (modern Nepal)
  • Four Noble Truths: Suffering (Dukkha), Origin (Samudaya), Cessation (Nirodha), Path (Magga).
  • Eightfold Path: Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.
  • Three Marks of Existence: Impermanence (Anicca), Suffering (Dukkha), No-self (Anatta).
  • Dependent Origination (Pratityasamutpada): Cycle of cause and effect.
  • Nirvana: Liberation from samsara.
  • Karma, compassion, and Middle Way (avoiding extremes).
  • Founded by Siddhartha Gautama (Buddha) in 6th–5th BCE.
  • Patronized by Ashoka (3rd BCE); spread across Asia.
  • Mahayana emergence (~1st CE); Vajrayana (~7th CE).
  • Peak in India: Maurya–Gupta–Pala eras.
  • Gautama Buddha: c. 563–483 BCE, Lumbini (Nepal), Shakya prince, enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, first sermon at Sarnath.
  • Ashoka: c. 304–232 BCE, Pataliputra, Maurya emperor, post-Kalinga conversion, propagated via edicts and missionaries.
  • Nagarjuna: c. 150–250 CE, South India, founder of Madhyamaka, Sunyata doctrine.
  • Vasubandhu: c. 4th–5th CE, Gandhara, Yogachara co-founder, Abhidharmakosha.
  • Asanga: c. 4th CE, Gandhara, Yogachara founder.
  • Dignaga: c. 480–540 CE, South India, Buddhist logic/epistemology.
  • Dharmakirti: c. 6th–7th CE, South India, expanded logic.
  • Buddhaghosa: 5th CE, Theravada commentator, Visuddhimagga.
  • Ashvaghosha: c. 1st–2nd CE, Kushan era, Buddhacharita.
  • Primary Texts:
    • Tipitaka (Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma Pitakas; Pali Canon).
    • Dhammapada, Jataka Tales, Milinda Panha.
    • Mahayana Sutras (Lotus Sutra, Heart Sutra, Prajnaparamita).
    • Visuddhimagga, Abhidharmakosha.
    • Ashoka’s Edicts.
  • Highlights:
    • Sermons and Jataka stories.
    • Stupas, chaityas, viharas (Sanchi, Ajanta).
    • Universities (Nalanda, Vikramshila).
    • Ashokan pillars and rock edicts.
  • Theravada (Pali Canon, prevalent in Sri Lanka/Southeast Asia).
  • Mahayana (Bodhisattva ideal, China/East Asia; sub-schools: Madhyamaka, Yogachara).
  • Vajrayana (Tantric, Tibet/Himalayas).
  • Early schools (18–24, e.g., Sthaviravada → Theravada; Mahasanghika → Mahayana influence).
  • Mahayana: Bodhisattva ideal (delay Nirvana to help others).
  • Key Bodhisattvas: Avalokiteshvara (compassion), Manjushri (wisdom), Maitreya (future Buddha), Vajrapani (power).
  • 1st Council: c. 483 BCE, Rajagriha (Rajgir), under Ajatashatru; presided by Mahakashyapa; compiled Vinaya & Sutta.
  • 2nd Council: c. 383 BCE, Vaishali, under Kalashoka; schism (Sthavira vs Mahasanghika).
  • 3rd Council: c. 250 BCE, Pataliputra, under Ashoka; presided by Moggaliputta Tissa; Abhidhamma compiled; missionaries sent.
  • 4th Council: c. 100 CE, Kashmir, under Kanishka; Mahayana consolidation.
  • Bodh Gaya (Mahabodhi Temple, Bihar): Enlightenment site; original shrine 3rd BCE (Ashoka), current ~5th–6th CE (Gupta), UNESCO.
  • Sarnath (Dhamek Stupa, Uttar Pradesh): First sermon; Ashokan pillar.
  • Lumbini (Nepal): Birthplace; Ashokan pillar, UNESCO.
  • Kushinagar (Uttar Pradesh): Parinirvana site.
  • Sanchi Stupa (Madhya Pradesh, 3rd BCE): Relics, UNESCO.
  • Ajanta Caves (Maharashtra, 2nd BCE–6th CE): Exclusively Buddhist paintings/sculptures (Jatakas, Buddha life).
  • Nalanda (Bihar, 5th CE): Monastic university.
  • Barabar Caves (Bihar, 3rd BCE): Earliest rock-cut.
  • Mauryas (Ashoka)
  • Kushans (Kanishka)
  • Guptas
  • Palas (Dharmapala)
  • Satavahanas
  • Gradual revival of Hinduism/Bhakti (assimilation, e.g., Buddha as Vishnu avatar).
  • Loss of royal patronage post-Gupta/Pala.
  • Internal divisions and tantric corruption (debated).
  • Turkish invasions (e.g., Nalanda destroyed 1193 CE).
Jainism c. 6th Century BCE–Ongoing
(Historical: Mahavira era; traditional prehistoric roots)		 Gangetic Plain (Magadha region, North India); Mahavira's birthplace: Kundagrama (near Vaishali, Bihar)
  • Ahimsa: Absolute non-violence towards all living beings.
  • Anekantavada: Multiplicity of viewpoints (many-sided reality).
  • Syadvada: Doctrine of conditional predication ("perhaps/maybe").
  • Aparigraha: Non-possession/non-attachment.
  • Satya (truth), Asteya (non-stealing), Brahmacharya (chastity) – Five Mahavratas.
  • Karma: Subtle matter binding the soul; liberation through its shedding.
  • Moksha: Liberation of the jiva (soul) from samsara.
  • 24 Tirthankaras: Ford-makers who rediscover and teach the path.
  • Pre-Mahavira tradition: Parshvanatha (23rd Tirthankara) revived four vows.
  • Mahavira (24th Tirthankara) systematized and added celibacy vow.
  • Strong patronage from kings (Bimbisara, Chandragupta) and merchants.
  • Schism into Digambara and Shvetambara (~2nd–1st BCE or later).
  • Flourished in South India under Western Gangas, Rashtrakutas, Hoysalas.
  • Rishabhanatha: Traditional first Tirthankara, associated with civilization origins.
  • Parshvanatha: c. 877–777 BCE (traditional), 23rd Tirthankara, revived Jainism.
  • Mahavira: c. 599–527 BCE (traditional), Kundagrama (Bihar), 24th Tirthankara, contemporary of Buddha.
  • Bhadrabahu: c. 4th BCE, last srutakevali, led southern migration with Chandragupta Maurya.
  • Sthulabhadra: c. 4th BCE, Shvetambara leader, presided over Pataliputra council.
  • Umasvati/Umaswami: c. 2nd–5th CE, author of Tattvartha Sutra (accepted by both sects).
  • Kundakunda: c. 2nd–3rd CE, Digambara acharya, key metaphysical texts (Samayasara, etc.).
  • Haribhadra: c. 6th–8th CE, Shvetambara scholar, promoted Anekantavada.
  • Primary Texts:
    • Agamas/Angas (Shvetambara canon: 45 texts, e.g., Acharanga, Kalpa Sutra, Bhagavati Sutra).
    • Tattvartha Sutra (Umasvati) – accepted by both sects.
    • Digambara texts: Shatkhandagama, Kashayapahuda.
    • Key works: Samayasara, Niyamasara, Pravachanasara (Kundakunda).
  • Highlights:
    • Kalpa Sutra (lives of Tirthankaras).
    • Jain influence in Tamil Sangam literature.
    • Monolithic statues (Gomateshwara), rock-cut caves, ornate temples.
  • Digambara ("sky-clad"): Monks nude; stricter asceticism; women need male rebirth for moksha.
  • Shvetambara ("white-clad"): Monks wear robes; women can attain moksha; idol worship common.
  • Shvetambara sub-sects: Murtipujaka (temple-worshipping), Sthanakavasi (non-idolatrous), Terapanthi (reformist, 18th CE).
  • 24 Tirthankaras as ideal conquerors (Jinas) and role models.
  • Path of extreme self-discipline and penance for soul purification.
  • No creator God; eternal universe.
  • 1st Council: c. 300 BCE, Pataliputra, presided by Sthulabhadra; compilation of Agamas (after famine-induced loss of oral knowledge).
  • 2nd Council: c. 512–513 CE, Vallabhi (Gujarat), presided by Devardhigani; final redaction of Shvetambara canon.
  • Shravanabelagola (Karnataka): Gomateshwara (Bahubali) statue, 981–983 CE, Ganga-Chola era; Mahamastakabhisheka site.
  • Dilwara Temples (Mount Abu, Rajasthan, 11th–13th CE): Exquisite marble work, Shvetambara.
  • Palitana (Shatrunjaya Hill) (Gujarat): Hundreds of temples, major tirtha.
  • Ranakpur Temple (Rajasthan, 15th CE): Vast Shvetambara temple with 1,444 pillars.
  • Sammed Shikharji/Parasnath Hill (Jharkhand): Most sacred; 20 Tirthankaras attained nirvana.
  • Girnar (Gujarat): Associated with Neminatha (22nd).
  • Udayagiri-Khandagiri Caves (Odisha, 1st–2nd BCE): Kharavela inscriptions.
  • Ellora Jain Caves (Maharashtra, 8th–10th CE): Rashtrakuta patronage.
  • Haryanka (Bimbisara)
  • Nanda and Maurya (Chandragupta Maurya)
  • Kharavela (Mahameghavahana, Kalinga)
  • Western Gangas, Kadambas
  • Rashtrakutas, Hoysalas
  • Chalukyas, Solankis
  • Never became majority religion; limited to trading communities.
  • Decline in patronage after medieval period.
  • Impact of Islamic invasions on northern centers.
  • Strong survival in western India (Gujarat, Rajasthan) and Karnataka.
- Philosphies (validated) -
Philosophy Time Period (Approximate) Location/Region of Origin Core Principles & Tenets Key Figures & Contributors
Vedic Philosophy (Early Vedic / Pre-Upanishadic phase; foundational to later Vedanta) ~1500 BCE – 800 BCE Sapta-Sindhu region (North-West India) with later expansion into the Gangetic Plains; cultural continuity with the Indus Valley Civilization debated among historians
  • Emphasis on rituals and sacrifices (Yajna) as means to sustain cosmic and social order.
  • Belief in multiple deities such as Indra, Agni, Varuna (largely henotheistic / monolatrous rather than strict polytheism).
  • Concept of cosmic order (Ṛta) governing nature, society, and morality.
  • Early and implicit concepts of Brahman (cosmic principle) and Atman (self), not yet systematized philosophically.
  • Focus on hymns and prayers seeking worldly prosperity, cattle, rain, victory, sons, and longevity.
  • Rishis (seer-sages) to whom the Vedic hymns are traditionally revealed (Vedas regarded as apaurusheya – not human-authored).
  • Families of priestly traditions and rishi lineages (e.g., Angiras, Bhrigus).
Upanishadic Philosophy (Later Vedic / Vedānta phase; philosophical culmination of the Vedas) ~800 BCE – 500 BCE Gangetic Plains (Kosala, Videha, Kuru–Panchala regions); core area of Later Vedic philosophical activity (not modern North-East India)
  • Focus on philosophical inquiry, introspection, and self-realization rather than ritual action.
  • Central concepts of Brahman (ultimate, absolute reality) and Atman (individual self).
  • Doctrine of Karma and Samsara, now understood as ethical causation governing rebirth.
  • Emphasis on knowledge (Jnana) as the primary path to liberation (Moksha).
  • Exploration of the nature of reality and consciousness, including identity of Atman and Brahman.
  • Shift from external ritualism (karma-kanda) to internal knowledge (jnana-kanda).
  • Yajnavalkya (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad) – leading metaphysical teacher, proponent of Atman-Brahman unity.
  • Uddalaka Aruni (Chandogya Upanishad) – teacher of the doctrine “Tat Tvam Asi”.
  • Shvetaketu (Chandogya Upanishad) – student figure through whom key teachings are conveyed.
  • Pippalada (Prashna Upanishad) – teacher responding to metaphysical questions of students.
Samkhya ~7th – 6th Century BCE (early philosophical roots; classical systematic formulation much later) Various regions of ancient India (pan-Indian philosophical tradition)
  • Dualistic philosophy: Purusha (pure consciousness) and Prakriti (primordial matter) as two independent, eternal realities.
  • Prakriti as the source of the material world, composed of three Gunas (Sattva, Rajas, Tamas) in dynamic equilibrium.
  • Evolution (pariṇāma) of the universe from Prakriti through a sequence of tattvas (ultimately 25 principles).
  • Emphasis on discrimination (Viveka) between Purusha and Prakriti as the means to liberation (Kaivalya).
  • Non-theistic (often termed atheistic) system: does not posit a creator God (Ishvara), though it accepts causation and moral order.
  • Kapila (traditional and legendary founder; associated with early Samkhya ideas).
  • Ishvara Krishna (c. 4th century CE), author of Samkhya Karika, the earliest extant systematic exposition of Samkhya philosophy.
Yoga (Classical / Pātañjala Yoga) ~2nd Century BCE – 2nd Century CE (classical systematic formulation; yogic ideas much earlier) Various regions of ancient India (pan-Indian philosophical and ascetic tradition)
  • System of physical, mental, and spiritual practices, with primary emphasis on mental discipline and liberation.
  • Eight limbs of Yoga (Ashtanga Yoga) as a graduated path of self-discipline and spiritual realization.
  • Focus on control and cessation of mental modifications (chitta-vritti-nirodha).
  • Accepts Samkhya metaphysics (Purusha–Prakriti dualism), but adds Ishvara (a special Purusha) as an object of devotion.
  • Emphasis on meditation (Dhyana) and absorption (Samadhi) as the culmination of yogic practice.
  • Patanjali – compiler/systematizer of the Yoga Sutras (four pādas: Samadhi, Sadhana, Vibhuti, Kaivalya).
Nyaya ~6th Century BCE – 2nd Century CE (early logical roots with classical systematic formulation later) Various regions of ancient India (pan-Indian logical and philosophical tradition)
  • System of logic and epistemology (theory of knowledge), concerned with correct reasoning.
  • Four Pramanas (sources of valid knowledge): Perception (Pratyaksha), Inference (Anumana), Comparison (Upamana), and Testimony (Shabda).
  • Emphasis on rigorous debate, syllogistic reasoning, and logical analysis.
  • Belief in liberation (Moksha) through right knowledge and removal of ignorance and false cognition.
  • Theistic system: accepts the existence of God (Ishvara) as an efficient cause of the world.
  • Gautama (also known as Akṣapāda Gautama), traditional author of the Nyaya Sutras.
  • Vatsyayana, author of the Nyaya Bhashya, the earliest extant authoritative commentary.
Vaisheshika ~6th Century BCE – 2nd Century CE (early atomistic roots with later classical formulation) Various regions of ancient India (pan-Indian naturalistic and philosophical tradition)
  • Atomistic pluralism: Universe composed of eternal, indivisible atoms (paramāṇu).
  • Seven categories (Padarthas): Dravya (substance), Guna (quality), Karma (action), Samanya (generality), Vishesha (particularity), Samavaya (inherence), Abhava (absence – added in later Vaisheshika development).
  • Emphasis on systematic understanding of the physical and material world.
  • Theistic system in later development, accepting the existence of God (Ishvara); early Vaisheshika was largely non-theistic, with theism emerging through Nyaya influence.
  • Kanada (also known as Ulūka), traditional author of the Vaisheshika Sutras.
Purva Mimamsa (Karma-Mīmāṃsā; earlier part of the Mīmāṃsā tradition) ~6th – 2nd Century BCE (early ritual hermeneutics; classical commentarial tradition later) Various regions of ancient India (pan-Indian tradition closely linked with Vedic ritual schools)
  • Emphasis on the interpretation and precise application of Vedic rituals (yajña).
  • Authority of the Vedas as eternal, authorless (apaurusheya), and infallible.
  • Focus on Dharma (duty) as known through Vedic injunctions (vidhi).
  • Belief in the intrinsic efficacy of rituals for achieving desired results through apūrva (unseen potency).
  • Emphasis on correct hermeneutical interpretation of Vedic texts using strict exegetical rules.
  • Jaimini – compiler/systematizer of the Mimamsa Sutras.
  • Shabara – author of the Shabara Bhashya, the earliest authoritative commentary.
Uttara Mimamsa (Vedanta; philosophical culmination of the Vedic tradition) ~500 BCE – 200 CE (early classical foundation; major school formulations much later) Various regions of ancient India (pan-Indian tradition with later regional schools)
  • System of philosophical interpretation of the Upanishads (Vedānta: “end of the Vedas”).
  • Emphasis on Brahman as the ultimate, absolute reality.
  • Various schools: Advaita (non-dualism), Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism), Dvaita (dualism), each offering distinct interpretations of Brahman, Atman, and the world.
  • Focus on knowledge (Jnana) as the path to liberation (Moksha), especially in Advaita; other schools also emphasize devotion (Bhakti) and divine grace.
  • Emphasis on inquiry into the nature of self (Atman) and ultimate reality.
  • Badarayana – author of the Brahma Sutras, foundational text of Vedanta.
  • Adi Shankara (8th century CE) – propounder of Advaita Vedanta.
  • Ramanuja (11th–12th century CE) – propounder of Vishishtadvaita Vedanta.
  • Madhvacharya (13th century CE) – propounder of Dvaita Vedanta.
Charvaka (Lokāyata; materialist and heterodox tradition) ~6th Century BCE (known primarily through fragmentary and polemical evidence) Various regions of ancient India (not confined to a single geographical area)
  • Materialistic and atheistic philosophy, denying the existence of God, soul, and supernatural entities.
  • Rejection of supernatural and metaphysical concepts such as Brahman, Atman, and moksha.
  • Emphasis on direct perception (Pratyaksha) as the primary valid source of knowledge; inference is rejected when it goes beyond sensory experience.
  • Hedonistic ethics: pursuit of pleasure and avoidance of pain, though often presented polemically by rival schools.
  • Rejection of Karma, Samsara, rebirth, and belief in an afterlife.
  • Brihaspati (traditional and legendary founder; attribution largely from hostile sources).
- Art and culture (validated) -
Category Details
Paintings
  • Bhimbetka Rock Shelters
    • Time: Upper Paleolithic to Mesolithic and Chalcolithic periods (~30,000 BCE to early historic times)
    • Location: Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh (Vindhya range, near Bhopal)
    • Prehistoric rock paintings depicting hunting scenes, dancing figures, animals (bison, deer, elephants), daily life, rituals, and community activities; executed using natural pigments such as red and white ochre
    • Technique: Rock art on cave walls and rock surfaces (not mural or fresco); multiple cultural layers indicating long continuity of habitation
    • Patronage: Prehistoric hunter-gatherer and early agrarian communities (no royal patronage)
    • Status: UNESCO World Heritage Site (2003)
  • Ajanta Caves
    • Time: ~2nd BCE–6th CE (major phase under Vakataka ruler Harishena)
    • Location: Aurangabad, Maharashtra
    • Buddhist murals depicting Jataka tales and Bodhisattvas; executed mainly in tempera / fresco-secco technique (painting on dry plaster), noted for narrative depth, expressive faces, and vibrant mineral colors
    • Patronage: Satavahanas (early phase), Vakatakas (later phase)
  • Bagh Caves
    • Time: ~5th–7th CE
    • Location: Madhya Pradesh
    • Buddhist-themed paintings stylistically similar to Ajanta, showing Gupta-period artistic influence with emphasis on secular elegance and use of natural pigments
    • Patronage: Regional rulers; strong Gupta artistic influence
  • Ellora Caves
    • Time: ~6th–9th CE
    • Location: Maharashtra
    • Hindu (Shiva, Vishnu), Buddhist, and Jain themes; paintings exist but sculpture predominates; Hindu caves include Krishna-related motifs
    • Patronage: Early Buddhist caves predate Rashtrakutas; Rashtrakutas mainly patronized the Hindu phase (Kailasa Temple)
  • Sittanavasal
    • Time: ~7th–9th CE
    • Location: Tamil Nadu
    • Jain paintings featuring the famous lotus pond (samavasarana symbolism), floral motifs, monks, and themes of spiritual purity; executed in fresco-secco technique, representing Pandyan art
    • Patronage: Pandyas
Temples
  • Dashavatara Temple
    • Time: ~5th CE
    • Location: Deogarh, Uttar Pradesh
    • Purpose: Vishnu worship; early structural stone temple in Nagara style with proto-latina shikhara
    • Patronage: Gupta dynasty; noted for sculptural panels such as Gajendramoksha and Nara–Narayana
  • Brihadeeswara Temple
    • Time: 1010 CE
    • Location: Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu
    • Purpose: Shiva worship; monumental expression of Chola imperial power in mature Dravida style
    • Patronage: Rajaraja Chola I; also known as Rajarajeshwaram; part of the Great Living Chola Temples (UNESCO)
  • Khajuraho Temples
    • Time: ~950–1050 CE
    • Location: Madhya Pradesh
    • Purpose: Hindu (Shiva, Vishnu) and Jain worship; renowned for intricate sculptural program including erotic (mithuna) figures symbolizing life, fertility, and tantric philosophy
    • Patronage: Chandela dynasty; Nagara style (Central Indian subtype)
  • Dilwara Temples
    • Time: ~11th–13th CE
    • Location: Mount Abu, Rajasthan
    • Purpose: Jain worship; famous for extremely intricate marble carvings and ornamental ceilings
    • Patronage: Solanki (Chaulukya) rulers of Gujarat and wealthy Jain merchants
  • Shore Temple
    • Time: ~7th–8th CE
    • Location: Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu
    • Purpose: Primarily Shiva worship with Vaishnava elements; early structural Dravida temple serving as a coastal landmark
    • Patronage: Pallava dynasty (Narasimhavarman II); part of the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram (UNESCO)
Pillars
  • Ashokan Pillar Inscriptions (Major & Minor Pillar Edicts)
    • Chronology: Reign of Ashoka, ~269–232 BCE
    • Classification (UPSC-Critical):
      • Major Pillar Edicts: Exactly 7 edicts (Edicts I–VII), issued in the later part of Ashoka’s reign
      • Minor Pillar Edicts: Multiple local / commemorative inscriptions (number not fixed), including Schism Edict and Buddhist commemorative records
    • Locations with Major Pillar Edicts:
      • Delhi–Topra (Delhi): All 7 Major Pillar Edicts; originally from Topra (Haryana), transported to Delhi by Firoz Shah Tughlaq; no capital survives
      • Lauriya–Nandangarh (Champaran, Bihar): All 7 Major Pillar Edicts; monolithic shaft (~35 ft); single-lion capital intact
      • Allahabad (Prayagraj) (UP): 6 Major Pillar Edicts; later reused for Samudragupta’s Prayag Prashasti; no capital survives
      • Lauriya–Araraj (Bihar): 6 Major Pillar Edicts; plain shaft; no capital
      • Rampurva (Bihar): 6 Major Pillar Edicts; originally had two capitals:
        • Bull capital – now preserved at Rashtrapati Bhavan, New Delhi
        • Lion capital – now preserved in Delhi
        pillar site is waterlogged and prone to damage
    • Locations with Ashokan Pillars but WITHOUT Major Pillar Edicts:
      • Sarnath (UP): Minor Pillar Edict (Schism Edict); famous four-lion capital (National Emblem of India); no Major Pillar Edicts
      • Nigali Sagar (Nepal): Minor Pillar Inscription; records Ashoka enlarging the stupa of Buddha Konakamana
      • Rummindei (Lumbini) (Nepal): Minor Pillar Inscription; records Buddha’s birthplace and Ashoka’s tax remission
      • Vaishali (Bihar): pillar with single-lion capital; no Major Pillar Edicts
      • Sankissa (UP): fragmentary pillar with elephant capital; no Major Pillar Edicts
    • Major Pillar Edicts – Core Themes:
      • Edict I: Prohibition of animal sacrifice; welfare orientation
      • Edict II: Medical facilities for humans and animals
      • Edict III: Respect for elders and moral conduct
      • Edict IV: Moral conquest (Dhamma) over material conquest
      • Edict V: Duties of Dhamma Mahamatras
      • Edict VI: Justice and accessibility of administration
      • Edict VII: Summary of Dhamma after 26 years of rule
    • Material & Style: Polished Chunar sandstone, monolithic shafts, bell-shaped capitals, high Mauryan polish
    • Patronage: Ashoka (Maurya dynasty)
    • UPSC-SAFE LOCK STATEMENT: Ashoka issued 7 Major Pillar Edicts at a few select sites, while Minor Pillar Edicts and commemorative inscriptions occur at several other locations; not all Ashokan pillars carry Major Pillar Edicts.
  • Samudragupta’s Allahabad Pillar Inscription
    • Time: ~350–375 CE
    • Location: Allahabad (Prayagraj, UP)
    • Purpose: Prayag Prashasti; records Aryavarta and Dakshinapatha conquests; praises Samudragupta as “Kaviraja”
    • Uniqueness: Sanskrit inscription in Gupta script on an Ashokan pillar; composed by Harisena
    • Patronage: Samudragupta (Gupta dynasty)
  • Heliodorus Pillar
    • Time: ~113 BCE
    • Location: Besnagar (Vidisha), Madhya Pradesh
    • Purpose: Dedication to Vasudeva (Vishnu) by Indo-Greek ambassador Heliodorus
    • Uniqueness: Garuda capital; Indo-Greek cultural synthesis; earliest epigraphic evidence of Vaishnavism
    • Patronage: Shunga period (Indo-Greek diplomatic context)
Stupas
  • Sanchi Stupa (Stupa No. 1)
    • Time: ~3rd century BCE (original brick stupa by Ashoka; major expansion and embellishment during 1st century BCE–1st century CE)
    • Location: Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh
    • Purpose: Buddhist relic worship; originally commissioned by Ashoka to enshrine relics of the Buddha
    • Architectural features: hemispherical dome (anda), harmika, central yasti with chhatras, four elaborately carved toranas depicting Jataka tales and Buddhist symbols
    • Patronage: Mauryas (foundation), Satavahanas and local guilds (later enlargement)
    • Status: UNESCO World Heritage Site
  • Amaravati Stupa (Mahachaitya)
    • Time: ~3rd century BCE–3rd century CE
    • Location: Amaravati (Dhanyakataka), Andhra Pradesh
    • Purpose: Buddhist worship and relic veneration; major center of Buddhist pilgrimage in the Deccan
    • Artistic features: highly intricate limestone reliefs, dynamic narrative panels, development of the Amaravati School of Art
    • Patronage: Satavahana dynasty and local donors
    • Note: Many sculptural panels are now housed in museums (Chennai, British Museum)
  • Bharhut Stupa
    • Time: ~2nd century BCE
    • Location: Bharhut, Madhya Pradesh
    • Purpose: Buddhist relic worship
    • Artistic features: stone railings (vedika) and gateways with narrative reliefs, extensive depiction of Jataka tales, Buddha represented symbolically (aniconic phase)
    • Inscriptions: Prakrit language in Brahmi script, valuable for early Buddhist history
    • Patronage: Shunga dynasty
Caves
  • Ajanta Caves
    • Time: ~2nd century BCE–6th century CE (two phases: Satavahana phase and Vakataka phase under Harishena)
    • Location: Maharashtra
    • Purpose: Buddhist monasteries and worship; combination of chaityas (prayer halls) and viharas (monastic residences)
    • Rock-cut architecture with world-famous murals and sculptures; among the finest examples of Buddhist art
    • Patronage: Satavahanas (early phase), Vakatakas (later phase)
    • Status: UNESCO World Heritage Site
  • Ellora Caves
    • Time: ~6th–9th century CE
    • Location: Maharashtra
    • Purpose: Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain worship; rare example of religious coexistence at one site
    • Total 34 caves: 12 Buddhist (1–12), 17 Hindu (13–29), 5 Jain (30–34)
    • Kailasa Temple (Cave 16): largest monolithic rock-cut temple in the world, dedicated to Shiva
    • Patronage: Multiple dynasties; Rashtrakutas primarily patronized the Hindu phase
    • Status: UNESCO World Heritage Site
  • Barabar Caves
    • Time: ~3rd century BCE
    • Location: Bihar
    • Purpose: Shelters for the Ajivika sect (not Buddhist); earliest example of rock-cut caves in India
    • Distinctive Mauryan polish; Lomas Rishi cave notable for earliest chaitya-arch façade
    • Patronage: Ashoka (Maurya dynasty)
  • Udayagiri–Khandagiri Caves
    • Time: ~2nd century BCE–1st century CE
    • Location: Odisha
    • Purpose: Jain monastic retreats
    • Hathi Gumpha inscription: records achievements of King Kharavela; crucial source for early Deccan history
    • Patronage: Kharavela (Mahameghavahana dynasty)
  • Elephanta Caves
    • Time: ~5th–8th century CE
    • Location: Maharashtra (Elephanta Island near Mumbai)
    • Purpose: Shaiva worship
    • Famous Trimurti (Sadashiva) sculpture, representing three aspects of Shiva
    • Patronage: Debated; attributed to either early Chalukyas (Badami) or Rashtrakutas
    • Status: UNESCO World Heritage Site
Other Structures
  • Mahabalipuram Rathas (Pancha Rathas / Pandava Rathas)
    • Time: ~7th century CE
    • Location: Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu
    • Purpose: Experimental rock-cut temple forms; architectural prototypes for later Dravida temples
    • Five monolithic rathas, each carved from a single rock, representing different shrine designs; not consecrated or used for active worship
    • Patronage: Pallava dynasty (Narasimhavarman I, Mamalla)
    • Status: Part of the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram (UNESCO)
  • Nalanda University
    • Time: ~5th–12th century CE
    • Location: Bihar
    • Purpose: Premier center of Buddhist learning and higher education
    • Large monastic-university complex with viharas, chaityas, classrooms, and vast libraries (Dharmaganja complex)
    • Patronage: Gupta dynasty (founder Kumaragupta I), later supported by Harsha and the Pala rulers
    • Significance: Attracted scholars from across Asia; destroyed around 1193 CE during Bakhtiyar Khilji’s invasion
  • Gomateshwara (Bahubali) Statue
    • Time: 983 CE
    • Location: Shravanabelagola, Karnataka
    • Purpose: Jain worship of Bahubali (Gomateshwara)
    • 57-foot-high monolithic granite statue; tallest free-standing monolithic statue in the world; depicts kayotsarga (standing meditation) posture
    • Patronage: Western Ganga dynasty; commissioned by Chamundaraya
    • Cultural note: Mahamastakabhisheka ceremony performed every 12 years
Ashokan Rock Edicts
  • Major Rock Edicts (14)
    • Time: ~269–232 BCE (Ashoka’s reign)
    • Nature: Set of 14 edicts (I–XIV); not all edicts occur at every site; Dhauli and Jaugada replace Edict XIII with Separate Kalinga Edicts
    • Locations & Uniqueness:
      • Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat): Inscribed on granite hill rock; Brahmi script; best-preserved set
      • Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand): Limestone rock; Brahmi script; northernmost Major Rock Edict site
      • Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha): Brahmi script; elephant sculpture above edicts; Edict XIII absent
      • Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): Brahmi script; fort site; Edict XIII absent
      • Shahbazgarhi (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan): Kharoshthi script; Indo-Greek cultural zone
      • Mansehra (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan): Kharoshthi script; inscriptions on rugged rock face
      • Sopara (near Mumbai, Maharashtra): Fragmentary Brahmi inscriptions; coastal trade linkage
    • Major Rock Edicts – Core Themes:
      • Edict I: Protection of animals; prohibition of certain animal sacrifices
      • Edict II: Medical care for humans and animals; mentions Antiochus II and southern kingdoms (Cholas, Pandyas, Satyaputras, Keralaputras)
      • Edict III: Moral conduct, obedience to elders, generosity
      • Edict IV: Spread of Dhamma through officials and persuasion rather than force
      • Edict V: Appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras; administrative innovation
      • Edict VI: King’s concern for justice; accessibility of administration
      • Edict VII: Religious tolerance and harmony
      • Edict VIII: Ashoka’s pilgrimage to Bodh Gaya; shift from pleasure tours to Dhamma tours
      • Edict IX: Condemnation of meaningless rituals
      • Edict X: Dhamma valued over fame and glory
      • Edict XI: Detailed explanation of Dhamma as ethical living
      • Edict XII: Mutual respect among religious sects
      • Edict XIII: Kalinga War remorse; non-violence policy; mentions Sri Lanka (Tamraparni) and unconquered southern kingdoms
      • Edict XIV: Summary and conclusion of Dhamma policy
    • Patronage: Ashoka (Maurya dynasty)
    • UPSC Note: Edict XIII is absent at Dhauli and Jaugada
  • Minor Rock Edicts
    • Time: ~269–232 BCE (earlier than Major Rock Edicts)
    • Nature: Short, personal proclamations emphasizing Ashoka’s conversion, urgency of Dhamma, and personal faith
    • Locations & Uniqueness:
      • Bhabru (near Jaipur, Rajasthan): Expresses Ashoka’s faith in Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha
      • Maski (Raichur, Karnataka): First inscription identifying Devanampiya Piyadassi as Ashoka
      • Gujarra (Datia, Madhya Pradesh): Mentions Ashoka explicitly
      • Rupnath (Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh): Early proclamation of Dhamma
      • Sahasram (Bihar): Urgent tone; early phase of Ashoka’s moral policy
    • Purpose: Early propagation of Dhamma and personal ethical commitment
    • Patronage: Ashoka (Maurya dynasty)
  • Separate Kalinga Edicts
    • Time: ~269–232 BCE
    • Nature: Two special edicts issued only for Kalinga region; not part of the 14 Major Rock Edicts
    • Locations & Uniqueness:
      • Dhauli (Odisha): Elephant sculpture; compassionate tone after Kalinga War
      • Jaugada (Odisha): Fort wall inscription; administrative focus
    • Purpose & Content:
      • Kalinga Edict I: Assurance of non-violence and humane governance
      • Kalinga Edict II: Welfare, justice, and appointment of local officers
    • Patronage: Ashoka (Maurya dynasty)
Languages
  • Vedic Sanskrit
    • Time: ~1500–500 BCE
    • Location: North-West India
    • Oral hymns (Vedas), precursor to Classical Sanskrit
  • Classical Sanskrit
    • Time: ~500 BCE–1200 CE
    • Location: Pan-India
    • Panini’s grammar, literary works (Kalidasa)
  • Prakrit
    • Time: ~3rd BCE–500 CE
    • Location: North/Central India
    • Vernacular, Jain texts, Ashokan edicts
  • Pali
    • Time: ~5th BCE–500 CE
    • Location: North India
    • Buddhist Tripitaka, simpler grammar
  • Tamil
    • Time: ~300 BCE–500 CE
    • Location: South India
    • Sangam literature, Dravidian
Scripts
  • Brahmi Script
    • Time: ~3rd century BCE onwards
    • Region: Most of the Indian subcontinent (except north-west)
    • Oldest widely used Indian script; written left to right
    • Used in:
      • Ashokan Rock Edicts and Pillar Edicts (Prakrit language)
      • Early Sanskrit inscriptions (Gupta period onwards)
      • Early Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions (South India)
    • Ancestor of most modern Indian scripts (Devanagari, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, etc.)
  • Kharoshthi Script
    • Time: ~3rd century BCE–3rd century CE
    • Region: North-West India and present-day Pakistan (Gandhara region)
    • Written right to left; derived from Aramaic script
    • Used mainly for:
      • Ashokan Major Rock Edicts at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra
      • Prakrit language in north-western Mauryan territories
    • Important UPSC distinction: Ashokan inscriptions are in Prakrit, but script differs — Brahmi in most regions, Kharoshthi in the north-west
  • Tamil-Brahmi Script
    • Time: ~3rd century BCE–3rd century CE
    • Region: Tamilakam (Tamil Nadu and adjoining areas)
    • Southern adaptation of Brahmi to suit Dravidian phonetics
    • Used for:
      • Early Tamil inscriptions
      • Sangam-age pottery inscriptions
  • Gupta Script
    • Time: ~4th–6th century CE
    • Region: North and Central India
    • Developed from Brahmi during the Gupta period
    • Used mainly for Sanskrit inscriptions (e.g., Prayag Prashasti of Samudragupta)
    • Direct precursor of Nagari / Devanagari script
  • Sharada Script
    • Time: ~8th–12th century CE
    • Region: Kashmir and north-western India
    • Derived from Gupta script; used mainly for Sanskrit texts
- Political, administrative, economic, etc systems (validated) -
System Time Period (Approximate) Location/Region Core Features & Structures Key Figures & Roles
Integrated data
Vedic Administration ~1500 BCE – 500 BCE (Early & Later Vedic phases) North-West India to Gangetic Plains
  • Nature of polity:
    • Tribal, kinship-based political organisation.
    • Gradual transition from pastoral tribal chiefdoms to territorial monarchies.
  • Kinghip:
    • Rajan was not absolute; authority limited by assemblies and customs.
    • Required ritual sanction and popular acceptance.
    • Protector of people and cattle (gopa, gopati).
  • Popular assemblies:
    • Sabha: Council of elders; judicial and advisory role.
    • Samiti: General assembly; participatory and political.
    • Vidatha: Early Vedic socio-religious assembly.
    • Gana: Clan or tribal council.
  • Administration:
    • No standing bureaucracy or salaried officials.
    • Functions carried out through clan-based functionaries.
  • Territorial units:
    • Jana → Vish → Grama.
  • Revenue system:
    • No land revenue.
    • King received voluntary offerings (Bali).
    • Economy centred on cattle wealth.
  • Military & justice:
    • No standing army; temporary tribal militias.
    • King acted as chief judge, guided by customary Dharma.
  • Political & Administrative Functionaries
    • Rajan:
      • Tribal chief or king.
      • Supreme political authority, yet constrained.
      • Chief judge and military leader.
    • Gramani:
      • Head of the village (Grama).
      • Maintained order and coordinated local affairs.
  • Religious & Ideological Functionaries
    • Purohita:
      • Chief priest and spiritual advisor to the king.
      • Performed yajnas to legitimise kingship.
      • Influenced political decisions through ritual authority.
  • Military Functionaries
    • Senani:
      • Commander of tribal military forces.
      • Led warriors during inter-tribal conflicts (Gavishthi).
  • Economic & Revenue Functionaries
    • Bhagadugha:
      • Collector of Bali (king’s share).
      • Did not function as a tax officer in the later sense.
  • Judicial & Advisory Roles
    • Sabha members:
      • Elders advising king and settling disputes.
    • Samiti participants:
      • Represented collective will of the tribe.
  • Intelligence, Communication & Support Roles
    • Spasa:
      • Spy or informer reporting to the king.
    • Suta:
      • Royal charioteer.
      • Messenger and chronicler of royal deeds.
    • Takshan:
      • Carpenter and artisan.
      • Built chariots and wooden structures.
Mauryan Administration ~321 BCE – 185 BCE Pan-India (capital: Pataliputra, Magadha)
  • Nature of polity:
    • Highly centralized and bureaucratic imperial monarchy.
    • The king was the supreme authority, assisted by a large council of officials.
    • Administration guided by Arthashastra (Kautilya) and royal edicts.
  • Administrative hierarchy:
    • Empire → Provinces → Districts → Villages.
    • Provinces governed by royal princes or high officials.
  • Provincial administration:
    • Major provinces at Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali, Suvarnagiri.
    • Provincial governors supervised revenue, justice, and military.
  • Urban administration:
    • Megasthenes describes a 30-member municipal board in Pataliputra.
    • Six committees handled industries, trade, foreigners, births/deaths, etc.
  • Revenue & economy:
    • Land revenue was the main income (usually 1/6th of produce).
    • Taxes on trade, tolls, mines, forests, irrigation.
    • State monopoly over mining, salt, arms, forests.
  • Judicial system:
    • King as the supreme judge.
    • Officials administered civil and criminal law.
    • Rajukas had magisterial powers.
  • Military system:
    • Large standing army (infantry, cavalry, elephants, chariots).
    • War office with six boards (Megasthenes).
  • Espionage & intelligence:
    • Highly developed spy system (Guda Purusha).
    • Monitored officials, public opinion, and potential revolts.
  • Ashokan innovations:
    • Dhamma as a state policy.
    • Edicts engraved on rocks and pillars for public communication.
    • Welfare measures for humans and animals.
  • Supreme Authority
    • Samrat:
      • Emperor and head of administration.
      • Issued orders, supervised officials, led foreign policy.
      • Examples: Chandragupta Maurya, Bindusara, Ashoka.
  • Central Administration (Mantriparishad)
    • Amatyas:
      • High-ranking civil servants.
      • Selected through testing and loyalty.
    • Mantrin:
      • King’s councilors for policy advice.
    • Purohita:
      • Chief priest and royal advisor.
  • Revenue & Finance
    • Samaharta:
      • Chief collector of revenue.
      • Assessed land revenue and taxes.
    • Sannidhata:
      • Chief treasurer.
      • Custodian of state treasury and storehouses.
  • Provincial & District Administration
    • Kumara / Aryaputra:
      • Royal prince governing provinces.
    • Pradesika:
      • District-level officer.
      • Toured every five years for inspection.
    • Rajuka:
      • Revenue and judicial officer.
      • Empowered to award punishments.
    • Yukta:
      • Subordinate official assisting Pradesika and Rajuka.
  • Village Administration
    • Gramika:
      • Village headman.
      • Maintained order and assisted revenue collection.
    • Gopa:
      • Supervised groups of villages.
  • Military Administration
    • Senapati:
      • Commander-in-chief of the army.
    • Antapala:
      • Officer guarding frontier regions.
  • Espionage & Internal Security
    • Guda Purusha:
      • Secret agents and spies.
      • Reported corruption, dissent, and loyalty of officials.
  • Ashokan Welfare Administration
    • Dhamma Mahamatras:
      • Special officers appointed by Ashoka.
      • Promoted moral conduct, social welfare, religious tolerance.
    • Rajukas (Ashokan role):
      • Instructed to be impartial and humane.
Gupta Administration ~4th CE – 6th CE North & Central India (capital: Pataliputra)
  • Nature of polity:
    • Monarchical system with divine kingship elements.
    • Less centralized than Mauryas; beginnings of feudal tendencies.
    • King regarded as protector of Dharma and social order.
  • Administrative structure:
    • Empire → Bhukti (province) → Vishaya (district) → Village.
    • Greater autonomy at provincial and local levels.
  • Provincial administration:
    • Bhuktis governed by Uparikas.
    • Often governors were princes or high-ranking officials.
  • Local administration:
    • Village assemblies and local bodies handled routine governance.
    • Guilds (Shrenis) played an important role in urban administration.
  • Revenue system:
    • Land revenue was the chief source of income.
    • Increase in land grants to Brahmins and officials.
    • Taxes paid in kind and cash (Bhaga, Hiranya).
  • Land grants & feudal features:
    • Agrahara and Brahmadeya grants became common.
    • Beneficiaries often received fiscal and administrative rights.
    • Beginning of intermediary landlords (Samantas).
  • Judicial system:
    • King as supreme judicial authority.
    • Dharmashastras influenced law and justice.
  • Military system:
    • Standing army with infantry, cavalry, elephants.
    • Feudatories required to supply troops.
  • Sources of information:
    • Prayag Prashasti (Samudragupta).
    • Eran, Bhitari, and land grant inscriptions.
  • Supreme Authority
    • Maharajadhiraja:
      • Paramount ruler and head of administration.
      • Assumed lofty titles (e.g., Vikramaditya).
      • Examples: Samudragupta, Chandragupta II.
  • Central Administration
    • Mantriparishad:
      • Council of ministers advising the king.
    • Sandhivigrahika:
      • Minister of war, peace, and diplomacy.
      • Handled treaties and foreign relations.
    • Kumaramatya:
      • High-ranking officer.
      • Often served as provincial governors or ministers.
  • Provincial Administration
    • Uparika:
      • Governor of a Bhukti (province).
      • Appointed by the king.
    • Bhogapati:
      • Officer assisting the Uparika.
  • District Administration
    • Vishayapati:
      • Head of a Vishaya (district).
      • Responsible for revenue and law & order.
    • Ayuktaka:
      • Subordinate official in district administration.
  • Village & Local Administration
    • Grama:
      • Basic unit of administration.
    • Gramikas / Gramapatis:
      • Village headmen.
      • Assisted in tax collection and dispute resolution.
    • Village Assemblies:
      • Handled irrigation, local disputes, and land records.
  • Revenue & Finance
    • Samaharta:
      • Chief revenue collector.
    • Hiranya & Bhaga:
      • Cash and produce taxes respectively.
  • Military Administration
    • Mahabaladhikrita:
      • Commander of the army.
    • Senapati:
      • Military general.
  • Feudal & Land Grant System
    • Samanta:
      • Feudatory chiefs or local rulers.
      • Provided military support to the king.
    • Agrahara / Brahmadeya Grantees:
      • Brahmins granted land with tax exemptions.
      • Often enjoyed administrative privileges.
Chola Administration ~9th CE – 13th CE South India (core areas: Thanjavur, Kaveri delta)
  • Nature of polity:
    • Hereditary monarchy with divine kingship ideology.
    • Highly centralized at the top but exceptionally decentralized at the local level.
  • Administrative hierarchy:
    • Empire → Mandalam (province) → Kottam / Valanadu → Nadu → Village.
    • Clear territorial divisions with well-defined responsibilities.
  • Local self-government (most distinctive feature):
    • Village assemblies exercised extensive autonomy.
    • Different types of assemblies existed based on village composition.
    • Committees (Varaiyams) handled specialized functions.
  • Village assemblies:
    • Ur: Assembly of non-Brahmin villages.
    • Sabha: Assembly of Brahmin villages (Agraharas).
    • Nagaram: Assembly of merchants in market towns.
  • Committees (Varaiyams):
    • Eri-Varaiyam – irrigation tanks.
    • Tottam-Varaiyam – gardens.
    • Pancha-Varaiyam – general administration.
    • Dharmavariyam – temples and charities.
    • Gold committee – treasury and loans.
  • Electoral system:
    • Detailed in the Uttaramerur inscriptions (Parantaka I).
    • Kudavolai system – selection by drawing lots.
    • Strict qualifications and disqualifications prescribed.
  • Revenue administration:
    • Land revenue was the primary source of income.
    • Systematic land surveys and classification.
    • Taxes paid in kind and cash.
  • Land categories:
    • Brahmadeya – land grants to Brahmins.
    • Devadana – land grants to temples.
    • Vellanvagai – taxable peasant land.
    • Eripatti – land reserved for irrigation tanks.
    • Salabhoga – land granted to educational institutions.
  • Military administration:
    • Standing army with infantry, cavalry, elephants.
    • Powerful navy controlling Bay of Bengal trade routes.
    • Military used for overseas expeditions (Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia).
  • Sources:
    • Uttaramerur inscriptions.
    • Leiden plates, temple inscriptions.
  • Central Authority
    • Chakravartin:
      • Supreme ruler and source of authority.
      • Examples: Rajaraja I, Rajendra I.
    • Perundaram:
      • High-ranking nobles and central officials.
      • Assisted the king in governance.
    • Sirudanam:
      • Lower-level officials and attendants.
  • Provincial Administration
    • Mandalam:
      • Largest administrative unit.
    • Valanadu / Kottam:
      • Intermediate administrative divisions.
    • Nadu:
      • District-level unit comprising several villages.
      • Administered by local assemblies and officials.
  • Local Self-Government
    • Sabha:
      • Assembly of Brahmin villages.
      • Highly autonomous; managed land, irrigation, justice.
    • Ur:
      • Assembly of non-Brahmin villages.
    • Nagaram:
      • Merchant guild assembly in urban centers.
  • Revenue Administration
    • Nattar:
      • Important local landholders.
      • Managed revenue and land records at Nadu level.
    • Kanakkar:
      • Accountants responsible for record-keeping.
  • Judicial Functions
    • Village assemblies acted as courts.
    • Cases related to land, irrigation, and social offenses.
  • Military Administration
    • Senapati:
      • Commander of the army.
    • Kaikkolaperumadai:
      • Royal bodyguards and standing troops.
  • Temple Administration
    • Temples functioned as:
      • Economic centers.
      • Landowners and employers.
      • Custodians of surplus wealth.
Military Systems (kept for redundency)
Vedic Military ~1500 BCE - 500 BCE Indus Valley & Gangetic Plains
  • Tribal militia, no standing army.
  • Chariots and bows as primary weapons.
  • Cattle raids (e.g., Dasharajna battle).
  • Focus on protecting tribal territory.
  • Senani: Military commander.
  • Rathis: Chariot warriors.
Mauryan Military ~321 BCE - 185 BCE Pan-India
  • Large standing army: infantry, cavalry, elephants, chariots.
  • Six-board war office (Arthashastra).
  • Espionage for intelligence (Gudhapurushas).
  • Kalinga War showcased might.
  • Senapati: Commander-in-chief.
  • Antapala: Border fortress commanders.
  • Mahabaladhikrita: Armed forces superintendent.
Gupta Military ~4th CE - 6th CE North & Central India
  • Feudal levies with royal army.
  • Emphasis on archery (Samudragupta’s coins).
  • Less centralized than Mauryas.
  • Conquests in Aryavarta, Dakshinapatha.
  • Mahadandanayaka: Chief commander.
  • Senapati: General.
  • Bhata: Feudal soldiers.
Chola Military ~9th CE - 13th CE South India & South-East Asia
  • Strong navy and infantry.
  • Naval conquests (Sri Lanka, Srivijaya).
  • Forts for defense (e.g., Gangaikonda Cholapuram).
  • Elite units for campaigns.
  • Senapati: Army/navy commander.
  • Kaikkolar: Elite infantry.
  • Naval Admirals: Led maritime expeditions.
Economic Systems (kept for redundency)
Vedic Economy ~1500 BCE - 500 BCE Indus Valley & Gangetic Plains
  • Agrarian and pastoral economy.
  • Barter system, cattle as wealth.
  • Bali: Voluntary tribute to king.
  • Early crops: Barley, wheat.
  • Rajan: Received Bali.
  • Gramani: Managed village resources.
Mauryan Economy ~321 BCE - 185 BCE Pan-India
  • State-controlled, agriculture-based.
  • Taxes: Bhaga (1/6th land), Hiranya (cash).
  • Coinage: Punch-marked silver Pana.
  • Trade via Silk Road, ports (Tamralipti).
  • Samaharta: Chief revenue collector.
  • Sannidhata: Treasurer.
  • Panyadhyaksha: Trade superintendent.
Gupta Economy ~4th CE - 6th CE North & Central India
  • Agrarian with trade boom.
  • Taxes: Bhaga (1/6th), Uparikara (vassal tax).
  • Gold coins (Dinaras), guilds (Srenis).
  • Trade with Rome (spices, silk).
  • Bhogikas: Revenue collectors.
  • Karanikas: Accountants.
Chola Economy ~9th CE - 13th CE South India
  • Agrarian with maritime trade.
  • Taxes: Kadamai (land), Opati (trade).
  • Irrigation (Grand Anicut), temple economy.
  • Trade with China, ports (Nagapattinam).
  • Nattar: Revenue officials.
  • Kanakkar: Accountants.
Other Systems (kept for redundency)
Judicial Systems ~1500 BCE - 13th CE Across Ancient India
  • Vedic: Sabha settled disputes.
  • Mauryan: King supreme, Rajukas judged.
  • Gupta: Mahadandanayaka as chief justice.
  • Chola: Sabha/Nattar courts, fines common.
  • Rajukas (Mauryan): Justice officers.
  • Mahadandanayaka (Gupta): Chief justice.
  • Sabha (Chola): Local judges.
Social Systems ~1500 BCE - 13th CE Across Ancient India
  • Vedic: Varna system (4 castes).
  • Mauryan: Flexible castes, slavery.
  • Gupta: Rigid castes, feudal hierarchy.
  • Chola: Temple-centric, Brahmin dominance.
  • Rajan (Vedic): Social leader.
  • Gramika (Mauryan): Village head.
Trade Systems ~6th BCE - 13th CE Across Ancient India
  • Uttarapatha: North trade route.
  • Dakshinapatha: South trade route.
  • Silk Road: Kushan trade with China.
  • Maritime: Chola trade with South-East Asia.
  • Panyadhyaksha (Mauryan): Trade overseer.
  • Srenis (Gupta): Guild leaders.
- Ports, trade routes, etc (validated) -
Category Time Period (Approximate) Location/Region Core Features & Trade Details Key Ports & Routes Associated Dynasties & Figures
Major Ports of Ancient India
Lothal ~2400 BCE – 1900 BCE Gujarat (near Gulf of Khambhat)
  • One of the earliest known dockyards, with brick-lined basin, spillway, and possible lock-gate mechanism.
  • Planned Harappan port-town with bead-making workshops.
  • Exported: Beads (carnelian), gemstones, cotton textiles, ivory objects.
  • Imported: Copper, tin, semi-precious stones from West Asia.
  • Trade links with Mesopotamia (Meluhha); Egyptian contact indirect.
 Ancient river channels linked to Arabian Sea trade Indus Valley Civilization
Muziris ~3rd BCE – 4th CE Kerala (Malabar Coast; identified with Pattanam/Kodungallur)
  • Major spice-export port, prominently mentioned in Periplus Maris Erythraei.
  • Exported: Black pepper, pearls, ivory, textiles.
  • Imported: Roman gold, wine, glassware, ceramics.
  • Pliny the Elder notes heavy Roman gold drain to India via Muziris.
 Maritime Silk Route / Indian Ocean monsoon routes Chera Dynasty
Bharuch (Barygaza) ~3rd BCE – 13th CE Gujarat (Narmada River estuary)
  • Major cosmopolitan port described in Periplus Maris Erythraei.
  • Key transshipment hub linking inland routes with Arabian Sea.
  • Exported: Cotton textiles, spices, agate, ivory.
  • Imported: Wine, coral, metals from Roman world.
 Western coastal maritime routes Mauryas, Guptas, later regional dynasties
Tamralipti ~3rd BCE – 8th CE West Bengal (Rupnarayana–Hooghly delta)
  • Major eastern seaport linked to Mauryan and Gupta trade networks.
  • Important Buddhist embarkation port (visited by Faxian, Xuanzang).
  • Exported: Muslin, silk, spices.
  • Trade with Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia (Suvarnabhumi).
 Bay of Bengal maritime routes Mauryas, Guptas
Poompuhar (Kaveripattinam) ~3rd BCE – 4th CE Tamil Nadu (Kaveri River mouth)
  • Principal Chola port described in Sangam literature (Silappadikaram).
  • Major center of Indo-Roman maritime trade.
  • Exported: Textiles, spices, pearls.
  • Imported: Roman gold coins, glassware.
 Coromandel Coast routes Early Cholas
Arikamedu ~2nd BCE – 2nd CE Puducherry (Coromandel Coast)
  • Indo-Roman trading settlement identified with “Poduke” of Periplus.
  • Archaeological finds include Roman amphorae and rouletted ware.
  • Exported: Textiles, gemstones, spices.
  • Imported: Roman wine, glassware.
 Coromandel Coast maritime routes Cholas, Pandyas
Sopara (Shurparaka) ~3rd BCE – 9th CE Maharashtra (north of Mumbai)
  • Ancient port-town with strong Buddhist associations.
  • Linked to Mauryan and Satavahana trade networks.
  • Exported: Cotton textiles, pearls.
  • Imported: Wine, metals from West Asia and Roman world.
 Western coastal routes Mauryas, Satavahanas
Kalyan (Kalyanpuri) ~1st CE – 10th CE Maharashtra (Thane region)
  • Important port connecting Western Deccan hinterland with the Arabian Sea.
  • Mentioned by Cosmas Indicopleustes.
  • Exported: Cotton textiles, rice, spices.
  • Imported: Copper, wine, luxury goods from Arabs and Romans.
 Konkan coast maritime routes Satavahanas, Western Kshatrapas
Barbaricum ~1st CE - 3rd CE Sindh (Indus delta, near present-day Karachi region)
  • Mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as a major Indus delta port.
  • Served as the maritime outlet for inland Indus trade.
  • Exported: Cotton textiles, semi-precious stones.
  • Imported: Roman silver, wine, luxury items (largely via Arabian intermediaries).
 Arabian Sea maritime trade routes Indo-Parthians, Kushans
Mandvi & Dwarka ~3rd BCE - early medieval period Gujarat coast (Kathiawar / Saurashtra Peninsula)
  • Important western coastal ports serving the Saurashtra region.
  • Primarily engaged in Arabian Sea trade with West Asia.
  • Exported: Cotton textiles, pearls, agricultural produce.
  • Later periods show indirect links with wider Indian Ocean trade networks.
 Arabian Sea routes Maitrakas of Valabhi; regional western Indian rulers
Odra Ports (Palur, Che-li-ta-lo) ~1st CE - 8th CE Odisha coast (ancient Kalinga region)
  • Ports of Kalinga actively involved in Southeast Asian maritime trade.
  • Exported: Elephants, rice, textiles, pepper.
  • Palur identified with ancient coastal Odisha.
  • Che-li-ta-lo is a Chinese transcription; exact identification remains debated.
 Bay of Bengal (Kalinga–Southeast Asia routes) Kalinga rulers; later Guptas
Nagasopaka (Sopara region) ~3rd BCE - early medieval period Maharashtra (Konkan coast)
  • Often identified with or closely associated with Sopara (Shurparaka).
  • Important Buddhist centre with nearby Ashokan inscriptions.
  • Functioned as part of the Sopara maritime trade complex rather than a distinct standalone port.
 Western maritime routes Mauryas; Satavahanas
Ghantasala ~2nd BCE - 3rd CE Andhra region (Krishna River delta)
  • Important eastern coastal port connected to Satavahana inland trade centres.
  • Exported: Spices, ivory, semi-precious stones.
  • Mentioned in Buddhist texts and classical sources as a maritime trade hub.
 Eastern maritime trade routes Satavahanas
Trade Routes of Ancient India
Uttarapatha ~6th BCE - 5th CE North India (Takshashila / Taxila to Pataliputra corridor)
  • Major northern land route facilitating long-distance inland trade.
  • Connected north-western regions with the Gangetic plain.
  • Goods traded: Silk, horses, spices, precious metals.
  • Under the Kushans, linked indirectly to Central Asian Silk Road networks.
 Connected inland centres; access to ports like Bharuch and Tamralipti via feeder routes Mauryas; Kushans
Dakshinapatha ~3rd BCE - 5th CE Central & South India (Magadha to Deccan and Tamilakam)
  • Major southern land route connecting the Gangetic plain with the Deccan and far south.
  • Enabled movement of goods from inland regions to eastern and western coastal ports.
  • Goods traded: Spices, textiles, pearls, metals.
 Linked inland regions to ports such as Muziris and Poompuhar Mauryas; Satavahanas; later Cholas
Silk Road ~2nd BCE - 14th CE North-West India via Central Asia
  • Overland transcontinental trade network linking India with Central Asia, China, and West Asia.
  • Goods exchanged: Silk, spices, precious stones, horses.
  • India’s participation strengthened under Kushan control of north-western regions.
 Linked inland north-western centres; indirect access to Indian ports Kushans; Guptas
Maritime Routes (Indian Ocean Trade) ~3rd BCE - 13th CE Eastern & Western coasts of India
  • Sea routes exploiting monsoon wind system.
  • Facilitated Indo-Roman trade in the west and Southeast Asian trade in the east.
  • Goods traded: Pepper, pearls, cotton textiles, silk.
 Muziris, Poompuhar, Tamralipti, Bharuch Cheras; Cholas; Pandyas; Mauryas
Kalinga–Suvarnabhumi Route ~3rd BCE - 8th CE Odisha (Kalinga coast) to Southeast Asia
  • Important eastern maritime route linking India with Southeast Asia.
  • Traders carried elephants, textiles, rice, pepper.
  • Played a role in the spread of Buddhism and Indian cultural influences in Southeast Asia.
 Palur and other Odisha ports → Suvarnabhumi Kalinga rulers; Guptas
Arabian–Red Sea Route ~1st CE - 6th CE Western Indian coast to Roman Egypt
  • Major Indo-Roman maritime route using monsoon navigation.
  • Exports from India: Pepper, pearls, ivory, cotton textiles.
  • Imports into India: Roman gold, wine, glassware.
 Muziris, Bharuch → Berenike → Alexandria Roman Empire; Cheras
Major Trade Goods
Spices ~3rd BCE - 13th CE Pan-India (major production in South India; redistribution role)
  • Key Indian export: Black pepper (high Roman demand).
  • Cinnamon and cloves largely sourced from Southeast Asia and redistributed via Indian ports.
  • Spices were high-value, low-bulk goods, ideal for long-distance maritime trade.
 Maritime routes (Arabian Sea & Bay of Bengal) Cheras; Cholas; later Indian Ocean trading powers
Textiles ~2400 BCE - 13th CE Pan-India (Indus region, Gujarat, Gangetic plains, Tamilakam)
  • Cotton textiles from Indus and western India; silk and fine cotton from Gangetic plains.
  • Muslin from Bengal highly prized in West Asia and Southeast Asia.
  • Indian textiles formed the backbone of both land and maritime trade.
 All major land and maritime routes Indus Valley Civilization; Guptas; Cholas
Gemstones ~2400 BCE - 13th CE Pan-India (regional specialisation)
  • Diamonds from central and southern India (Golconda region).
  • Carnelian beads produced in Gujarat (Lothal, Khambhat).
  • Semi-precious stones widely exported as luxury items.
 Maritime routes and overland Silk Road connections Indus Valley Civilization; Mauryas; regional kingdoms
- Foreign visitors along with their important works (validated) -
Foreign Travelers to Ancient India (6th Century BCE–11th Century CE)
Traveler Time Period Origin Observations and Contributions Key Works Associated Indian Dynasty/Region
Scylax of Caryanda c. 515 BCE Greece (Caryanda)
  • Commissioned by Persian Emperor Darius I to explore the Indus River and map routes to the Arabian Sea.
  • Provided early geographical and navigational information on North-West India.
  • His accounts contributed to Greek knowledge of India, preserved through Herodotus.
 Periplus (lost; cited by Herodotus) North-West India (Achaemenid Persian satrapy)
Megasthenes c. 302–298 BCE Seleucid Empire (Greek)
  • Ambassador of Seleucus I Nicator to Chandragupta Maurya’s court at Pataliputra.
  • Described Mauryan administration, urban planning, agriculture, military, and society.
  • Proposed a seven-fold social division (Greek interpretation, not varna system).
  • Included mythical elements, reducing reliability in parts.
 Indica (lost; fragments preserved by Strabo, Arrian, Diodorus) Mauryan Empire (Magadha)
Deimachus c. 300 BCE Seleucid Empire (Greek)
  • Envoy of Antiochus I to Bindusara’s court.
  • Wrote about Indian geography and society.
  • Later criticized by Strabo for exaggeration.
 Indica (fragmentary) Mauryan Empire (Magadha)
Dionysius c. 2nd Century BCE Ptolemaic Egypt (Greek)
  • Possibly sent as a diplomatic visitor during Hellenistic–Indian contacts.
  • Information survives only indirectly and remains uncertain.
 Unknown (fragmentary references) Mauryan or Post-Mauryan India
Apollonius of Tyana c. 1st Century CE Roman Empire (Greek)
  • Philosopher who visited Taxila.
  • Described Indian ascetics and philosophical traditions.
  • Account recorded later by Philostratus; semi-legendary in nature.
 Life of Apollonius (by Philostratus) Indo-Parthian / Early Kushan region (Punjab)
Faxian (Fa-Hien) c. 399–414 CE China
  • Buddhist monk who visited India during Chandragupta II’s reign.
  • Focused on Buddhist monasteries, scriptures, and practices.
  • Noted social stability and mild governance under the Guptas.
 Fo-Kuo-Ki (A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms) Gupta Empire
Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) c. 629–645 CE China
  • Studied at Nalanda during Harsha’s reign.
  • Provided detailed accounts of administration, economy, caste, and religion.
  • Documented decline of Buddhism in some regions.
 Si-Yu-Ki (Records of the Western Regions) Harsha’s Empire (North India)
Yijing (I-Tsing) c. 671–695 CE China
  • Travelled to India by sea.
  • Studied at Nalanda and documented monastic rules.
  • Provided valuable information on Sanskrit learning and maritime trade.
 A Record of Buddhist Practices Late Guptas / Early Palas
- Important terms (validated) -
Category Term Meaning/Significance
Social & Administrative Agrahara Land or village granted by a king, often to Brahmins, typically tax-exempt to support religious and educational activities.
Amla Revenue official or agent, particularly in medieval administration (including Mughal period), responsible for revenue assessment and collection.
Ayukta Official in Mauryan administration, primarily tasked with revenue collection and local governance.
Brahmadeya Land gifted to Brahmins, similar to Agrahara, often tax-free to support Vedic learning and rituals.
Chaturvarnya The four-fold social division (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) as outlined in Vedic texts.
Devadana Land granted to temples for maintenance and religious activities, common in South Indian kingdoms like Chola.
Eripatti Land in Chola administration reserved for maintaining irrigation tanks, ensuring agricultural productivity.
Gahapati Householder or wealthy peasant, often a landowner in ancient texts, significant in Buddhist and Jain contexts.
Ghatikas Educational institutions or centers of learning in South India, often attached to temples, fostering Vedic and secular studies.
Grama Village, the basic administrative unit in ancient Indian governance.
Gramini Village headmen, responsible for local administration and dispute resolution.
Jajmani System System of economic interdependence between castes in rural areas, based on hereditary service exchange.
Nattar Local notables or elite landholders in Chola Nadu, forming part of village and district assemblies rather than formal revenue officials.
Rajukas Officers appointed by Ashoka to guide social conduct, administer justice, and propagate Dhamma.
Sabhaiyars Members of the Sabha, village assemblies in Chola administration, handling local governance and temple affairs.
Salabhoga Land grant made specifically to Brahmin educational institutions or scholars, especially in South Indian kingdoms.
Samanta Feudal lord or vassal king in post-Gupta and medieval India, owing allegiance to a larger ruler.
Taniyurs Large villages or urban centers in Chola administration, often with autonomous governance.
Ti-shas Minor administrative functionaries mentioned in limited ancient inscriptions; term is obscure and not widely attested.
Ur Village assembly leaders in Chola administration, managing local governance and community affairs.
Political & Administrative Arz-i-Mamalik Minister in charge of the army of the entire kingdom, prominent in later medieval administration.
Bherighosha Sound of war drums, symbolizing Ashoka’s early policy of military conquest, notably in the Kalinga War.
Bhukti A province in the Gupta administrative system, governed by an Uparika.
Dhammaghosha Sound of Dhamma, signifying Ashoka’s shift to cultural conquest through propagation of Buddhist principles.
Gaulmika Military-cum-administrative officer in Satavahana administration, in charge of rural security and local forces.
Janapada Territorial state in the later Vedic period, precursor to Mahajanapadas.
Kottams Larger administrative units in the Chola kingdom, comprising multiple Nadus.
Mahadandanayaka Chief judicial officer in ancient and medieval Indian kingdoms, overseeing justice administration.
Mahajanapada Sixteen powerful kingdoms/republics in 6th century BCE, such as Magadha and Kosala.
Mahamatras & Ayuktas Higher officials in Mauryan administration, responsible for governance and oversight.
Mandala Territorial or political unit; in Arthashastra also refers to a circle of states forming a foreign policy system.
Nadu Districts in Chola administration, comprising multiple villages, managed by Nattar.
Purohita Chief priest or royal advisor, guiding rulers on religious and political matters.
Saulkika and Sulkadhyaksha Tax officers in ancient India, responsible for collecting customs and tolls.
Uparika Provincial governor in Gupta administration, overseeing Bhuktis.
Vimshatipati Officer in charge of 20 villages in Gupta administration, managing local governance.
Vishayapati District officer in Gupta administration, responsible for local revenue and law enforcement.
Vellanvagai Non-Brahmin agricultural land in Chola administration, subject to regular taxation.
Economic Abwab Extra-legal charges or cesses exacted by landlords, often in medieval India.
Amil Revenue official responsible for tax collection in ancient and medieval periods.
Balisadhakas Revenue collectors or officials mentioned in early sources; term is debated and sparsely attested.
Bhaga Royal share of agricultural produce, typically one-sixth, as a form of tax.
Bhandagarika Treasurer in Sakya and Lichchhavi republics, managing state finances.
Bal system Early form of tribute or levy in Vedic society, later evolving into formal taxation.
Dronavapa Unit of land measurement, referring to an area sown with one drona of seed.
Grihapati Independent landowners or householders, often wealthy peasants.
Grāmakapatis Wealthy peasants who controlled village resources and land.
Hiranya Tax paid in cash, often in gold, in ancient Indian kingdoms.
Iskka & Satnama Obscure and unreliable coin terms; not standard in ancient Indian numismatics and unsafe for UPSC.
Kara General tax levy, often on land or produce, in ancient India.
Karsapana Standard unit of silver punch-marked coin in ancient India.
Kshetra Cultivated land, often measured for taxation purposes in ancient India.
Kulika Head of an artisan guild or skilled craft association in ancient India.
Kulyavapa Land measurement unit, larger than Dronavapa, used in ancient agricultural contexts.
Nigama Market town or trading center in ancient India, fostering commerce.
Nivartana Land measurement unit, often used in Gupta inscriptions for tax assessments.
Pana Silver punch-marked coin, widely used in Mauryan and post-Mauryan periods.
Pataka Minor unit of land measurement mentioned in some ancient records; limited administrative importance.
Samaharta Head of tax assessment in Mauryan administration, overseeing revenue collection.
Sanadhata Chief custodian of the treasury and storehouses in Mauryan administration.
Vessa Pali term referring to the Vaishya social group, associated with trade and agriculture.
Vetti Forced labor system in Chola administration, often for public works.
Vishti Forced labor by peasants, common in Gupta period for state projects.
Religious & Philosophical Alvars Vaishnava saint-poets of early medieval South India, known for devotional hymns.
Anvikshiki "Looking at"; logical reasoning or philosophy, emphasized in Arthashastra.
Apabhramsha Later stage of Prakrit language development, used in Jain and secular texts.
Aranyakas "Forest Books"; Vedic texts focused on philosophical and ritualistic interpretations.
Ardha-Magadhi Eastern dialect of Prakrit, used in early Jain texts like the Agamas.
Arhat Enlightened being in Buddhism or Jainism, having attained liberation.
Bodhisattva Enlightened being who delays Nirvana to help others, central to Mahayana Buddhism.
Dharmashastras Texts dealing with religious, social, and legal duties, e.g., Manusmriti.
Nayanars Shaiva saint-poets of early medieval South India, known for Tamil devotional hymns.
Paramitas Perfections or virtues (e.g., generosity, morality) in Mahayana Buddhism for attaining enlightenment.
Sramana Ascetic movements, including Jainism and Buddhism, emphasizing renunciation.
Tirthankara Spiritual teachers in Jainism, e.g., Mahavira, who guide souls to liberation.
Upanishads Philosophical texts forming the core of Vedantic thought, exploring metaphysics.
Vattakirutal Sangam-era Tamil practice of fasting unto death, often by kings or warriors for honor.
Art & Architecture Amphorae Roman pottery; large oval jars with narrow necks, used in Indo-Roman trade.
Antarala Vestibule or antechamber connecting the mandapa and sanctum in a temple.
Ardhamandapa Hall preceding the sanctum in a temple, often used for rituals.
Chaitya A Buddhist apsidal prayer hall containing a stupa, used for congregational worship.
Gandhara Art Greco-Buddhist art style, blending Indian and Hellenistic elements, prominent in Kushan period.
Gopuram Ornate temple gateway tower, characteristic of South Indian Dravidian architecture.
Mandapa Pillared hall in a temple, used for gatherings and rituals.
Mathura Art Indigenous Indian sculpture style, known for Buddhist, Jain, and Hindu icons.
Prasada Palace or temple structure; in architectural context refers to monumental or elevated buildings.
Shikhara Temple spire or tower, typical of North Indian Nagara architecture.
Stambha Pillar, often inscribed, e.g., Ashokan pillars, symbolizing royal authority.
Vimana Tower over the sanctum in South Indian temples, distinct from Shikhara.
Literature & Language Agamas Shaiva, Vaishnava, and Shakta religious texts prescribing temple rituals, theology, and worship practices.
Akam Sangam love poems, focusing on personal and emotional themes in Tamil literature.
Brahmi Ancient Indian script, used in Ashokan edicts and early inscriptions.
Kharosthi Ancient script used in northwest India, especially in Gandhara region.
Mahabharata Epic Hindu text, attributed to Vyasa, narrating the Kurukshetra War.
Pali Language of early Buddhist scriptures, used in Theravada texts.
Prakrit Middle Indo-Aryan languages, used in Jain texts and early dramas.
Puranam War and heroic theme (puram) in Sangam literature, dealing with kingship, battles, and valor.
Ramayana Epic Hindu text, attributed to Valmiki, narrating the life of Rama.
Sangam Assembly of Tamil poets, producing classical Tamil literature (c. 300 BCE–300 CE).
Sataka Literary genre consisting of a collection of one hundred verses, e.g., Bhartrihari’s Shatakatraya.
Tamilakam Ancient Tamil region, encompassing Chola, Chera, and Pandya territories.
Tripitaka Buddhist scriptures, comprising Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma Pitakas.
Vedas Ancient Hindu scriptures (Rig, Yajur, Sama, Atharva), forming the basis of Vedic culture.
- The Importance of Ancient Indian History - Understanding the Foundations of Civilization - Early humans in India transitioned from hunting-gathering to agriculture (Mehrgarh, 7000 BCE), leading to settled life. - The Indus Valley Civilization (Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro) displayed advanced urban planning, drainage, and trade systems. - Agriculture, metalworking, and textile industries formed the economic base of early societies. - Political Unification and State Formation - Ancient rulers sought to unify India under one rule, reinforcing political and cultural integration. - Notable examples: - 3rd Century BCE - Ashoka ruled almost the entire subcontinent, spreading Buddhism and administrative uniformity. - 4th Century CE - Samudragupta expanded rule from North to South India, linking diverse regions. - 7th Century CE - Harshavardhana controlled North India before being challenged by Pulakesin II. - Despite political fragmentation, administrative systems like tax collection and local governance remained similar. - Cultural and Linguistic Integration - Sanskrit and Prakrit shaped early Indian literature, while Tamil flourished in South India. - Brahmi script, first used in Ashoka's inscriptions, evolved into modern Indian scripts. - The Ramayana and Mahabharata created a shared cultural identity across the subcontinent. - Pilgrimage sites (Varanasi, Rameshwaram, Puri) reinforced religious and cultural unity. - Religious and Philosophical Evolution - Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism originated in India, shaping spiritual traditions worldwide. - The concept of Dharma (moral duty) was central to Indian thought and governance. - The Bhakti and Sufi movements later promoted religious harmony and social reform. - Cultural Synthesis and Foreign Influences - India absorbed influences from Greeks, Scythians, Hunas, and Turks, enriching its traditions. - Indo-Greek rulers like Menander adopted Buddhism, contributing to cross-cultural exchange. - The Gandhara and Mathura schools of art reflect Greco-Buddhist artistic fusion. - Science, Technology, and Knowledge Systems - Aryabhata (5th century CE) proposed Earth's rotation and accurately calculated pi. - The concept of zero in mathematics and the decimal system, developed in India, revolutionized mathematics. - Sushruta Samhita documented advanced surgical techniques, including plastic surgery. - The Iron Pillar of Delhi (4th century CE) showcases India's advanced metallurgy. -
