However, the establishment of the Bhikkhuni Sangha came with certain regulations, known as the Eight Garudhammas (heavy rules), which placed nuns in a subordinate position to monks, regardless of seniority. - Liberal and Democratic Nature: - Compared to Brahmanism, Buddhism was more inclusive, accepting people regardless of caste or gender. - Spread of Buddhism in Non-Vedic Regions - Buddhism found fertile ground for conversion in regions outside Vedic influence, particularly in Magadha. - The people of Magadha readily accepted Buddhism because they were looked down upon by orthodox Brahmanas. - Magadha was considered outside Aryavarta (the holy land of Aryas), making its people more open to non-Vedic traditions. - Even today, north Bihar communities prefer not to be cremated south of the Ganga in Magadha, reflecting this ancient tradition. - Buddha's Personality and Preaching Method - Tackling Evil with Goodness: - Buddha promoted non-violence, compassion, and love as responses to hatred and evil. - Calm and Poised Nature: - He remained unprovoked by slander or abuse and tackled his opponents with wit and wisdom. - Example: - When an ignorant person abused him, Buddha listened silently and then asked (anecdote from Akkosa Sutta): - “My son, if a person does not accept a present, what happens to it?” - The person replied, “It remains with the one who offered it.” - Buddha responded, “My son, I do not accept your abuse.” - Use of Pali Language and Organized Religious Order - Use of Pali, the common spoken language, helped spread Buddhist teachings widely among the masses. - Buddha established the Sangha (religious order), which was open to all, irrespective of caste or gender. - Monks had to follow strict rules and regulations, including vows of continence, poverty, and faith. - Royal Patronage and Global Spread - Rapid Expansion During Buddha's Lifetime: - The kingdoms of Magadha, Kosala, and Kausambi, along with several republican states, adopted Buddhism. - Ashoka's Role in the Expansion of Buddhism: - Around 200 years after Buddha's death, Maurya King Ashoka embraced Buddhism, making it a major turning point. - Through his missionaries, Ashoka spread Buddhism to Central Asia, West Asia, and Sri Lanka, transforming it into a world religion. - Buddhism's Continued Influence: - Even though Buddhism later declined in India, it remains strongly rooted in Sri Lanka, Burma, Tibet, China, Japan, and other parts of South, Southeast, and East Asia. - Sects of Buddhism - Hinayana (Lesser Vehicle/The School of the Elders) - Believes Buddha was a teacher, not a god. - Does not accept idol worship. - Follows original Pali texts (Theravada Buddhism). - Spread to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos. - Theravada is the only surviving branch of the Hinayana group. - Mahayana (The Greater Vehicle) - Believes Buddha was divine. - Encourages idol worship. - Emphasizes Bodhisattvas (future Buddhas) like Avalokiteshvara, Manjushri. - Spread to China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam. - Vajrayana (Diamond Vehicle/The Thunderbolt Vehicle) - Tantric Buddhism (Mystical Practices, Mantras, Mandalas, Rituals). - Dalai Lama (Tibetan Buddhism) follows Vajrayana. - Spread to Tibet, Mongolia, Bhutan. - Important Buddhist Literature -

- Causes of the Decline of Buddhism - Transformation into Ritualism and Ceremonialism - Initial Spirit of Reform Lost: - Like many religions, Buddhism began with a reformist zeal but gradually succumbed to the rituals and ceremonies it originally denounced. - Influence of Brahmanism: - Over time, Buddhism absorbed many elements of Brahmanism, the very system it had opposed. - To counter Buddhism, Brahmanas reformed their practices, emphasizing: - Preservation of cattle wealth - Promise of heaven to women and Sudras, making their religion more inclusive. - Shift from Simplicity to Idol Worship: - By the first century A.D., large-scale idol worship became common in Buddhism. - Devotees made rich offerings, which led to increasing materialism among Buddhist monks. - Separation from the Common People - Abandonment of Pali Language: - Initially, Buddhism spread widely using Pali, the language of the common people. - However, monks later adopted Sanskrit, a language of intellectual elites, making Buddhism less accessible. - Monks Isolated from Society: - Buddhist monks withdrew from active engagement in people's daily lives. - The monasteries became self-sufficient and wealthy, reducing monks' interaction with the broader society. - Corruption and Degeneration of Monasteries - Accumulation of Wealth: - Generous royal grants and devotee offerings made Buddhist monasteries extremely wealthy. - Nalanda and other monasteries controlled revenues from hundreds of villages. - Moral Decline: - By the 7th century A.D., monasteries became centers of luxury and corruption, contradicting Buddha's original teachings. - The rise of Vajrayana Buddhism introduced esoteric rituals, including tantric practices. - Perception of Women: - The presence of women in monasteries led to further moral degeneration. - Buddha's warning to Ananda: - “If women were not admitted into monasteries, Buddhism would have lasted for thousands of years. But because they have been admitted, it will last only five hundred years.” - Turkish Invasions and Destruction of Monasteries - Targeting of Buddhist Monasteries: - Due to their immense wealth, Buddhist monasteries became prime targets for Turkish invaders. - Nalanda and other Buddhist centers were attacked, leading to the massacre of monks. - Survival in Neighboring Regions: - Some monks fled to Nepal and Tibet, ensuring Buddhism's survival outside India. - Extinction in India: - By the 12th century A.D., Buddhism had practically disappeared from its land of origin. - Assimilation into Hinduism - Buddha became an incarnation of Vishnu in Hinduism. - Importance and Influence of Buddhism - Social and Economic Impact - Awareness of Social Problems: - Buddhism recognized the growing economic inequalities in 6th century B.C. northeast India, caused by: - Iron ploughshare agriculture - Expansion of trade and coin usage - To address this, Buddhism discouraged accumulation of wealth, believing poverty led to hatred, cruelty, and violence. - The Buddha recommended: - Providing grain to farmers - Wealth to traders - Wages to laborers - The poor were encouraged to give alms to monks, with the promise of wealth in their next life. - Monastic Code and Opposition to Materialism: - The Buddhist code of conduct for monks was a reaction to material excesses. It: - Imposed restrictions on food, dress, and sexual behavior. - Forbade monks from accepting gold and silver or engaging in trade. - These rules were later relaxed, but initially, they resembled primitive communism, reminiscent of early tribal society. - This discipline partially opposed the growing use of money, private property, and luxury in the 6th century B.C. - Contradictions and Strengthening of Social Hierarchy: - While Buddhism sought to mitigate social inequalities, it also reinforced the new social order: - Debtors were barred from joining the Sangha, benefiting moneylenders. - Slaves were not admitted, indirectly supporting slave owners. - These rules reflected Buddhism's adjustment to changing material conditions rather than revolutionary opposition. - Similarities and Differences with Brahmanism - Despite renouncing the world and criticizing Brahmanical greed, Buddhist monks: - Did not participate in production but lived on alms and donations like Brahmanas. - Emphasized family obligations, private property, and political authority. - Supported social class order, though: - Brahmanas justified varna by birth. - Buddhists defined varna by action and attributes. - Buddhism primarily focused on individual salvation (Nirvana), offering an escape for monks but requiring lay followers to conform to existing social conditions. - Inclusivity and Influence on Brahmanical Society - Women and Sudras in Buddhism: - Buddhism provided social upliftment by allowing women and Sudras to convert. - Under Brahmanism, they were denied: - The sacred thread - The right to read the Vedas - Conversion to Buddhism freed them from these marks of inferiority. - Promotion of Non-Violence and Cattle Protection: - Buddhism emphasized non-violence and respect for animal life. - The Suttanipata (early Buddhist text) described cattle as: - Annada vannada sukhada (givers of food, beauty, and happiness). - This teaching opposed the slaughter of animals, influencing later Brahmanical emphasis on cow sanctity. - Intellectual and Cultural Contributions - Rise of Rationalism: - Buddhism encouraged critical thinking, promoting: - Logical reasoning over superstition. - Merit-based judgment rather than blind faith. - Literary Development: - Buddhist scholars significantly enriched Pali literature. - Three categories of early Pali texts: 1. Teachings of the Buddha 2. Rules for the Sangha 3. Philosophical exposition of Dhamma - Apabhramsa writings in East India during the Middle Ages also originated from Buddhist monks. - Growth of Educational Institutions: - Buddhist monasteries evolved into residential universities. - Prominent centers of learning: - Nalanda and Vikramasila (Bihar) - Valabhi (Gujarat) - Impact on Art and Architecture - Sculpture and Artistic Representation: - The first human statues worshipped in India were likely Buddha images. - Stone panels depicting Buddha's life were created at: - Gaya (Bihar) - Sanchi and Bharhut (Madhya Pradesh) - From the 1st century A.D., Buddha's panel images became common. - Fusion of Greek and Indian Art: - Gandhara Art (Northwest India) blended Indian and foreign artistic styles. - Kushan influence promoted Buddhist art in the delta region. - Cave Architecture: - Buddhist monks carved residential caves in: - Barabar Hills (Gaya, Bihar) - Nasik (Western India) - Buddhism left a profound mark on Indian society, culture, education, and art, even though it declined as an organized religion. - Modern Revival of Buddhism - Swami Vivekananda spread Buddhist ideas in the West. - B.R. Ambedkar led the Dalit Buddhist movement (Navayana Buddhism) in 1956. - Unlike Theravāda, Mahāyāna, or Vajrayāna, Navayana is not a classical sect but a reformation movement within Buddhism. - Dalai Lama & Tibetan Buddhism have gained global influence. - Territorial States and the First Magadhan Empire - Rise of Large Territorial States in the Sixth Century B.C - Impact of Iron Technology - The widespread use of iron in eastern Uttar Pradesh and western Bihar facilitated the growth of large territorial states. - Iron weapons strengthened the warrior class, making them a key force in state formation. - Iron agricultural tools allowed peasants to produce surplus food grains, exceeding their own consumption needs. - Role of Surplus Production - The extra produce was collected by princes to: - Support military forces. - Maintain administrative structures. - The surplus also sustained urban centers, which emerged in the sixth century B.C.. - Expansion and Strengthening of Territorial Identity - With increased resources, people expanded their land at the cost of neighboring areas. - The rise of large states with towns as their centers of power reinforced the territorial concept. - Allegiance shifted from the jana (tribe) to the janapada (territory), marking a significant change in political identity. - This transformation played a crucial role in shaping early Indian statehood and governance. - The Mahajanapadas: The Sixteen Great States - Geographical Distribution - During the age of the Buddha, 16 large states, known as mahajanapadas, emerged. - These states were mostly located north of the Vindhyas, extending from the north-west frontier to Bihar. - Among them, Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, and Avanti were the most powerful. - - - 16 Mahajanpadas table -

- Remember through alphabetical sequence - A3 – C1 – G1 – K4 – M3 – P1 – S1 – V2 - Major Mahajanapadas 1. Anga - Located in modern Monghyr and Bhagalpur districts. - Capital: - Champa, inhabited since the sixth century B.C. - Eventually annexed by Magadha. 2. Magadha - Covered Patna, Gaya, and parts of Shahabad. - Became the leading state of its time. 3. Vajji (Wajjis Confederacy) - Located north of the Ganga in Tirhut. - Confederation of eight clans, with the Lichchhavis as the most powerful. - Capital: - Vaisali (modern Basarh, Vaisali district). 4. Kasi - Capital: - Varanasi (earliest habitation at Rajghat, c. 700 B.C.). - Initially powerful but later subjugated by Kosala. 5. Kosala - Encompassed eastern Uttar Pradesh. - Capital: - Sravasti (modern Sahet-Mahet). - Included Ayodhya (not significantly settled before the sixth century B.C.). - Governed the Sakyas of Kapilavastu (Buddha's birthplace, identified with Piprahwa, Basti district). - Neighboring Mallas, whose territory included Kusinara (modern Kasia, Deoria district), where Buddha passed away. 6. Vatsa - Located along the Yamuna, with its capital at Kausambi. - Originally a Kuru clan, they migrated from Hastinapur. - Strongly fortified capital, strategically located near the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna. 7. Kuru and Panchala - Situated in western Uttar Pradesh. - Lost political significance after the Later Vedic period. 8. Avanti - Located in central Malwa and Madhya Pradesh. - Divided into two parts: - North: - Capital Ujjain (eventually the more dominant center). - South: - Capital Mahishamati. - Developed ironworking and strong fortifications. - Political Struggles and Magadha's Supremacy - The period from the sixth century B.C. onward was marked by constant struggles for dominance among these states. - Ultimately, Magadha emerged victorious, laying the foundation for an Indian empire. - Rise and Growth of the Magadhan Empire - Emergence of Magadha - Haryanka Dynasty - Bimbisara (544 B.C. - 492 B.C.) - Magadha rose to prominence under Bimbisara, a contemporary of Gautama Buddha. - He initiated a policy of conquests and expansion, which culminated in the Kalinga war under Ashoka. - Territorial Expansion: - Annexed Anga and placed it under his son Ajatasatru, who governed from Champa. - Strengthened Magadha through marriage alliances: - First wife: - Princess of Kosala (sister of Prasenajit), bringing a revenue-rich Kasi village as dowry. - Second wife: - Chellana, a Lichchhavi princess from Vaisali. - Third wife: - Daughter of the chief of the Madra clan of Punjab. - These alliances enhanced diplomatic prestige and facilitated westward and northward expansion. - Magadha's Rivalry with Avanti - Avanti (Capital: Ujjain) was Magadha's strongest rival. - King Chandra Pradyota Mahasena of Avanti fought Bimbisara but later formed an alliance. - Bimbisara displayed diplomatic acumen: - Sent royal physician Jivaka to treat Pradyota when he was ill. - Received an embassy from Gandhara, showcasing Magadha's growing political influence. - By the 6th century B.C., Bimbisara had established Magadha as the dominant power with control over 80,000 villages (conventional figure). - Strengthening of Magadha's Capital - The earliest capital of Magadha was Rajgir (Girivraja). - It was surrounded by five hills with stone fortifications, making it impregnable. - Ajatasatru's Reign and Expansion (492-460 B.C.) - Ascended the throne by killing his father, Bimbisara. - His rule marked the peak of Haryanka power, with an aggressive expansionist policy. - Major wars - Wars with Kosala - Conflict with Kosala led to prolonged wars. - Eventually, Ajatasatru triumphed, forcing the Kosalan king to: - Give his daughter in marriage to Ajatasatru. - Leave Kasi under Magadhan control. - War Against Vaisali (Lichchhavis) - Despite being of Lichchhavi descent (through his mother), Ajatasatru attacked Vaisali, claiming they had allied with Kosala. - Used diplomatic manipulation to create internal divisions among the Lichchhavis. - Military innovations: - War engine (catapult-like) to hurl stones. - Chariot with a rotating mace, enabling mass killings. - Took 16 years to subjugate Vaisali, expanding Magadha further. - Rivalry with Avanti - Avanti, having defeated the Vatsas of Kausambi, now threatened Magadha. - To counter this, Ajatasatru fortified Rajgir. - However, the invasion never materialized during his reign. - Udayin (460-444 B.C.) and the Shift to Pataliputra - Strategic move: - Built a fort at Pataliputra, located at the confluence of the Ganga and Son rivers. - This centralized location made Pataliputra the power center of Magadha. - The Sisunaga Dynasty and Avanti's Fall - Udayin's successors (Sisunagas) temporarily shifted the capital to Vaisali. - Their greatest achievement was defeating Avanti (Ujjain), ending a 100-year rivalry. - Avanti was absorbed into Magadha, remaining under its control until the Mauryan era. - The Nanda Dynasty (Most Powerful Rulers of Magadha) - The Nandas succeeded the Sisunagas and expanded Magadha further. - Mahapadma Nanda: - Conquered Kalinga, bringing back a Jina idol as a war trophy. - Subjugated Kosala, likely after a rebellion. - Declared himself ekarat (sole sovereign), destroying other ruling princes. - Military Strength - Maintained a massive army: - 200,000 infantry (on foot) - 60,000 cavalry (horse/elephant riding) - 6,000 war elephants - Efficient taxation system funded this large military force. - Alexander's Invasion (326 B.C.): - Nandas' strength deterred Alexander from advancing eastward. - Decline of the Nandas - Later Nanda rulers became weak and unpopular. - Their rule ended with the rise of the Mauryan Empire, under which Magadha reached its peak of glory. - Causes of Magadha's Success - The expansion and dominance of the Magadhan empire in the two centuries preceding the rise of the Mauryas can be attributed to a combination of strategic, geographical, economic, military, and societal factors. - While ambitious rulers such as Bimbisara, Ajatasatru, and Mahapadma Nanda played a crucial role in its growth through conquests and diplomacy, several other factors contributed significantly to Magadha's success. - Geographical and Strategic Advantages - Magadha enjoyed a favorable geographical position in the age of iron. The richest iron deposits were located near Rajgir, enabling the Magadhan rulers to equip their armies with superior iron weapons. - The kingdom's two capitals, Rajgir and Pataliputra, were strategically located: - Rajgir was surrounded by five hills, making it naturally impregnable in an era without advanced siege technology. - Pataliputra occupied a pivotal position at the confluence of the Ganga, Gandak, and Son rivers, facilitating easy communication and movement of troops in all directions. - The natural water barriers of the Son, Ganga, and Punpun rivers made Pataliputra a formidable water-fort (Jaladurga), providing exceptional defense. - Agricultural Prosperity and Economic Strength - Magadha lay at the center of the fertile middle Gangetic plain, where the land was highly productive due to heavy rainfall. - The region produced varieties of paddy, allowing for agricultural surplus, which the rulers could tax to sustain a strong state. - The rise of towns and trade contributed to economic prosperity. The rulers collected tolls from commercial activities, ensuring wealth accumulation to maintain a powerful army. - Military Superiority - Magadha pioneered the large-scale use of elephants in warfare, giving it a strategic advantage over its rivals. Elephants were effective in: - Storming fortresses - Marching through marshy and rugged terrain - Crushing enemy formations - According to Greek sources, the Nandas maintained a massive force of 6,000 elephants, which played a crucial role in their military campaigns. - Political and Administrative Efficiency - The Magadhan rulers employed both fair and ruthless means to expand their kingdom and consolidate power. - The ability to generate significant revenue through taxation and trade allowed them to maintain a large standing army. - The shift of capital from Rajgir to Pataliputra strengthened the state's administrative efficiency and control over expanding territories. - Unorthodox Social Structure - Magadha's population included Kiratas and Magadhas, groups considered low in the Brahmanical hierarchy. However, this racial and cultural admixture led to a society more open to expansionist and unorthodox policies. - The region was relatively newly Aryanized, which made its rulers and people more dynamic and ambitious compared to older, more traditional kingdoms influenced by Vedic orthodoxy. - Rivalry and Competition - The most serious competitor of Magadha was Avanti, with its capital at Ujjain. Avanti also had access to iron ore in eastern Madhya Pradesh, allowing it to forge high-quality weapons. - However, Magadha eventually defeated Avanti after a century-long struggle, solidifying its dominance in northern India. - Conclusion - The combination of geographical advantages, economic strength, military innovation, political ambition, and a flexible social structure enabled Magadha to defeat rival kingdoms and establish the first great empire in Indian history. - These factors laid the foundation for the eventual rise of the Maurya dynasty, under which Magadha reached its peak. - Iranian and Macedonian Invasions - Iranian Invasion of North-West India - While north-east India saw the gradual expansion of the Magadhan empire, the situation in north-west India during the first half of the sixth century B.C. was markedly different. - Political Disunity in North-West India - The region was fragmented, with small principalities such as: - Kambojas - Gandharas - Madras - These states frequently fought among themselves, lacking a strong kingdom like Magadha to unite them. - Moreover, the region was prosperous and easily accessible via the Hindu Kush passes, making it vulnerable to external invasions. - Iranian Expansion into India - Around 516 B.C., the Achaemenian ruler Darius I took advantage of this political disunity and invaded north-west India. - He annexed Punjab (west of the Indus) and Sindh, incorporating them into the Iranian empire as its twentieth satrapy (province). - This satrapy included: - Sindh - North-west frontier - Part of Punjab west of the Indus - Economic and Military Significance of the Indian Satrapy - This Indian province was the most fertile and populous in the Achaemenian empire. - It paid 360 talents (A talent was a significant measure of weight, roughly 26-30 kg (57-66 lbs) of gold) of gold in annual tribute, contributing one-third of Iran's total revenue from its Asian provinces. - Indian soldiers were also recruited into the Iranian army. - Xerxes, the successor of Darius, deployed Indian troops in his prolonged war against the Greeks. - Continued Iranian Rule Until Alexander's Invasion - Iranian control over north-west India continued for nearly two centuries. - India remained a part of the Achaemenian empire until Alexander the Great's invasion in the fourth century B.C. - Results of Indo-Iranian Contact - The Indo-Iranian interaction lasted for approximately 200 years, significantly influencing trade, culture, and administration in India. - Economic Impact: Trade and Commerce - The contact fostered Indo-Iranian trade, as evidenced by the presence of Iranian coins in the north-west frontier region. - However, the continuation of punch-marked coins in India was not a direct result of Iranian influence. - Cultural Influence: Writing System - One of the most notable influences was the introduction of the Kharosthi script by Iranian scribes. - Characteristics of the Kharosthi script: - Written from right to left, similar to Arabic. - Used in Ashokan inscriptions in north-west India during the third century B.C. - Continued to be in use until the third century A.D. - Artistic Influence: Mauryan Sculpture - The monuments of Ashoka's time, particularly the ball-shaped capitals, were inspired by Iranian models. - In architecture, the capital is the topmost member of a column, mediating between the column and the load it supports. - - Administrative and Linguistic Influence - Iranian influence is evident in the preamble of Ashoka's edicts and the use of certain words. - Example: - The Iranian term “dipi” (meaning inscription) was replaced by “lipi” in Ashokan inscriptions. - Indirect Influence: Greek Interest in India - Through the Iranians, the Greeks became aware of India's vast wealth. - This knowledge aroused Greek interest, eventually leading to Alexander's invasion of India. - Alexander's Invasion of India - Background: Greek-Iranian Conflict - In the fourth century B.C., the Greeks and Iranians fought for world supremacy. - Under Alexander of Macedonia, the Greeks defeated the Iranians, conquering Asia Minor, Iraq, and Iran. - Defeating the Persian Empire (the biggest power of that time) is one of the main reasons why Alexander the Great is praised so much - Achaemenid Persian Empire was one of the largest and most powerful empires of the ancient world. A relatively small kingdom (Macedonia) defeated a superpower. - He died as an undefeated ruler - - - From Iran, Alexander marched to India, attracted by its great wealth. - Greek historians like Herodotus described India as a fabulous land, further tempting Alexander. - His invasion was also driven by: - Geographical curiosity, as he believed the eastern side of India was connected to the Caspian Sea. - Aspirations to surpass mythical conquerors. - Political Condition of North-West India - The region was divided into independent monarchies and tribal republics. - These rulers were deeply connected to their land but failed to unite against a common enemy. - Two prominent rulers: - Ambhi (Prince of Taxila) - submitted to Alexander. - Ambhi of Taxila readily surrendered, providing troops and treasure. - Porus (Kingdom between Jhelum & Chenab) - resisted him. - Porus resisted at the Battle of Jhelum - though defeated, his bravery impressed Alexander, who restored his kingdom and made him an ally. - The Khyber Pass remained unguarded, making invasion easier. - Alexander's Campaign in India (326-325 B.C.) - After conquering Iran, Alexander moved to Kabul and then entered India through the Khyber Pass. Took five months to reach the Indus. - Advanced up to the Beas River, but could not proceed further. - Halt at the Beas River - Alexander wanted to march eastward, but his army refused due to: - War-weariness and homesickness after ten years of campaigning. - The hot Indian climate and disease outbreaks. - Fierce resistance from Indian forces along the Indus. - Reports of Magadha's Nanda dynasty, whose massive army greatly outnumbered Alexander's forces. - Despite repeated appeals, his soldiers refused to continue. - Alexander lamented: - “I am trying to rouse (To wake up or awaken someone) the hearts that are disloyal and crushed with craven (Completely lacking courage; cowardly) fears.” - Forced to retreat, his dream of an eastern empire remained unfulfilled. - Return and Aftermath - On his return, Alexander defeated several small republics along the way. - He stayed in India for 19 months (326-325 B.C.), mostly engaged in fighting. - He had little time to organize his conquests but made some administrative arrangements: - Most conquered states were restored to their rulers who accepted his authority. - His own territorial possessions were divided into three provinces, each under a Greek governor. - He founded several cities to maintain Greek influence. - Alexandria (Egypt) - The most famous city, founded in 331 BCE. - Became a major center of learning, trade, and culture. - Home to the Great Library of Alexandria and the Lighthouse of Alexandria (one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World). - Alexandria Arachosia (Afghanistan) - Modern-day Kandahar. - A key administrative and military base in the eastern part of Alexander's empire. - Alexandria Eschate ("The Furthest") (Tajikistan) - Located in present-day Khojand (Tajikistan). - Marked the easternmost expansion of Alexander's conquests. - Alexandria Bucephalous (Pakistan) - Founded in honor of Bucephalus, Alexander's beloved horse, after it died following the Battle of the Hydaspes (326 BCE). - Likely near modern Jhelum in Pakistan. - Alexandria on the Indus (Pakistan) - Founded near modern-day Uch, Pakistan. - Served as a key military and trade center on the Indus River. - Alexandria Margiana (Turkmenistan) - Modern Merv, Turkmenistan. - Built as a defensive settlement on the empire's northeastern frontier. - Alexandria in the Caucasus (Afghanistan) - Modern Begram, Afghanistan. - Became a major trade hub connecting Central Asia with India. - Effects of Alexander's Invasion - First Contact Between Ancient India and Europe - Alexander's invasion marked the first direct contact between ancient India and Europe. - His campaign was a triumphant success, adding an Indian province to his empire, larger than the territory conquered by Iran. - However, the Greek hold on India was short-lived, as the Mauryas soon took over. - Indo-Greek Interaction and Trade - The most significant result of Alexander's invasion was the direct Indo-Greek connection in multiple fields. - His campaign opened four major routes by land and sea, facilitating trade and movement of Greek merchants and craftsmen. - Greek Settlements in India - Even before Alexander's invasion, some Greeks lived in north-west India. - After the invasion, more Greek settlements were established, including: - Alexandria in the Kabul region - Boukephala on the Jhelum - Alexandria in Sindh - Although these areas later came under the Mauryas, Greek settlers continued to live under Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka. - Geographical Contributions - Alexander was deeply interested in geography and explored the Indian Ocean at the mouth of the Indus. - He sent his friend Nearchus with a fleet to explore the coastline from the Indus to the Euphrates, searching for harbors. - His historians provided valuable geographical records, helping establish a chronology of Indian events. - Observations on Indian Society and Economy - Greek historians recorded important social and economic details, including: - The sati system, where widows self-immolated on their husband's pyre. - The sale of girls in marketplaces by poor parents. - The fine breed of oxen in north-west India, leading Alexander to send 200,000 oxen to Macedonia. - The flourishing carpentry industry, with carpenters specializing in chariots, boats, and ships. - Political Impact: Rise of the Maurya Empire - Alexander's invasion weakened the power of petty states in north-west India, creating a power vacuum. - This facilitated the expansion of the Maurya empire. - Chandragupta Maurya is believed to have observed Alexander's military tactics, which later helped him overthrow the Nanda dynasty and establish the Maurya empire. - State and Varna Society in the Age of the Buddha - Material Life in North India (c. 6th Century B.C.) - The material life of North India, particularly in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, can be reconstructed using Pali texts, Sanskrit Sutra literature, and archaeological evidence. - The sixth century B.C. marks the beginning of the Northern Black Polished Ware (NBP) phase, characterized by a glossy, fine-quality pottery used as tableware for the wealthy. - - This period also saw the introduction of iron implements for agriculture and crafts, the emergence of metallic money, and the use of burnt bricks and ring wells, which appeared in the mid-NBP phase (c. 3rd century B.C.). - Urbanization and Settlements - The NBP phase marked India's second urbanization, as the first urban phase (Harappan civilization) had disappeared by c. 1500 B.C., leaving a gap of about 1,000 years without towns. - By the 6th century B.C., new towns emerged in the middle Gangetic basin. - Many towns mentioned in Pali and Sanskrit texts, such as Kausambi, Sravasti, Ayodhya, Kapilavastu, Varanasi, Vaisali, Rajgir, Pataliputra, and Champa, have been excavated and show habitation signs from the NBP phase. - Wooden palisades in Patna, possibly from Maurya or pre-Maurya times, suggest fortifications in some towns. - Buildings were mostly made of mud-brick and wood, though Pali texts mention seven-storied palaces, which have not been found. - Excavated structures appear unimpressive, but the material remains indicate a significant population increase compared to the earlier Painted Grey Ware settlements. - Artisans, Merchants, and Guilds - Many towns began as seats of government but evolved into market centers inhabited by artisans and merchants. - Specialization in crafts developed due to guild systems and localization: - Saddalaputta at Vaisali had 500 potters' shops. - 18 artisan guilds are mentioned, with specific references to smiths, carpenters, leather workers, and painters. - Merchants lived in designated streets, such as “vessa” (merchants' streets) in Varanasi and ivory workers' streets. - Craftsmanship was hereditary, with sons learning their family trade. - Trade and Transport - Craft products, including fine textiles, ivory objects, and pottery, were transported over long distances. - Large-scale trade is indicated by frequent references to 500 cartloads of goods. - All major cities were located on riverbanks and trade routes, interconnected as follows: - Sravasti linked to Kausambi and Varanasi. - Traders traveled from Kosala and Magadha via Mathura to Taxila. - Routes extended from Mathura to Ujjain and the Gujarat coast. - Eastern routes went from Sravasti through Kapilavastu, Kusinara, Vaisali, and Patna to Rajgir and Champa (near modern Bhagalpur). - Currency and Economic Transactions - The terms “iskka” and “satamana” in Vedic texts likely refer to early coins, though actual coins date only from the 6th century B.C.. - Before coins, barter and cattle were common exchange mediums. - The earliest metallic coins, appearing in Gautama Buddha's time, were mostly silver, with some copper. - These were punch-marked coins, featuring symbols like hills, trees, fish, bulls, elephants, and crescents. - The first hoards of these coins have been found in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Magadha, with some early coins also found in Taxila. - The Pali texts show extensive monetary usage, with wages and prices being paid in coins, and even the price of a dead mouse being estimated in money. - Role of Writing - Writing likely began before Ashoka (3rd century B.C.). - The earliest records, possibly written on perishable materials, have not survived. - Writing facilitated: - Trade documentation and bookkeeping. - Tax collection and military administration. - Compilation of laws and rituals. - Development of measurement texts like Sulvasutras, aiding in land demarcation. - Rural Settlements and Agriculture - Though rural settlements from the NBP phase remain largely unexcavated, a strong rural base was essential for urbanization. - Cities relied on peasants' taxes, tributes, and agricultural produce. - Peasants purchased iron tools such as axes, adzes, knives, razors, nails, and sickles, found in early layers at Kausambi. - Pali texts mention three types of villages: - Typical villages, inhabited by various castes and communities, led by a bhojaka (village headman). - Craft villages, such as a carpenters' village near Varanasi, which served as market hubs. - Border villages, located at the edge of forests, mainly inhabited by fowlers and hunters. - Land was divided into family-allotted plots, cultivated with family labor and hired agricultural workers. - Fields were fenced, and irrigation channels were dug collectively under the supervision of the village headman. - Peasants paid one-sixth of their produce as tax, collected directly by royal agents, with no intermediate landlords. - Some villages were granted to Brahmanas and merchants. - Large plots were worked by slaves and agricultural laborers. - Wealthy peasants, called grāmakapatis, were similar to Vaishyas. - Crops and Agricultural Advancements - Rice was the staple (A basic or essential item) crop in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. - Various types of paddy (rice in its husk before processing) and paddy fields are described in Pali texts. - Large-scale paddy transplantation began in the age of Buddha, significantly increasing yields. - Other crops included barley, pulses, millet, cotton, and sugarcane. - Agricultural progress was driven by iron ploughshares and fertile alluvial soil between Allahabad and Rajmahal. - Technological Advancements and Resource Utilization - Iron played a key role in clearing forests and expanding cultivation. - Iron tools were hardened for greater durability. - Tools from Rajghat (Varanasi) indicate the use of iron ore from Singhbhum and Mayurbhanj. - Iron supplies boosted crafts and agriculture, supporting economic growth. - Economic Transformation - The economic landscape of this period contrasts sharply with earlier Vedic rural economies in western Uttar Pradesh and chalcolithic economies in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. - A fully developed food-producing economy emerged in the middle Gangetic basin, supporting non-agricultural populations. - This economic surplus enabled long-term taxation, standing armies, and the rise of large territorial states. - Conclusion - The material culture of 6th century B.C. North India was marked by rapid urbanization, economic expansion, and technological progress. - The interplay between agriculture, trade, currency, and governance laid the foundation for the emergence of large kingdoms and a complex socio-economic structure. - This period saw the transformation of the middle Gangetic basin into a thriving center of urban life, commerce, and state formation. - Administrative System - Rise of Kosala and Magadha - During this period, many states existed, but only Kosala and Magadha emerged as powerful. - Both were ruled by hereditary monarchs belonging to the Kshatriya varna. - The Jatakas mention that oppressive kings and chief priests were sometimes expelled by the people, but such events were rare. - The king held the highest official status and enjoyed special protection of his person and property. - Only great religious leaders, like the Buddha, could challenge the king's authority. - The king was primarily a warlord, leading his kingdom to victory, as seen in the careers of Bimbisara and Ajatasatru. - Role of Officials - The king ruled with the help of various officials, both high and low. - Higher officials were called mahamatras and performed various functions, including: - Mantrin (minister) - Senanayaka (commander) - Judge - Chief accountant - Head of the royal harem - A separate class of officers called ayuktas may have performed similar functions in some states. - Administration and Ministers - The king's administration relied on capable ministers. - Varsakara of Magadha weakened the Lichchhavis of Vaisali, helping Ajatasatru conquer the republic. - Dirghacharayana of Kosala supported the king of Kosala. - Most high-ranking officials and ministers were recruited from the Brahmana class, but they were not from the king's own clan. - Revenue and Payment System - In Kosala and Magadha, despite the circulation of punch-marked silver coins, influential brahmanas and sethis were paid through village revenue grants. - Unlike in later Vedic times, the king did not need clan approval to grant revenue rights. - However, these grants only provided revenue—they did not include administrative authority. - Village Administration - The village headman managed rural administration. - Originally, headmen led tribal regiments and were called gramini (leader of a grama or tribal military unit). - As agriculture and plough cultivation became common, the gramini evolved into a village headman in pre-Mauryan times. - They were known by different titles: - Gramabhojaka - Gramini - Gramika - King Bimbisara is said to have summoned 86,000 gramikas, showing their importance and direct links to the king. - Duties of Village Headmen - The village headmen were responsible for: - Assessing and collecting taxes from villagers - Maintaining law and order in the locality - Sometimes, oppressive headmen were punished by the villagers. - Army and Taxation - Expansion of the Army - The real increase in state power is seen in the formation of a large professional army. - At the time of Alexander's invasion, the Nanda ruler of Magadha maintained: - 20,000 cavalry - 200,000 infantry - 2,000 horse-chariots - 4,000 elephants - Chariots were losing importance in both northeast and northwest India, where they had been introduced by the Aryans. - Rulers in northwest India had fewer elephants than the Magadhan kings but maintained a comparable number of horses. - The possession of numerous elephants gave Magadhan princes a military advantage. - State Revenue and Taxation - Maintaining a large, long-service army required significant state resources. - The Nandas were known for their enormous wealth, which likely helped sustain their army. - However, there is no clear record of how they raised taxes from the people. - Taxation System - A firm fiscal system was established, where: - Kshatriyas (warriors) and Brahmanas (priests) were exempt from taxation. - The tax burden fell on the peasants (mainly Vaishyas or Grihapatis). - The Bal system, which was originally a voluntary payment by tribesmen in Vedic times, became a compulsory tax under the king. - Balisadhakas (tax officers) were appointed to collect this tax. - The king collected one-sixth of the produce as tax from peasants. - Tax Collection and Payment - Taxes were assessed and collected by royal agents with the help of village headmen. - The advent of writing may have helped improve the tax system. - Payments were made in both cash and kind (refers to goods or services rather than money): - Punch-marked coins suggest tax payments in cash. - In northeastern India, payments were often made in paddy. - Peasants were also subjected to forced labor for royal projects. - The birth stories of the Buddha mention peasants fleeing their kingdom to escape excessive taxation. - Taxes on Artisans and Traders - Artisans had to work one day per month for the king. - Traders paid customs duties on the sale of their goods. - Tolls were collected by officers known as saulkika ( remember like Sulka(toll) + ika (Adhikari)) or sulkadhyaksha ((Sulka(toll)) + Adhyaksha(Supervisor)). - Decline of Popular Assemblies - The sabha and samiti were no longer summoned by kings, leading to the decline of popular assemblies in post-Vedic times. - These assemblies were originally tribal institutions, but as tribes dissolved into varna and caste groups, they lost their significance. - In small kingdoms, assemblies may have functioned effectively in the Vedic period. - However, in large states like Kosala and Magadha, holding big assemblies became impractical. - Reasons for their decline: - Difficulty in communication across large states. - Integration of non-Vedic people who did not fit into the old tribal system. - Rise of the Parishad and Republican Assemblies - Instead of large assemblies, a small council called Parishad, consisting exclusively of Brahmanas, emerged. - However, assemblies continued to flourish in smaller republican states like: - Sakyas - Lichchhavis - The Republican Experiment - Geographical Presence and Origins - The republican system of government existed primarily in: - The Indus basin - The Indus basin republics may have been remnants of Vedic tribes, though some may have evolved from earlier monarchies. - The foothills of the Himalayas in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar - In Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, the republican system might have been influenced by old tribal ideals of equality, which did not grant much prominence to the raja. - Structure of Republican Governance - Real power in these republics lay with tribal oligarchies (Power is concentrated in the hands of a small group) rather than a single ruler. - Composition of the Ruling Class - In the republics of the Sakyas and Lichchhavis, the ruling class belonged to the same clan and varna. - In Vaisali, the Lichchhavis had 7707 rajas in the assembly, but brahmanas were not included. - In post-Maurya republics like the Malavas and Kshudrakas, both kshatriyas and brahmanas were granted citizenship, but slaves and hired laborers were excluded. - In one state on the Beas River in Punjab, membership was restricted to those who could supply at least one elephant to the state—making it a typical oligarchy in the Indus basin. - Administrative Machinery - The administrative system in the Sakya and Lichchhavi republics was simple and included: - Raja (Chief) - Uparaja (Vice-King) - Senapati (Commander) - Bhandagarika (Treasurer) - The Lichchhavis reportedly had seven courts to try the same case one after another, though this might be an exaggeration. - Unlike monarchies, certain states in the Buddha's time were ruled by leaders responsible to assemblies, rather than by hereditary kings. - Thus, while political power was not shared equally, the republican tradition in India dates back at least to the age of the Buddha. - Differences Between Republics and Monarchies - Revenue and Administration - In monarchies, the king alone claimed all revenue from the peasants. - In republics, every tribal oligarch (raja) had a share of the revenue. - Among the Lichchhavis, each of the 7707 rajas maintained his own storehouse and administration. - Military Organization - Monarchies maintained a regular standing army and did not allow any private military forces within their territory. - In republics, each raja had his own small army under his senapati, leading to competition among them. - Role of the Brahmanas - In monarchies, brahmanas held significant influence. - In republics, they were excluded from governance, and law-books did not recognize these states. - Governance Model - Monarchies functioned under a single ruler. - Republics operated through oligarchic assemblies rather than individual leadership. - Decline of the Republican Tradition - The republican tradition weakened after the Maurya period. - Even before the Mauryas, monarchies were stronger and more widespread. - Ancient thinkers saw kingship as the most common and stable form of government. - Buddhist Explanation of Kingship's Origin - The Digha Nikaya (an early Buddhist Pali text) describes the origins of kingship: - In the earliest times, humans lived harmoniously. - With the emergence of private property, conflicts arose over land and women. - To resolve disputes, people elected a chief responsible for law and order. - In exchange for protection, they offered him a portion of their paddy. - This elected chief became the king, marking the birth of kingship and the state. - Social Orders and Legislation - Origins of the Legal and Judicial System - The Indian legal and judicial system originated during this period. - Previously, society was governed by tribal law, which did not recognize class distinctions. - Over time, the tribal community became clearly divided into four varnas: - Brahmanas (priests and teachers) - Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors) - Vaisyas (peasants and taxpayers) - Sudras (laborers serving the other three classes) - The Dharmasutras formalized the duties of each varna, and both civil and criminal laws were based on varna divisions. - Discrimination Against the Sudras - The higher the varna, the purer it was considered, and the higher the moral conduct expected. - Sudras suffered severe social and legal discrimination: - Denied religious and legal rights - Excluded from upanayana (sacred thread ceremony) - Severely punished for crimes against higher varnas, while crimes against them were punished lightly - Shunned by higher varnas, their food was avoided, and intermarriage was prohibited - Denied high positions and expected to work as slaves, artisans, or agricultural laborers - Even Buddhism and Jainism did not significantly improve the status of the Sudras. - Though they were admitted into new religious orders, their overall social position remained low. - Gautama Buddha visited assemblies of brahmanas, kshatriyas, and grihapatis (householders), but there is no mention of an assembly of sudras. - Administration of Civil and Criminal Law - Royal agents administered law and imposed harsh punishments, including: - Scourging (to whip, punish, or cause great suffering) - Beheading - Tearing out the tongue - Criminal punishments often followed the principle of revenge (“tooth for tooth, eye for eye”). - Integration of Non-Vedic Tribes - Although brahmanical law-books framed laws based on varna hierarchy, they also accommodated the customs of non-Vedic tribal groups. - Many indigenous tribes were gradually absorbed into the brahmanical social order. - Some were assigned fictitious social origins, while others were allowed to follow their own customs. - Economic and Political Developments - The age of the Buddha was crucial in shaping Indian polity, economy, and society: - Agriculture flourished, particularly in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, due to the use of iron tools in alluvial areas. - Food production increased, allowing for tax collection from peasants. - Large states emerged, funded by regular taxes and tributes. - To maintain social order, the varna system was institutionalized, clearly defining the roles of each class: - Kshatriyas - rulers and warriors - Brahmanas - priests and teachers - Vaisyas - peasants and taxpayers - Sudras - laborers serving all three classes - The Age of the Mauryas - Chandragupta Maurya and the Foundation of the Maurya Dynasty - Origins and Rise to Power - Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya dynasty, but his origins remain debated: - Brahmanical tradition states he was born to Mura, a Sudra woman in the Nanda court. - Earlier Buddhist tradition identifies him as a Kshatriya from the Maurya clan in Gorakhpur, near the Nepalese Terai. - Taking advantage of the weakness and unpopularity of the Nanda dynasty, he overthrew them with the help of Chanakya (Kautilya) and established Mauryan rule. - Conquests and Expansion - Greek writer Justin claims Chandragupta overran the whole of India with an army of 600,000 soldiers—though this is uncertain. - He successfully defeated Seleucus I Nicator, the Greek viceroy ruling west of the Indus. - Following a peace treaty, Chandragupta: - Gained control over eastern Afghanistan, Baluchistan, and the Indus region. - Gave 500 war elephants to Seleucus in return. - Extent of the Mauryan Empire - Chandragupta built a vast empire covering: - Bihar, Orissa, Bengal - Western and north-western India - The Deccan - The Mauryan Empire excluded: - Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and parts of north-eastern India. - In the north-west, the Mauryas controlled territories beyond those held by the British Empire centuries later. - Imperial Organization Under Chandragupta Maurya - Sources of Information - The Mauryan administration was highly elaborate, as described by: - Megasthenes, a Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus to Chandragupta Maurya's court. - Lived in Pataliputra and wrote about its administration and that of the empire. - His original account is lost, but fragments appear in later Greek writings, compiled into a book. - Kautilya's Arthashastra, though compiled later, contains authentic information on Mauryan governance and economy. - Centralized Monarchy - Chandragupta Maurya was an autocrat, holding absolute power. - Arthashastra states that his happiness lay in the happiness of his subjects, though it is unclear how closely he followed this ideal. - Megasthenes mentions a royal council advising the king, but its role was not binding. High-ranking officers were chosen from among these councillors. - Provincial and Urban Administration - The empire was divided into provinces, each governed by a prince from the royal family. - Provinces were further subdivided into smaller administrative units. - Major Mauryan cities included Pataliputra, Kausambi, Ujjain, and Taxila. - Pataliputra's administration was handled by six committees of five members each, responsible for: - Sanitation - Care of foreigners - Birth and death registration - Regulation of weights and measures - Other civic functions - Central Government and Economic Control - The central government maintained two dozen departments, regulating social and economic activities, particularly near the capital. - The state controlled major economic activities to ensure financial stability: - New land was cultivated using peasants and Sudra laborers. - Taxes on peasants ranged from one-fourth to one-sixth of the produce. - Irrigation fees were collected from those using state-provided water. - Emergency crop production was imposed when necessary. - Tolls were levied on goods entering towns. - The state had monopolies on mining, liquor sales, and weapon manufacturing. - Mauryan Military Strength - The Mauryas maintained a vast military, as recorded by Pliny and Megasthenes: - 600,000 foot soldiers - 30,000 cavalry - 9,000 elephants - 8,000 chariots (mentioned in another source) - A possible navy - Military administration was managed by a board of 30 officers, divided into six committees (five members each), overseeing: - Infantry - Cavalry - Elephants - Chariots - Navy - Transport - The Mauryan military was nearly three times larger than the Nanda army, owing to a larger empire and greater resources. - Conclusion - Chandragupta established an efficient administrative system with a strong financial base. - The combination of a centralized monarchy, provincial governance, economic control, and military strength enabled the Mauryan Empire to flourish and expand. - Bindusara (c. 297-273 BCE) - Son of Chandragupta - Expanded the empire towards Deccan (South India). - Known as "Amitraghata" (Slayer of Enemies). - Maintained relations with Greek rulers like Antiochus I. - Asoka (273-232 B.C.) - Accession to the Throne - Chandragupta Maurya was succeeded by his son Bindusara, who maintained relations with Greek princes. - Asoka, Bindusara's son, is considered the greatest Mauryan ruler. - Buddhist tradition portrays him as cruel in his early years, claiming he killed 99 brothers to seize the throne. - However, this statement is legendary and lacks historical credibility. - His biography, written by Buddhist scholars, contains fictional elements and cannot be taken literally. - Asokan Edicts (official orders, proclamations, or decrees issued by an authority): A Historical Source - Nature and Distribution - Asoka was the first Indian king to communicate directly with the people through inscriptions. - His edicts were engraved on: - Rocks - Polished stone pillars (mounted with capitals) - Caves - Found across the Indian subcontinent, as well as in Kandahar, Afghanistan. - Composition and Language - Asoka issued 44 royal orders, each with multiple copies. - The inscriptions were written in different languages and scripts: - Prakrit language and Brahmi script (majority of the empire). - Kharosthi script (north-western region). - Aramaic and Greek (Kandahar region). - Significance - Placed along ancient highways, making them accessible to the public. - Provide valuable insights into: - Asoka's policies (both external and domestic). - His governance style and moral teachings. - The extent of his empire and its administration. - Impact of the Kalinga War - The Turning Point in Asoka's Rule - After ascending the throne, Asoka fought only one major war—the Kalinga War. - According to his 13th Major Rock Edict, the war resulted in: - 100,000 people killed - 150,000 taken as prisoners - Many more perished due to war-related suffering. - The war deeply affected Asoka, causing him grief (Deep sorrow, especially due to loss) and remorse (a deep feeling of regret or guilt for a wrong committed), particularly due to the suffering of Brahmin priests and Buddhist monks. - As a result, he abandoned physical conquest (bherighosha) and adopted a policy of cultural conquest (dhammaghosha). - Asoka's Own Words (13th Major Rock Edict) - In his edicts, Asoka expresses deep remorse over the war: - “On conquering Kalinga, the Beloved of the Gods felt remorse, for when an independent country is conquered, the slaughter, death, and deportation of the people is extremely grievous… The Beloved of the Gods considers victory by Dhamma to be the foremost victory.” - Shift to Dhamma and Foreign Policy - Asoka now focused on ideological expansion, urging: - Tribal peoples and frontier kingdoms to see him as a father and obey him with confidence. - His officials to propagate the principles of dhamma across the empire. - He no longer considered foreign conquests legitimate but instead sought to influence other regions ideologically. - His foreign policy involved: - Sending ambassadors of peace to Greek kingdoms in Western Asia and Greece. - Undertaking welfare measures for people and animals in foreign lands—a unique initiative for that era. - According to Buddhist tradition, sending Buddhist missionaries to Sri Lanka and Central Asia to spread dhamma. - Pragmatism (a philosophy or approach that emphasizes practicality, real-world results, and problem-solving over abstract theories or ideals) in Governance - Despite his transformation, Asoka was not an extreme pacifist (someone who believes in peace and opposes war or violence): - He retained Kalinga after its conquest and integrated it into the Maurya Empire. - There is no evidence that he disbanded the massive army inherited from Chandragupta Maurya. - While urging tribal people to follow dharma, he also threatened action against those who violated social order. - Administrative Reforms Under Dhamma - Within the empire, Asoka introduced officers called rajukas, who had the power to: - Reward people for good conduct. - Punish them if necessary to maintain order. - His policy of consolidation (the act of strengthening, uniting, or making something more stable and effective) through dhamma had practical success: - The Kandahar inscription suggests that hunters and fishermen abandoned their traditional killing practices, possibly adopting settled agricultural life. - Internal Policy and Buddhism - Asoka's Conversion to Buddhism - Asoka was converted to Buddhism after the Kalinga War. - According to tradition: - He became a monk and undertook pilgrimages (dharma yatras) to Buddhist shrines. - He made huge donations to the Buddhist community. - Buddhist Council and Missionary Work - A Buddhist council was held under the chairmanship of Asoka's brother. - Missionaries were sent to: - South India - Sri Lanka - Burma - Other countries to spread Buddhism - Rummindei Pillar Inscription of Asoka - The inscription is in Brahmi script and written in Prakrit language. - It marks the birthplace of Buddha (Lumbini) and states: - “When King Devanampriya Priyadarsin had been anointed ( to be chosen, blessed, or consecrated for a special role, often in a religious or ceremonial context) for twenty years, he came himself and worshiped (this spot), because the Buddha Sakyamuni was born here. (He) both caused to be made a stone bearing wall and caused a stone pillar to be set up (in order to show) that the Blessed One was born here. The village of Lumbini was exempted from bali (tribute), and bhaga (the royal share of the produce) was reduced to one-eighth.” - - Governance and Administration - Asoka followed the ideal of paternal kingship, repeatedly reminding his officials that he considered his subjects as his children. - His officials (rajukas and dharmamahamatras) were instructed to: - Propagate dhamma among various social groups, including women. - Administer justice fairly. - Ensure the welfare of the people as representatives of the king. - Social and Religious Policies - Rituals and Animal Protection: - He disapproved of rituals, especially those performed by women. - He forbade the killing of certain birds and animals. - He completely prohibited animal slaughter in the capital. - He interdicted (to prohibit, forbid, or restrict something, often by legal or authoritative order) excessive social revelries (lively and noisy celebrations, often involving drinking, dancing, and festivity). - Broad Religious Outlook: - Asoka's dharma was not sectarian (strong loyalty to a particular group, especially in religion or politics); it aimed at preserving the social order. - It emphasized: - Obedience to parents. - Respect for Brahmanas and Buddhist monks. - Compassion towards slaves and servants. - These values were common to both Buddhism and Brahmanism. - Asoka's Teachings and Social Order - Asoka emphasized living in harmony: - Compassion towards animals. - Proper behavior towards relatives. - Strengthening the family institution and social classes. - His teachings focused on moral and ethical living rather than religious conversion. - Unlike Buddhist teachings, he never spoke about nirvana—instead, he stated that good behavior would lead to heaven. - His policies aimed at tolerance and maintaining social order, rather than promoting a sectarian faith. - Asoka's Place in History - - Asoka's Achievements - Asoka is regarded as one of the greatest missionary (a person who is sent to spread religious beliefs, provide humanitarian aid, or promote a cause, usually in foreign lands) rulers in ancient history. - His zeal (great enthusiasm, passion, or dedication toward a cause, goal, or belief) and devotion helped him achieve significant success both domestically and internationally. - Contrary to the belief that his pacific policies weakened the Maurya Empire, his reign saw remarkable accomplishments. - Political and Cultural Unification - Asoka politically unified India, strengthening it further through: - One dharma (ethical code). - One language (Prakrit in most regions). - One script (Brahmi, widely used in inscriptions). - Despite favoring Brahmi, he respected and accommodated: - Other scripts like Kharosthi, Aramaic, and Greek. - Languages such as Greek, Prakrit, and Sanskrit. - Various religious sects, including non-Buddhist and even anti-Buddhist groups, to whom he also made donations. - His tolerant religious policy ensured no forced imposition of Buddhism on his subjects. - Missionary and Administrative Policies - Asoka was deeply committed to missionary activities. - He deputed officials to far-flung regions of his empire, which: - Strengthened administration. - Promoted cultural integration between the Gangetic heartland and distant provinces like: - Kalinga - Lower Deccan - Northern Bengal - Policy of Peace and Non-Aggression - Asoka is historically significant for his policy of peace, non-aggression, and cultural conquest. - Unlike his predecessors, he renounced military conquest after the Kalinga war. - His vision stood in stark contrast (difference between things or the act of comparing to highlight differences) to: - Kautilya's Arthashastra, which advocated continuous expansion. - The Magadhan rulers before him, who followed an aggressive military approach. - Asoka's ideals were unique, as no Indian king before him had pursued such a pacifist policy. - A similar example existed only in Egypt, where Akhenaten (14th century BCE) had adopted a pacific (Calm, peaceful, or avoiding conflict) policy. - However, Asoka was likely unaware of Akhenaten's precedent (an earlier event, decision, or action that serves as an example or guide for future situations). - Despite having ample resources and a large army, he never waged war again after Kalinga's conquest. - Limitations of Asoka's Policy - His policy did not leave a lasting impact on his viceroys and vassals. - After his retirement in 232 BCE, many of them declared independence in their regions. - Neighboring powers were not influenced by his peaceful approach. - Within 25 years of his departure, foreign forces invaded India's northwestern frontiers. - Other rulers included - Dasaratha Maurya (c. 232-224 BCE) - Grandson of Ashoka - The empire started weakening. - Samprati (c. 224-215 BCE) - Promoted Jainism - Little expansion or administration. - Salisuka (c. 215-202 BCE) - Weak ruler - Faced internal revolts. - Devavarman (c. 202-195 BCE) - Lost territories - The empire shrank further. - Satadhanvan (c. 195-187 BCE) - Short reign - Empire decline continued - Brihadratha (c. 187-185 BCE) - Last Mauryan ruler - Killed by Pushyamitra Shunga, a Brahmin general, who founded the Shunga Dynasty. - Significance of the Maurya Rule - State Control in the Mauryan Empire - The King's Authority and Dharma - The Brahmanical law-books emphasized that the king should govern according to the Dharmashastras and existing customs. - Kautilya's Arthashastra advised the king to uphold dharma when the varna-ashrama system weakened. - The king was regarded as dharmapravartaka (promulgator of social order). - Ashoka's inscriptions explicitly stated that royal orders were supreme over other laws, and he actively promoted dharma through officials. - Rise of Royal Absolutism - The assertion of absolute monarchy was a natural consequence of the military expansion by Magadhan rulers. - Kingdoms such as Anga, Vatsali, Kasi, Kosala, Avanti, and Kalinga were annexed into the Magadhan Empire, leading to greater centralized control over all aspects of life. - Military dominance eventually evolved into coercive state control over administration, economy, and society. - Vast Bureaucratic Machinery - The state maintained an extensive bureaucracy, unparalleled in earlier Indian history. - A sophisticated espionage system supported the administration: - Spies gathered intelligence on foreign threats and government officers. - Some spies also manipulated superstitions to extract money from the public. - Government Officials and Salaries - High-ranking functionaries, known as ti-shas, were primarily paid in cash. - Major officials and their salaries: - Minister (Mantri), High Priest (Purohita), Commander-in-Chief (Senapati), and Crown Prince (Yuvaraja) - Paid up to 48,000 panas. - Lower-ranked officers - Paid 60 panas, with some receiving as little as 10-20 panas. - This led to massive income disparity between high and low-level officials. - Economic Regulations - State Control and Administration - According to Kautilya's Arthashastra, the Mauryan state appointed 27 superintendents (adhyakshas) to regulate various economic activities, including: - Agriculture: - Providing irrigation facilities and regulating water supply. - Trade and Commerce: - Managing markets and ensuring fair transactions. - Weights and Measures: - Standardizing trade practices. - Crafts and Industries: - Overseeing weaving, spinning, and mining. - Megasthenes mentions that land measurement and water distribution were carefully regulated, similar to Egyptian practices. - Taxation System - The Mauryan period marked a significant development in taxation. Kautilya lists numerous taxes levied on: - Peasants, artisans, and traders - Land and produce - The administration prioritized tax assessment over storage. Key officials included: - Samaharta - Head of tax assessment. - Sanadhata - Chief custodian of the treasury and storehouses. - Epigraphic evidence suggests that taxes were collected in kind, with rural granaries serving as reserves for famine and drought relief. - Currency and Economy - The Mauryan economy relied on punch-marked silver coins bearing the symbols of: - Peacock - Hill and crescent (a curved, moon-like shape) - These coins were widely circulated, aiding in: - Tax collection and salary payments - Market transactions across the empire - Social and Labor Organization - Role of Slavery - A notable social development was the employment of slaves in agriculture. - Megasthenes claimed not to have seen slaves in India. - However, domestic slaves had existed since Vedic times. - The Mauryan state maintained large farms worked by: - Slaves (possibly including 150,000 war captives from Kalinga). - Hired laborers. - Despite this, ancient Indian society was not a slave society like Greece or Rome. Instead, shudras served as laborers, artisans, and domestic workers under the higher varnas. - Infrastructure and Transportation - Roads and Communication - The Mauryan administration maintained an extensive road network that enabled trade and governance: - Pataliputra to Nepal (via Vaisali and Champaran). - Himalayan foothills route (connecting Vaisali, Champaran, Kapilavastu, Kalsi, Hazara, and Peshawar). - Northwestern India to Patna (as described by Megasthenes). - Kalinga to Andhra and Karnataka, improving connectivity in southern India. - The strategic location of Pataliputra facilitated movement in all directions, enhancing royal control over a vast territory. - Population and Military - The Mauryas ruled over a relatively small population: - The army numbered around 650,000 soldiers. - If 10% of the population served in the army, the total population would be around 6.5 million. - Ashokan inscriptions suggest that state control was strongest in the Middle Gangetic region, but weaker in the extreme east and south. - Art and Architecture - Stone Masonry and Pillars - The Mauryan period witnessed a major transformation in architecture: - Use of stone masonry on a large scale. - Megasthenes compared Pataliputra's palace to the grandeur of Iran's capital. - Excavations at Kumhrar (Patna) reveal remnants of an 80-pillared hall. - - Mauryan artisans excelled in stone polishing, seen in: - Highly polished stone pillars, set up across the empire. - Each pillar made of a single sandstone piece, with sculpted capitals featuring lions or bulls. - - - Cave Architecture - Mauryan rulers pioneered rock-cut caves for monks. - The Barabar Caves (30 km from Gaya) are the earliest examples. - This architectural tradition later spread to western and southern India. - - - Causes of the Fall of the Maurya Empire - The Magadhan empire, which had been established through successive wars culminating in the conquest of Kalinga, began to disintegrate after the exit of Ashoka in 232 BCE. Several factors contributed to the decline and eventual fall of the Maurya Empire. - Brahmanical Reaction - Ashoka's policies led to growing resentment among the Brahmanas. Although he adopted a tolerant approach and asked people to respect Brahmanas, his measures—such as prohibiting the killing of animals and birds and criticizing superfluous rituals—significantly affected their income. - The Brahmanas, who depended on sacrifices and rituals for their livelihood, suffered due to the anti-sacrifice stance of Buddhism and Ashoka's policies. - Despite Ashoka's efforts to maintain religious harmony, the Brahmanas desired a government that favored them and preserved their traditional privileges. - Some of the new kingdoms that emerged after the fall of the Maurya Empire were ruled by Brahmanas, such as the Sungas and Kanvas in the east and the Satavahanas in the Deccan. These dynasties revived Vedic sacrifices, which Ashoka had neglected. - Financial Crisis - The enormous expenditure on maintaining the army and bureaucracy led to a severe financial strain on the Maurya treasury. - The Mauryas had the largest army and the largest regiment of officers in ancient India, which required extensive resources. - Despite imposing numerous taxes, it became difficult to sustain such a vast administrative structure. - Ashoka's generous donations to Buddhist monks further depleted state finances. - In the final stages of the empire, the treasury became so exhausted that gold images were reportedly melted to cover expenses. - Oppressive Rule in the Provinces - Misrule and oppressive administration in various provinces contributed to the empire's decline. - During Bindusara's reign, the people of Taxila complained about the tyranny of corrupt bureaucrats (dushtamatyas). Ashoka resolved the issue temporarily, but the problem persisted when he became emperor. - The Kalinga edicts suggest that Ashoka was deeply concerned about oppression in the provinces. He instructed the mahamatrus (officials) not to mistreat townspeople. - To improve administration, he introduced the rotation of officers in key regions like Tosali (Kalinga), Ujjain, and Taxila. - Despite these measures, discontent continued, and after Ashoka's retirement, regions like Taxila were quick to rebel against Maurya rule. - Spread of New Material Knowledge in Outlying Areas - The spread of technological and agricultural advancements weakened the Maurya Empire's dominance. - Magadha had initially expanded due to its material advantages, such as the early use of iron tools and weapons. - However, as knowledge of these techniques spread to central India, the Deccan, and Kalinga, the core Gangetic region lost its unique advantage. - With access to better tools and resources, peripheral provinces developed independently and formed new kingdoms. - This explains the emergence of the Sungas and Kanvas in central India, the Chetis in Kalinga, and the Satavahanas in the Deccan. - Neglect of the North-West Frontier - Ashoka's focus on missionary activities left the north-western frontier vulnerable to external threats. - In the third century BCE, Central Asia witnessed constant tribal movements, particularly among the Scythians, who relied on cavalry warfare. - In response to these threats, the Chinese ruler Shih Huang Ti (247-210 BCE) built the Great Wall of China around 220 BCE to protect his empire. - However, Ashoka did not take similar measures to secure India's frontiers. - As a result, when the Scythians advanced, they pushed the Parthians, Sakas, and Greeks towards India. - The Greeks, who had established a kingdom in Bactria (north Afghanistan), became the first to invade India in 206 BCE, triggering a series of invasions that continued until the beginning of the Christian era. - Final Collapse and the Rise of the Sungas - The Maurya Empire ultimately fell in 185 BCE when Pushyamitra Sunga, a Brahmana and general of the last Maurya king, Brihadratha, usurped (to take power, a position, or rights forcefully or without legal authority) the throne. - Pushyamitra Sunga is said to have killed Brihadratha in public and declared himself ruler of Pataliputra. - The Sungas ruled over Pataliputra and central India, actively reviving Brahmanical traditions through Vedic sacrifices. - They reportedly persecuted Buddhists, marking a significant shift from the Maurya policies of religious tolerance. - The Kanvas, another Brahmana dynasty, succeeded the Sungas and continued to rule over the remnants of the Maurya Empire. - Thus, a combination of financial instability, administrative inefficiencies, regional rebellions, technological diffusion, and foreign invasions led to the eventual downfall of the Maurya Empire. - Central Asian Contacts and Their Results - - Around 200 B.C., India did not witness the rise of a large empire like that of the Mauryas. However, this period was marked by extensive and intimate contacts between Central Asia and India. - In eastern India, central India, and the Deccan, the Mauryas were succeeded by native dynasties such as the Sungas, Kanvas, and Satavahanas. - In north-western India, power shifted to several ruling dynasties from Central Asia. - The Indo-Greeks - Around 200 B.C., a series of invasions took place, beginning with the Greeks from Bactria, a region south of the Oxus River in present-day northern Afghanistan. These invaders came in successive waves, sometimes ruling simultaneously in different regions. - Causes of Indo-Greek Invasions - The weakness of the Seleucid Empire, which controlled Bactria and parts of Iran (Parthia), made the region vulnerable. - - Seleucid Empire (312–63 BC) was a major Hellenistic Greek state in Western Asia founded by Seleucus I Nicator, one of Alexander the Great’s generals - The Scythian (nomadic warrior people who lived in the Eurasian steppes (modern-day Ukraine, southern Russia, and Central Asia)) tribes put increasing pressure on the Greek rulers in Bactria, forcing them to retreat. - With the construction of the Great Wall of China, the Scythians could no longer push eastward, so they turned their attention towards the Greeks and Parthians, ultimately leading the Bactrian Greeks to invade India. - The successors of Ashoka were too weak to resist these foreign invasions. - Greek Rule in India - The Indo-Greeks (Bactrian Greeks) were the first to invade India, expanding their control over north-western India by the early 2nd century B.C. - They occupied a larger territory than that conquered by Alexander, reportedly advancing as far as Ayodhya and Pataliputra. - However, the Greeks failed to establish a unified rule in India, with two Greek dynasties ruling simultaneously in north-western India. - Menander (165-145 B.C.) - The most famous Indo-Greek ruler, also known as Milinda, ruled from Sakala (modern Sialkot, Punjab). - He invaded the Ganga-Yamuna Doab and later converted to Buddhism under the influence of Nagasena. - Their philosophical discussions were compiled in the famous book Milinda Panho (The Questions of Milinda). - Significance of Indo-Greek Rule - Coinage: - The Indo-Greeks were the first rulers in India to issue coins definitively attributed (A quality, feature, or trait that belongs to a person, thing, or idea) to individual kings. - Unlike the early punch-marked coins, which cannot be assigned to specific dynasties, Greek coins provided clear attributions. - They were also the first to introduce gold coins in India, a trend that expanded under the Kushans. - - Art and Culture: - Greek rule introduced Hellenistic artistic elements in north-western India, which contributed to the development of Gandhara art. - The Sakas - The Sakas were Iranian-speaking nomadic tribes closely related to the Scythians, who lived in the Central Asian steppes and later migrated into South Asia, Persia, and China. - Steppes refer to a vast, semi-arid, grass-covered plain that is largely treeless - - After the Greeks, the Sakas emerged as the next major foreign rulers in India, controlling a much larger territory than their predecessors. - They established five branches of rule, each with its seat of power in different regions of India and Afghanistan: - Afghanistan - Punjab, with Taxila as the capital - Mathura, where they ruled for about two centuries - Western India, where they continued to rule until the 4th century A.D. - Upper Deccan - - Resistance Against the Sakas - The Sakas faced little effective resistance from Indian rulers. - Around 58 B.C., a king of Ujjain successfully fought against them and drove them out. - He adopted the title Vikramaditya, and his victory led to the establishment of the Vikrama Samvat era in 58 B.C. - Vikram Samvat is the traditional lunar calendar of India for determining Hindu festivals (Diwali, Holi, etc.) - The title Vikramaditya became prestigious, similar to how Roman emperors adopted the title Caesar. - As a result, 14 rulers in Indian history later adopted the title Vikramaditya, especially in western India and the western Deccan until the 12th century A.D. - Saka Rule in Western India - Among the different Saka branches, only those in western India held power for a long duration—about four centuries. - The most famous Saka ruler in India was Rudradaman I (A.D. 130-150). - His rule extended over Sindh, Kutch, and Gujarat, and he also recovered territories from the Satavahanas, including: - Konkan - Narmada Valley - Malwa - Kathiawar - Contributions of Rudradaman I - He is remembered for repairing and improving the Sudarshana Lake in Kathiawar, which had been used for irrigation since Mauryan times. -
