He was a great patron of Sanskrit - Despite being of foreign origin, he issued the first-ever long inscription in pure Sanskrit, whereas earlier long inscriptions in India were composed in Prakrit. - The Parthians - - The Parthians were an Iranian people who established the Parthian Empire (247 BCE - 224 CE) in Persia (modern Iran). - After the Sakas, the Parthians established their rule in north-western India. In many ancient Indian Sanskrit texts, both groups are mentioned together as Saka-Pahlavas because they ruled parallelly for some time. - Origins and Expansion - The Parthians originally lived in Iran and later migrated to India. - Unlike the Greeks and the Sakas, they controlled only a small portion of north-western India during the 1st century A.D. - Key Parthian Ruler - The most famous Parthian king was Gondophernes. - It is believed that during his reign, St. Thomas came to India to propagate Christianity. - Who Was St. Thomas? - St. Thomas, also known as Thomas the Apostle or "Doubting Thomas", was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus Christ. He is best known for: - Doubting Jesus' Resurrection - He initially refused to believe that Jesus had risen from the dead until he saw and touched Jesus' wounds. - Missionary Work in India - According to Christian tradition, he traveled to India to spread Christianity. - Martyrdom in India - The suffering or death of a person because of their religious or ideological beliefs - He was believed to be martyred in Chennai (Tamil Nadu), India. - Integration into Indian Society - Over time, the Parthians, like the Sakas, became an integral part of Indian polity and society. - The Kushans - - The Kushans, also known as the Yuechis or Tocharians, were a nomadic tribe from the steppes of North Central Asia near China. - They first occupied Bactria (North Afghanistan), displacing the Sakas, and gradually moved into the Kabul Valley. By crossing the Hindukush, they seized Gandhara, replacing the Greek and Parthian rule. - Eventually, they expanded their empire over the lower Indus basin and greater Gangetic basin, creating a vast domain extending from Khorasan in Central Asia to Varanasi in India. Their rule unified territories across five modern countries, fostering cultural interactions. - Kushan Dynasties - The Kushan rule was marked by two successive dynasties: 1. The Kadphises Dynasty (c. A.D. 50 - 78) - Founded by chiefs of the Kadphises house and lasted 28 years. - Kadphises I issued copper coins south of the Hindukush, imitating Roman coins. - Kadphises II minted a large number of gold coins and expanded the kingdom east of the Indus. 2. The Kanishka Dynasty (A.D. 78 - 230) - Extended Kushan power over Upper India and the Lower Indus Basin. - Issued gold coins with higher gold content than the Gupta coins. - Their inscriptions were found in north-western India, Sindh, Mathura, Sravasti, Kausambi, and Varanasi, indicating rule over the greater Gangetic basin. - Major Kushan Capitals - Purushapura (Peshawar) - The primary capital, where Kanishka built a monastery and a massive stupa. - Mathura - The secondary capital, evidenced by Kushan coins, inscriptions, sculptures, and structures. - Kanishka: The Greatest Kushan Ruler - Despite suffering defeats against the Chinese, Kanishka is historically significant for: - Starting the Saka era in A.D. 78, which is still used by the Government of India. - Saka Samvat was adopted on March 22, 1957 as the National Calender of India on recommendation of Calender Reform Committee - It is debated who started Saka era, but this book mentions this, but other sources mention Satvahana king started the saka era - Patronizing Buddhism and holding a Buddhist council in Kashmir, finalizing the doctrines of Mahayana Buddhism. - Supporting Sanskrit literature and art, significantly influencing Indian culture. - - Decline of the Kushan Empire - Kanishka's successors ruled north-western India until A.D. 230. - Some later rulers had Indianized names, such as Vasudeva. - The Kushan Empire in Afghanistan and west of the Indus was overthrown in the mid-3rd century A.D. by the Sassanian Empire of Iran. - However, Kushan principalities survived in India for about a century. - Kushan influence persisted in Kabul Valley, Kapisa, Bactria, Khorezm, and Sogdiana (modern Bokhara and Samarkand) until the 3rd and 4th centuries. - Archaeological Findings - Kushan coins, inscriptions, and terracottas have been found across Central Asia. - A huge Kushan palace at Toprak-Kala in Khorezm (3rd-4th century A.D.) contained administrative archives with inscriptions in Aramaic script and the Khorezmian language. - Mnemonic to remember order of invasions - Ghee Shakkar vala Paratha Khao Ho? - Ghee -> Indo-Greeks - Shakkar -> Sakas - vala -> _x - Paratha -> Indo-Parthians - Khao -> Kushanas - Ho -> White Hunas - Impact of Central Asian Contacts on India - Structures and Pottery - Construction Advances: - The Saka-Kushan phase marked a significant advancement in construction, with multiple structural layers found in northern India. - Architectural Features: - Extensive use of burnt bricks for flooring. - Tiles for both flooring and roofing. - Brick wells became common. - Pottery Developments: - Red ware pottery, found in plain and polished forms with fine fabric. - Notable types include sprinklers and spouted channels. - Similarities with thin red pottery from Kushan layers in Soviet Central Asia. - Techniques extended to regions like Farghana, indicating cultural exchange. - Trade and Technology - Cultural Integration: - Sakas and Kushans settled permanently in India, adopting Indian script, language, and religion. - Military Contributions: - Introduced better cavalry and large-scale horse riding. - Popularized reins and saddles, visible in Buddhist sculptures. - Enthusiastic horsemen, evidenced by terracotta figures from Begram, Afghanistan. - Some foreign horsemen used heavy armor, spears, lances, and possibly rope stirrups. - Attire Influences: - Introduced turbans, tunics, trousers, and long coats. - Afghan and Punjabi turbans, and sherwanis, evolved from these influences. - Brought in caps, helmets, and boots, widely used by warriors. - Economic Influence: - Established strong trade ties with Central Asia. - India received gold from the Altai Mountains and possibly via Roman trade. - The Kushans controlled the Silk Route, bringing immense wealth through tolls. - First rulers in India to issue gold coins on a large scale. - Polity - Feudatory System: - Central Asian rulers imposed their rule over many native princes. - The Kushans adopted the title "King of Kings," showing supremacy over smaller rulers. - Divine Kingship: - Kushan kings were called “Sons of God.” - Inspired by Chinese kingship, adapted in India to emphasize royal authority. - Manu's laws reinforced the king's divine status. - Government Structure: - Introduced the satrap system, dividing the empire into satrapies. - Some regions had hereditary dual rule (father and son ruling jointly). - Less centralization under these rulers. - Social Classification: - Sakas and Parthians were seen as fallen Kshatriyas. - The concept of "fallen Kshatriyas" was a way to categorize certain groups of people who were considered to have once belonged to the Kshatriya varna (the warrior and ruling class) but had lost their status. This loss of status was often due to a failure to uphold their traditional duties or by not adhering to the Dharma (righteous conduct) associated with their caste. - Large-scale assimilation of foreigners into Indian society occurred during the post-Maurya period. - Military Governorship: - The Greeks introduced the concept of military governors (strategos) to maintain control. - - New Elements in Indian Society - Cultural Assimilation: - Greeks, Sakas, Parthians, and Kushans gradually lost their separate identity. - They were absorbed into Indian society as Kshatriyas. - Vishnu texts supported this assimilation, as seen in Kushan ruler Vasudeva's name, linked to Krishna. - Religion - Religious Conversions: - Some foreign rulers embraced Vaishnavism (worship of Vishnu). - Greek ambassador Heliodorus erected a pillar in honor of Vishnu in Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh. - A few rulers adopted Buddhism, such as Menander, who engaged in debates with the Buddhist teacher Nagasena. - The Kushans worshipped both Shiva and Buddha, with their images appearing on coins. - The Origin of Mahayana Buddhism - Transformation of Buddhism: - Foreign influence led to changes in Buddhism, making it more accessible. - The original puritanical form was too abstract (Something that exists as an idea but not as a physical object) for foreigners. - A new sect, Mahayana (Great Wheel), emerged, emphasizing Buddha's image worship. - Those rejecting Mahayana were called followers of Hinayana (Lesser Vehicle). - Kanishka's Patronage (a supporter or sponsor): - Convened a Buddhist council in Kashmir to engrave Buddhist teachings on copper sheets. - Built many stupas in Buddha's memory. - Gandhara Art - Artistic Patronage: - Foreign rulers actively supported Indian art and literature. - The Kushan empire facilitated interaction between Indian, Greek, and Roman artisans. - Gandhara Art: - Developed in the northwestern frontier, blending Graeco-Roman and Indian styles. - Buddha images featured Graeco-Roman hairstyles. - - Mathura Art: - Mathura remained a hub of indigenous art. - Produced the famous headless statue of Kanishka. - Created numerous Buddha and Mahavira images. - The Mathura Museum holds the largest Kushan-era sculpture collection. - - Southern Developments: - Rock-cut Buddhist caves emerged in Maharashtra. - Nagarjunakonda and Amaravati in Andhra Pradesh became major Buddhist art centers. - Early Buddhist panels are found in Gaya, Sanchi, and Bharhut (2nd century B.C.). - - Literature and Learning - Sanskrit Literature: - Foreign rulers promoted Sanskrit. - Earliest kāvya-style inscription by Rudradaman (c. A.D. 150). - Prakrit continued for inscriptions until the 4th century A.D. - Notable Writers: - Aśvaghoṣa, under Kushan patronage, wrote Buddhacharita (Buddha's biography) and Saundarananda. - Growth of Mahayana Buddhism led to avadānas (Buddhist tales), e.g., Mahāvastu and Divyāvadāna. - Theatrical Influence: - Greek influence introduced curtains (yāvanikā) to Indian theatre. - Science and Technology - Astronomy & Astrology: - Indian texts adopted Greek planetary movement terms. - Indian astrology absorbed Greek ideas; the term horāśāstra was derived from “horoscope.” - Medicine & Chemistry: - Charaka and Sushruta pioneered medicine, botany, and chemistry. - Charakasamhitā detailed herbal medicines and chemical processes. - Indian medicine (auṣadhi) relied on plants (oṣadhi). - Technological Advancements: - - Central Asian influence seen in trousers and long boots (Kanishka depicted wearing them). - Leather shoe-making possibly began in this period. - Kushan copper and gold coins imitated Roman coins. - Diplomatic ties with Rome: - Indian embassies sent to Emperor Augustus (A.D. 27-28) and Trajan (A.D. 110-120). - Roman contacts may have influenced Indian glass-making, which flourished during this era. - - The Age of the Satavahanas - Political History of the Satavahanas - The Satavahanas, considered identical to the Andhras mentioned in the Puranas, were the most important native successors of the Mauryas in the Deccan and central India. However, while the Puranas speak only of Andhra rule, the name “Andhra” does not appear in Satavahana inscriptions. - According to some Puranas, the Andhras ruled for 300 years, a period now attributed to the Satavahana dynasty. - Early Satavahana Rule - The earliest Satavahana inscriptions date back to the first century B.C., when they defeated the Kanvas and established their power in parts of central India. However, their initial stronghold was not in Andhra, but in Maharashtra, where most of their early inscriptions have been found. - They established their rule in the upper Godavari valley, a region that remains agriculturally rich in present-day Maharashtra. - Gradually, the Satavahanas expanded their rule over Karnataka and Andhra. Their greatest rivals were the Sakas, who had established dominance in the upper Deccan and western India. At one point, the Satavahanas lost their territories in Maharashtra and western India to the Sakas. - Gautamiputra Satakarni (A.D. 106-130) - The fortunes of the Satavahana dynasty were revived by Gautamiputra Satakarni (A.D. 106-130). He: - Called himself the only Brahmana. - Defeated the Sakas and destroyed many Kshatriya rulers. - Eliminated the Kshaharata lineage, to which his adversary Nahapana belonged. - Overstruck more than 8,000 silver coins of Nahapana found near Nasik, proving his conquest. - Occupied Malwa and Kathiawar, which were under Saka control. - Gautamiputra Satakarni's empire extended from Malwa in the north to Karnataka in the south, possibly exerting general authority over Andhra. - Later Satavahana Kings (A.D. 130-220) - The successors of Gautamiputra Satakarni ruled until A.D. 220. - Vasisthiputra Pulumayi (A.D. 130-154) - His coins and inscriptions found in Andhra indicate that by the mid-2nd century, Andhra was fully integrated into the Satavahana kingdom. - Established his capital at Paithan (Pratisthan) on the Godavari in Aurangabad district. - Continued conflict with the Sakas, who sought control over Konkan and Malwa. - Rudradaman I (A.D. 130-150) - Saka Ruler of Saurashtra (Kathiawar) - Defeated the Satavahanas twice but did not destroy them due to matrimonial alliances. - Yana Sri Satakarni (A.D. 165-194) - Recovered North Konkan and Malwa from the Sakas. - Promoted trade and navigation. - His coins have been found across Andhra, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat, indicating extensive influence. - - Aspects of Material Culture Under the Satavahanas - The material culture of the Deccan under the Satavahanas was a fusion of local traditions and northern influences. - Iron Usage and Metallurgy - The megalith builders of the Deccan were already familiar with iron tools and agriculture. - Before circa 200 B.C., a few iron hoes were in use, but their number increased significantly in the first two or three centuries of the Christian era. - The form of hoes remained largely unchanged from the megalithic to the Satavahana phase, except that they were now fully socketed. - Other iron tools from this period include: - Socketed hoes - Sickles, spades, ploughshares - Axes, adzes, razors - Tanged and socketed arrowheads and daggers - A blacksmith's shop has been discovered at a site in Karimnagar district, indicating advanced ironworking. - The iron ores of Karimnagar and Warangal were likely exploited, as evidence of iron mining dates back to the megalithic phase. - Gold and Coinage - Gold workings from the early Christian centuries have been found in the Kolar fields. - Unlike the Kushans, the Satavahanas did not issue gold coins, but likely used gold as bullion (form of bars, ingots, or coins). - Their coinage primarily consisted of: - Lead coins, which are common in the Deccan. - Potin, copper, and bronze coins. - The Ikshvakus, who succeeded the Satavahanas, also issued their own coins. - Both the Satavahanas and Ikshvakus seem to have exploited the mineral resources of the Deccan. - Agriculture and Economy - The people of the Deccan practiced paddy transplantation. - The Krishna-Godavari delta developed into a major rice-producing region in the first two centuries A.D. - Cotton production was another key feature of the Deccan's economy. - Foreign accounts describe Andhra as famous for its cotton products. - The economy was strong enough to sustain a large military force. According to Pliny, the Andhra kingdom maintained: - 100,000 infantry - 2,000 cavalry - 1,000 elephants - Urbanization and Infrastructure - Contact with north India introduced new elements of material culture, such as: - Coins - Burnt bricks - Ring wells - By 200 B.C. - A.D. 200, sites like Peddabankur (Karimnagar district) show: - Regular use of fire-baked bricks. - Flat, perforated roof tiles for durable structures. - 22 brick wells dating to the second century A.D., facilitating dense habitation. - Covered underground drains leading waste water into soakage pits. - Towns emerged in: - Maharashtra by the first century B.C., with several crafts flourishing. - Eastern Deccan a century later. - Pliny mentions that Andhra in the western Deccan had: - 30 walled towns. - Numerous villages. - Inscriptions and excavations confirm the existence of several towns in the second and third centuries A.D. - Increasing trade activity is indicated by numerous Roman and Satavahana coins. These coins appeared earlier in western Deccan and about a century later in eastern Deccan (Godavari-Krishna region). - Pattern of Administration Under the Satavahanas - Divine Kingship and Royal Ideals - The Satavahana rulers upheld the royal ideals set forth in the Dharmashastras. - The king was portrayed as the upholder of dharma and was assigned divine attributes. - The Satavahana king was compared to legendary figures such as: - Rama, Bhima, Kesava, Arjuna - Supernatural forces, to emphasize his divinity and prowess. - Administrative Structure - The Satavahanas retained some administrative units from the Ashokan period: - The district was called “ahara”, the same term used during Ashoka's reign. - Officials were known as “amatyas” and “mahamatras”, similar to those in Mauryan administration. - Military and Feudal Elements - The administration had strong military influences, evident in key appointments: - The senapati (commander) was also appointed as the provincial governor. - Since tribal communities in the Deccan were not fully Hinduized or reconciled to Satavahana rule, military control was necessary. - In rural areas, administration was handled by the gaulmika, who led a military regiment consisting of: - 9 chariots - 9 elephants - 25 horses - 45 foot soldiers - - The head of the army platoon was stationed in the countryside to maintain peace and order. - Military influence is further evident in inscriptions mentioning: - “Kataka” (military camps) - “Skandhavaras” (military settlements), which also functioned as administrative centers when the king was present. - This highlights the coercive nature of Satavahana rule. - Land Grants and Religious Patronage - The Satavahanas initiated the practice of granting tax-free villages to: - Brahmanas - Buddhist monks - The cultivated fields and villages granted to them were declared free from interference by: - Royal policemen - Soldiers - Other royal officials - These granted lands became autonomous enclaves within the kingdom. - Buddhist monks promoted peace and social order by preaching good conduct and respect for authority. - Brahmanas helped enforce the varna system, which contributed to social stability. - Feudal Hierarchy and Feudatories - The Satavahana kingdom had a three-tiered system of feudatories: - 1. Raja (King) - The highest-ranked feudatory, with the right to mint coins. - 2. Mahabhoja - The second-grade feudatory. - 3. Senapati - The third-grade feudatory. - These feudatories and landed beneficiaries held significant local authority, shaping the decentralized nature of Satavahana rule. - Religion Under the Satavahanas - Promotion of Brahmanism - The Satavahana rulers identified as Brahmanas and symbolized the triumph of Brahmanism. - They actively performed Vedic sacrifices, including: - Ashvamedha (horse sacrifice) - Vajapeya (royal consecration sacrifice) - They worshipped several Vaishnava deities, such as: - Krishna - Vasudeva - Other Vaishnava gods - Brahmanas were granted liberal sacrificial fees, reinforcing their religious authority. - Support for Buddhism - Despite their Brahmanical inclinations, the Satavahanas patronized Buddhism, particularly the Mahayana sect. - Buddhist monks received land grants, facilitating the growth of monastic institutions. - Buddhism flourished in: - Nagarjunakonda and Amaravati (Andhra Pradesh) - Became major centers of Buddhist culture. - Nasik and Junar (Western Deccan, Maharashtra) - Buddhism thrived here due to the patronage of traders. - Under the Ikshvakus (successors of the Satavahanas), Buddhism continued to receive strong support. - Architecture Under the Satavahanas - Rock-Cut Temples and Monasteries - The Satavahana period saw the creation of rock-cut temples and monasteries in the north-western Deccan (Maharashtra). - This tradition began around 200 BC, about a century before the Satavahanas. - Two major structures were: - Chaitya (Temple): - A large hall with numerous columns. - The most famous chaitya is at Karle (Western Deccan), measuring: - 40 meters long, 15 meters wide, 15 meters high. - A remarkable example of rock-cut architecture. - - Vihara (Monastery): - A central hall accessed through a doorway from a front verandah. - Excavated near chaityas as residences for monks during the rainy season. - Nasik has three viharas, carrying inscriptions of Nahapana and Gautamiputra, dating to the 1st-2nd centuries A.D. - Buddhist Architecture in Andhra - Rock-cut architecture also existed in Andhra Pradesh (Krishna-Godavari region), but the region was better known for its free-standing Buddhist structures. - The most notable Buddhist monuments include: - Stupas: - Found across 125 km around Ellora. - Most famous stupas: - Amaravati Stupa: - Originated around 200 BC, but completely rebuilt in the late 2nd century A.D. - Dimensions: - Dome 53 meters across the base. - 33 meters in height. - Covered with sculptures depicting scenes from Buddha's life. - - Nagarjunakonda: - Flourished under the Ikshvakus (successors of the Satavahanas). - Contained Buddhist stupas and the earliest Brahmanical brick temples. - - Language Under the Satavahanas - Official Language: Prakrit - All inscriptions were composed in Prakrit and written in the Brahmi script, similar to the Asokan period. - Literary Contributions: - Some Satavahana kings may have authored books in Prakrit. - The Gathasaptasati, a collection of 700 verses in Prakrit, is attributed to King Hala. - However, the text appears to have been edited much later, possibly after the 6th century A.D. - The Dawn of History in the Deep South - Transition to the Historical Period in South India - Markers of the Historical Period - Several key elements define the beginning of the historical period: - Large-scale rural settlements practicing plough agriculture with iron implements. - Formation of the state system. - Rise of social classes. - Use of writing. - Beginnings of written literature. - Megalithic Culture in Peninsular India - These historical elements were absent in the Kaveri delta until around 200 B.C. - Before this, the uplands of the peninsula were inhabited by megalith builders. - Their actual settlements are rare, but their graves (megaliths) provide insights into their culture. - Megaliths were stone-circled graves, containing skeletons, pottery, and iron objects. - - Material Culture of the Megalithic People - They used various types of pottery, but black-and-red ware was most popular. - They buried goods with the dead, likely believing in an afterlife. - Grave goods suggest their sources of livelihood: - Weapons: - Arrowheads, spearheads, tridents (later associated with Shiva). - Agricultural tools: - Hoes, sickles (fewer in number compared to weapons). - The prevalence of weapons suggests that agriculture was not very advanced. - Geographical Spread and Variations - Megaliths are found across upland areas of the peninsula, with a concentration in eastern Andhra and Tamil Nadu. - Their beginnings can be traced to around 1000 B.C., lasting until 1st century B.C., and in some places, even into the early Christian era. - The Cholas, Pandyas, and Cheras (mentioned in Ashokan inscriptions) were likely in the megalithic phase of material culture. - Burial Practices: - In southern Tamil Nadu, skeletons were placed in urns made of red pottery, often without stone circles or many grave goods. - In the Krishna-Godavari valley, the dominant practice was cist burial or pit burial with stone circles. - Despite using iron, megalithic people relied on upland areas for settlement rather than plains or lowlands. - Transition to Settled Agriculture and State Formation - By the beginning of the Christian era, or slightly earlier, they: - Moved from uplands to fertile river basins and marshy deltaic regions. - Adopted wet paddy cultivation. - Established villages and towns. - Developed social classes. - Influences from the North: - Contact with northern traders, conquerors, and Jain and Buddhist missionaries introduced new elements of material culture. - These changes laid the foundation for state formation in South India. - By the 1st century A.D., the history of the deep south becomes clearer through written records, Greek and Roman accounts, and archaeological evidence. - Three Early Kingdoms - - The southern end of the Indian peninsula, located south of the Krishna River, was divided into three major kingdoms: Chola, Pandya, and Chera (Kerala). - These kingdoms were mentioned in Ashoka's inscriptions (3rd century B.C.), indicating that they lay outside the Maurya Empire, in what is now Tamil Nadu and Kerala. - Pandya Kingdom - The Pandyas are first mentioned by Megasthenes, who noted their kingdom was renowned for pearls. - He also recorded that the kingdom was ruled by a woman and claimed that seven-year-old mothers existed there, which suggests the presence of a matriarchal society. - The Pandya territory covered the southernmost and southeastern regions of the peninsula, corresponding to modern Tirunelveli, Ramnad, and Madurai. - Madurai, the Pandya capital, derived its name from the Tamil word for Mathura. - Sangam literature (compiled in Tamil academies in the early Christian era) mentions Pandya rulers but lacks a connected historical account. - The Pandyas profited from trade with the Roman Empire and even sent embassies to Emperor Augustus. - Brahmanas held considerable influence, and the Pandya kings performed Vedic sacrifices in the early centuries of the Christian era. - Chola Kingdom - The Chola kingdom, also known as Cholamandalam or Coromandel, was located northeast of the Pandya territory, between the Pennar and Velur rivers. - Uraiyur, a major center for cotton trade, was the Cholas' political hub. - In the mid-2nd century B.C., a Chola king named Elara conquered Sri Lanka and ruled for nearly 50 years. - A more detailed Chola history begins in the 2nd century A.D. with Karikala (c. A.D. 100), the most famous early Chola ruler. - - He founded Puhar (Kaveripattanam) and built 160 km of embankments along the Kaveri River using the labor of 12,000 Sri Lankan captives. - Puhar (Kaveripattanam) became a major trade and commerce center with a large dock, as confirmed by excavations. - The Cholas gained wealth from cotton trade and maintained a navy that sailed to the Ganga, Irrawaddy, and the Malaya Archipelago. - Decline of the Cholas: - After Karikala, Chola power declined rapidly. - Kaveripattanam was destroyed, and the neighboring Cheras and Pandyas expanded at the Cholas' expense. - The Pallavas from the north further weakened them. - From the 4th to the 9th century A.D., the Cholas played only a marginal role in South Indian history. - Chera (Kerala) Kingdom - The Chera kingdom lay west and north of Pandya land, covering the modern Kerala region between the sea and the mountains. - It was as significant as the Chola and Pandya kingdoms due to its trade with the Romans. - The Romans stationed two regiments at Muziris (Cranganore) to protect their trade interests and even built a temple to Augustus there. - The most notable event in Chera history was their war against the Cholas (c. A.D. 150): - The Cheras killed the father of Chola king Karikala, but their own king was also killed. - Later, they formed a matrimonial alliance with the Cholas. - The Chera king allied with the Pandyas against the Cholas but was defeated. - It is said that the Chera king, wounded in the back, committed suicide out of shame. - The greatest Chera ruler was Senguttuvan (the Red Chera), known for his victories over rivals and securing his cousin's throne. - - He is said to have crossed the Ganga, but this is likely an exaggeration. - After the 2nd century A.D., Chera power declined, and there is no record of their history until the 8th century A.D. - Economic and Cultural Significance of These Kingdoms - These three kingdoms were engaged in continuous warfare with each other and Sri Lanka. - Despite frequent wars, they thrived due to natural resources and trade. - Their primary exports included: - Spices, especially pepper, in high demand in the Western world. - Ivory from elephants. - Pearls from the sea. - Precious stones from their mines. - Fine textiles, including muslin and silk. - Uraiyur was especially noted for its cotton trade. - Early Tamil poems describe intricate silk weaving and cotton fabric as thin as a snake's skin. - Trade connections extended to the Greek and Hellenistic kingdoms of Egypt and Arabia, as well as the Malaya Archipelago and China. - Tamil words for rice, ginger, and cinnamon were adopted into the Greek language, showing linguistic influence. - Trade flourished when Egypt became a Roman province and the monsoons were discovered (early 1st century A.D.), leading to a boom in commerce with Rome. - However, as Roman trade declined, these kingdoms also weakened and decayed. - - The Purse and the Sword - Sources of Revenue - Trade and Customs Duties - Trade, both foreign and internal, was a major source of royal income. - Customs officials operated in Puhar to collect duties. - Transit taxes were imposed on merchants transporting goods. - Soldiers patrolled roads to ensure merchant safety and prevent smuggling. - Spoils of War - War plunder (to steal goods, especially by force, often during war, raids, or conflicts) contributed significantly to the treasury. - Agricultural Revenue - The primary and most stable source of income was agriculture. - The king claimed a share of agricultural produce, though the exact proportion is unknown. - The fertile regions of the peninsula produced: - Grains like paddy, ragi - Cash crops like sugarcane, pepper, turmeric - Fruits of various kinds - The Kaveri delta was exceptionally productive, with a saying that “the space where an elephant could lie down could feed seven people.” - The Military System - Composition of the Army : - Chariots drawn by oxen - Elephants - Cavalry - Infantry - Role of Elephants and Horses - Elephants played a crucial role in warfare. - Horses were imported by sea into the Pandya kingdom. - Military Leadership and Equipment - Nobles, princes, and army captains rode elephants. - Commanders drove chariots. - Foot soldiers and cavalry wore leather sandals for foot protection. - Rise of Social Classes - Role of Taxes in Society - Taxes funded both the professional army and royal patronage of poets and priests. - Poets and priests, primarily Brahmanas, were highly respected and generously rewarded by kings. - King Karikala is said to have gifted one poet 1.6 million gold pieces. - Other rewards included cash, land, chariots, horses, and even elephants. - Brahmanas and Social Structure - The Brahmanas first appeared in Tamil lands during the Sangam Age. - An ideal king was expected never to harm the Brahmanas. - Tamil Brahmanas consumed meat and wine. - Absence of the Traditional Varnas - Kshatriyas and Vaishyas are not explicitly mentioned in Sangam texts as regular varnas. - However, a warrior class existed: - Military captains were given the title enadi at a formal ceremony. - - Civil and military offices under both the Cholas and Pandyas were held by vailaias (rich peasants). - - The Ruling Class and Peasantry - The ruling caste was known as arasar, and they intermarried with the vailaias. - The vailaias (fourth caste) were the dominant peasantry, owning the majority of the land: - Rich peasants owned land but did not plow it themselves, employing laborers instead. - Poor peasants worked directly on the land. - Agricultural labor was mainly done by women of the lowest class (Aadaisi-yar), who were similar to slaves. - Lower-Class Artisans and Laborers - Pulaiyans: - Low-class artisans who made ropes, charpoys, and mats from animal skins. - Outcasts and forest tribes: - Lived in extreme poverty, surviving on daily earnings. - Social Inequalities - Sharp divisions between the rich and the poor existed: - The rich lived in brick houses. - The poor lived in huts and humble dwellings. - Merchants in cities resided in upper-story buildings. - Caste and religion did not yet strictly enforce social hierarchy. - Brahmanas and ruling classes dominated society, but the rigid caste distinctions of later periods had not yet fully developed. - Beginnings of Brahmanism - Influence of Brahmanism - Tamil society in the early centuries of the Christian era was influenced by Brahmanism, but its impact was limited: - Confined to a small part of Tamil territory. - Affected mainly the upper levels of Tamil society. - Royal Patronage of Vedic Traditions - Kings performed Vedic sacrifices, showcasing their association with Brahmanical traditions. - Brahmanas, as followers of the Vedas, engaged in philosophical disputes, possibly with Jainas and Buddhists. - Popular Religious Practices - The chief local deity worshipped by the people was Murugan (Subramaniya). - - Vishnu worship is also mentioned but may have been a later development. - Funerary Practices - The megalithic tradition of providing for the dead persisted. - People offered paddy to the deceased. - Cremation was introduced, but inhumation (burial) from the megalithic phase continued. - Tamil Language and Sangam Literature - The Sangam Assemblies - The Sangam was a college or assembly of Tamil poets, likely held under royal patronage. - The exact number of Sangams and their duration remain uncertain. - A Tamil commentary (8th century A.D.) claims: - Three Sangams lasted for 9,990 years. - Attended by 8,598 poets. - 197 Pandya kings acted as patrons. - These claims are exaggerated, but a Sangam was definitely held in Madurai under royal patronage. - Compilation of Sangam Literature - The available Sangam literature was compiled between A.D. 300-600. - The chronological classification of the texts into early, middle, and late strata is still unclear. - Descriptions in Sangam texts align with: - Greek and Roman accounts. - Archaeological findings. - Writing and Inscriptions - The art of writing was known to Tamils before the Christian era. - Over 70 short inscriptions in the Brahmi script have been found in natural caves (mainly in the Madurai region). - These inscriptions: - Contain an early form of Tamil mixed with Prakrit words. - Date back to 2nd-1st centuries B.C. - Coincide with the arrival of Jaina and Buddhist missionaries in the region. - Inscribed potsherds from excavations confirm the existence of written Tamil at the beginning of the Christian era. - Given this evidence, it is unsurprising that a significant body of Sangam literature was produced in the early centuries of the Christian era, though it was formally compiled by A.D. 600. - Crafts, Trade and Towns in the Post-Maurya Age - - Crafts and Economic Developments (200 B.C.-A.D. 200) - Growth of Crafts and Artisans - The period of Sakas, Kushans, Satavahanas, and early Tamil states was one of the most prosperous in terms of crafts and commerce. - Artisans and Craftsmen: - The Digha Nikaya (pre-Maurya) mentions about 24 occupations. - The Mahavastu (this period) lists 36 kinds of workers in Rajgir. - The Milinda Panho records 75 occupations, 60 of which are craft-based. - Though craftsmen were mainly associated with towns, excavations show their presence in villages as well. - In Karimnagar (Telangana), craftsmen like carpenters, blacksmiths, goldsmiths, and potters lived in separate quarters. - Agricultural laborers lived at one end of the settlement. - Mining and Metallurgy - Eight major metalworking crafts involved: - Gold, silver, lead, tin, copper, brass, iron, and precious stones. - Other metals: Brass, zinc, antimony, and red arsenic. - Iron technology advanced significantly: - Kushan and Satavahana layers contain numerous iron artifacts. - Special progress in iron manufacture was seen in Telangana (Andhra). - Weapons, balance rods, socketed axes, hoes, sickles, ploughshares, razors, and ladles found in Karimnagar and Nalgonda districts. - Indian iron and steel (including cutlery) were exported to Abyssinian ports and highly valued in Western Asia. - Textile and Dyeing Industry - Cloth-making and silk-weaving flourished. - Mathura was a major center for a special type of cloth called sataka. - Dyeing Industry: - Thrived in South India. - Brick-built dyeing vats found in Uraiyur (Tiruchirapalli, Tamil Nadu). - Similar vats excavated at Arikamedu. - These belong to 1st-3rd centuries A.D., a period when the handloom textile industry thrived. - Increased oil production due to the use of the oil wheel. - Luxury and Specialized Crafts - Ivory work, glass manufacture, and bead cutting were prominent. - Excavations in Kushan sites reveal many such products. - Indian ivories found in Afghanistan and Rome resemble those from Satavahana sites in Deccan. - Glass objects from Rome found in Taxila and Afghanistan. - Glass-blowing knowledge entered India around the beginning of the Christian era. - Bead-cutting became widespread, with large numbers of semi-precious stone beads in post-Maurya layers. - Coin-minting: - Coins were made from gold, silver, copper, bronze, lead, and potin. - Fake Roman coins were also produced. - Coin-moulds found in north India and Deccan. - A Satavahana coin-mould could produce six coins at a time. - Terracotta and Sculptural Art - Terracotta production flourished, mainly for urban elite. - Found in large quantities in Kushan and Satavahana sites, especially: - Yelleshwaram (Nalgonda district) - largest number of terracottas and their moulds. - Kondapur (near Hyderabad) - another major center. - Terracotta popularity declined in the Gupta and post-Gupta periods, coinciding with urban decline. - Guilds (associations of craftsmen or merchants) and Economic Organizations - Artisans were organized into guilds, playing a key role in economic life. - Guilds in Maharashtra (2nd century A.D.): - Lay Buddhists deposited money with guilds of potters, oil millers, and weavers to support monks. - Guilds in Mathura: - A chief deposited money with the flour-makers' guild to feed 100 Brahmanas daily. - At least two dozen guilds are known from texts. - Most artisans, based on inscriptions, were concentrated in: - Mathura region. - Western Deccan (major trade route areas). - Trade and Economic Expansion (200 B.C.-A.D. 200) - Roman Trade and Monsoon Navigation - India's trade with the eastern Roman Empire flourished. - Initially, much of the trade was overland, but it was disrupted by Sakas, Parthians, and Kushans (1st century B.C.). - Parthians (Iran) imported iron and steel from India but hindered (obstructed, delayed, or made difficult) trade beyond Iran. - Sea trade expanded (1st century A.D.) with the discovery of monsoon winds, allowing: - Faster sailing across the Arabian Sea. - Access to western ports like Broach ((Bharuch) - Gujarat) and Sopara (Maharashtra). - Eastern ports like Arikamedu (Tamil Nadu) and Tamralipti (West Bengal). - Broach was the most important port, receiving: - Goods from Satavahana, Saka, and Kushan kingdoms. - Imports from Rome and West Asia. - Major Trade Routes - Northwestern Routes (linking Kushan and Saka territories to Broach): - Two major routes converged at Taxila and connected to the Silk Road (Central Asia). - Route 1: - Ran north to south from Taxila to lower Indus basin, then to Broach. - Route 2 (Uttara-patha): - More frequently used. - Taxila → Punjab → Western Yamuna coast → Mathura → Ujjain → Broach. - Eastern Route: - Kausambi (near Allahabad) → Ujjain, linking with western routes. - - Conclusion - The Saka-Kushan-Satavahana period saw unprecedented growth in crafts, metallurgy, textiles, and luxury goods. - Artisans thrived in guilds and were key to urban and religious economic systems. - Trade networks flourished, especially Roman trade via monsoon navigation. - Urban handicrafts, terracotta art, and coin-minting played a vital role in economic expansion. - Foreign Trade with Rome - Nature of Trade - The trade between India and Rome was significant but focused on luxury goods rather than daily necessities. - South India was the first region to establish trade with Rome, as evident from the discovery of early Roman coins in Tamil kingdoms, which were outside Satavahana control. - Major exports from India to Rome included: - Spices (especially from South India) - Muslin (lightweight, finely woven cotton fabric), pearls, jewels, and precious stones (from Central and South India) - Iron goods, particularly cutlery - India's Role in Transit Trade - India acted as an intermediary in trade between China, Central Asia, and the Roman Empire. - Silk was traditionally sent from China to Rome via the Silk Road (passing through North Afghanistan and Iran). - The Parthian control of Iran disrupted this route, leading to alternative trade routes through: - North-western India to western Indian ports - The east coast of India, from where it was sent to the West - As a result, India engaged in significant transit trade in silk. - Roman Imports to India - Key Roman goods exported to India included: - Wine amphorae and pottery (found in Tamluk, Arikamedu, and South India) - Lead (used by the Satavahanas for coin minting, imported in coiled strips) - Roman trade mainly influenced South India and the Satavahana kingdom, with limited penetration into North India. - Despite this, the Kushan-controlled north-western subcontinent engaged in trade with the eastern Roman Empire. - The Roman conquest of Mesopotamia (A.D. 11) and Emperor Trajan's campaigns in the Persian Gulf further facilitated trade. - Roman Influence in India - Roman trade goods and cultural influences reached north-western India and Afghanistan. - At Begram (north of Kabul), artifacts of Western origin were discovered, including: - Large glass jars (from Italy, Egypt, and Syria) - Bronze stands, steel yards, weights, Greco-Roman statues, jugs, and alabaster vessels - Taxila (modern Surkap in Pakistan) revealed Greco-Roman bronze sculptures, silver ornaments, bronze pots, and coins of Emperor Tiberius. - Despite these finds, certain Roman goods (e.g., Arretine pottery) were largely confined to South India. - Both the Satavahanas and the Kushans profited from Roman trade, though the Satavahanas benefited the most. - Impact of Roman Trade on India's Economy - A major Roman export to India was gold and silver coins. - Around 85 Roman coin hoards have been found across India, most of them in the south. - The Roman historian Pliny (A.D. 7) lamented that Rome was being drained of gold due to its trade with India. - Complaints arose in A.D. 22 about the excessive Roman expenditure on Indian pepper (for exotic flavor, medicinal properties, and status as a luxury item), which was called “yavanapriya” (beloved of the Greeks) in Sanskrit. - Similar concerns arose over high prices paid for Indian steel cutlery. - The trade imbalance was so severe that Rome eventually restricted imports of Indian pepper and steel. - Use of Roman Gold in India - Roman gold coins were valued for their intrinsic worth and possibly used in large transactions. - The Kushans issued many gold coins, but not all were minted from Roman gold. - India had a history of gold trade, dating back to the tribute paid to the Iranian Empire in the 5th century B.C. - Potential sources of Indian gold included: - Central Asia - Karnataka - Gold mines in Dhalbhum (South Bihar) - Contact with Rome influenced Indian coinage, leading to the dinar-type gold coins, which became widespread under the Guptas. - However, gold coins were not used in daily transactions, which were conducted using coins made of lead, potin, or copper. - Expansion of the Money Economy - Lead and copper deposits in Andhra allowed for extensive coin minting. - The Satavahanas issued lead or potin coins, while the Kushans produced large numbers of copper coins. - Other ruling groups using copper and bronze coins included: - The Nagas (Central India) - The Yaudheyas (Eastern Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab, and Uttar Pradesh) - The Mitras (rulers of Kausambi, Mathura, Avanti, and Ahichhatra in Uttar Pradesh) - The deep penetration of the money economy in this period coincided with: - The growth of arts and crafts - India's thriving trade with Rome - Urban Settlements - The expansion of crafts, commerce, and the increasing use of money led to the prosperity of numerous towns during this period. - Urban Centers in North India - Several important towns, such as Vaisali, Pataliputra, Varanasi, Kausambi, Sravasti, Hastinapur, Mathura, and Indraprastha (Purana Quila in New Delhi), are mentioned in literary texts and described by Chinese pilgrims. - Most of these towns flourished during the Kushan period (1st-2nd century A.D.), as evidenced by archaeological findings, including terracotta figures found in Ter (Osmanabad district). - Excavations reveal that agate, jasper, and carnelian were extensively worked for bead manufacturing after 200 B.C., utilizing raw materials from the trap bedrock of the Sipra River. - - Urban Centers in the Satavahana Kingdom - The Satavahana kingdom witnessed urban growth parallel to the Kushan and Saka regions. - Major towns of this period include Tagar (Ter), Paithan, Dhanyakataka, Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Broach, Sopara, Arikamedu, and Kaveripattanam. - Excavations indicate well-developed structures, particularly those from the Kushan period at Nagarjunakonda. - - Excavation Findings and Structural Developments - Prosperous Kushan phases have been identified in sites across Bihar (Chirand, Sonpur, Buxar) and Eastern Uttar Pradesh (Ghazipur). - Other thriving urban sites during the Kushan period include Sohgaura, Bhita, Kausambi, Shringaverapur (near Allahabad), Atranjikhera, Meerut, and Muzaffarnagar. - Mathura (Sonkh excavation) reveals seven Kushan layers, compared to only one Gupta layer, indicating a decline in urban activity after the Kushans. - Punjab (Jullundar, Ludhiana, Ropar) and Haryana also show strong evidence of Kushan-era urban development. - Gupta-era structures were often built with reused Kushan bricks, suggesting a decline in urbanization post-Kushan rule. - Ujjain, the most important town in the Saka kingdom (Malwa & western India), held a strategic position at the intersection of major trade routes. - Trade and Urban Growth - Towns flourished due to thriving trade with the Roman Empire and Central Asia. - Urban centers in Punjab and Western Uttar Pradesh prospered as they lay along the north-western (Uttarapatha) trade route, stretching from Mathura to Taxila. - The Kushan Empire ensured security on trade routes, facilitating economic growth. - However, the decline of the Kushan Empire (3rd century A.D.) severely impacted urban settlements. - Decline of Urban Centers - The Roman Empire banned trade with India in the 3rd century A.D., leading to economic setbacks. Few reasons include: - Severe Gold & Silver Drain - Rome imported luxury goods from India (spices, silk, pearls, and cotton) but exported very little in return. - Political Instability in Rome - The Crisis of the Third Century (235-284 CE) saw frequent civil wars, economic collapse, and invasions. - Rise of the Sassanian Empire (224 CE) - The Sassanian Persians (modern Iran) became powerful and blocked Roman trade routes to India. - Decline of Roman Economy - Overreliance on slave labor, debased currency, and internal corruption weakened Rome's economy. - Without trade, artisans and merchants lost their livelihood, resulting in the decline of urban centers. - Archaeological evidence from the Deccan suggests a reduction in urban settlements after the Satavahana phase. - Thus, while urbanization peaked under the Kushans and Satavahanas, its decline was marked by political instability and trade restrictions imposed by Rome. - The Rise and Growth of the Gupta Empire - Background - Emergence of Post-Mauryan Powers - After the decline of the Maurya Empire, two significant powers emerged: - Satavahanas (Deccan & South) - Kushans (North India) - The Satavahanas brought political stability and economic prosperity through trade with the Roman Empire. - The Kushans played a similar role in northern India. - Both empires collapsed by the mid-3rd century AD. - Rise of the Gupta Empire - The Gupta Empire emerged from the ruins of the Kushan Empire. - The Guptas possibly had Vaishya origins. - Although not as vast as the Maurya Empire, they successfully unified northern India for over a century (335-455 AD). - Their original kingdom included Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. - Uttar Pradesh was the core region, as evident from Gupta coins and inscriptions. - The center of power was likely at Prayag (modern Allahabad). - Continuity from the Kushans - The Guptas possibly succeeded the Kushans in Uttar Pradesh without any major time gap. - Archaeological evidence shows that Gupta antiquities immediately follow Kushan remains. - The Guptas adopted military advancements from the Kushans: - Saddles, reins, buttoned coats, trousers, and boots → Ensured greater mobility - Cavalry-based warfare → Similar to the Kushan military strategy - Coins depict horsemen, emphasizing the role of cavalry over chariots & elephants. - Economic and Material Advantages - The Guptas controlled fertile lands in Madhyadesa (Bihar & Uttar Pradesh). - They had access to iron ores in central India & south Bihar, strengthening military capability. - Trade links with the Byzantine Empire (Eastern Roman Empire) boosted their economy. - Due to these advantages, they expanded their rule over: - Anuganga (Middle Gangetic Basin) - Prayag (modern Allahabad) - Saketa (modern Ayodhya) - Magadha - Eventually, this expansion led to the formation of an all-India empire. - Transition from the Kushans & Murundas - Kushan rule in northern India ended around 230 AD. - Central India fell under the Murundas, possibly related to the Kushans. - The Murundas ruled until 250 AD, after which their power declined. - By 275 AD, the Gupta dynasty emerged as the dominant force. - Rulers - Sri Gupta (c. 240-280 CE) - Founder of the Gupta dynasty - Ruled a small kingdom in Magadha (Bihar). - Ghatotkacha (c. 280-319 CE) - Son of Sri Gupta - Expanded the kingdom slightly. - Chandragupta I and the Foundation of Gupta Empire - The first prominent Gupta ruler was Chandragupta I. - He strengthened his position through a strategic marriage with a Lichchhavi princess from Nepal. - The Guptas were possibly Vaishyas, and this marriage into a Kshatriya family enhanced their royal legitimacy. - Took the title "Maharajadhiraja" (King of Kings). - Chandragupta I was an influential ruler, as he: - Started the Gupta Era in 319-320 AD → Marked the beginning of Gupta rule. - Established a stable political base that facilitated future Gupta expansion. - Samudragupta (335-380 AD) - Expansion of the Gupta Kingdom - Samudragupta, the son and successor of Chandragupta I, significantly expanded the Gupta Empire. - Unlike Ashoka, who promoted peace and non-aggression, Samudragupta thrived on war and conquest. - His court poet, Harishena, recorded his military exploits in a long inscription at Allahabad, on the same pillar that carries Ashoka's peaceful edicts. - Patron of arts and music (depicted playing the veena on coins). - Conquests of Samudragupta - His military campaigns can be divided into five groups: - Group One: Conquest of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab - Defeated local princes and incorporated their kingdoms into the Gupta Empire. - Group Two: Subjugation of the Eastern Himalayan and Frontier States - A "frontier" refers to a transitional zone or borderland between a dominant power and less controlled or independent neighboring territories, often characterized by a mix of cultures and interactions. - Defeated rulers of Nepal, Assam, Bengal, and other republics in Punjab. - Group Three: Control over the Vindhya Forest Kingdoms (Atavika Rajyas) - Brought the tribal forest kingdoms under Gupta authority. - Group Four: Victories in Eastern Deccan & South India - Defeated twelve rulers from the eastern Deccan and Tamil Nadu. - Reached Kanchi (Tamil Nadu), where the Pallavas accepted his suzerainty. - Unlike in the north, he defeated but later liberated these rulers. - Group Five: Defeat of the Sakas and Kushans - Ousted the Sakas and Kushans, some of whom ruled in Afghanistan. - Several distant rulers submitted to him. - Influence Beyond India - Samudragupta's power was recognized even outside India. - A Chinese source mentions that Meghavarman, the ruler of Sri Lanka, sent a missionary to seek permission to build a Buddhist temple at Gaya. - Samudragupta granted this request, leading to the development of a major monastic center. - Legacy - The Allahabad inscription suggests that Samudragupta was never defeated in battle. - Due to his military brilliance and conquests, he is often called “The Napoleon of India.” - He successfully unified a vast part of India, and his influence extended across the subcontinent. - - Chandragupta II (A.D. 380-412) - Peak of Gupta power - Expansion of the Gupta Empire - Chandragupta II expanded the empire through marriage alliances and military conquests. - He married his daughter, Prabhavati, to a Vakataka prince (a Brahmana ruler of central India). - After the prince's death, his young son succeeded him, making Prabhavati the virtual (something that exists in effect but not physically) ruler. - Prabhavati governed with the assistance of an official sent by Chandragupta II, allowing him to exercise indirect control over the Vakataka kingdom. - This control provided strategic advantages, enabling him to conquer western Malwa and Gujarat, which had been under Saka rule for nearly four centuries. - Significance of the Western Conquest - The victory over Malwa and Gujarat gave Chandragupta II access to the western seacoast, a region famous for trade and commerce. - This boosted the prosperity of Malwa, particularly its chief city, Ujjain. - Ujjain became so important that Chandragupta II is believed to have made it the second capital of the Gupta Empire. - Military Achievements and the Iron Pillar Inscription - The Iron Pillar inscription near Qutb Minar, Delhi, glorifies the achievements of a king named Chandra. - If Chandra is identified as Chandragupta II, it suggests he established Gupta authority in north-western India and a significant part of Bengal. - Title of Vikramaditya & Patronage of Scholars - Chandragupta II adopted the title Vikramaditya, originally used by a ruler of Ujjain in 58 B.C. to mark his victory over the Sakas. - His court at Ujjain was adorned by many scholars, including the Aryabhata, Varahamihira. renowned poet Kalidasa and lexicographer Amarasimha. - Fa-Hsien's Visit to India (399-414 A.D.) - During Chandragupta II's reign, the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Fa-Hsien visited India. - He wrote an elaborate account of Indian society, providing valuable insights into Gupta-era life. - - Kumaragupta I (c. 415-455 CE) - Maintained the empire's prosperity - Established Nalanda University. - Faced threats from Pushyamitras and Hunas. - Skandagupta (c. 455-467 CE) - Fought the Huna invasions - Weakened the empire by defending against Hunas (White Huns). - After his death, the empire started declining. - Successors (Decline Phase) (c. 467-550 CE) - Puru Gupta (467-473 CE) - Narasimhagupta Baladitya (473-495 CE) - Buddhagupta (495-540 CE) - Vishnugupta (c. 540-550 CE) - Last known Gupta ruler - Fall of the Gupta Empire - Huna Invasions and Military Decline - After Chandragupta II, his successors faced invasions by the Hunas from Central Asia in the second half of the fifth century A.D. - Initially, Skandagupta successfully resisted the Hunas, but his successors proved weak against them. - The Hunas excelled in horsemanship, possibly used metal stirrups, and were skilled archers, achieving military success in both Iran and India. - By 485 A.D., the Hunas occupied eastern Malwa and central India, with Punjab and Rajasthan also falling under their control. - The Gupta Empire shrank significantly at the beginning of the sixth century due to these invasions. - Yasodharman's Challenge to Gupta Authority - The Huna power was later overthrown by Yasodharman of Malwa. - Yasodharman dealt the final, decisive blow to the Hunas, effectively breaking their power in India. - After defeating the foreign invaders, he didn't hand the land back to the Guptas. Instead, he turned around and challenged the Gupta Emperor’s authority. - In 532 A.D., Yasodharman successfully challenged the Guptas and erected pillars of victory to commemorate his conquests across northern India. - Though his rule was short-lived, it severely weakened the Guptas. - Rise of Feudatories and Regional Powers - Several governors and feudatories appointed by the Guptas began asserting independence: - North Bengal and Samatata (Southeast Bengal) rulers became autonomous. - The Later Guptas of Magadha emerged as a separate power in Bihar. - The Maukharis, with their capital at Kanauj, rose to power in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. - Independent princes in northern Madhya Pradesh issued land grants in their own name, though they still used the Gupta era for dating. - The rulers of Valabhi established authority in Gujarat and western Malwa. - The princes of Thaneswar gained control in Haryana and eventually moved towards Kanauj. - Economic Decline and Loss of Trade - The loss of western India by the end of the fifth century deprived the Guptas of wealth from trade and commerce, severely impacting their economy. - Land grants for religious and other purposes further weakened state revenues, making it difficult to maintain a large professional army. - Decline in foreign trade also affected economic stability: - A silk weaver guild migrated from Gujarat to Malwa in 473 A.D. and took up non-productive professions, indicating reduced demand for their goods. - The benefits of Gujarat's trade gradually disappeared. - Currency Debasement and the Final Decline - From the mid-fifth century, the Gupta kings tried to maintain their gold currency by reducing the gold content, but this failed to restore stability. - After Skandagupta II's reign (A.D. 467), almost no Gupta coins or inscriptions were found in western Malwa and Saurashtra, indicating a complete loss of control over the region. - Though the Imperial Guptas continued to rule until the mid-sixth century, their glory had faded a century earlier. - Life in the Gupta Age - System of Administration - Monarchical Structure and Kingship - Unlike the Mauryas, the Gupta rulers adopted grand titles such as paramesvara, maharajadhiraja, and paramabhattaraka, reflecting their supremacy over lesser kings within their empire. - Kingship was hereditary, but the absence of a strict primogeniture system (system or practice where the eldest son inherits the entire estate, throne, or position of the father) led to succession disputes, allowing chiefs and high officials to exploit uncertainties. - The Guptas maintained strong ties with the Brahmanical order by making generous gifts to Brahmanas, who, in turn, glorified the king as Vishnu, the preserver. Coins often depicted the goddess Lakshmi as Vishnu's consort. - Military Organization - The size of the Gupta army is unknown, but the king maintained a standing army, supplemented by forces from feudatories. - Military tactics evolved, with cavalry and horse archery gaining prominence, while chariots became obsolete. - Taxation and Revenue Administration - Land taxes increased, while trade and commerce taxes declined. - The king collected taxes ranging from one-fourth to one-sixth of agricultural produce. - Villagers were required to provide food and supplies for the army and royal officers. In central and western India, peasants were subjected to vishti (forced labor) for serving the army and officials. - Judicial System - The Gupta period saw the development of a structured legal system with separate civil and criminal laws. - Criminal law covered offenses like theft and adultery, while civil law addressed disputes over property and inheritance. - Laws varied according to varna distinctions. - The king, assisted by Brahmana priests, was responsible for upholding justice. Guilds had autonomy in governing their own affairs. - Bureaucracy and Administration - The Gupta administrative system was less elaborate than that of the Mauryas. - The most important officials were the kumaramatyas, appointed by the king and likely paid in cash. - Unlike the Mauryas, the Guptas (who were probably of Vaisya origin) recruited officials beyond the upper varnas. - Offices became hereditary, consolidating power but weakening central control. - Provincial and Local Governance - The empire was divided into divisions (bhuktis), each governed by an uparika. - Bhuktis were further divided into districts (vishayas), administered by vishaya-patis. - In eastern India, vishayas were subdivided into vithis, which contained multiple villages. - Role of Village and Urban Administration - The village headman gained importance, managing local affairs with the help of elders. No land transaction could occur without their approval. - Urban administration relied on professional guilds (shrenis) consisting of artisans, merchants, and scribes, who governed town affairs. - Artisans and bankers had their own guilds, which regulated their members and enforced trade laws. - Guilds flourished in places like Vaisali, Bhita, Mandasor, and Indore, enjoying immunities and self-governance. - Feudalism (social, economic, and political system in which land was the main source of power) in the Gupta Empire - The empire was largely managed by feudatories, many of whom were subjugated by Samudragupta. - Vassal chiefs had three primary obligations: 1. Attending the Gupta court. 2. Paying tribute. 3. Offering daughters in marriage to the ruling family. - Feudatory chiefs received charters, marked with the royal Garuda seal, granting them autonomy in their regions. - Land Grants and Economic Impact - The Gupta period saw an increase in fiscal and administrative land grants, particularly in Madhya Pradesh. - Religious beneficiaries (Brahmanas) received tax-free land and were authorized to collect taxes from peasants. These villages were exempt from royal jurisdiction. - It is unclear whether state officials were compensated with land grants, though the circulation of gold coins suggests that higher officials were paid in cash. - Economic Changes: Decline of Trade and Rise of Landed Classes - Fa-hsien's accounts indicate that Magadha had thriving cities and wealthy Buddhist patrons. - However, foreign trade declined significantly after A.D. 550, particularly with the Eastern Roman Empire, which learned silk production, reducing India's silk exports. - As early as the mid-5th century, a silk-weaving guild from western India (Lata) migrated to Mandasor, where members abandoned their trade due to declining demand. - Emergence of Landed Aristocracy - Land grants to priests facilitated agricultural expansion but reduced local peasants to lower socio-economic status. - In central and western India, peasants were subjected to forced labor (vishti), increasing their burdens. - Social and Religious Developments During the Gupta Period - Brahmana Supremacy and Caste System - The Guptas, originally Vaisyas, were elevated to Kshatriya status by the brahmanas. - Brahmanas gained wealth and privileges through numerous land grants, as outlined in the law-book of Narada. - They depicted Gupta rulers as possessing divine attributes, strengthening their influence. - Caste Expansion and Integration of Foreigners - The caste system expanded due to the assimilation of foreigners and tribal groups. - Many foreign conquerors, including the Hunas, were assigned Kshatriya status. The Hunas were later classified as one of the thirty-six Rajput clans, and some Rajputs still carry the title Huna. - Tribal chiefs integrated into brahmanical society were granted high status, while common tribal members were often assigned a lower caste. - Status of Sudras and Women - Sudras and women gained some social privileges, such as the right to listen to the epics and Puranas. - Krishna worship became accessible to them. - From the seventh century onward, Sudras were increasingly identified as agriculturists rather than servants or laborers. - Increase in Untouchability - The number of untouchables, especially the Chandalas, grew during this period. - Fa-hsien observed that Chandalas lived outside villages, worked in trades related to meat, and were considered polluting by upper castes. - Religious Transformations - Decline of Buddhism - Buddhism lost royal patronage under the Guptas. - While Fa-hsien noted its presence, it had declined significantly, especially in Magadha. - Rise of Brahmanism and Vaishnavism - Vishnu and Shiva became the most revered deities, with Vishnu emerging as the protector of the varna system. - Key texts such as the Vishnupurana and Vishnusmriti were compiled in his honor. - By the fourth century A.D., the Bhagavad Gita promoted devotion to Krishna and reinforced caste duties. - Religious Practices and Festivals - Idol worship in temples became widespread. - Agricultural festivals were integrated into religious traditions, providing income for priests. - Religious Tolerance - The Gupta rulers did not persecute Buddhists or Jains. - Buddhism itself had absorbed several Hindu elements, reducing religious conflicts. - Art and Culture During the Gupta Period - Patronage of Art and Literature - - The Gupta period is often called the “Golden Age” of ancient India, though economically, some northern Indian towns declined. - The Guptas possessed a large amount of gold and issued the most gold coins. - Princes and wealthy individuals supported artists and scholars. - Samudragupta is depicted on his coins playing the vina (lute), showcasing his musical patronage. - Chandragupta II is credited with maintaining the Nine Luminaries—great scholars at his court. - Akbar modeled his court after the ancient Indian tradition of the "Navaratnas" (Nine Gems). - Religious Influence on Art - Ancient Indian art was primarily inspired by religion. - Buddhism had earlier led to the construction of stone pillars, cave carvings, and stupas (dome-shaped relic structures). - The Gupta period saw an evolution in Buddhist and Hindu art, with significant advancements in sculpture and painting. - - Buddhist Art and Architecture - The Gupta period produced some of the most exquisite Buddhist artworks. - A 2-meter-high bronze Buddha statue was discovered in Sultanganj, Bhagalpur. - Fa-hsien reported seeing a 25-meter-high copper Buddha statue, but it is no longer traceable. - - Notable Buddhist art centers: - Sarnath and Mathura - produced beautiful Buddha images. - Ajanta paintings - the finest example of Gupta-era Buddhist art, depicting scenes from Gautama Buddha's life and earlier Buddhas. - The Ajanta paintings are known for their lifelike depictions and vibrant colors, which have remained intact for over 14 centuries. - - Rise of Hindu Iconography - As supporters of Brahmanism, the Guptas saw the emergence of Hindu deities in sculpture. - - Images of Vishnu, Shiva, and other gods appeared, often arranged in a hierarchical pantheon: - The chief deity is depicted larger in size. - Retainers and subordinate gods appear smaller, symbolizing social and divine hierarchy. - - Architecture - The Gupta period saw limited architectural achievements, primarily brick and stone temples: - Bhitargaon (Kanpur) - a notable brick temple. - Bhitari (Ghazipur) and Deogarh (Jhansi) - other examples of Gupta brick architecture. - The Buddhist university at Nalanda, established in the fifth century, had its earliest brick structures from this period. - Literature During the Gupta Period - Secular Literature - The Gupta period was remarkable for the production of secular literature. - Bhasa wrote thirteen plays, but Kalidasa's works made this era truly famous. - Kalidasa - The Greatest Sanskrit Poet & Dramatist - Author of famous plays like Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta, and Raghuvamsha. - Abhijnanasakuntalam is considered one of the world's greatest literary works. - Abhijnanashakuntalam was one of the first Indian works translated into European languages, alongside the Bhagavad Gita. - Known as the Shakespeare of India. - Patronized by Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya). - Vishnu Sharma - The Author of Panchatantra - Wrote Panchatantra, a collection of moral stories using animal characters. - One of the earliest works of political science and ethics. - Sudraka - The Playwright - Wrote Mrichchhakatika (The Little Clay Cart), a famous Sanskrit drama. - It depicted the life of common people, traders, and courtesans. - Distinctive Features of Gupta Plays: - All plays from this period were comedies—no tragedies are known. - Language variation: - Higher-class characters spoke Sanskrit, while women and Shudras used Prakrit. - Religious Literature - The Ramayana and Mahabharata were likely compiled, expanded, and refined in the 4th century A.D. - Ramayana: - Depicts Rama's exile and his battle against Ravana to rescue Sita. - Emphasizes ideal family relationships: - A son must obey his father. - A younger brother must obey his elder brother. - A wife must be faithful to her husband. - Theme: - The triumph of righteousness (Rama) over evil (Ravana). - Mahabharata: - Narrates the conflict between the Pandavas and Kauravas over kingship. - Highlights the idea that “kingship knows no kinship.” - The Bhagavad Gita, part of the Mahabharata, teaches: - One must perform their duties based on caste and rank without expecting rewards. - Theme: - Victory of righteousness over evil. - Puranas: - Compiled during the Gupta period, these texts contained myths, legends, and sermons for educating common people. - This period also saw the compilation of Smritis (law-books in verse), with commentaries on them emerging later. - Development of Sanskrit Grammar - Sanskrit grammar was further refined, based on the works of Panini and Patanjali. - Patanjali (Influence in Gupta Period) - Earlier, he wrote the Mahabhashya on Sanskrit grammar. - His work influenced linguistics and yoga studies in the Gupta era. - Amarasimha - The Lexicographer - Amarasimha, a scholar in Chandragupta I's court, compiled Amarakosa, a Sanskrit thesaurus (dictionary) memorized by students. - Important for linguistic studies and Sanskrit grammar. - Classical Literary Style - The Gupta period was a golden phase of classical literature, known for its ornate Sanskrit style. - Key literary trends: - Verse gained prominence over prose. - Commentaries on existing texts began to emerge. - Science and Technology During the Gupta Period - Mathematics and Astronomy - Aryabhata (476 CE - 550 CE) - The Mathematician & Astronomer - Aryabhata, a mathematician from Pataliputra, wrote the Aryabhatiya, a key mathematical and astronomical text, which showcased his expertise in various calculations. - Introduced the concept of zero and the decimal system. - Explained the heliocentric theory (Earth rotates on its axis). - Calculated pi (π ≈ 3.1416) and the approximate value of a year (365.25 days). - Brahmagupta - Mathematician & Astronomer (Later Gupta Period, 598 CE) - Wrote Brahmasphutasiddhanta, which expanded Aryabhata's work. - First to use zero as a number and describe negative numbers. - Varahamihira - The Astronomer & Astrologer - Author of Brihat Samhita, an encyclopedia on astronomy, astrology, and meteorology. - Introduced the concept of horoscopy in India. - Stated that the Earth is spherical. - Other important works - A Gupta inscription from 448 A.D. (Allahabad) indicates that the decimal system was known in India by the early 5th century. - In astronomy, the Romaka Sidhanta was compiled, incorporating Greek influences. - Medical science - Dhanvantri - The Father of Ayurveda - Court physician of the Guptas, regarded as the pioneer of Ayurveda. - Wrote about surgical techniques, medicinal herbs, and treatments. - Geography - Shanku - The Geographer - Contributed to geography and cartography (map-making). - Wrote about land measurement techniques. - Metallurgy and Craftsmanship - Gupta craftsmen excelled in iron and bronze work. - Bronze Buddha images were mass-produced, aided by advancements in iron technology. - The Mehrauli Iron Pillar (Delhi), manufactured in the 4th century A.D., is a remarkable example of iron craftsmanship: - Originally it was probably installed at Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh) and later shifted to Delhi under Delhi Sultanate as a symbol of power and authority - It has remained rust-free for over 1,500 years. - Western iron foundries could not replicate such a feat until recent centuries. - Unfortunately, later artisans failed to build upon this metallurgical expertise. - - Spread of Civilization in Eastern India - Signs of Civilization in Eastern India (4th-7th Century A.D.) - Defining Civilization - A society is considered civilized if it possesses: - Writing skills, a taxation system, and law enforcement mechanisms. - Social classes and specialized roles in priestly, administrative, and productive functions. - The ability to produce surplus goods, supporting both producers (artisans, peasants) and non-producing consumers. - Delayed Civilization in Eastern India - In eastern Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, West Bengal, Bangladesh, and Assam, these elements appeared much later. - Before the mid-4th century A.D., no significant written records exist in these regions. - Spread of Civilization (4th-7th Century A.D.) - This period saw the expansion of an advanced rural economy, formation of state systems, and social class distinctions in: - Eastern Madhya Pradesh - Orissa - Eastern and Southeast Bengal - Assam - The distribution of Gupta-era inscriptions in these regions demonstrates this cultural diffusion. - Role of Land Grants in Cultural Expansion - Many inscriptions are land grant records issued by feudatory princes and others. - These grants were primarily for religious purposes, benefiting: - Brahmanas and Buddhists - Vaishnavite temples and Buddhist monasteries - The beneficiaries of these grants played a crucial role in spreading and strengthening civilization. - A region-wise analysis helps understand this process in detail. - Political and Cultural Developments in Orissa and Eastern & Southern Madhya Pradesh - Early State Formation and Trade in Kalinga (Coastal Orissa) - Kalinga (Coastal Orissa, south of the Mahanadi) rose to prominence under Ashoka, but a strong state was established only in the 1st century B.C. under Kharavela, who advanced as far as Magadha. - In the 1st and 2nd centuries A.D., Orissa's ports engaged in trade of pearls, ivory, and muslin, with archaeological evidence from Sisupalgarh (Kalinganagari, 60 km from Bhubaneswar) indicating Roman trade connections. - However, northern Orissa did not experience significant state formation or commercial activity. - Gupta Conquests and State Expansion (4th-6th Century A.D.) - Samudragupta's conquests (4th century A.D.) included Kosala and Mahakantara (covering parts of northern and western Orissa). - From the second half of the 4th century to the 6th century, multiple regional states emerged, with at least five identifiable kingdoms: - Matharas (Pitṛbhaktas) - Dominated the region between Mahanadi and Krishna rivers. - Vasisthas - Ruled in south Kalinga near Andhra. - Nalas - Controlled the forest areas of Mahakantara. - Manas - Occupied coastal Orissa, beyond the Mahanadi. - Each state developed systems of taxation, administration, and military organization. The Nalas and Manas also introduced their own coinage. - The rulers favored Brahmanas through land grants, performed Vedic sacrifices, and sought power, prestige, and legitimacy. - Economic and Administrative Advancements - Advanced culture spread beyond the coastal regions into other parts of Orissa and Eastern Madhya Pradesh. - The discovery of Nala gold coins in Bastar (Madhya Pradesh) suggests an economy with large-scale monetary transactions. - Manas-issued copper coins, indicating the use of metallic currency among artisans and peasants. - States increased revenue by creating new fiscal units in rural areas: - Matharas established Mahendrabhoga (in the Mahendra mountains). - Dantayavagubhoga district, supplying ivory and rice-gruel for administrators, was formed in a less developed area. - Brahmanical land grants (agraharas): - These lands funded religious and educational activities. - Some grants remained taxable, unlike those in other parts of India. - Agricultural improvements: - Brahmana-led cultivation expansion in tribal, forest, and red soil regions. - The introduction of detailed seasonal divisions: - Earlier there were three seasons of four months each. - Under the Matharas (5th century A.D.) the year was divided into 12 lunar months, improving weather-based agricultural planning. - Spread of Writing and Sanskritization - Writing was known in coastal Orissa since the 3rd century B.C., with Prakrit inscriptions continuing until the mid-4th century A.D. - From A.D. 350 onward, Sanskrit became the dominant language, spreading beyond the coastal region, north of the Mahanadi. - Sanskrit's influence extended to Brahmanical religion, law, and social structures: - Royal charters began quoting Puranas and Dharmasastras. - Kings claimed to uphold the varna system and align themselves with the Gangetic cultural traditions. - The holy dip at Prayag (confluence of Ganga and Yamuna) became a symbol of spiritual merit, attracting victorious kings. - Bengal - Early Writing and Settlements - Writing was prevalent in north Bengal during Asoka's time, as evidenced by an inscription in Bogra district. - Local settlements maintained storehouses filled with coins and food grains for Buddhist monks, indicating tax payments and surplus production. - Prakrit and Buddhism were known in this region. - In the second century B.C., an inscription from Noakhali (south-east Bengal) also confirms knowledge of Prakrit and Brahmi script. - Political Developments (4th-6th Century A.D.) - By the mid-4th century, a ruler with the title of Maharaja governed Pokhatna (Damodara, Bankura district). He was a devotee of Vishnu and possibly granted a village to a deity. - By the 5th and 6th centuries, the region between the Ganga and Brahmaputra (now Bangladesh) had become a settled, Sanskrit-educated region. - Around A.D. 550, Gupta governors became independent and ruled north Bengal, though parts may have been under Kamarupa. - Local vassal rulers, called Samaniya Maharajas, developed administrative and military structures, including horses, elephants, foot soldiers, and boats for taxation and warfare. - By A.D. 600, the area was known as Gauda, with Sasanka as its ruler, a rival of Harsha. - Land Transactions and Agriculture - Between A.D. 432-433, numerous land sale records on copper plates were found in Pundravardhanabhukti (north Bengal, now mostly in Bangladesh). -
