Land was often bought using gold coins (dinara) and granted for religious purposes, making it tax-exempt. - These records indicate an active local administration involving scribes, merchants, artisans, and landowners under Gupta-appointed governors. - Most land grants describe the land as uncultivated and tax-free, implying expansion of agriculture and settlement. - Development in Deltaic Bengal (Samatata & Vanga) - The deltaic region (Brahmaputra basin, Samatata) acknowledged Samudragupta's authority. - South-east Bengal was likely not ruled by Brahmanized princes, lacking Sanskrit and the varna system, unlike north Bengal. - Around A.D. 525, a structured state emerged, covering Samatata and parts of Vanga, issuing gold coins in the late 6th century. - By the 7th century, the Khadga kingdom (Dacca area), Lokanatha's Brahmana feudatory kingdom, and the Ratas (Comilla area) had formed. - These rulers issued land grants and created agraharas (Brahmana land endowments). - Social and Cultural Progress - Sanskrit culture spread, leading to sophisticated poetic meters by the second half of the 7th century. - Fiscal and administrative units, like Dandabhukti (border of Bengal and Orissa), were created to manage tribal populations and promote Sanskrit-based culture. - Vardhamanabhukti (Burdwan) emerged as a center in the 7th century. - Land grants in Faridpur (south-east Bengal) and Comilla show the transformation of forested and waterlogged regions into cultivated lands. - Formation of Multiple States (Mid-5th to 7th Century) - This period saw the rise of nearly half a dozen states, some independent and others feudatory. - Each state had a military camp, maintained cavalry, elephants, boats, and tax-collection systems. - Expansion occurred through warfare and land grants to Buddhists and Brahmanas. - The rise in land endowments led to the appointment of an Agrithartkahad officer to oversee them. - Land Ownership and Governance - Initially, land was owned collectively by tribes and communities, with grants given to priests. - Later, individual families gained land ownership, but the community still influenced sales and donations. - Over time, kings claimed more land and rights, enabling them to grant land and collect taxes. - Sanskrit, the official language of the Puranas and Dharmasastras, was known to administrative functionaries, emphasizing the spread of Brahmanical culture. - Conclusion - The 5th-7th centuries marked a crucial phase in Bengal's history, with political consolidation, land expansion, and cultural Sanskritization. - The transition from tribal to organized state systems signified the advancement of civilization in the region. - Assam - Early Settlements and Political Developments - Kamarupa, covering the Brahmaputra basin, gained prominence in the 7th century. - However, excavations in Ambari (near Gauhati) indicate settlements existed as early as the 4th century A.D. - In the same period, Samudragupta received tributes from Davaka (possibly in Nowgong district) and Kamarupa, suggesting their rulers were tribute-collecting chiefs from tribal peasantry. - Growth of Settlements and Cultural Influence - Excavations confirm developed settlements in Ambari by the 6th and 7th centuries, supported by inscriptions. - By the early 6th century, Sanskrit and writing were in active use. - Kamarupa kings adopted the title “Yarman,” a designation found across northern, central, and southern India. - They solidified their power through land grants to Brahmanas. - Rise of Bhaskaravarman (7th Century) - Bhaskaravarman emerged as a powerful ruler, controlling much of the Brahmaputra basin and areas beyond. - Buddhism gained influence in Kamarupa during this time. - The Chinese traveler Hsuan Tsang (Hieun Tsang) visited Kamarupa, further documenting its development. - The Formative Phase of Eastern India (4th-7th Century) - Spread of Civilization and Cultural Developments - Different parts of eastern India gained prominence at varying times, but their formative phase spanned from the 4th to the 7th century. - This period saw the spread of writing, Sanskrit learning, Vedic rituals, Brahmanical social classes, and state systems across: - Eastern Madhya Pradesh - North Orissa - West Bengal - Bangladesh - Assam - Gupta influence played a key role in stimulating cultural and state formation, as seen in: - Direct rule over north Bengal and north-west Orissa - Use of the Gupta era in inscriptions across the region - Political and Economic Advancements - New states emerged in Bengal, where rulers built strong military camps with elephants, horses, and boats, funded by taxation from rural communities. - 5th-6th centuries marked major developments, including: - Large-scale writing and use of Sanskrit - Formation of a varna-based society - Growth of Buddhism, Brahmanism, Saivism, and Vaishnavism - Decline of communal land authority, with private property and land transactions using gold coins - Agriculture and trade flourished, supported by: - Iron ploughshare agriculture - Wet paddy cultivation (noted by Kalidasa in Vanga) - High-quality sugarcane production in north Bengal - Growth of crafts and a food-surplus economy - Expansion into Outlying Regions - The decline of the Gupta empire coincided with rapid development in previously remote and less-inhabited areas, such as: - Red soil regions of West Bengal, north Orissa, and Chotanagpur plateau, which were difficult to cultivate - Jungle areas with alluvial soil and heavy rainfall in Bangladesh and the Brahmaputra basin - These regions, once ruled by tribal chiefs, gradually integrated into state systems and became part of historical records. - Harsha and His Times - Harsha's Kingdom (A.D. 606-647) - Political Background and Rise of Harsha - The Gupta empire ruled northern and western India for about 160 years, with power centered in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, until its decline in the mid-6th century. - Following their fall, northern India fragmented into multiple kingdoms. - The White Hunas dominated Kashmir, Punjab, and western India from around A.D. 500. - North and western India were divided among several feudatories, who took control of the former Gupta territories. - Gradually, one ruling family from Thanesar (Haryana) expanded its control over these feudatories. - The leader responsible for this consolidation of power was Harshavardhana (A.D. 606-647). - Kanauj: The New Political Center - Harsha shifted his capital from Thanesar to Kanauj, which then became a major political and military center. - Decline of Pataliputra: - Pataliputra had thrived on trade, commerce, and taxation from traders using its four river routes. - However, with the decline of trade and scarcity of money, officials and soldiers were instead compensated through land grants, reducing Pataliputra's importance. - Rise of Kanauj: - With its strategic location in the doab (Farrukhabad, Uttar Pradesh), Kanauj emerged as a key fortified military center. - Unlike the plains, Kanauj's elevated position made it easier to defend. - Troops could be moved swiftly using both land and water routes, allowing control over the eastern and western doab. - Its emergence under Harsha symbolized the transition from a pre-feudal to a feudal political order in northern India. - Sources of Harsha's Reign - Banabhatta, his court poet, chronicled his life in the Harshacharita. - Chinese traveler Hsuan Tsang (Hieun Tsang) visited India in the 7th century A.D., staying for 15 years and providing valuable insights. - Harsha's inscriptions mention various taxes and officials, reflecting the administrative system of his time. - Extent of Harsha's Empire and Challenges - Harsha is often termed the last great Hindu emperor of northern India, but this is only partially true. - His direct rule extended over Rajasthan, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Orissa, with his influence spreading beyond these regions. - Several peripheral states acknowledged his sovereignty, but he never controlled the entire Indian subcontinent. - His southward expansion was checked at the Narmada River by Pulakesin II, the Chalukyan ruler of Karnataka and Maharashtra (capital: Badami, modern Bijapur district). - Despite this setback, Harsha faced no major opposition and succeeded in bringing political unity to a significant part of India. - Administration Under Harsha - Feudal and Decentralized Governance - Harsha's administration followed a structure similar to the Gupta system but became more feudal and decentralized over time. - His empire relied heavily on feudatories, who played a crucial role in governance and military support. - Military Strength: - Harsha reportedly had an army of 100,000 horses and 60,000 elephants, a number far exceeding that of the Mauryas (who had 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants despite controlling a much larger territory). - This vast military force was possible because Harsha could mobilize his feudatories, who provided foot soldiers and horses in times of war. - Land Grants and Revenue System - Land grants continued under Harsha, given to priests for religious services and officers as rewards for their service. - Administrative Charters: - Officers received land grants via charters, similar to earlier practices. - These grants provided privileges to priests as seen in previous dynasties. - Hsuan Tsang's Account: - Harsha's revenue was divided into four parts: 1. Royal expenditures (for the king's needs). 2. Scholars and education. 3. Public servants and administration. 4. Religious purposes. - Ministers and high-ranking officials were granted land, marking the beginning of feudal practices in administration. - Law and Order - Harsha's administration struggled with maintaining internal security. - Robbery and Crime: - Despite Harsha's efforts, robbery was common. Even Hsuan Tsang, a royal guest, was robbed during his travels. - Harsh Punishments: - Robbery was considered treason, and the punishment was amputation of the right hand. - However, due to the influence of Buddhism, punishments were often softened, and criminals were instead imprisoned for life. - Hsuan Tsang's Account of Harsha's Reign - Journey and Purpose - The Chinese pilgrim Hsuan Tsang visited India during Harsha's reign, leaving China in A.D. 629 and returning in A.D. 645. - His primary purpose was to study at the Buddhist university of Nalanda (Bihar) and collect Buddhist texts. - He spent several years at Harsha's court, traveling extensively across India. - His account provides a richer and more detailed description of India's economic, social, and religious life compared to Fa-hsien's earlier account. - Observations on Cities - Declining Cities: - Pataliputra and Vaisali had lost their former glory. - Rising Cities: - Prayag (Allahabad) and Kanauj in the Gangetic doab had become prominent political and cultural centers. - Society and Social Classes - Brahmanas and Kshatriyas: - Lived simple lives, in contrast to the nobles and priests, who enjoyed luxurious lifestyles. - Sudras as Agriculturists: - Hsuan Tsang's account is significant as he describes Sudras as agriculturalists, unlike earlier texts, which portrayed them as servants of the three higher varnas. - Untouchables and Social Exclusion: - He mentions scavengers and executioners as untouchables, living outside villages. - They consumed garlic and onions, and their presence was announced loudly so others could avoid contact with them. - Buddhism and Nalanda Under Harsha - State of Buddhism - During Hsuan Tsang's visit, Buddhism had fragmented into 18 sects. - Many old Buddhist centers had declined, but Nalanda emerged as the most prominent. - Nalanda University - Nalanda was a renowned Buddhist university, reportedly housing 10,000 students, all of whom were monks. - Excavations reveal an impressive complex, constructed and renovated over 700 years (5th century A.D. onward). - However, evidence suggests the monastery could not have accommodated 10,000 monks. - I-tsing account - By A.D. 670, Chinese pilgrim I-tsing recorded only 3,000 monks, which seems a more realistic estimate. - The university was financially supported by revenues from 200 villages. - Nalanda remained a major monastic center during Harsha's reign. - - Harsha's Religious Policy - Initially a Shaivite, Harsha later became a great patron of Buddhism. - He followed a tolerant religious policy, supporting multiple faiths. - He organized a grand assembly at Prayag, attended by tributary princes, ministers, and nobles. - An image of Buddha was worshipped. - Hsuan Tsang delivered discourses. - At the end of the event, Harsha made generous donations, keeping only his personal clothing. - Hsuan Tsang describes Harsha as kind, courteous, and helpful, with free movement granted to the pilgrim across the empire. - Harsha as a Literary Patron - Harsha was a literary figure, having authored three plays. - He patronized scholars, including his court poet Banabhatta. - Banabhatta's Harshacharita provides a glorified account of Harsha's early life, written in an ornate ( highly decorative, elaborate, and intricate form of expression in art, architecture, literature, or speech) style that influenced later writers. - Formation of New States and Rural Expansion in the Peninsula - The New Phase (c. A.D. 300-750) - - Political Developments - This period marks the second historical phase in the regions south of the Vindhyas, continuing some trends from the first phase (c. 200 B.C. - A.D. 300) while introducing new developments. - First Phase (200 B.C. - A.D. 300): - Satavahanas dominated the Deccan. - Tamil kingdoms ruled the southern districts of Tamil Nadu. - Northern Tamil Nadu, southern Karnataka, southern Maharashtra, and the land between the Godavari and the Mahanadi remained under external political control, lacking independent states. - Second Phase (A.D. 300-750): - Between A.D. 300 and 600, around two dozen states emerged, as evidenced by land charters. - - By the seventh century, three major states had solidified their power: - Pallavas of Kanchi - Chalukyas of Badami - Pandyas of Madurai - Economic and Agrarian Changes - The first historical phase was characterized by: - Thriving crafts. - Internal and external trade. - Extensive coin usage. - Numerous towns. - The second phase saw a decline in trade, towns, and coinage - A significant feature of this period was the large-scale land grants to Brahmanas, often tax-free. - These land grants indicate that new areas were brought under cultivation, leading to agrarian expansion and rural settlement growth. - Religious and Cultural Shifts - This period saw the rise of Brahmanism, replacing earlier Buddhist and Jain influences. - First Phase (200 B.C. - A.D. 300): - Buddhist monuments were widespread in Andhra and Maharashtra. - Jainism and Buddhism were present in southern Tamil Nadu. - Second Phase (A.D. 300-750): - Jainism became confined to Karnataka. - Vedic sacrifices were frequently performed by kings across the peninsula. - The construction of stone temples for Shiva and Vishnu began: - Pallavas initiated temple-building in Tamil Nadu. - Chalukyas of Badami built temples in Karnataka. - By the end of this phase, South India had transformed from a land of megaliths to a land of temples. - Linguistic Changes - Before A.D. 400, inscriptions in Andhra, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu were primarily in Prakrit. - The Brahmi inscriptions in Tamil Nadu also contained Prakrit words. - From A.D. 400 onwards, Sanskrit became the official language in the peninsula, and most charters were composed in it. - States of the Deccan and South India - The Vakatakas (Successors of the Satavahanas) - Ruled northern Maharashtra and Vidarbha (Berar). - Were Brahmanas and issued numerous land grants to fellow Brahmanas. - Actively promoted Brahmanical religion and performed Vedic sacrifices. - Played a role in North Indian politics: - Chandragupta II married his daughter, Prabhavati Gupta, into the Vakataka royal family. - With their support, he conquered Gujarat and parts of Western India from the Sakas (late 4th century A.D.). - Served as a conduit for transmitting Brahmanical ideas and social institutions to the South. - The Chalukyas of Badami - Overthrew the Vakatakas and ruled the Deccan for nearly two centuries (until A.D. 757). - Eventually displaced by their feudatories (individuals or states that owe allegiance and provide service), the Rashtrakutas. - Claimed descent from: - Brahman, Manu, or the Moon (likely for legitimacy). - Boasted of ruling at Ayodhya, though they were likely a local Kanarese people elevated under Brahmanical influence. - Established their kingdom in western Deccan (early 6th century A.D.): - Capital at Vatapi (modern Badami, Karnataka). - Later branched into several ruling houses but remained the dominant power in the Deccan. - No other Deccan power was as significant until the rise of Vijayanagar in the late medieval period. - - The Ikshvakus - Emerged in the Krishna-Guntur region after the decline of the Satavahanas. - Likely a local tribe that adopted the name “Ikshvaku” to assert antiquity. - Left behind monuments at Nagarjunakonda and Dharanikota. - Initiated the practice of land grants in the Krishna-Guntur region (several copper plate charters discovered). - The Pallavas - Supplanted the Ikshvakus. - Origin: - “Pallava” means “creeper” (Sanskrit equivalent of Tamil “tondai”). - Possibly a local tribe that established authority in Tondainadu (land of creepers). - Initially had a reputation as uncivilized or even robbers (Tamil word “Pallava” also means “robber”). - Extended authority over southern Andhra and northern Tamil Nadu. - Established capital at Kanchi (modern Kanchipuram), which became a center of temple-building and Vedic learning. - The Kadambas - Early rivals of the Pallavas, ruling northern Karnataka (4th century A.D.). - Founded by Mayurasarman: - Came to Kanchi for education but was driven out. - Set up camp in a forest and, with the help of local tribes, defeated the Pallavas. - Though later defeated, was recognized as a ruler by the Pallavas. - Religious influence: - Performed 18 Ashvamedha sacrifices. - Generously granted villages to Brahmanas. - Capital: - Vaijayanti (Banavasi, North Kanara, Karnataka). - The Western Gangas - Established rule in southern Karnataka (4th century A.D.). - Kingdom located between: - Pallavas (east). - Kadambas (west). - Often feudatories of the Pallavas. - Distinguished from the Eastern Gangas of Kalinga. - Early capital: - Kolar (possibly influenced by its gold mines). - Religious and Economic Influence - Land Grants: - The Pallavas, Kadambas, and Chalukyas extensively granted villages to Brahmanas, often tax-free. - These grants: - Expanded agrarian settlements. - Allowed Brahmanas to collect dues directly from peasants. - Granted up to 18 types of immunities, including exemption from taxes and forced labor. - Religious Patronage: - Pallavas, Kadambas, and Chalukyas performed major Vedic sacrifices (Ashvamedha, Vayapeya). - Boosted priestly class wealth, often at the expense of peasants. - The Kalabhra Revolt (6th Century A.D.) - A social and political uprising against the land-grant-based Brahmanical system. - Led by the Kalabhras, who are depicted as “evil rulers” in later sources. - Overthrew numerous kings and ruled Tamil land. - Revoked Brahmadeya (Brahmana land grants), redistributing land. - Possibly inclined toward Buddhism, as they patronized Buddhist monasteries. - Suppressed through joint efforts of: - Pandyas, Pallavas, and Chalukyas of Badami. - Some traditions claim they even imprisoned the Chola, Pandya, and Chera kings. - The scale of the revolt suggests it impacted areas beyond Tamil land. - The confederacy (union of independent states, groups, or entities) against the Kalabhras indicates that the revolt challenged the prevailing social and political order in South India. - Conflict Between the Pallavas and the Chalukyas - Background - The Pallavas of Kanchi and the Chalukyas of Badami fought for supremacy in peninsular India from the 6th to 8th centuries. - The Pandyas of Madurai and Tinnevelly played a minor role in the conflict. - Despite both dynasties patronizing Brahmanism, performing Vedic sacrifices, and granting land to Brahmanas, they clashed over plunder, prestige, and territorial control. - The Krishna-Tungabhadra doab was the main battleground, later contested between the Vijayanagar and Bahmani kingdoms. - Pulakesin II and Early Conflicts (609-642 A.D.) - The conflict intensified during the reign of Pulakesin II (609-642 A.D.), the most famous Chalukya king. - His achievements are recorded in the Aihole inscription, composed by his court poet Ravikirti. - He overthrew the Kadambas of Banavasi and subjugated the Gangas of Mysore. - He repelled Harsha's army at the Narmada, preventing northern expansion into the Deccan. - Pulakesin II nearly reached Kanchipuram, but the Pallavas ceded their northern provinces to maintain peace. - Around 610 A.D., he seized the Krishna-Godavari region, establishing the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi. - However, his second invasion of Pallava territory failed, leading to his downfall. - Pallava Counterattack Under Narasimhavarman I (630-668 A.D.) - Narasimhavarman I (630-668 A.D.) defeated Pulakesin II around 642 A.D., capturing Vatapi (Badami). - He took the title Vatapikonda (Conqueror of Vatapi). - He also defeated the Cholas, Cheras, Pandyas, and Kalabhras. - Renewed Conflict and Chalukya Victory (8th Century A.D.) - After a brief pause in the late 7th century, the conflict resumed in the early 8th century. - Vikramaditya II (733-745 A.D.), a Chalukya king, invaded Kanchi three times. - In 740 A.D., he decisively defeated the Pallavas, ending their dominance in southern India. - Despite this, the Pallava ruling house survived for another century. - The Chalukya victory was short-lived, as their empire fell to the Rashtrakutas in 757 A.D.. - Temples in Early Medieval India - Rise of Temple Worship - Alongside Vedic sacrifices, the worship of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva gained popularity, especially the last two. - From the 7th century, the Alvar saints promoted the Vaishnavite tradition, while the Nayanmars popularized the Shaivite tradition. - Nayanmars -> Nandi -> Shaivite - Alwars -> Not Shaivite -> Vaishnavite - Pallava Temples (7th-8th Century A.D.) - The Pallava kings constructed numerous stone temples to house these deities. - At Mahabalipuram - Seven Rath Remple - The most famous are the seven ratha temples at Mahabalipuram, built in the 7th century by Narasimhavarman I. - - Shore Temple - Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram) also houses the Shore Temple, a notable structural temple. - At Kanchipuram - Kailasanatha Temple - Several other structural temples were built at Kanchipuram, including the Kailasanatha Temple (8th century A.D.). - - Trick to remember Pallavas temple: - - Chalukya Temples (7th-8th Century A.D.) - The Chalukyas of Badami built numerous temples, particularly at Aihole, which contains around 70 temples (c. 610 A.D. onward). - Temple construction continued in Badami and Pattadakal, where ten temples were built in the 7th and 8th centuries. - Notable temples at Pattadakal: - Papanatha Temple (c. 680 A.D.) - Features a low, stunted tower in northern style. - Virupaksha Temple (c. 740 A.D.) - Built in southern style, measuring 40 meters with a high, square, storied tower (sikhara). - Temple walls are adorned with sculptures from the Ramayana. - Trick to remember Chalukyas temple: - - Temple Maintenance and Patronage - Before the 8th century, temple maintenance was likely funded by taxes collected by the king. - After the 8th century, land grants to temples became common, often recorded on temple walls. - Some temples in Karnataka under the Chalukyas were built by Jain traders. - While common people primarily worshipped village gods with offerings of paddy and toddy, they may have also contributed to major temples for religious and social status. - Demands on the Peasantry - Need for Resources - Enormous resources were required for: - Wars - Art and literature - Religious patronage - Administration - These resources were largely extracted from the peasantry. - Types of Taxation and Extractions - Both the Vakataka (Vidarbha & Maharashtra) and Pallava (Southern Andhra & Northern Tamil Nadu) kingdoms imposed similar burdens on agrarian communities. - Key demands included: - Land tax - A portion of the agricultural produce. - Benevolence tax - Payments in cereals and gold. - Resource extraction: - Trees like palmyra were tapped for salt, sugar, and liquor. - Hidden treasures and deposits in villages belonged to the king. - Natural goods tax: - Peasants had to provide flowers, milk, wood, and grass. - Forced labor (Vishti) - Peasants could be compelled to work for the state without pay. - Additional Peasant Obligations - During royal visits and army movements, villagers had to: - Supply bullocks for carts. - Provide cots, charcoal, ovens, cooking pots, and attendants. - Impact on Peasantry - These demands placed a heavy burden on the labor and produce of rural communities. - Many of these taxes were exempted for Brahmanas through 18 types of immunities granted from the 4th century A.D. onward. - Over time, state extractions from the peasantry increased further. - Rural Expansion - Increase in Agricultural Production - The heavy demands of the king on the peasantry suggest that the agricultural output must have increased. - Tax collection and state expansion would not have been possible without higher agricultural productivity. - Formation of New States - During this period, new states emerged in the trans-Vindhyan regions. - These states consisted of feudatory chiefdoms—small states within larger states. - Each state, whether paramount (supreme, most important, or having the highest authority) or feudatory, required: - Its own army. - Its own taxation system. - An administrative machinery. - Priestly and other supporters. - The survival and expansion of these states depended on resources from their rural base. - Rural proliferation and increased agricultural production became essential. - Role of Brahmanas in Rural Growth - In tribal areas, land grants to Brahmanas helped integrate local peasants into the agrarian economy. - The Brahmanas introduced: - Better cattle preservation methods. - Improved agricultural techniques. - In labor-scarce areas, sharecroppers and weavers were assigned to Brahmanas, as seen in an early Pallava grant. - This contributed to the spread of new cultivation techniques and the growth of rural communities. - Types of Villages in South India - Three main types of villages existed: - Ur - The most common type, inhabited by peasant castes. - Land was likely held in common. - The village headman collected and paid taxes on behalf of the community. - Mainly found in southern Tamil Nadu. - Sabha - Consisted of Brahmadeya villages (granted to Brahmanas) and Agrahara villages. - Brahmana landowners had individual rights but conducted activities collectively. - Nagaram - Villages dominated by traders and merchants. - Possibly formed due to the decline of trade, which led merchants to settle in villages. - Rural Administration - In Chalukya territories, village elders (Mahajana) managed local affairs. - The period A.D. 300 - A.D. 750 saw significant rural expansion, better land utilization, and structured village organization. - Social Structure - Dominance of Princes and Priests - Society was dominated by princes and priests. - Princes claimed Brahmana or Kshatriya status, though many were originally local tribal chiefs. - These chiefs were elevated to the second varna due to their benefactions to priests. - Priests legitimized the rulers by: - Creating respectable family trees. - Tracing their lineage to ancient solar and lunar dynasties. - This process secured legitimacy for the rulers in the eyes of the people. - Role of Priests - The priests were mainly Brahmanas, though Jain and Buddhist monks also held similar status. - They gained power and influence due to land grants. - Peasantry and Social Hierarchy - Below the princes and priests was the peasantry, divided into numerous peasant castes. - In the Brahmanical system, most of them were likely classified as Sudras. - Peasants and artisans were expected to: - Produce goods. - Render services. - Make payments. - Failure to do so was seen as a violation of dharma (norms). - The Age of Kali and Restoration of Order - When the social order collapsed, it was called the age of Kali. - It was the king's duty to restore peace and order. - Many rulers, including the Vakataka, Pallava, Kadamba, and Western Ganga kings, adopted the title Dharma-Maharaja (King of Dharma). - Simhavarman, the founder of Pallava power, was credited with restoring dharma. - He is said to have suppressed the Kalabhras, a group that had disrupted the existing social order. - India's Cultural and Commercial Interactions with the World - Indian Law and Maritime Travel - Medieval lawgivers forbade crossing the seas, implying isolation - The prohibition on crossing the seas, often referred to as Kala Pani (literally "black water") or Samudra Ullanghana ("crossing the ocean"), was a significant taboo in certain sections of Hindu society, especially among upper castes like Brahmins. - Here are some examples of the implications of this taboo: - Social Exclusion and Loss of Caste: - The primary consequence of violating the Kala Pani prohibition was the potential loss of one's caste or social status, leading to social ostracism. Mahatma Gandhi, for example, was excommunicated from his caste after traveling to Britain to study law. - Difficulty in Maintaining Ritual Purity: - One of the reasons cited for the prohibition was the difficulty in maintaining ritual purity and performing daily religious observances on a ship or in a foreign land. This concern was so significant that Maharaja Sawai Madho Singh II even carried Ganga water with him when he traveled to England in 1901 to avoid drinking foreign water,. - Mutiny Among Soldiers: - During the British colonial period, the reluctance of high-caste Indian soldiers to cross the seas for military campaigns led to instances of discontent and even mutiny, as they feared losing their faith and caste status. - Impact on Trade and Travel: - While Indian traders had a history of maritime activity, particularly from the southern kingdoms, the Kala Pani proscription likely influenced the degree and nature of their engagement in overseas ventures, with some accounts suggesting that the taboo contributed to a reluctance among some Hindus to engage in extensive maritime trade during the Portuguese Age of Exploration,. - Opposition to Priests Visiting Foreign Lands: - In recent times, controversies have arisen over priests or religious figures who have traveled overseas. For instance, in 2007, the ascension of Sugunendra Tirtha to the Udupi Krishna Temple was opposed by some seers because he had visited foreign countries, committing the offense of saagarolanga,. - However, India maintained extensive contacts with Asia, West Asia, and the Roman Empire since ancient times. - Harappan traders engaged with Mesopotamian cities (2400-1700 B.C.), as evidenced by discovered seals. - From the Christian era onward, India traded with China, Southeast Asia, and the Roman Empire. - The Silk Route and land connections facilitated commerce and cultural exchange. - Spread of Buddhism and Cultural Exchange - Buddhism played a key role in India's interactions with Sri Lanka, Burma, China, and Central Asia. - Ashoka (3rd century B.C.) likely sent missionaries to Sri Lanka, leading to permanent Buddhist influence. - Brahmi inscriptions (2nd-1st century B.C.) found in Sri Lanka confirm early Buddhist presence. - Buddhism spread to Burma (Myanmar), where Theravada Buddhism flourished, inspiring temple and statue construction. - Burmese and Sri Lankan Buddhists produced an extensive Buddhist literary corpus, surpassing India's. - Even after Buddhism declined in India, it remained dominant in Burma and Sri Lanka. - Buddhism's Expansion into Central and East Asia - Kanishka's reign (2nd century A.D.) saw increased Indian Buddhist missions to China, Central Asia, and Afghanistan. - Buddhism spread from China to Korea and Japan, prompting Chinese pilgrimages to India (e.g., Fa-hsien, Hsuan Tsang). - Dunhuang in China became a major Buddhist center. - India adopted silk-growing techniques from China, while China learned Buddhist painting from India. - Buddhism in Afghanistan and Central Asia - Afghanistan and Central Asia became major Buddhist centers. - Begram and Bamiyan (Afghanistan) housed numerous Buddhist statues and monasteries. - Bamiyan had the tallest rock-cut Buddha statue (early Christian era) and many monastic caves. - In March 2001, they were deliberately destroyed by the Taliban - Buddhism thrived here until Islam replaced it (7th century A.D.). - Central Asia preserved Indian Buddhist stupas, monasteries, inscriptions, and manuscripts. - Kushan rule helped spread Prakrit (Kharosthi script) to Central Asia. - - Indian Influence in Southeast Asia - Southeast Asia absorbed Indian culture, mostly through Brahmanical traditions rather than Buddhism. - Burma (Myanmar) had strong Buddhist influences, with extensive remains from the Gupta period. - India's trade and settlements (1st century A.D.) in Java (Indonesia) called it Suvarnadvipa (Island of Gold). - Pallavas established colonies in Java (early Christian era). - Champa (Vietnam) and Kamboja (Cambodia) were Indianized kingdoms with Sanskrit as the official language. - Srivijaya and Hindu Influence in Southeast Asia - Sumatra (Srivijaya Kingdom, 5th-10th century A.D.) became a center of Indian culture. - Kamboja (Cambodia), founded in the 6th century A.D., was a Shiva-worshipping kingdom and a Sanskrit learning hub. - Champa (Southern & Northern Vietnam) was a major Vedic and Dharmashastra education center. - Angkor Wat (Cambodia), built in medieval times, surpasses Borobudur in grandeur. - The Ramayana and Mahabharata influenced Indonesian culture, with folk plays and Sanskrit-influenced Bahasa Indonesia. - - Indian Ocean Trade and Cultural Exchange - Indian settlements thrived in the Indian Ocean until the 13th century. - Trade, not just religion, played a vital role in cultural exchange. - Suvarnabhumi and Suvarnadvipa (Southeast Asia) indicate Indian interest in gold trade. - Indians adopted: - Gold coin minting from Greeks and Romans. - Silk cultivation from China. - Betel leaf farming from Indonesia. - Cotton farming spread from India to China & Central Asia. - Indian art, religion, script, and language had a profound impact, but cultures evolved uniquely, never becoming exact replicas of Indian traditions. - Transformation of the Ancient Phase - Social Crisis and the Origin of Land Grants - The transformation of ancient Indian society into medieval society was primarily driven by the practice of land grants. - While charters suggest that kings granted land to acquire religious merit and that monks and priests required land for performing religious rites, the real reason behind this practice was a deep social crisis that disrupted the ancient order. - The Crisis of the Varna System - Ancient Indian society functioned based on the varna system, where: - Vaishyas (peasants) engaged in productive activities and paid taxes. - Shudras (laborers) provided essential services. - The taxes collected from the vaishyas allowed the king to: - Pay salaries to officials and soldiers. - Reward priests. - Purchase luxury goods from merchants and artisans. - However, in the third and fourth centuries A.D., this system faced a severe breakdown. Puranic texts describe a situation where: - Social classes abandoned their assigned functions. - The lower orders sought to claim the status and privileges of the higher orders. - Peasants refused to pay taxes and resisted forced labor. - This led to varna-sankara (the intermixture of social classes) and the weakening of traditional social barriers. Oppression by the ruling classes, heavy taxation, and lack of royal protection fueled this crisis. - In Puranic literature, this disorder was referred to as Kaliyuga—a time of moral and social decay. - Response to the Crisis - To restore order, rulers implemented several measures: - Coercive Measures - The law-book of Manu urged that vaishyas and shudras should strictly adhere to their designated roles, potentially leading to forceful suppression. - Land Grants to Priests and Officials - Instead of directly collecting taxes, kings granted land to Brahmanas and state officials as payment for their services. This had several advantages: - The burden of tax collection and law enforcement was transferred to the new landowners. - These beneficiaries could directly manage rebellious peasants. - It encouraged the cultivation of new lands. - By settling Brahmanas in newly conquered tribal areas, the ruling classes sought to spread Brahmanical culture and instill loyalty to the king. - Thus, land grants became a crucial strategy to stabilize the social and political system, shaping the transition from ancient to medieval India. - Decline of Central Control - From the fifth century A.D., land grants became increasingly common. These grants, especially to Brahmanas, significantly weakened royal authority by transferring key administrative and fiscal powers to local beneficiaries. - Impact of Land Grants to Brahmanas - Exemption from Taxes - Villages granted to Brahmanas were made tax-free, meaning all revenues that previously went to the king were now collected by the Brahmanas. - Administrative Autonomy - The beneficiaries gained the right to govern the people in the donated villages. - Exclusion of Royal Officials - Government officers and royal retainers were not allowed to enter the gifted villages, reducing central oversight. - Judicial Authority - Initially, the king retained the right to punish thieves, but by later periods, the beneficiaries were given full judicial authority over criminal offenses. - Thus, the Brahmanas not only collected taxes but also maintained law and order, effectively acting as independent rulers within their granted villages. Since these grants were permanent, royal power was steadily eroded from the end of the Gupta period. - Weakening of Royal Authority - In earlier periods, such as the Maurya era, taxation and law enforcement were strictly under state control: - Mauryas: - Taxes were assessed and collected by royal agents, and law and order were maintained by the central administration. - Kushans & Early Guptas: - The state continued to pay officials in cash, supported by a steady supply of copper and gold coins. - However, from the sixth century A.D., a major shift occurred: - Officials Paid in Land Revenues - Law-books of the time recommended rewarding services with land instead of cash. - Harshavardhana's Era: - Public officials, including governors, ministers, magistrates, and officers, were granted land for their personal upkeep. - A quarter of royal revenue was set aside for rewarding top officials. - Consequences - These grants created powerful local vested interests that operated independently of the central government. - As more regions became autonomous pockets, the king's direct control over taxation and law enforcement weakened. - The shift from salaried officials to land-holding elites further fragmented central authority, accelerating the decline of strong, centralized rule. - Thus, land grants—both to religious figures and government officials—played a key role in dismantling central control, paving the way for feudal structures in medieval India. - New Agrarian Economy - A significant transformation occurred in the agrarian economy as land grants became more widespread. - The landed beneficiaries, such as Brahmanas and religious institutions, neither cultivated the land themselves nor collected revenues directly. Instead, the actual work was done by peasants and sharecroppers, who were attached to the land without legal ownership. - Cultivation by Peasants and Sharecroppers - According to the Chinese pilgrim I-tsing, most Indian monasteries had their lands cultivated by servants and other workers. - Hsuan Tsang describes the Shudras as agriculturists, suggesting that by this time, they no longer worked primarily as slaves or agricultural laborers but possibly occupied the land temporarily. - This shift was particularly evident in the old settled regions of North India. - Expansion of Land Grants in Tribal Areas - From the fifth-sixth centuries A.D., land grants to Brahmanas increased significantly, particularly in tribal areas. - In these regions, agriculturists were placed under the direct control of religious beneficiaries, especially the Brahmanas. - Restricted Mobility of Peasants and Artisans - From the sixth century onwards, peasants and sharecroppers were increasingly bound to the land in backward and mountainous regions like Orissa and the Deccan. - Over time, this practice spread to the Ganga basin and North India, where: - Peasants and artisans were restricted from leaving the villages granted to beneficiaries. - They were expected to remain in the same village to fulfill its agricultural and economic needs. - Thus, the agrarian economy gradually moved towards a more rigid and localized structure, limiting social and economic mobility while strengthening the control of landowning beneficiaries. - Decline of Trade and Towns - From the sixth century A.D., trade began to decline significantly. The end of long-distance trade weakened urban economies, leading to the decay of towns and a shift in social organization. - Decline of Trade - End of Foreign Trade: - Trade with the western Roman Empire ended in the third century. - The silk trade with Iran and Byzantium ceased in the mid-sixth century. - Some commerce continued with China and Southeast Asia, but its benefits were largely taken by Arab merchants, who acted as middlemen. - By the pre-Muslim period, the Arabs had practically monopolized India's export trade. - Decline in Coinage: - The long decline of trade is evident from the scarcity of gold coins after the sixth century. - This decline was not limited to North India but also affected South India. - Decay of Towns - Flourishing Towns Under Earlier Dynasties: - Under the Satavahanas and Kushans, towns thrived in West and North India. - Some cities continued to exist during the Gupta period, but post-Gupta times saw the ruin of many old commercial centers. - Archaeological Evidence of Urban Decline: - Excavations show that several towns began to decline during the Gupta period and mostly disappeared in post-Gupta times. - Examples include: - Haryana and East Punjab - Purana Qila (Delhi), Mathura, Hastinapur, Sravasti, Kausambi (near Allahabad), Rajghat (Varanasi), Chirand, Vaisali, Pataliputra - Hsuan Tsang's Observations: - The Chinese pilgrim Hsuan Tsang visited several towns once associated with the Buddha but found them almost deserted or in ruins. - Shift to Rural Economy: - With limited markets for exports, artisans and merchants abandoned urban centers and migrated to the countryside to take up agriculture. - In the late fifth century, a group of silk weavers from the western coast migrated to Mandasor (Malwa), abandoned silk weaving, and adopted new professions. - The decay of trade and towns forced villages to become self-sufficient, producing oil, salt, spices, and cloth on their own. - Changes in Social Organization - Transformation of Vaisyas' Status: - In the Gangetic basin, vaisyas were traditionally free peasants. - However, land grants introduced landlords between peasants and the king, effectively reducing the status of the vaisyas to that of shudras. - Spread of the Modified Social Order: - The modified Brahmanical social order expanded from North India to Bengal and South India due to land grants given to Brahmanas (brought from the north) in the fifth-sixth centuries. - In outlying regions, society became simplified into two major classes: - Brahmanas (landlords and religious elites) - Shudras (peasants and laborers) - Thus, the decline of trade and urban life led to greater ruralization, self-sufficient village economies, and significant shifts in social hierarchy, reinforcing land-based economic structures. - Changes in the Varna System - The traditional varna system, which divided society into four main varnas (Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas, and Sudras), underwent significant modifications due to land grants and political changes. - Emergence of Landed Classes and Social Mobility - Frequent seizures of power and land grants led to the rise of new categories of landowners. - Individuals who acquired land and power sought higher social status, even if they originally belonged to a lower varna. - Challenge to the Traditional System: - According to the Dharmasastras, varna-based hierarchy determined social and economic rights. - However, economically prosperous individuals from lower varnas created a contradiction between wealth and social status. - Adjustments in Social Classification: - The need to recognize new landed elites led to modifications in written texts. - Varehamihira, an astrologer from the sixth century, followed the old practice of prescribing house sizes based on varna. - However, he also classified houses based on the ranks of ruling chiefs, indicating a shift toward land-based social status rather than strict varna divisions. - Rise of Castes and Sub-Castes - From the seventh century onwards, the varna system fragmented into numerous castes and sub-castes, leading to a more complex jati (caste) hierarchy. - Expansion of Mixed Castes: - An eighth-century Purana mentions that thousands of mixed castes were formed due to intermarriage, particularly between vaisya women and lower-caste men. - This led to the further division of Sudras and untouchables into multiple sub-castes. - Fragmentation of Brahmanas and Rajputs: - The Brahmanas and Rajputs (who emerged as a dominant force in politics and society by the seventh century) also developed many sub-castes. - Territorial and Occupational Basis of Caste: - Due to limited mobility in the economy, even people engaged in the same occupation became divided into separate castes based on their geographical location. - Integration of Tribals into Hindu Society: - Many tribal communities were absorbed into the Hindu caste system due to the land grants given to Brahmanas in tribal regions. - These groups were mostly classified as Sudras or mixed castes, with each tribe being assigned a separate caste status. - Conclusion - Thus, while varna remained a theoretical framework, actual social divisions became more fluid yet rigid with the emergence of land-based hierarchies, regional caste divisions, and the integration of tribal communities into the caste order. - Cultural Developments (6th-7th Centuries A.D.) - The sixth and seventh centuries marked significant cultural transformations, including the rise of regional identities, linguistic changes, and script diversification. - Formation of Regional Identities - Several sub-national units emerged, such as Andhra, Assam, Bengal, Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Orissa, Rajasthan, and Tamil Nadu. - These identities were recognized by both Indian and foreign sources: - Hsuan Tsang, the Chinese traveler, mentions several nationalities. - Visakhadatta (6th-century author) describes people from different regions with distinct customs, clothing, and languages. - Jaina texts (8th century) list 18 major nationalities, detailing their physical traits, languages, and character. - Sanskrit Literature and Ornate Style - Sanskrit continued as the language of the ruling class since the 2nd century A.D. - Due to royal opulence and grandeur, Sanskrit prose and poetry became verbose and highly ornate. - This ornate style gained popularity from the 7th century onwards. - Bana, a leading Sanskrit writer, exemplifies this florid prose style. - Despite being difficult to imitate, his works influenced medieval Sanskrit writers. - Development of Regional Languages - From the 7th century A.D., regional languages began evolving from Prakrit dialects. - Buddhist writings (Eastern India) show early forms of Bengali, Assamese, Maithili, Oriya, and Hindi. - Jaina Prakrit texts reveal the origins of Gujarati and Rajasthani. - Factors behind linguistic diversification: - The breakup of the Gupta Empire led to the rise of independent principalities, reducing countrywide communication. - The decline of trade further isolated regions, accelerating the growth of distinct languages. - Emergence of Regional Scripts - Before the 7th century, a single script (with minor variations) was used across India, from Maurya to Gupta times. - A Gupta-era scholar could read inscriptions from different parts of the country. - After the 7th century, distinct regional scripts emerged, making cross-regional reading difficult. - Each region adopted its own script, requiring multiple script knowledge to read post-Gupta inscriptions. - Conclusion - The 6th-7th centuries saw the rise of regional cultural identities, the transformation of Sanskrit literature, the birth of regional languages, and the divergence of scripts, marking a major shift in India's cultural landscape. - Bhakti and Tantricism - Development of Regional Styles in Sculpture and Temple Construction - From the seventh-eighth centuries, every region in India began to develop its own style of sculpture and temple construction. South India, in particular, became a hub of stone temples, where both stone and bronze were the primary media for representing divinities. - The production of bronze statues flourished, especially in: - South India - primarily for Brahmanical temples. - Eastern India - mainly for Buddhist temples and monasteries. - Although the same gods and goddesses were worshipped across India, regional variations emerged in their artistic depictions. - Religious Hierarchy in Post-Gupta Times - During the post-Gupta period, Hindu divinities were organized in hierarchical ranks, mirroring the stratification in society based on: - Ritual status - Landed property - Military power - The most supreme deities—Vishnu, Shiva, and Durga—were placed at the top, presiding over minor gods and goddesses who were relegated to the roles of attendants and retainers. This hierarchical arrangement was reflected in both art and literature. - Additionally, monastic organizations of the Jainas, Saivites, and Vaishnavites were also divided into five ranks, with the Acharya (chief monk) occupying the highest status, often coronated in a manner similar to a prince. - Rise of the Bhakti Movement - From the seventh century A.D., the Bhakti cult spread across India, particularly in South India. The Bhakti tradition emphasized: - Devotional surrender to a personal god. - Making offerings to the deity in return for receiving prasada (divine favor). - A relationship akin to feudal dependence, where devotees' devotion mirrored the tenant-landlord relationship in society. - The Spread of Tantricism - One of the most remarkable religious developments from the sixth century A.D. was the rise of Tantricism, which gained prominence as: - Large numbers of Brahmanas received land grants in regions like Nepal, Assam, Bengal, Orissa, Central India, and the Deccan. - Tantric texts, shrines, and practices began to appear around the same time. - Tantricism was inclusive, admitting both women and Sudras into its ranks. - Tantric practices placed significant emphasis on: - Magic rituals aimed at fulfilling material desires. - Curing ailments and injuries using mystical techniques. - Incorporation of aboriginal tribal customs into Brahmanical traditions. - Over time, Tantric rituals—which originally stemmed from tribal traditions—were systematized, compiled, and promoted by Brahmanas. However, they were later distorted to cater to the interests of wealthy patrons. - Integration of Tantricism into Major Religions - Tantric practices were not confined to Hinduism; they influenced multiple religious traditions, including: - Jainism - Buddhism - Saivism - Vaishnavism - From the seventh century A.D., Tantricism remained a dominant force throughout medieval India. Numerous medieval manuscripts discovered across India contain extensive references to Tantricism and astrology, often presenting the two as interwoven concepts. - Thus, in the sixth and seventh centuries, significant transformations occurred in polity, society, economy, language, script, and religion. These changes marked the transition from ancient India to medieval India, shaping the foundations of the medieval period. - Sequence of Social Changes - Early Society in Pre-Vedic Times - Lack of Written Records - No written texts exist for studying society during pre-Vedic times. - Archaeological evidence serves as the primary source of information. - Paleolithic Age (Old Stone Age) - People lived in small groups in hilly areas. - Subsistence depended on: - Hunting wild animals. - Gathering wild fruits and vegetation roots. - Transition to Food Production - Towards the end of the Stone Age and the beginning of the Metal Age, humans: - Learned to cultivate crops. - Began to live in permanent houses. - Neolithic and Chalcolithic Settlements - Communities primarily lived in upland regions, near hills and rivers. - Early peasant villages emerged in the Indus basin, gradually leading to urban centers. - Rise and Fall of Urbanization - The Harappan civilization developed with: - Well-planned cities. - Large and small houses for different social classes. - After its decline, urbanism did not reappear in India for nearly a thousand years. - Tribal and Pastoral Phase - Pastoral Society in the Rig Vedic Period - The Rig Vedic society was primarily pastoral and semi-nomadic. - Cattle and horses were the chief possessions, and wealth was measured in terms of cattle. - The term “gau” (cow) appears 176 times in the earlier portions of the Rig Veda. - A wealthy person was called “gomat” (owner of cattle). - Wars were fought for cattle, and the raja's main duty was to protect them, earning him titles like “gopa” (protector of cows) and “gopati” (lord of cows). - The importance of cattle is also reflected in family terminology: - A daughter was called “duhitr” (one who milks the cow). - The buffalo, an unfamiliar animal to the Vedic people, was called “govala” (cow-haired). - References to agriculture in the Rig Veda are fewer compared to cattle-rearing. - Wealth Distribution and Tribal Economy - People produced only enough for subsistence, with limited surplus. - The chief's wealth came mainly from: - War spoils taken from enemy tribes. - Tributes (bali) exacted from defeated or hostile tribes. - Voluntary gifts given by tribal kinsmen in return for leadership and military protection. - Periodical sacrifices served as events for distributing these gifts and tributes. - Priests received the largest share for their religious services. - Princes and priests sought unequal wealth distribution, although voluntary contributions from tribesmen remained significant. - Ordinary tribal members received a share (amsa or bhaga), distributed in folk assemblies attended by rajas and tribal followers. - Social Structure and Property - Despite the presence of artisans, peasants, priests, and warriors, society remained: - Tribal - Pastoral - Semi-nomadic - Egalitarian (no rigid class structure). - Forms of property: - Spoils of war and cattle were the primary wealth. - Women slaves were given as gifts, but their numbers were likely small. - Gifts of cereals were rare since large-scale agriculture was not yet developed. - Social hierarchy: - High ranks existed, but social classes had not yet emerged. - Princes and priests employed women slaves for domestic service, but a formal serving order (Sudras) had not yet developed. - Agriculture and the Origin of Upper Orders - Transition to Agriculture - As the Vedic people migrated from Afghanistan and Punjab to western Uttar Pradesh, they became full-fledged agriculturists. - Later Vedic settlements persisted for two to three centuries, leading to the emergence of territorial chiefdoms. - Economic Contributions and Social Structure - Peasants contributed tributes that enabled princes to perform sacrifices and reward priests. - Nobles and warriors, supported by peasant tributes, also paid the priests. - Peasants supplied food to craftsmen such as smiths, chariot-makers, and carpenters, who primarily served the warrior class. - However, despite these economic developments, the peasant economy did not yet support trade and urbanization, which became prominent only in the age of the Buddha. - The society did not use metallic money at this stage. - Absence of Taxation and Professional Army - The Vedic communities lacked a formal taxation system and professional army. - Taxes were collected by the prince's kinsmen rather than appointed officials. - Payments made to the king resembled sacrificial offerings to the gods rather than structured taxation. - The tribal militia of the pastoral era evolved into a peasant militia. - The vis (tribal peasantry) formed the sena (armed host) and was referred to as bala (force) in later Vedic times. - The army for the asvamedha horse sacrifice consisted of: - Kshatriyas (military captains and leaders, armed with bows, quivers, and shields). - Vis (peasants) (rank-and-file members, armed with sticks). - Rituals reinforced the subjugation of the vaisyas (peasants) under the warrior nobles. - Weak Development of Taxation and Ruling Class - The transition from tribal warriors to a tax-paying agrarian society was still in its early stages. - Agriculture relied on wooden ploughshares, and cattle were indiscriminately slaughtered in sacrifices, limiting surplus production. - As a result, peasants could not pay regular taxes. - Princes were not entirely disconnected from peasants and were expected to support agriculture, sometimes even ploughing the land themselves. - The rajanya (nobles) ruled over their peasant kinsmen but depended on the peasant militia for warfare. - Land grants required the consent of the tribal peasantry, preventing a sharp distinction between rulers and the ruled. - Varna System of Production and Government - Transformation of Society Through Iron Technology - The introduction of iron tools for crafts and cultivation led to a shift from a relatively egalitarian Vedic society to a fully agricultural and class-divided social order by the sixth century B.C. - The clearing of forests in the middle Gangetic basin, one of the most fertile regions in the world, enabled the establishment of numerous rural and urban settlements. - This agricultural expansion facilitated the rise of large territorial states and ultimately the formation of the Magadhan empire. - Agricultural Surplus and Labor Specialization - The use of iron ploughshares, sickles, and other tools allowed peasants to produce a surplus beyond their subsistence needs. - This surplus supported artisans who provided tools, clothing, and luxury items, as well as weapons for the ruling classes. - Production techniques in post-Vedic times advanced significantly compared to the Vedic age. - The accumulation of large tracts of land led to the need for additional labor, including slaves and hired workers. - Unlike the Vedic period, where family-based farming was the norm, wage labor and slavery became common during the age of the Buddha. - In the Mauryan period, large state farms employed slaves, including the 150,000 people captured in Kalinga by Ashoka, who were put to work in farms and mines. - However, in general, most slaves in ancient India were used for domestic work, while small peasants remained the dominant force in production, occasionally aided by slaves and hired laborers. - Taxation, Administration, and the Role of the Varna System - With increased production, surplus wealth was collected by the ruling classes through both administrative and religious means. - Kings appointed tax-collectors to assess and collect revenue. - To reinforce social obedience, the varna system was formalized: - The three higher varnas were ritually distinguished from the Sudras, the fourth and lowest varna. - The twice-born (Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, and Vaisyas) were entitled to Vedic education and sacred thread investiture, while Sudras were excluded and assigned to serve the higher varnas. - Some law-givers even restricted slavery to Sudras alone. - The twice-born were considered citizens, while Sudras were effectively treated as non-citizens. - Social Hierarchy and Economic Distinctions - Within the twice-born ranks, further divisions emerged: - Brahmanas were forbidden from ploughing or engaging in manual labor. - The higher varnas developed disdain for manual labor, leading to the marginalization of craftsmen and the emergence of untouchability. - The Vaisyas, though part of the twice-born, worked as peasants, herdsmen, artisans, and traders. - Crucially, they were the primary taxpayers whose contributions sustained the Kshatriyas and Brahmanas. - The Kshatriyas were responsible for collecting taxes from peasants and tolls from traders and artisans, allowing them to pay their priests and officials in both cash and kind. - Differentiation in Economic Privileges - The rate of interest on loans varied by varna: - Brahmanas - 2% - Kshatriyas - 3% - Vaisyas - 4% - Sudras - 5% - Sudra guests were only provided food if they had performed work for the host. - While these rules, outlined in the Dharma Sastras (law-books), may not have been strictly enforced, they reflect the social norms of the time. - Conflicts and Cooperation Between Priests and Warriors - The Brahmanas and Kshatriyas, both dependent on the tributes, taxes, and labor of peasants and artisans, occasionally clashed over the division of social surplus. - Kshatriyas resented the Brahmanas' claim to the highest status in society. - Despite these tensions, they resolved their differences in the face of opposition from Vaisyas and Sudras. - Ancient texts emphasize their interdependence: - Kshatriyas could not prosper without Brahmanas, and Brahmanas could not thrive without Kshatriyas. - Their mutual cooperation was deemed essential for ruling and sustaining society. - Social Crisis and the Rise of Landed Classes - The Functioning and Decline of the Old Order - For several centuries, the social and economic system in the Gangetic basin functioned effectively, supporting the rise of successive large states. - The first and second centuries A.D. witnessed a period of booming trade, urbanization, and artistic flourishing. - This phase reached its peak around the third century A.D., after which its progressive role began to decline. - By the third century A.D., a deep social crisis emerged, reflected in the Puranic descriptions of the Kali age, written in the third and fourth centuries A.D. - Social Crisis: Breakdown of the Varna System - The Kali age was marked by varna-samkara, or the intermixture of varnas, indicating a disruption of traditional roles: - Vaisyas and Sudras (peasants, artisans, and laborers) either refused to perform their assigned productive roles or declined to pay taxes and provide labor. - Varna boundaries concerning marriage and social interactions were increasingly disregarded. - In response, epics and legal texts emphasized the need for danda (coercion) to enforce social order: - Manu explicitly stated that Vaisyas and Sudras should not be allowed to deviate from their designated duties. - Kings were portrayed as restorers and upholders of the varna system. - Shift in Taxation and Administration - Coercion alone was insufficient to compel peasants to pay taxes and laborers to work. - Instead of collecting taxes centrally and redistributing them among priests, military chiefs, and administrators, the state adopted a more decentralized system: - Land revenues were assigned directly to these groups for their support, a sharp departure from earlier Vedic practices. - Previously, only the community could grant land to priests and possibly princes, but now the raja (king) seized this power and distributed land to influential individuals. - These beneficiaries were not only granted land but also given administrative authority, including the power to maintain law and order. - Land Grants and Expansion into Tribal Areas - To secure additional revenue, expanding kingdoms sought to integrate tribal areas into their tax base. - This was achieved by granting land in these backward regions to enterprising Brahmanas, who: - Introduced new agricultural methods to the local population. - Taught loyalty and discipline to the tribal inhabitants. - Spread Ayurveda medicine and agricultural knowledge, increasing overall production. - Promoted literacy through the use of Prakrit and Sanskrit. - Impact of Land Grants on Society - The process of granting land helped extend civilization to the deep south and far east, a movement that had been initiated earlier by traders, Jainas, and Buddhists. - These grants facilitated the incorporation of aboriginal peasants into the Hindu social order, where they were categorized as Sudras. - Over time, Sudras came to be recognized as peasants and agriculturists, as reflected in early medieval texts. - Decline of Independent Vaisya Peasants and Rise of Feudalism - In developed areas, land grants weakened the position of independent Vaisya peasants, who previously held economic significance. - As a result, Vaisyas and Sudras became socially and economically closer from the Gupta period onward. - The most significant consequence of land grants was the emergence of a class of landlords who lived off the produce of peasants. - By the 5th-6th centuries A.D., this transformation laid the foundation for a new social structure—feudalism. - Legacy in Science and Civilization - Religion and the Formation of Social Classes - Agrarian Society and the Influence of Religion - Despite the presence of towns during the Harappan civilization and from the Maurya to the Gupta period, ancient Indian civilization was not as urbanized as those of Greece and Rome. - The vast expanse of the Indian subcontinent, with much of it located far from the sea, limited trade and commerce, making Indian life primarily agrarian. - Compared to Western cultures, religion played a far greater role in shaping Indian society, influencing economy, polity, art, and literature. - Apart from Hinduism, India gave rise to Jainism and Buddhism, which later spread to Japan, Central Asia, and beyond. - While Christianity arrived in India around the first century A.D., it did not gain much prominence in ancient times. - Buddhism eventually declined within India, though it significantly contributed to the diffusion of Indian art, language, and literature in neighboring regions. - Religion and Social Class Structure - Unlike in other ancient societies where social classes were defined and enforced primarily by the state, in India, varna laws were upheld by both the state and religion. - The duties of priests, warriors, peasants, and laborers were believed to have been divinely ordained and codified in religious law. - Punishments for violating these duties involved both secular penalties and religious penances, varying according to varna status. - Over time, varnas (social classes) and jatis (castes) came to be seen as hereditary, reinforced by both legal and religious frameworks. - The Role of Dharma in Social Stability - The varna system ensured that: - Brahmanas served as priests. - Kshatriyas acted as rulers and warriors. - Vaishyas engaged in production and taxation. - Sudras performed labor and servitude. - Religious doctrines strongly indoctrinated individuals into accepting their roles: - The Bhagavad Gita taught that one must adhere to their own dharma rather than take up another's, as it was considered dangerous. - The lower classes toiled in the belief that fulfilling their dharma would earn them a better life in the next world or rebirth. - Reduction of Social Conflict through Religious Indoctrination - This religious conditioning helped reduce social tensions between the producing classes and the ruling elite, which included princes, priests, officials, soldiers, and merchants. - In contrast to Greece and Rome, where slaves and laborers worked under the threat of physical coercion, in India: - Vaishyas and Sudras labored willingly, believing in the religious sanctity of their duties. - The need for harsh coercion was minimized, as people were mentally conditioned to accept their social roles. - Philosophical Systems in Ancient India - Idealism and the Search for Truth - Indian thinkers deeply explored the nature of reality, considering the world to be an illusion (maya) and pondering the relationship between the soul (atman) and God (Brahman). - No other civilization is believed to have delved as profoundly into this philosophical question as India. - Ancient India became renowned for its contributions to philosophy and spiritualism, particularly through the Upanishads, which emphasized the pursuit of real knowledge and the abandonment of material life. - Many Western philosophers admired Indian thought: - The German philosopher Schopenhauer found solace in the Vedas and Upanishads, claiming they consoled him in life and would console him after death. - Western thinkers continue to be drawn to the Upanishads, as they seek answers to human problems brought about by modern technology. - Materialism in Indian Philosophy - Despite its strong spiritual tradition, India also developed materialist schools of thought that rejected the idea of divine creation. - Sankhya system - The Sankhya system, founded by Kapila (c. 580 B.C.), contained materialist elements: - It argued that the soul (purusha) attains liberation through real knowledge. - Real knowledge is acquired through observation, inference, and words. - It denied the existence of God, asserting that the world is not created by a divine being but by nature and is governed by natural forces. - Charvaka and the Lokayata System - The most radical materialist philosophy in ancient India was developed by Charvaka (c. 6th century B.C.), whose system is known as Lokayata. - Core beliefs of Lokayata philosophy: - Only what is experienced through the senses is real. - Anything beyond direct perception—including gods and an afterlife—is dismissed as non-existent. - This philosophy rejected spiritual doctrines, making it a stark contrast to the dominant idealist schools. - The Coexistence of Idealism and Materialism - Ancient India saw the simultaneous development of both idealist and materialist philosophies. - While the Upanishads promoted detachment from the material world, thinkers like Charvaka championed a purely rational and empirical worldview. - These diverse philosophical traditions highlight the depth and breadth of Indian thought, ranging from spiritual introspection to rational skepticism. - Indian Craftsmanship and Material Culture - Advancements in Dyeing and Colors - Indian craftsmen made significant progress in material culture, excelling in various fields of production. - They were highly skilled in dyeing and creating long-lasting, vibrant colors. - The durability of Indian pigments is evident in the Ajanta and Ellora paintings, which have remained intact for centuries. - Mastery in Steel Production - India was a pioneer in steelmaking, developing advanced metallurgical techniques before other civilizations. - Indian steel, later known as wootz, was exported to many countries from early times. - Indian craftsmen produced exceptionally strong steel swords, unmatched by any other civilization. - These swords were highly sought after across Asia and Europe, reinforcing India's reputation in metallurgy. - Political Organization in Ancient India - Experiments in Democracy - Alongside Greece, India was one of the few countries to experiment with some form of democracy in ancient times. - Ashoka: A Model Ruler - Ashoka, one of India's greatest rulers, initially expanded his empire through military conquest. - Despite his victory over Kalinga, he renounced aggression and adopted a policy of peace. - His reign, along with that of other Indian rulers, emphasized religious tolerance, ensuring that the beliefs of all communities were respected. - Science and Mathematics in Ancient India - Interconnection of Religion and Science - In ancient India, religion and science were deeply intertwined. - Astronomy developed significantly because planets were considered gods, leading to their detailed observation. - Understanding planetary movements was essential for predicting seasons and weather, which were crucial for agriculture. - Grammar and linguistics evolved due to the Brahmanical emphasis on the precise recitation of Vedic prayers. - Panini, in the 4th century B.C., systematized Sanskrit grammar in his work, Ashtadhyayi. - Mathematics and Numerical Innovations - By the 3rd century B.C., mathematics, astronomy, and medicine developed as separate disciplines. - India made three fundamental contributions to mathematics: - Notation system - Decimal system - Use of zero - The earliest epigraphic evidence of the decimal system is from the 5th century A.D. - Indian numerals were later adopted by the Arabs, who introduced them to the Western world. - Though called Arabic numerals in English, the Arabs themselves referred to them as Hindsa (Indian numerals). - These numerals were used in Ashokan inscriptions from the 3rd century B.C. - Zero and Algebra - Zero was discovered in India around the 2nd century B.C., treated as a separate numeral. - The earliest recorded use of zero in Arabia dates to A.D. 87, and it spread to Europe through Arab traders. - Both Indians and Greeks contributed to algebra, but Western Europe adopted it via Arab scholars, who had earlier learned it from India. - Geometry and Trigonometry - Apastamba - Apastamba (2nd century B.C.) developed practical geometry for altar construction. - His work defined acute, obtuse, and right angles. - Aryabhata - Aryabhata (A.D. 476-500) formulated rules for finding the area of a triangle, leading to the origin of trigonometry. - Suryasiddhanta, a major astronomical text, had no equivalent in contemporary Greece. - Advancements in Astronomy - Aryabhata (5th century A.D.) and Varahamihira (6th century A.D.) were renowned astronomers. - Aryabhata: - Calculated planetary positions using Babylonian methods. - Discovered the causes of solar and lunar eclipses. - Estimated the Earth's circumference, a measurement considered accurate even today. - Recognized that the Sun is stationary and the Earth rotates. - His work, Aryabhatiya, remains a significant text. - Varahamihira (author of Brihatsamhita, 6th century A.D.): - Stated that the Moon orbits the Earth and the Earth orbits the Sun. - Utilized Greek astronomical knowledge but made original contributions in planetary observations. - Applied Sciences: Chemistry and Metallurgy - Indian craftsmen made significant contributions to chemistry: - Invented lasting dyes and discovered the blue color. - Indian blacksmiths were pioneers in steel manufacturing. - Indian steel, known later as wootz, was exported globally. - Ancient Indian Medicine - Early Medical Practices - Ancient Indian physicians studied anatomy, devised methods for diagnosing diseases, and prescribed medicinal treatments. - The Atharva Veda contains the earliest references to medicines, but remedies were often mixed with magical charms and spells, preventing medicine from developing on scientific principles. - Contributions of Sushruta and Charaka - During the post-Maurya period, India saw the rise of two great Ayurvedic scholars: - Sushruta - Author of Sushruta Samhita - Sushruta is believed to have lived around 600 BCE during the Vedic period of ancient India. - His Sushruta Samhita describes surgical techniques for: - Cataract removal - Treatment of stone disease - Various other ailments - He listed 121 surgical instruments used in operations. - Emphasized diet and cleanliness in disease treatment. - Charaka - Author of Charaka Samhita, 2nd century A.D. - His Charaka Samhita is considered an encyclopedia of Indian medicine. - It describes diseases such as: - Various fevers - Leprosy - Hysteria (Mirgi) - Tuberculosis (though he may not have recognized its infectious nature). - Contains the names of numerous plants and herbs used as medicines. - Useful for the study of ancient Indian flora and early chemistry. - Impact on Future Medical Development - Indian medicine evolved based on Charaka's foundational principles. - Ayurveda continued to develop, influencing medical practices in India and beyond. - Ancient Indian Contributions to Geography - Knowledge of Indian Geography - Ancient Indians had limited knowledge of lands outside India. - The epics and Puranas describe India's: - Rivers - Mountain ranges - Pilgrimage sites - Different regions - Though they were aware of China and Western countries, they lacked clear knowledge of their exact locations and distances from India. - Navigation and Shipbuilding - Ancient Indians gained some knowledge of navigation. - They made contributions to the craft of shipbuilding. - However, due to: - The seats of power being far from the coast. - The absence of maritime threats. - Indian rulers did not prioritize naval advancements. - Ancient Indian Contributions to Art and Literature - Art and Architecture - Ancient Indian masons (re skilled workers who build or repair structures using stone, brick, or concrete) and craftsmen created remarkable works of art. - Ashoka's monolithic pillars: - Known for their shining polish, similar to Northern Black Polished Ware. - The technique used to achieve this polish remains a mystery. - These pillars were topped with animal statues, especially lions. - The Lion Capital of Ashoka was later adopted as India's national emblem. - Ajanta Caves and Paintings - The Ajanta cave temples date from 2nd century B.C. to 7th century A.D. - Ajanta paintings: - Appeared in 2nd century A.D., mostly during Gupta times. - Themes were taken from Buddha's previous incarnations and ancient literature. - The technique, lines, and colors displayed a level of proficiency unmatched before the European Renaissance. - Ajanta is regarded as the birthplace of Asian art. - Spread of Indian Art - Indian art influenced regions from Central Asia and China to Southeast Asia. - Gandhara Art: - A fusion of Indian, Central Asian, and Hellenistic styles. - The first Buddha statue was created in this style. - Though its features were Indian, elements like drapery and head presentation reflected Greek influence. - South Indian temples served as models for Southeast Asian architecture, including: - Angkor Wat (Hindu-Buddhist temple complex) in Cambodia. - Borobudur (Buddhist temple) in Java (Island in Indonesia). - Education and Literature - Nalanda University - One of the earliest residential universities, attracting students from India, Tibet, and China. - Strict admission standards: - Only students who passed the test of the dvarapandita (scholar at the gate) were admitted. - Housed thousands of monks engaged in learning, philosophy, and meditation. - Indian Literature - Rig Veda: - The earliest Indo-Aryan literary work. - Provides insights into Aryan culture. - Gupta Period Literature: - The works of Kalidasa, especially Abhijnanasakuntalam, which has been translated into many global languages.
