Why Not Others?: - Option (b) places Chandela with Panamalai, which is incorrect since Chandela architecture is associated with Khajuraho. - Option (c) misplaces Gupta architecture, as Deogarh, not Panamalai, represents their temple-building efforts. - Option (d) mismatches Khajuraho and Deogarh, which belong to different dynasties. - Other Architectural Contributions: - Maurya: - Stupas (Sanchi, Bharhut), Ashokan pillars - Satavahana: - Amaravati stupa - Rashtrakuta: - Ellora Kailasanatha temple - Hoysala: - Belur, Halebidu temples - Vijayanagara: - Hampi temples - Connection to Other Topics: - Related to ancient and medieval Indian architecture (e.g., Q95 [2015] on temple styles). - Can link to questions on rock-cut architecture (e.g., Q62 [2013] on Ajanta and Elephanta caves). - Connects with artistic influences in South and North India (e.g., Q41 [2016] on Dravidian vs Nagara style). - Key Takeaway: - Understanding temple architecture across dynasties helps in analyzing artistic developments, political patronage, and religious symbolism in Indian history. - Q21: Which one of the following statements regarding Ashoka stone pillars is incorrect? - Options: (a) These are highly polished (b) These are monolithic (c) The shaft of pillars is tapering in shape (d) These are parts of architectural structures - Answer: (d) These are parts of architectural structures - Analysis: - Why (d) is Incorrect?: - Ashoka's pillars were standalone monuments, not parts of architectural structures like temples or stupas. - These pillars were erected independently across the Mauryan Empire to propagate Dhamma (Buddhist teachings and moral edicts). - Explanation of Other Options: - (a) Highly Polished: - Correct—Mauryan pillars exhibit the famous "Mauryan polish," giving them a smooth, glossy finish. - (b) Monolithic: - Correct—Each pillar was carved from a single block of sandstone, primarily from the Chunar region (Uttar Pradesh). - (c) Tapering Shaft: - Correct—The shafts were slightly tapered, creating a slender and elegant appearance. - Ashokan Pillar Characteristics: - Material: - Sandstone, mainly from Chunar and Mathura. - Shape: - Monolithic, tapering, and highly polished. - Capitals: - Usually adorned with animal sculptures (e.g., the famous lion capital of Sarnath, now India's national emblem). - Locations: - Found in Sarnath, Sanchi, Lauriya Nandangarh, Rampurva, and other Mauryan sites. - Broader Context: - Links to Mauryan Art: - Ashokan pillars represent the earliest known examples of imperial propaganda through monumental inscriptions. - Compare with Persian Achaemenid pillars (e.g., those at Persepolis), which influenced Ashokan style. - Related to Mauryan Stupas: - While pillars stood alone, stupas (e.g., Sanchi) were religious architectural structures. - Connection to Other Topics: - Can be linked to questions on Mauryan art (e.g., Q102 [2014] on Gandhara vs. Mauryan art). - Related to epigraphy and inscriptions (e.g., Q78 [2017] on Ashokan edicts). - Key Takeaway: - Ashokan pillars were independent structures used for political and religious messaging, not architectural components of temples or stupas. - Q22: Which one of the following scripts of ancient India was written from right to left? - Options: (a) Brahmi (b) Nandnagari (c) Sharada (d) Kharosthi - Answer: (d) Kharosthi - Analysis: - Why (d) Kharosthi?: - Kharosthi was a script used primarily in the northwestern region of the Indian subcontinent, particularly in Gandhara (modern-day Pakistan and Afghanistan). - It was derived from the Aramaic script, which was written from right to left, and retained this writing direction. - Characteristics of Kharosthi: - Period: - Used between the 4th century BCE and the 3rd century CE. - Usage: - Primarily in inscriptions and Buddhist texts (e.g., Gandharan Buddhist manuscripts). - Decline: - Replaced by Brahmi-derived scripts over time. - Explanation of Other Options: - (a) Brahmi: - Incorrect—Brahmi, the most widely used script in ancient India, was written from left to right. - It is the precursor of most modern Indian scripts, including Devanagari, Tamil, and Kannada. - (b) Nandnagari: - Incorrect—A variant of the Nagari script, used in medieval India, written from left to right. - Mainly used in Sanskrit texts. - (c) Sharada: - Incorrect—Sharada, an early script of the northwestern region (modern Kashmir), was written from left to right. - Precursor to Gurmukhi script. - Other Prevalent Scripts in Ancient India: - Brahmi: - The oldest attested script in India (from at least the 3rd century BCE). - Left-to-right direction. - Grantha: - Used in South India for Sanskrit texts. - Developed from Brahmi. - Gupta Script: - Prevalent during the Gupta period (4th-6th century CE). - Evolved into later Nagari and regional scripts. - Siddham: - Developed from Gupta script. - Used for Buddhist texts and spread to East Asia. - Tamil-Brahmi: - Variant of Brahmi used for Tamil inscriptions. - Found in Sangam-era records. - Broader Context: - Links to Ancient Scripts: - Can be connected to questions on epigraphy (e.g., Q56 [2016] on Ashokan inscriptions). - Related to Gandhara art and Indo-Greek influences. - Indo-Greek Connection: - Kharosthi was used in coinage of Indo-Greek and Kushan rulers, showing cross-cultural exchanges. - Key Takeaway: - Kharosthi is the only major ancient Indian script written from right to left, reflecting Persian and Aramaic influences. - Q23: The famous dialogue between Nachiketa and Yama is mentioned in the: - Options: (a) Chhandogyopanishad (b) Mundakopanishad (c) Kathopanishad (d) Kenopanishad - Answer: (c) Kathopanishad - Analysis: - Why (c) Kathopanishad?: - The Kathopanishad contains the dialogue between Nachiketa, a young seeker, and Yama, the god of death. - Nachiketa, after being sent to Yama's abode by his father, seeks knowledge of the ultimate truth (Brahman) and the nature of the soul (atman). - Yama instructs him on the immortality of the soul, karma, and self-realization. - Explanation of Other Options: - (a) Chhandogyopanishad: - Incorrect—A part of the Sama Veda, it discusses metaphysical concepts, including the famous "Tat Tvam Asi" (You are That) teaching. - (b) Mundakopanishad: - Incorrect—Belongs to the Atharva Veda, focusing on Brahman and the two types of knowledge (higher and lower). - (d) Kenopanishad: - Incorrect—Explains the supremacy of Brahman over the senses and mind, belonging to the Sama Veda. - Key Teachings of Kathopanishad: - Concept of Atman: - Yama explains that the soul (atman) is eternal and beyond death. - The Path to Liberation: - Yama describes two paths—Preyas (the pleasant) and Shreyas (the good)—emphasizing the importance of choosing wisdom over material pleasures. - Parallels with the Bhagavad Gita: - Some verses of the Kathopanishad are found in the Bhagavad Gita (e.g., discussions on the indestructibility of the soul). - Broader Context: - Links to Questions on Upanishads: - Similar to Q67 [2012] on "Tat Tvam Asi" and Q98 [2017] on Vedantic philosophy. - Can connect to questions on Hindu metaphysics and spiritual dialogues (e.g., Q45 [2015] on Bhagavad Gita). - Key Takeaway: - The Kathopanishad, through the Nachiketa-Yama dialogue, emphasizes the imperishable nature of the soul and the pursuit of spiritual wisdom. - Q24: Milindapanho is in the form of a dialogue between the king Menander and Buddhist monk: - Options: (a) Nagasena (b) Nagarjuna (c) Nagabhatta (d) Kumarilabhatta - Answer: (a) Nagasena - Analysis: - Why (a) Nagasena?: - The Milindapanho (Questions of Milinda) is a Pali Buddhist text written in the form of a dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander I (Milinda) and the Buddhist sage Nagasena. - The text discusses deep philosophical questions related to Buddhist doctrines, including the nature of self (anatta), karma, and Nirvana. - Explanation of Other Options: - (b) Nagarjuna: - Incorrect—Nagarjuna was a 2nd-3rd century CE Mahayana Buddhist philosopher and founder of the Madhyamaka school. - (c) Nagabhatta: - Incorrect—Nagabhatta was a Gurjara-Pratihara ruler, not related to Buddhist philosophy. - (d) Kumarilabhatta: - Incorrect—Kumarilabhatta was a 7th-8th century CE Mimamsa philosopher who defended Vedic rituals against Buddhist critiques. - Key Teachings of Milindapanho: - Concept of Anatta (No-Self): - Nagasena explains that there is no permanent "self"; the individual is just an aggregate of five skandhas (form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness). - The Chariot Analogy: - Nagasena compares the self to a chariot, arguing that just as a chariot is a combination of its parts, a person is a combination of mental and physical elements. - Karma and Rebirth: - The text discusses how actions (karma) shape future existences without a permanent self. - Historical Significance: - Menander I (c. 165 - 130 BCE): - A powerful Indo-Greek ruler known for his patronage of Buddhism. - After his discussions with Nagasena, he is said to have embraced Buddhism. - Text's Influence: - Considered one of the earliest instances of Buddhist dialogues influencing later philosophical traditions. - Helps in understanding the interaction between Hellenistic and Buddhist thought. - Broader Context: - Links to Questions on Buddhist Texts: - Similar to Q45 [2014] on Tripitaka and Q78 [2016] on Jataka Tales. - Can connect to questions on Greek influence on Buddhism (e.g., Q39 [2012] on Gandhara Art). - Key Takeaway: - The Milindapanho is a key Buddhist text illustrating the spread of Buddhism into Hellenistic culture through philosophical dialogue. - Q25: Which one of the following edicts mentions the personal name of Ashoka? - Options: (a) Kalsi (b) Rummindei (c) Special Kalinga Edict (d) Maski - Answer: (d) Maski - Analysis: - Why (d) Maski?: - The Maski Edict is a Minor Rock Edict where Ashoka explicitly mentions his name as Devanampiya Piyadassi (Beloved of the Gods, Piyadassi). - This was the first edict discovered that confirmed Ashoka's identity with the title Piyadassi, resolving a historical debate. - Explanation of Other Options: - (a) Kalsi: - Incorrect—Kalsi contains Major Rock Edict 13, which describes the Kalinga War and its consequences but does not mention Ashoka's name. - (b) Rummindei: - Incorrect—Rummindei Edict (also called the Lumbini Edict) records Ashoka's visit to Lumbini, the birthplace of Buddha, and his tax concessions for the region but does not mention his name. - (c) Special Kalinga Edict: - Incorrect—These edicts (found at Dhauli and Jaugada) deal with Ashoka's special governance policies for Kalinga but do not mention his personal name. - All Major and Minor Ashokan Edicts and Their Features: - Major Rock Edicts (14 in total, found in Girnar, Kalsi, Dhauli, Jaugada, etc.): - Edict 1 (Animal Protection Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Prohibition of animal slaughter and festive killings. - Edict 2 (Medical Care Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Welfare measures including medical treatment for humans and animals, extended to neighboring regions including the Sangam Kingdoms (Cholas, Pandyas, Cheras, Satyaputras, Keralaputras) in South India, showcasing Ashoka's outreach beyond his empire. - Edict 3 (Moral Conduct Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Encouragement of generosity and proper behavior. - Edict 4 (Dhamma Promotion Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Importance of Dhamma and its spread. - Edict 5 (Dhamma Mahamatra Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras for welfare administration. - Edict 6 (King's Administration Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - The role of the king in administration and justice. - Edict 7 (Religious Tolerance Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Promotion of religious tolerance. - Edict 8 (Buddhist Pilgrimage Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Ashoka's pilgrimage to Buddhist sites. - Edict 9 (Ritual Condemnation Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Condemnation of ceremonies and rituals. - Edict 10 (Dhamma over Fame Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Dhamma is superior to fame and glory. - Edict 11 (Explanation of Dhamma Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Further elaboration of Dhamma principles. - Edict 12 (Religious Harmony Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Emphasis on religious harmony and mutual respect. - Edict 13 (Kalinga War Edict): - Found at Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Description of the Kalinga War and its consequences, including Ashoka's remorse; lists unconquered southern neighbors—the Sangam Kingdoms (Cholas, Pandyas, Satyaputras, Keralaputras)—alongside Kalinga, indicating Mauryan diplomatic awareness. - Edict 14 (Dhamma Summary Edict): - Found at Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Summary of Ashoka's Dhamma policies. - Minor Rock Edicts (Found in Bhabru, Maski, Gujarra, etc.): - Bhabru Edict: - Found near Bairat (Jaipur, Rajasthan): - Ashoka declares himself a Buddhist and mentions Buddhist texts he reveres. - Maski Edict: - Found near Maski (Raichur, Karnataka): - First edict to explicitly mention Ashoka by name as Devanampiya Piyadassi. - Gujarra Edict: - Found near Datia (Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh): - Also mentions Ashoka's name, similar to Maski. - Pillar Edicts (7 Major Edicts, found in Delhi-Topra, Lauriya-Nandangarh, etc.): - Pillar Edict 1 (Animal Welfare Edict): - Found at Delhi-Topra (Delhi), Lauriya-Nandangarh (Champaran, Bihar), Allahabad (Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh): - Prohibition of animal sacrifice. - Pillar Edict 2 (Public Welfare Edict): - Found at Delhi-Topra (Delhi), Lauriya-Nandangarh (Champaran, Bihar), Allahabad (Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh): - Ashoka's charity and medical facilities for all. - Pillar Edict 3 (Respect and Duty Edict): - Found at Delhi-Topra (Delhi), Lauriya-Nandangarh (Champaran, Bihar), Allahabad (Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh): - Respect for parents, teachers, and elders. - Pillar Edict 4 (Dhamma Over Wealth Edict): - Found at Delhi-Topra (Delhi), Lauriya-Nandangarh (Champaran, Bihar), Allahabad (Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh): - Dhamma is superior to material wealth. - Pillar Edict 5 (Dhamma Officers Edict): - Found at Delhi-Topra (Delhi), Lauriya-Nandangarh (Champaran, Bihar), Allahabad (Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh): - Appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras for public welfare. - Pillar Edict 6 (Justice and Fairness Edict): - Found at Delhi-Topra (Delhi), Lauriya-Nandangarh (Champaran, Bihar), Allahabad (Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh): - Instruction on fairness and impartiality in administration. - Pillar Edict 7 (Dhamma Consolidation Edict): - Found at Delhi-Topra (Delhi), Lauriya-Nandangarh (Champaran, Bihar): - Summary of Ashoka's Dhamma policies. - Separate Edicts (Special Kalinga Edicts in Dhauli and Jaugada, Odisha): - Special Kalinga Edict 1: - Found at Dhauli (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha): - Describes different governance policies for Kalinga, emphasizing non-violence. - Special Kalinga Edict 2: - Found at Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha): - Ensures justice and welfare administration for the people of Kalinga. - Historical Significance: - The Maski Edict played a crucial role in identifying the historical Ashoka and proving that the Mauryan emperor was the same as the Piyadassi mentioned in earlier inscriptions. - These edicts provide valuable insights into Ashoka's administrative policies, ethical governance, and promotion of Dhamma. - Key Takeaway: - The Maski Edict is historically significant as it explicitly names Ashoka, confirming his identity in inscriptions. - Q26: The following map shows four of the sixteen Mahajanapadas that existed in ancient India. The places marked A, B, C and D respectively are: - - Options: (a) Matsya, Cedi, Kosala, Anga (b) Surasena, Avanti, Vatsa, Magadha (c) Matsya, Avanti, Vatsa, Anga (d) Surasena, Cedi, Kosala, Magadha - Answer: (c) Matsya, Avanti, Vatsa, Anga - Analysis: - Matsya Mahajanpada comprised the present day Jaipur-Bharatpur-Alwar area of Rajasthan - Avanti was one of the most important ones and its core area comprises the present day Ujjain district of Madhya Preadesh - Vatsa with its capital at Kausambi was another powerful Mahajanapada, annexed by Magadha. - Anja Mahajanapada was in Gangetic valley - Q27: In the Mahayana Buddhism, the Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara was also known as: - Options: (a) Vajrapani (b) Manjusri (c) Padmapani (d) Maitreya - Answer: (c) Padmapani - Analysis: - A Bodhisattva in Buddhism is a being who seeks enlightenment (Bodhi) not just for themselves but for the benefit of all sentient beings. - Why (c) Padmapani? - Avalokitesvara, the Bodhisattva of Compassion in Mahayana Buddhism, is often depicted holding a lotus (Padma), which is why he is also called Padmapani. - He is considered the embodiment of boundless compassion and is revered in various Buddhist traditions, especially in Tibet and East Asia. - Explanation of Other Options: - (a) Vajrapani: - Incorrect—Vajrapani is the Bodhisattva of Power and is often depicted holding a vajra (thunderbolt). - (b) Manjusri: - Incorrect—Manjusri is the Bodhisattva of Wisdom, depicted holding a sword to cut through ignorance. - (d) Maitreya: - Incorrect—Maitreya is the future Buddha, who is prophesied to appear when the teachings of Gautama Buddha have faded. - Important Bodhisattvas in Mahayana Buddhism: - Avalokitesvara (Padmapani): - Bodhisattva of Compassion, depicted with a lotus. - Worshipped as Guanyin in China and Kannon in Japan. - Manjusri: - Bodhisattva of Wisdom, depicted with a sword and a book (Prajnaparamita). - Vajrapani: - Bodhisattva of Power and Protector of Buddha's teachings. - Maitreya: - The future Buddha who will appear in the next age. - Depicted sitting on a throne, waiting to descend to earth. - Ksitigarbha: - Bodhisattva of the Underworld, protector of souls in Buddhist hells. - Samantabhadra: - Bodhisattva of Practice and Meditation, often depicted with an elephant. - Akasagarbha: - Bodhisattva of Space and Infinite Wisdom. - Symbolism of Avalokitesvara: - He is known for his thousand-armed form (Sahasrabhuj Lokeshvara) to help countless beings. - He is worshipped in different names and forms across cultures: - In Tibet, as Chenrezig. - In China, as Guanyin. - In Japan, as Kannon. - Broader Context: - Links to Questions on Mahayana Buddhism: - Related to Q34 [2016] on Buddhist councils and Q42 [2018] on different Bodhisattvas. - Can be connected to questions on Buddhist iconography in art and sculpture, such as Gandhara and Ajanta paintings. - Key Takeaway: - Avalokitesvara, also called Padmapani, is the Bodhisattva of Compassion, widely venerated in Mahayana Buddhism, symbolizing mercy and protection. - Mahayana Buddhism emphasizes the role of Bodhisattvas, enlightened beings who delay Nirvana to help others achieve liberation. - Q28: The silver coins issued by the Guptas were called: - Options: (a) Rupaka (b) Karshapana (c) Dinara (d) Pana - Answer: (a) Rupaka - Analysis: - Why (a) Rupaka?: - The Gupta Empire issued silver coins called Rupaka, which followed the weight standard of the Western Kshatrapas. - These coins typically featured the king's portrait on one side and a deity or Garuda on the other. - Explanation of Other Options: - (b) Karshapana: - Incorrect—Karshapana was an ancient punch-marked coin used in the Mauryan period, not the Gupta era. - (c) Dinara: - Incorrect—Dinara was the name of gold coins issued by the Gupta rulers, modeled after the Roman Aureus. - (d) Pana: - Incorrect—Pana was a currency used in earlier periods, particularly in the Mauryan empire. - Coinage System of the Gupta Empire: - Gold Coins (Dinara): - The most prominent coins of the Gupta period, showcasing rulers and Hindu deities like Vishnu and Lakshmi. - Silver Coins (Rupaka): - Issued mainly in western India, influenced by the earlier Kshatrapa coinage. - Copper Coins: - Used for smaller transactions, but not as widely circulated as gold and silver coins. - Important Gupta Rulers and Their Coinage: - Chandragupta I (c. 319 - 335 CE): - Issued gold Dinara coins, depicting himself and his queen, Kumaradevi. - Samudragupta (c. 335 - 375 CE): - Issued various types of coins, including Standard Type, Archer Type, and Battle Axe Type. - Chandragupta II (c. 375 - 415 CE): - Introduced silver Rupaka coins after defeating the Western Kshatrapas. - Kumaragupta I (c. 415 - 455 CE): - Issued coins with Kartikeya and Garuda insignia. - Skandagupta (c. 455 - 467 CE): - Issued coins depicting Vishnu's Garuda and war-related imagery. - Broader Context: - Links to Questions on Ancient Indian Economy: - Similar to Q42 [2015] on Mauryan currency and Q63 [2017] on Kushana coinage. - Can connect to questions on trade, commerce, and monetary systems in ancient India. - Key Takeaway: - The Gupta period saw an advanced coinage system, with Rupaka being the standard silver currency, alongside gold Dinara and lesser-used copper coins. - Q29: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: - List-I (Author): A. Varahamihira B. Vishakhadatta C. Sudraka D. Bilhana - List-II (Work): 1. Prabhakaravardhana 2. Mrichchhakatika 3. Brihat-Samhita 4. Devi-Chandraguptam 5. Vikramankadeva-Charita - Options: (a) A-3, B-4, C-2, D-5 (b) A-3, B-2, C-4, D-5 (c) A-5, B-4, C-2, D-3 (d) A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2 - Answer: (a) A-3, B-4, C-2, D-5 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Gupta and post-Gupta periods (4th-11th centuries A.D.) were a high point for Indian literature, producing works in astronomy, drama, and poetry. This question pairs notable authors with their works, spanning scientific treatises (Varahamihira), Sanskrit plays (Vishakhadatta, Sudraka), and historical poetry (Bilhana). - These works reflect the cultural and intellectual diversity of ancient India, often tied to royal patronage. - Correct Matches Explained: - Varahamihira - Brihat-Samhita (A-3): - A 6th-century astronomer and polymath, Varahamihira wrote Brihat-Samhita, an encyclopedic work covering astronomy, astrology, architecture, and omens, influential in Gupta scientific traditions. - Vishakhadatta - Devi-Chandraguptam (B-4): - Vishakhadatta, a Gupta-era playwright, is attributed with Devi-Chandraguptam, a political drama about Chandragupta Maurya and the rise of his dynasty. - Sudraka - Mrichchhakatika (C-2): - Sudraka, a playwright of uncertain date but likely from the early post-Gupta period, is credited with Mrichchhakatika (The Little Clay Cart), which blends romance and social commentary. - Bilhana - Vikramankadeva-Charita (D-5): - Bilhana, an 11th-century Kashmiri poet, wrote Vikramankadeva-Charita, a poetic biography of Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI. - Why Not Others?: - (b) A-3, B-2, C-4, D-5: - Incorrect—This option misassigns Vishakhadatta’s work, pairing him with Mrichchhakatika instead of Devi-Chandraguptam. - (c) A-5, B-4, C-2, D-3: - Incorrect—Varahamihira is incorrectly paired with Vikramankadeva-Charita, and Bilhana is misassigned to Brihat-Samhita. - (d) A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2: - Incorrect—Varahamihira is wrongly associated with Prabhakaravardhana, a king, not a work, and other mismatches occur in the pairings. - Literary Genres Represented: - Scientific Treatise: - Brihat-Samhita: Astronomy and astrology, blending science with practical knowledge. - Sanskrit Drama: - Mrichchhakatika and Devi-Chandraguptam: Political and social narratives, rooted in Gupta theatrical traditions. - Historical Poetry: - Vikramankadeva-Charita: Courtly eulogy, typical of medieval India. - Other Notable Works by These Authors: - Varahamihira: - Pancha-Siddhantika: Treatise on five astronomical systems, complementing Brihat-Samhita. - Vishakhadatta: - Mudrarakshasa: Political drama about Chandragupta Maurya and Chanakya, often UPSC-tested (e.g., Q18 [1996]). - Sudraka: - Mrichchhakatika is his only widely recognized work, though authorship is debated. - Bilhana: - Chaurapanchasika: Romantic poetry, showcasing his versatility beyond historical themes. - Related Figures: - Kalidasa: - Gupta-era poet and playwright (e.g., Abhijnanashakuntalam), contemporary of Vishakhadatta and Sudraka, known for Sanskrit-Prakrit usage (e.g., Q105 [2015-I]). - Bhasa: - Pre-Gupta playwright, influenced later drama (e.g., Svapnavasavadatta), setting the stage for Gupta works (e.g., Q150 [2024-I]). - Aryabhata: - 5th-century astronomer, peer of Varahamihira, authored Aryabhatiya, impacting scientific literature (e.g., Q84 [2012-I]). - Harisena: - Gupta poet, wrote the Allahabad Pillar inscription, akin to Bilhana's courtly style (e.g., Q76 [2006]). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Gupta cultural achievements (e.g., Q18 [1996] on Vishakhadatta), literary traditions (e.g., Q4 [1995] on Prakrit), or medieval poetry (e.g., Q142 [2022-I] on Chalukyas). - Key Takeaway: - Matching authors to works reveals the diversity of Gupta and post-Gupta literature, from science (Varahamihira) to drama (Vishakhadatta, Sudraka) to poetry (Bilhana). - Q30: Which one of the following was a common institution in the village system of ancient India? - Options: (a) Chaturvedimangalam (b) Parishad (c) Ashtadikgaja (d) Manigrama - Answer: (b) Parishad (book is saying option d, but option b makes more sense) - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In ancient India, village systems were the backbone of agrarian society, especially during Vedic and post-Vedic periods (c. 1500 BCE-600 CE). Local institutions managed community affairs, with the Parishad being a common assembly of learned Brahmins or elders that advised on religious, legal, and social matters. - These bodies were prominent in Vedic texts and continued in various forms into later periods, reflecting decentralized governance. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Chaturvedimangalam: - Incorrect—Refers to a South Indian Brahmin settlement endowed with land (common in Chola period, 9th-13th centuries CE), not a widespread village institution in ancient India. - (c) Ashtadikgaja: - Incorrect—Means "eight elephants of the directions," a term for eight poets in the court of Vijayanagara king Krishnadevaraya (16th century CE), unrelated to ancient village systems. - (d) Manigrama: - Incorrect—A medieval South Indian merchant guild (e.g., in Chola inscriptions), not a common village institution but a trade-specific organization. - Role of Parishad: - The Parishad, often comprising Vedic scholars or village elders, acted as a council for dispute resolution, education, and upholding Dharma, as seen in texts like the Rigveda and Dharmashastras (e.g., Manu Smriti). - Village Institutions in Ancient India: - Sabha: - Village assembly for general community decisions, broader than Parishad, mentioned in Rigveda (e.g., 10.191). - Samiti: - Larger tribal or regional gathering, less localized than Parishad, also Vedic in origin (e.g., Atharvaveda 7.12). - Gramani: - Village headman, a key administrative figure alongside Parishad, responsible for local leadership (Rigveda 10.62). - Panchayat: - Council of five elders, evolved from Vedic assemblies, common in later texts for village justice (e.g., Yajnavalkya Smriti). - Gana: - Tribal or clan council, prevalent in Vedic and post-Vedic republics (e.g., Licchavis), influencing village governance. - Vidatha: - Early Vedic assembly for ritual and social functions, possibly a precursor to Parishad (Rigveda 3.38). - Related Figures: - Yajnavalkya: - Vedic sage (c. 1200 BCE), linked to Parishad-like assemblies in Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, known for legal and philosophical contributions (e.g., Q2 [1995] on Gargi). - Manu: - Author of Manu Smriti (c. 200 BCE-200 CE), codified roles of village councils like Parishad in social governance. - Kautilya: - Mauryan-era scholar (c. 300 BCE), described local governance in Arthashastra, including village-level bodies (e.g., Q18 [1996] on Vishakhadatta). - Harsha: - 7th-century ruler, his records (e.g., by Bana) mention village councils, evolving from earlier Parishads (e.g., Q63 [2002]). - Broader Connection: - Ties to questions on Vedic society (e.g., Q2 [1995] on Brahmavadinis), Mauryan administration (e.g., Q25 [1997] on Ashoka), or Chola local governance (e.g., Q40 [1999] on Uttiramerur). - Key Takeaway: - Parishad was a vital village institution in ancient India, reflecting the role of scholarly councils in local governance, distinct from later specialized bodies like guilds or courts. - Q31: The Badami rock inscription of Pulakesin I is dated in the Saka year 465. If the same were to be dated in Vikrama Samvat, the year would be: - Options: (a) 601 (b) 300 (c) 330 (d) 407 - Answer: (a) 601 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Pulakesin I (r. 543-566 CE), founder of the Chalukya dynasty of Badami, issued the Badami rock inscription, dated Saka year 465. The Saka era begins in 78 CE, while the Vikrama Samvat starts in 58 BCE. Converting between these eras requires adjusting for their respective starting points. - The Chalukyas of Badami (6th-8th centuries CE) were a major South Indian power, and their inscriptions often used the Saka era, reflecting regional chronological traditions. - Calculation: - Saka Year 465 + Saka Era start (78 CE) = 465 + 78 = 543 CE. - Vikrama Samvat Year = 543 CE + Vikrama Samvat offset (58 years from 58 BCE to 1 CE) = 543 + 58 = 601. - Thus, Saka 465 corresponds to Vikrama Samvat 601. - Why Not Others?: - (b) 300: - Incorrect—Vikrama Samvat 300 = 300 - 58 = 242 CE, far earlier than Saka 465 (543 CE). - (c) 330: - Incorrect—Vikrama Samvat 330 = 330 - 58 = 272 CE, still too early for 543 CE. - (d) 407: - Incorrect—Vikrama Samvat 407 = 407 - 58 = 349 CE, not matching 543 CE. - Chronological Systems in Ancient India: - Saka Era: - Starts 78 CE, linked to Kushana king Kanishka, widely used in South India (e.g., Chalukya inscriptions). - Vikrama Samvat: - Starts 58 BCE, attributed to King Vikramaditya, prevalent in North India. - Gupta Era: - Starts 320 CE, used by the Gupta dynasty (e.g., Q3 [1995]). - Kali Era: - Starts 3102 BCE, mythological, less common in inscriptions (e.g., Q3 [1995]). - Conversion Formulae: - Saka to CE: - Saka Year + 78 = CE Year. - CE to Vikrama Samvat: - CE Year + 58 = Vikrama Samvat Year. - Vikrama Samvat to CE: - Vikrama Samvat Year - 58 = CE Year. - Related Figures: - Pulakesin I: - Chalukya founder (r. 543-566 CE), issued the Badami inscription, established dynasty's power in Deccan (e.g., Q142 [2022-I] on Chalukyas). - Kanishka: - Kushana ruler (1st-2nd century CE), associated with Saka era's origin (78 CE), known for Buddhist patronage (e.g., Q57 [2001]). - Vikramaditya: - Legendary king (possibly Malwa ruler or Chandragupta II), linked to Vikrama Samvat (58 BCE) (e.g., Q3 [1995]). - Kirttivarman I: - Son of Pulakesin I (r. 566-597 CE), continued Chalukya inscriptions, maintaining Saka era usage. - Broader Connection: - Ties to questions on Chalukya history (e.g., Q142 [2022-I]), era conversions (e.g., Q3 [1995] on eras), or inscription dating (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Gupta records). - Key Takeaway: - Converting Saka 465 (543 CE) to Vikrama Samvat 601 highlights the interplay of India's dating systems, with Pulakesin I's inscription anchoring Chalukya history. - [1998] - Q32: Many of the Greeks, Kushanas and Shakas embraced Buddhism rather than Hinduism because: - Options: (a) Buddhism was in the ascendant at that time (b) they had renounced the policy of war and violence (c) caste-ridden Hinduism did not attract them (d) Buddhism provided easier access to Indian society - Answer: (c) caste-ridden Hinduism did not attract them - Analysis: - Historical Context: - During the post-Mauryan period (c. 200 BCE-300 CE), foreign groups like the Greeks (Indo-Greeks), Kushanas, and Shakas (Indo-Scythians) entered Northwest India. This era saw Buddhism flourishing under royal patronage (e.g., Ashoka), while Hinduism was rooted in Vedic traditions and caste hierarchy (varna system). - These foreign rulers often adopted Buddhism, as evident in inscriptions, coins, and art (e.g., Gandhara school), reflecting its appeal over Hinduism's rigid social structure. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Buddhism was in the ascendant at that time: - Partially true—Buddhism was prominent (e.g., Mauryan support), but its rise alone doesn't explain their preference; caste was a stronger factor. - (b) they had renounced the policy of war and violence: - Incorrect—These groups were warrior cultures (e.g., Kushanas under Kanishka); their conversion wasn't about pacifism but practicality and acceptance. - (d) Buddhism provided easier access to Indian society: - Plausible—Buddhism's egalitarian ethos aided integration, but caste aversion (option c) is the more direct and historically supported reason. - Appeal of Buddhism to Foreigners: - Buddhism rejected caste distinctions, offering a universal doctrine (e.g., Four Noble Truths) that appealed to outsiders without hereditary social barriers, unlike Hinduism's varna system (Brahmins, Kshatriyas, etc.) which excluded foreigners as mlecchas (barbarians). - Patronage of stupas, monasteries, and trade routes (e.g., Silk Road) by these rulers further aligned with Buddhism's monastic and mercantile support base. - Socio-Religious Dynamics: - Vedic Hinduism: - Emphasized caste and ritual purity, less accessible to foreigners lacking Vedic lineage. - Buddhism: - Open to all (sangha welcomed diverse converts), spread via trade and royal support (e.g., Ashoka's edicts). - Jainism: - Also egalitarian but less widespread than Buddhism during this period. - Related Figures: - Menander I (Milinda): - Indo-Greek king (c. 155-130 BCE), converted to Buddhism, famed for Milinda Panha dialogues with Nagasena (e.g., Q152 [2024-I]). - Kanishka: - Kushana ruler (c. 127-150 CE), major Buddhist patron, convened Fourth Buddhist Council, used Saka era (e.g., Q57 [2001]). - Rudradaman I: - Shaka ruler (c. 130-150 CE), Junagadh inscription shows Sanskrit adoption but Buddhist leanings among Shakas. - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), set the stage for Buddhism's appeal to later foreign rulers with his Dhamma policies (e.g., Q25 [1997]). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Indo-Greek rulers (e.g., Q57 [2001] on Kanishka), Ashokan legacy (e.g., Q5 [1995]), or cultural synthesis (e.g., Q86 [2013-I] on Gandhara art). - Key Takeaway: - The Greeks, Kushanas, and Shakas favored Buddhism over Hinduism due to its rejection of caste, offering a more inclusive path for foreign integration into Indian society. - Q33: The Ashoka major rock edicts which tell us about the Sangam Kingdom include rock edicts: - Options: (a) I and X (b) I and XI (c) II and XIII (d) II and XIV - Answer: (c) II and XIII - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ashoka (r. 268-232 BCE), the Mauryan emperor, inscribed his Major Rock Edicts across his empire to propagate Dhamma and record his reign. The Sangam Kingdom refers to the Tamil polities of the Cholas, Cheras, and Pandyas in South India (c. 300 BCE-300 CE), known from Sangam literature like Tolkappiyam. - Edicts II and XIII mention these southern neighbors, reflecting Mauryan awareness of regions beyond direct control. - Correct Edicts Explained: - Rock Edict II: - Mentions providing medical aid and planting herbs, extending to the territories of the Cholas, Pandyas, and others, showing Ashoka's welfare outreach. - Rock Edict XIII: - Lists southern kingdoms (Cholas, Pandyas, Satyaputras, Keralaputras) alongside Kalinga, detailing Ashoka's regret over conquest and his shift to Dhamma, indicating diplomatic relations. - Why Not Others?: - (a) I and X: - Incorrect—Edict I bans animal sacrifices, X praises Dhamma over fame; neither references Sangam kingdoms. - (b) I and XI: - Incorrect—Edict XI discusses Dhamma gifts and morality, no mention of southern kingdoms. - (d) II and XIV: - Incorrect—Edict XIV outlines edict uniformity, not Sangam specifics; only II relates to the south. - Ashoka's Southern Outreach: - Edicts II and XIII highlight Ashoka's engagement with Tamil kingdoms as frontier states, not under Mauryan rule but influenced by his policies, suggesting trade or cultural ties. - Sangam Kingdoms Overview: - Cholas: - Coastal Tamil rulers, later prominent in medieval period (e.g., Q40 [1999] on Chola villages). - Cheras: - West coast rulers (Kerala), known for trade with Romans. - Pandyas: - Southern Tamil kings, famed for pearl fisheries. - Satyaputras and Keralaputras: - Lesser-known Tamil chieftains, also in Edict XIII. - Related Figures: - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), authored the edicts, shifted to Buddhism post-Kalinga (e.g., Q5 [1995]). - Kanishka: - Kushana ruler (c. 127-150 CE), later Buddhist patron, contrasting Ashoka's earlier outreach (e.g., Q32 [1998]). - Karikala Chola: - Early Chola king (c. 2nd century CE), Sangam figure, possibly contemporary with Ashokan references. - Nedunjeliyan: - Pandya king from Sangam texts (e.g., Silappadikaram), representing the southern kingdoms' era. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Ashokan inscriptions (e.g., Q5 [1995] on Priyadarsi), Mauryan-South India relations, or Sangam history (e.g., Q40 [1999] on Chola administration). - Key Takeaway: - Rock Edicts II and XIII reveal Ashoka's diplomatic and welfare outreach to the Sangam kingdoms, underscoring Mauryan influence in South India without direct conquest. - Q34: Which of the following pairs are correctly matched? - Pairs: 1. Mrichchakatikam—Shudraka 2. Buddhacharita—Vasuvandhu 3. Mudrarakshasha—Vishakadatta 4. Harshacharita—Banabhatta - Options: (a) 1, 2, 3 and 4 (b) 1, 3 and 4 (c) 1 and 4 (d) 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 1, 3 and 4 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ancient Indian literature spans various genres—drama, poetry, and biography—reflecting cultural and intellectual achievements from the Gupta period (4th-6th centuries CE) to later eras. This question tests authorship of key works from this tradition, spanning roughly 1st to 7th centuries CE. - Correctness of Pairs: - 1. Mrichchakatikam—Shudraka: - Correct—Shudraka, traditionally dated to the Gupta period, is credited with Mrichchakatikam (The Little Clay Cart), a Sanskrit play blending romance and social realism (e.g., Q4 [1995]). - 2. Buddhacharita—Vasuvandhu: - Incorrect—Buddhacharita, an epic poem on Buddha's life, was written by Ashvaghosha (c. 1st-2nd century CE), a Buddhist poet. Vasubandhu (4th-5th century CE) was a philosopher who wrote Abhidharmakosha, not this work. - 3. Mudrarakshasha—Vishakadatta: - Correct—Vishakadatta, a Gupta-era playwright, authored Mudrarakshasha, a political drama about Chandragupta Maurya and Chanakya (e.g., Q29 [1998]). - 4. Harshacharita—Banabhatta: - Correct—Banabhatta, a 7th-century poet at Harsha's court, wrote Harshacharita, a biographical account of Emperor Harsha (e.g., Q63 [2002]). - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1, 2, 3 and 4: - Incorrect—Pair 2 (Buddhacharita—Vasuvandhu) is wrong; Ashvaghosha, not Vasubandhu, is the author. - (c) 1 and 4: - Incorrect—Misses Pair 3 (Mudrarakshasha—Vishakadatta), which is correct. - (d) 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Pair 2 is wrong, and it omits correct Pairs 1 and 4. - Literary Genres Represented: - Drama: - Mrichchakatikam and Mudrarakshasha: Sanskrit plays with social and political themes. - Epic Poetry: - Buddhacharita: Narrative of Buddha's life, rooted in Buddhist tradition. - Biography: - Harshacharita: Courtly prose-poetry chronicling Harsha's reign. - More info on their works: - Shudraka: - Mrichchakatikam is the only major work attributed to him. - Ashvaghosha: - Also wrote Saundarananda, another Buddhist epic. - Vishakadatta: - Also credited with fragments of Devi-Chandraguptam (e.g., Q29 [1998]). - Banabhatta: - Also authored Kadambari, a romantic prose work. - Related Figures: - Kalidasa: - Gupta-era poet (e.g., Abhijnanashakuntalam), contemporary of Shudraka and Vishakadatta (e.g., Q105 [2015-I]). - Ashvaghosha: - Buddhist poet (c. 1st-2nd century CE), true author of Buddhacharita, linked to Kanishka's court (e.g., Q32 [1998]). - Vasubandhu: - Philosopher (4th-5th century CE), wrote Abhidharmakosha, not Buddhacharita, often confused due to Buddhist context. - Harsha: - 7th-century ruler, patron of Banabhatta, subject of Harshacharita (e.g., Q63 [2002]). - Broader Connection: - Ties to questions on Gupta literature (e.g., Q4 [1995] on Prakrit), Buddhist texts (e.g., Q152 [2024-I]), or Harsha's reign (e.g., Q63 [2002]). - Key Takeaway: - Correct matches (Shudraka—Mrichchakatikam, Vishakadatta—Mudrarakshasha, Banabhatta—Harshacharita) highlight key literary figures, with Buddhacharita misattributed to Vasubandhu instead of Ashvaghosha. - Q35: What is the correct chronological order in which the following appeared in India? - Items: 1. Gold coins 2. Punch marked silver coins 3. Iron plough 4. Urban culture - Options: (a) 3, 4, 1, 2 (b) 3, 4, 2, 1 (c) 4, 3, 1, 2 (d) 4, 3, 2, 1 - Answer: (d) 4, 3, 2, 1 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The timeline of ancient India spans the Harappan civilization (c. 3300-1300 BCE) to the post-Mauryan period (c. 200 BCE-300 CE). This question traces technological and economic developments across these phases. - Chronological Order Explained: - 4. Urban culture: - Earliest—Appeared with the Harappan civilization (c. 2600-1900 BCE), marked by cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro with planned streets and drainage (e.g., Q1 [1995]). - 3. Iron plough: - Next—Emerged in the later Vedic period (c. 1000 BCE), linked to iron technology in the Gangetic plains, boosting agriculture (e.g., Painted Grey Ware sites). - 2. Punch marked silver coins: - Followed—Introduced around 6th-5th centuries BCE during the Mahajanapadas (e.g., Magadha), standardized trade with silver coins bearing punch marks. - 1. Gold coins: - Latest—Appeared in the post-Mauryan period (c. 1st century BCE-1st century CE), notably under Kushanas (e.g., Kanishka's gold dinaras), influenced by Indo-Greek and Roman trade. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 3, 4, 1, 2: - Incorrect—Iron plough (c. 1000 BCE) predates urban culture (c. 2600 BCE), reversing the order. - (b) 3, 4, 2, 1: - Incorrect—Iron plough before urban culture is wrong; urban culture is far earlier. - (c) 4, 3, 1, 2: - Incorrect—Gold coins (1st century BCE-CE) before punch marked silver coins (6th-5th centuries BCE) is out of sequence. - Key Developments Timeline: - Harappan Urbanization: - c. 2600-1900 BCE: Urban culture with advanced planning, no metals like iron yet. - Iron Age: - c. 1000 BCE: Iron plough introduced, aiding settled agriculture in North India. - Early Coinage: - c. 600-400 BCE: Punch marked silver coins, linked to Mahajanapadas and trade. - Gold Coinage: - c. 1st century BCE-CE: Gold coins under Kushanas, reflecting wealth and foreign influence. - Archaeological Evidence: - Urban Culture: - Harappan sites (e.g., Lothal, Gujarat; Dholavira, Gujarat). - Iron Plough: - Iron tools from PGW sites (e.g., Hastinapur, Uttar Pradesh). - Punch Marked Coins: - Found across Gangetic plains (e.g., Taxila, Punjab). - Gold Coins: - Kushana mints (e.g., Mathura, Uttar Pradesh). - Related Figures: - Harsha: - 7th-century ruler, reflects later urban continuity, not the origin (e.g., Q63 [2002]). - Bimbisara: - Magadhan king (c. 6th century BCE), linked to punch marked coins' era (e.g., Q25 [1997] on Ashoka's context). - Kanishka: - Kushana ruler (c. 127-150 CE), introduced gold coins, marking their peak (e.g., Q32 [1998]). - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), postdates punch marked coins, predates gold coins (e.g., Q5 [1995]). - Broader Connection: - Ties to questions on Harappan urbanism (e.g., Q1 [1995]), Iron Age technology (e.g., Q142 [2022-I] on Chalukyas' context), or coinage evolution (e.g., Q57 [2001] on Kanishka). - Key Takeaway: - The sequence—urban culture (Harappan), iron plough (Vedic), punch marked silver coins (Mahajanapadas), gold coins (Kushanas)—maps India's progression from urban beginnings to advanced trade economies. - Q36: Statements - Assertion (A): According to Ashoka's edicts social harmony among the people was more important than religious devotion. - Reason (R): He spread ideas of equity instead of promotion of religion. - Options: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A and R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ashoka (r. 268-232 BCE), after the Kalinga War, shifted from conquest to Dhamma—a moral code emphasizing tolerance, compassion, and social harmony—reflected in his edicts (Major Rock, Pillar, and Minor). These inscriptions, spread across India (e.g., Dhauli, Odisha), aimed to unify a diverse empire. - Evaluation of Assertion (A): - True—Ashoka's edicts prioritize social harmony over religious devotion. For example, Major Rock Edict 12 (Girnar, Gujarat) promotes harmony among sects rather than devotion to one faith, and Edict 7 stresses tolerance over ritualistic piety. - Evaluation of Reason (R): - True—Ashoka's Dhamma focuses on equity, respect, and ethical conduct (e.g., Edict 11 on generosity to all), not promoting any single religion, including Buddhism, despite his personal leanings (e.g., Bhabru Edict, Rajasthan). - Correct Explanation—R explains A because Ashoka's emphasis on equity (e.g., equal treatment of all sects, welfare in Edict 2) directly supports social harmony as a higher goal than religious devotion. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Both A and R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A: - Incorrect—R (equity) directly underpins A (social harmony), as equity fosters unity across diverse groups, aligning with Ashoka's intent. - (c) A is true but R is false: - Incorrect—R is true; Ashoka's edicts (e.g., Edict 9 condemning rituals) show he prioritized ethical equity over religious promotion. - (d) A is false but R is true: - Incorrect—A is true; edicts consistently elevate harmony (e.g., Edict 13's remorse and outreach) over devotion. - Ashoka's Dhamma Principles: - Social Harmony: - Edict 12: Encourages mutual respect among religions to reduce conflict. - Equity: - Edict 5: Dhamma Mahamatras ensure welfare for all classes, not just one faith. - Non-Religious Focus: - Edict 9: Critiques empty rituals, favoring moral actions. - Evidence from Edicts: - Major Rock Edict 2: - Welfare extended to all, including Sangam Kingdoms, showing universal equity (Junagadh, Gujarat). - Major Rock Edict 13: - Lists diverse neighbors (e.g., Cholas, Pandyas) with a call for peace, not religious conformity (Dhauli, Odisha). - Pillar Edict 6: - Fair administration for all subjects, emphasizing justice over faith (Delhi-Topra, Delhi). - Related Figures: - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), crafted Dhamma post-Kalinga, named in Maski Edict (Raichur, Karnataka) (e.g., Q5 [1995]). - Kanishka: - Kushana ruler (c. 127-150 CE), later Buddhist patron, contrasts Ashoka's broader equity focus (e.g., Q32 [1998]). - Manu: - Lawgiver (c. 200 BCE-200 CE), his caste-based Dharma differs from Ashoka's equitable Dhamma (e.g., Q30 [1998]). - Harsha: - 7th-century ruler, blended religion and governance, unlike Ashoka's secular tilt (e.g., Q34 [1998]). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Ashokan policies (e.g., Q33 [1998] on Sangam outreach), religious tolerance (e.g., Q32 [1998] on Buddhism), or social structures (e.g., Q30 [1998] on Parishad). - Key Takeaway: - Ashoka's edicts prioritize social harmony through equity (A and R true), with R explaining A by showing his focus on universal ethics over religious promotion. - Q37: Which of the following pairs are correctly matched? - Pairs: 1. Lothal: Ancient dockyard 2. Sarnath: First Sermon of Buddha 3. Rajgir: Lion capital of Ashoka 4. Lothal: Ancient dockyard: - Correct—Lothal (Gujarat), a Harappan site, is famed for its dockyard, possibly the world's earliest, linked to maritime trade (c. 2400 BCE) (e.g., Q1 [1995]). - 2. Sarnath: First Sermon of Buddha: - Correct—Sarnath (near Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh) is where Buddha delivered his First Sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) c. 5th century BCE, marked by the Dhamekh Stupa. - 3. Rajgir: Lion capital of Ashoka: - Incorrect—Rajgir (Bihar) was a Magadhan capital and site of the First Buddhist Council (c. 483 BCE), but the Lion Capital, Ashoka's iconic pillar symbol, is from Sarnath (c. 250 BCE), not Rajgir. - 4. Nalanda: Great seat of Buddhist learning: - Correct—Nalanda (Bihar) was a renowned Buddhist university, flourishing from the 5th century CE under Gupta patronage, visited by Hiuen Tsang (7th century CE). - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1, 2, 3 and 4: - Incorrect—Pair 3 (Rajgir: Lion capital) is wrong; the Lion Capital is at Sarnath. - (b) 3 and 4: - Incorrect—Pair 3 is incorrect, and it misses correct Pairs 1 and 2. - (d) 1 and 2: - Incorrect—Omits Pair 4 (Nalanda), which is correct. - Significance of Sites: - Lothal: - Harappan port, evidence of early trade with Mesopotamia (modern Gujarat). - Sarnath: - Buddhist pilgrimage site, also home to Ashoka's Lion Capital (modern Uttar Pradesh). - Rajgir: - Early political and Buddhist center, not linked to the Lion Capital (modern Bihar). - Nalanda: - Pinnacle of Buddhist education, with vast libraries and monasteries (modern Bihar). - Correct Locations and Associations: - Lothal: - Dockyard, not Buddhist or Ashokan (Gujarat). - Sarnath: - First Sermon and Lion Capital, not Rajgir (Uttar Pradesh). - Rajgir: - Buddhist councils and Gridhrakuta Hill, not Lion Capital (Bihar). - Nalanda: - University, not a sermon or dock site (Bihar). - Related Figures: - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), erected the Sarnath Lion Capital, not at Rajgir (e.g., Q5 [1995]). - Buddha: - Siddhartha Gautama (c. 5th century BCE), gave his First Sermon at Sarnath, shaping its legacy. - Hiuen Tsang: - Chinese pilgrim (7th century CE), documented Nalanda's grandeur, not Lothal or Rajgir. - Key Takeaway: - Correct matches are Sarnath (First Sermon) and Nalanda (Buddhist learning), while Lothal's dockyard is right but Rajgir's Lion Capital belongs to Sarnath. - Q38: Which one of the following ancient Indian records is the earliest royal order to preserve food-grains to be utilised during the crises in the country? - Options: (a) Sohgaura Copper-plate (b) Rummindei Pillar-edict of Ashoka (c) Prayaga-prasasti (d) Mehrauli Pillar inscription of Chandra - Answer: (a) Sohgaura Copper-plate - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ancient Indian inscriptions often served as royal decrees or records of significant events, ranging from pre-Mauryan times (c. 6th century BCE) to the Gupta period (4th-6th centuries CE). This question focuses on early evidence of state-managed crisis preparedness through food-grain preservation. - Correct Option Explained: - (a) Sohgaura Copper-plate: - Earliest—Dated to c. 3rd century BCE (possibly pre-Mauryan or early Mauryan), found near Gorakhpur (Uttar Pradesh), this copper-plate inscription mentions the construction of granaries (kostokat_storage) to store grain for use during famines or crises, making it the earliest known royal order of its kind. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Rummindei Pillar-edict of Ashoka: - Incorrect—Dated to c. 250 BCE (Ashoka's reign, 268-232 BCE), found at Lumbini (Nepal), it records Ashoka's visit to Buddha's birthplace and tax exemptions, with no mention of food-grain preservation. - (c) Prayaga-prasasti: - Incorrect—Dated to c. 335 CE, the Allahabad Pillar inscription (Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh) by Samudragupta's court poet Harisena praises the Gupta king's conquests, not crisis management like grain storage. - (d) Mehrauli Pillar inscription of Chandra: - Incorrect—Dated to c. 375-415 CE (likely Chandragupta II), found in Delhi, it commemorates victories (e.g., against the Sakas), with no reference to food-grain preservation. - Significance of Granaries in Ancient India: - Pre-Mauryan/Mauryan: - Sohgaura's granaries reflect early state planning for famine relief, predating Ashoka's welfare measures. - Mauryan: - Ashoka's Edict 2 (c. 250 BCE) mentions welfare like medical aid, but not specific grain storage orders. - Gupta: - Later inscriptions focus on conquests or piety, not crisis-specific grain reserves. - Chronological Context: - Sohgaura Copper-plate: - c. 3rd century BCE, possibly pre-Mauryan or early Mauryan. - Rummindei Pillar-edict: - c. 250 BCE, mid-Mauryan. - Prayaga-prasasti: - c. 335 CE, early Gupta. - Mehrauli Pillar: - c. 375-415 CE, Gupta peak. - Related Figures: - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), known for welfare (e.g., Edict 2), not granaries (e.g., Q5 [1995]). - Samudragupta: - Gupta king (r. 335-375 CE), Prayaga-prasasti records conquests, not food policy (e.g., Q76 [2006]). - Chandragupta II: - Gupta ruler (r. 375-415 CE), Mehrauli inscription celebrates victories, not granaries. - Kautilya: - Mauryan advisor (c. 300 BCE), Arthashastra mentions granaries, but Sohgaura is the earliest physical record. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Mauryan administration (e.g., Q33 [1998]), Gupta inscriptions (e.g., Q76 [2006]), or early economic planning (e.g., Q35 [1998] on coins). - Key Takeaway: - The Sohgaura Copper-plate (c. 3rd century BCE) is the earliest royal order for food-grain preservation, predating Ashoka's edicts and Gupta records focused on other themes. - Q39: The concept of Eight-fold path forms the theme of: - Options: (a) Dipavamsa (b) Divyavadana (c) Mahaparinibbana Sutta (d) Dharma Chakara Pravartana Sutta - Answer: (d) Dharma Chakara Pravartana Sutta - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Eight-fold Path is a core Buddhist teaching, outlined by Gautama Buddha (c. 5th century BCE) as the path to Nirvana, comprising right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration. This question tests knowledge of Buddhist texts from the Pali Canon and later chronicles. - Correct Option Explained: - (d) Dharma Chakara Pravartana Sutta: - Correct—Also known as the "Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma," this sutta records Buddha's First Sermon at Sarnath (c. 5th century BCE), where he introduced the Four Noble Truths and the Eight-fold Path as the Middle Way to end suffering. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Dipavamsa: - Incorrect—A 4th-century CE Sinhalese chronicle narrating Buddhist history in Sri Lanka, not focused on the Eight-fold Path but on monastic lineage. - (b) Divyavadana: - Incorrect—A Sanskrit Buddhist text (c. 2nd-3rd century CE) with moral tales (e.g., Ashoka's stories), not centered on the Eight-fold Path. - (c) Mahaparinibbana Sutta: - Incorrect—Part of the Pali Canon (Digha Nikaya), it describes Buddha's last days and Parinirvana (c. 483 BCE), emphasizing his final teachings but not the Eight-fold Path as its theme. - Buddhist Texts and Their Themes: - Dharma Chakara Pravartana Sutta: - Eight-fold Path and Four Noble Truths, foundational teaching (Pali Canon). - Mahaparinibbana Sutta: - Buddha's death and final instructions, not the Eight-fold Path's origin. - Dipavamsa: - Historical narrative of Buddhism's spread, not doctrinal focus. - Divyavadana: - Didactic stories, not a systematic exposition of the Path. - Eight-fold Path in Context: - Introduced in the First Sermon (Sarnath), it guides ethical conduct, mental discipline, and wisdom, contrasting with extreme asceticism or indulgence, as per Buddha's Middle Way. - Related Figures: - Gautama Buddha: - Siddhartha (c. 5th century BCE), delivered the Dharma Chakara Pravartana Sutta at Sarnath (e.g., Q37 [1998]). - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), promoted Buddhism, linked to Divyavadana tales (e.g., Q5 [1995]). - Ananda: - Buddha's attendant, recited Mahaparinibbana Sutta at the First Council (Rajgir, Bihar). - Nagasena: - Later monk (c. 2nd century BCE), discussed Buddhist doctrine with Menander, not tied to these texts (e.g., Q32 [1998]). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Buddhist sites (e.g., Q37 [1998] on Sarnath), Ashokan spread of Buddhism (e.g., Q33 [1998]), or doctrinal evolution (e.g., Q32 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - The Dharma Chakara Pravartana Sutta, Buddha's First Sermon, uniquely centers on the Eight-fold Path, distinguishing it from other texts like chronicles or death narratives. - Q40: The given map relates to: - - Options: (a) Kanishka at the time of his death (b) Samudragupta after the close of his South Indian campaign (c) Ashoka towards close of his reign (d) Empire of Thaneswar on the eve of Harsha's accession - Answer: (c) Ashoka towards close of his reign - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ancient Indian empires varied in scope, from the northwest-focused Kushanas (1st-2nd century CE) to the pan-Indian Mauryas (3rd century BCE) and Guptas (4th century CE), and the regional Thaneswar (7th century CE). Without the map, the answer hinges on typical UPSC patterns and territorial logic. - Evaluation of Options: - (a) Kanishka at the time of his death: - Kanishka (r. c. 127-150 CE), a Kushana ruler, controlled Northwest India (modern Punjab, Kashmir, parts of Uttar Pradesh), Central Asia, and parts of the Gangetic plains (e.g., Mathura). His empire didn't extend deep into South India or the Deccan. - (b) Samudragupta after the close of his South Indian campaign: - Samudragupta (r. 335-375 CE), a Gupta king, conquered much of North India and conducted a South Indian campaign (c. 350 CE), subduing kings in the Deccan and Tamil regions (e.g., Prayaga-prasasti). His empire spanned the Gangetic plains, parts of Central India, and had tributary states in the south, but not direct control over the far south. - (c) Ashoka towards close of his reign: - Ashoka (r. 268-232 BCE), Mauryan emperor, ruled a vast empire after the Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE), covering modern North India (Punjab to Bengal), the Deccan (up to Karnataka), and Kalinga (Odisha). Edicts (e.g., Dhauli, Odisha; Girnar, Gujarat) and references to Sangam Kingdoms (Edict 13) suggest influence, not control, in the far south (Tamil Nadu, Kerala). - (d) Empire of Thaneswar on the eve of Harsha's accession: - Thaneswar (c. 606 CE), under Prabhakaravardhana, was a smaller North Indian kingdom (modern Haryana, parts of Punjab, Uttar Pradesh) before Harsha (r. 606-647 CE) expanded it. It didn't span the Deccan or South India at accession. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Kanishka: - Incorrect—His empire was northwest-centric, lacking the pan-Indian reach of Ashoka or Samudragupta's southern campaigns. - (b) Samudragupta: - Incorrect—While extensive, his direct control didn't match Ashoka's breadth (e.g., no Gujarat or full Deccan), and southern gains were tributary, not annexed. - (d) Thaneswar: - Incorrect—Far smaller, limited to North India pre-Harsha, unlike the broader empires of others. - Territorial Extents: - Kanishka: - Northwest India, Central Asia, parts of Gangetic plains (c. 1st-2nd century CE). - Samudragupta: - North India, Deccan, tributary South India (c. 350 CE). - Ashoka: - Pan-Indian (Punjab to Odisha, down to Karnataka), influence in Tamil regions (c. 232 BCE). - Thaneswar: - Haryana, parts of Punjab, Uttar Pradesh (c. 606 CE). - Map Deduction: - Map shows a vast empire from Northwest India to the Deccan, with influence (not control) in the far south, Ashoka's reign (c. 232 BCE) fits best, as per his edict locations (e.g., Junagadh, Gujarat; Bhubaneswar, Odisha) and Edict 13's southern references (Cholas, Pandyas). - Related Figures: - Kanishka: - Kushana ruler (r. c. 127-150 CE), northwest empire, Buddhist patron (e.g., Q32 [1998]). - Samudragupta: - Gupta king (r. 335-375 CE), South Indian campaign, Prayaga-prasasti (e.g., Q38 [1998]). - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), widest empire, edict-based governance (e.g., Q33 [1998]). - Harsha: - Thaneswar ruler (r. 606-647 CE), expanded post-accession, not pre- (e.g., Q34 [1998]). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Ashokan edicts (e.g., Q33 [1998]), Gupta conquests (e.g., Q38 [1998]), or Kushana rule (e.g., Q32 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - Ashoka's empire towards his reign's end (c. 232 BCE) likely matches the map's pan-Indian scope, outstripping Kanishka's northwest focus, Samudragupta's tributary south, and Thaneswar's initial small size. - [1999] - Q41: From the third century AD when the Hun invasion ended the Roman Empire, the Indian merchants relied more and more on the: - Options: (a) African trade (b) West-European trade (c) South-East Asian trade (d) Middle-Eastern trade - Answer: (c) South-East Asian trade - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Huns' invasions (e.g., under Attila, c. 5th century CE) disrupted the Western Roman Empire, collapsing by 476 CE. This ended the lucrative Indo-Roman trade (c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE) via the Red Sea and Mediterranean, pushing Indian merchants to seek new markets from the 3rd century CE onward. - Correct Option Explained: - (c) South-East Asian trade: - Correct—From the 3rd-4th centuries CE, Indian merchants increasingly focused on South-East Asia (e.g., Funan, Champa, Srivijaya in modern Cambodia, Vietnam, Indonesia). Archaeological evidence (e.g., Oc Eo port) and texts (e.g., Buddhist accounts) show trade in spices, textiles, and cultural exchange, boosted by the rise of Indianized kingdoms. - Why Not Others?: - (a) African trade: - Incorrect—Trade with East Africa (e.g., Axum, modern Ethiopia) existed via the Red Sea, but it declined post-Roman collapse and was less significant than South-East Asian routes. - (b) West-European trade: - Incorrect—Western Europe was fragmented after Rome's fall (e.g., Dark Ages), with no direct maritime trade replacing the Roman network until much later. - (d) Middle-Eastern trade: - Incorrect—Middle Eastern trade (e.g., via Persian Gulf) persisted with Sassanids, but it was a conduit, not a primary market, and didn't match South-East Asia's growing demand. - Shift in Trade Patterns: - Pre-3rd Century: - Indo-Roman trade dominated (e.g., pepper, gems via Muziris, Kerala to Rome). - Post-3rd Century: - South-East Asian trade rose, with Indian goods (e.g., cotton, beads) and culture (e.g., Hinduism, Buddhism) spreading to Funan and beyond. - Evidence of South-East Asian Trade: - Archaeological: - Indian pottery, beads at Oc Eo (Vietnam), Kedah (Malaysia). - Literary: - Buddhist Jatakas and Chinese records (e.g., Fa-Hien, 5th century CE) note Indian ships in South-East Asia. - Cultural: - Angkor Wat (Cambodia), Borobudur (Indonesia) reflect Indian influence from this period. - Related Figures: - Fa-Hien: - Chinese pilgrim (c. 399-414 CE), documented Indian maritime activity in South-East Asia. - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), earlier spread Buddhism, laying cultural trade foundations (e.g., Q33 [1998]). - Samudragupta: - Gupta king (r. 335-375 CE), his era saw trade shift east as Roman links waned (e.g., Q40 [1998]). - Kanishka: - Kushana ruler (r. c. 127-150 CE), earlier Indo-Roman trade peak, pre-Hun disruption (e.g., Q32 [1998]). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Ashokan cultural spread (e.g., Q33 [1998]), Gupta trade (e.g., Q40 [1998]), or Buddhist influence (e.g., Q39 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - Post-3rd century CE, with Roman trade disrupted by Huns, Indian merchants pivoted to South-East Asia, fostering economic and cultural ties evident in archaeology and Indianized kingdoms. - Q42: The following persons came to India at one time or another: 1. Fa-Hien, 2. I-Tsing, 3. Megasthanese, 4. Hieun-Tsang. The correct chronological sequence of their visits is: - Options: (a) 3, 1, 2, 4 (b) 3, 1, 4, 2 (c) 1, 3, 2, 4 (d) 1, 3, 4, 2 - Answer: (b) 3, 1, 4, 2 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Foreign travelers visited India across centuries, documenting its culture, politics, and religion. This question spans the Seleucid (4th century BCE) to Tang (7th century CE) periods, testing chronological awareness. - Chronological Sequence Explained: - 3. Megasthanese: - Earliest—c. 302-298 BCE, Greek ambassador from Seleucus I to Chandragupta Maurya's court, wrote Indica about Mauryan India. - 1. Fa-Hien: - Next—c. 399-414 CE, Chinese Buddhist pilgrim during Chandragupta II's Gupta reign, visited Buddhist sites (e.g., Sarnath). - 4. Hieun-Tsang (Xuanzang): - Followed—c. 629-645 CE, Chinese monk during Harsha's rule, documented Nalanda and other centers. - 2. I-Tsing (Yijing): - Latest—c. 671-695 CE, Chinese pilgrim in the late 7th century, studied at Nalanda during its post-Harsha decline. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 3, 1, 2, 4: - Incorrect—I-Tsing (2) before Hieun-Tsang (4) reverses their order (671 CE vs. 629 CE). - (c) 1, 3, 2, 4: - Incorrect—Fa-Hien (399 CE) before Megasthanese (302 BCE) is out of sequence. - (d) 1, 3, 4, 2: - Incorrect—Fa-Hien before Megasthanese is wrong, as 399 CE follows 302 BCE. - Timeline of Visits: - Megasthanese: - c. 302-298 BCE, Mauryan period. - Fa-Hien: - c. 399-414 CE, Gupta period. - Hieun-Tsang: - c. 629-645 CE, Harsha's reign. - I-Tsing: - c. 671-695 CE, post-Harsha. - Purpose and Records: - Megasthanese: - Political account (Indica) of Mauryan court (Pataliputra, Bihar). - Fa-Hien: - Buddhist pilgrimage, recorded Gupta prosperity (e.g., Q41 [1998]). - Hieun-Tsang: - Detailed Buddhist study, Nalanda focus (Bihar) (e.g., Q37 [1998]). - I-Tsing: - Monastic rules and Nalanda's later phase. - Related Figures: - Scylax of Caryanda (Greek, c. 515 BCE) - Time Period: - Under Persian Emperor Darius I - Observations: - Sent by Darius I to explore the Indus River and its tributaries (modern-day Pakistan). - His accounts contributed to early Greek knowledge of India. - Described Indian customs, trade routes, and geography. - Megasthenes (Greek, c. 302-298 BCE) - Time Period: - Chandragupta Maurya's reign - Book: - Indica (Now lost, but referenced by later historians like Strabo and Arrian) - Observations: - First detailed Greek account of India. - Described the Mauryan capital Pataliputra, administration, caste system, and agriculture. - Mentioned mythical creatures (gold-digging ants, mouthless people). - Deimachus (Greek, c. 300 BCE) - Time Period: - Bindusara's reign (Son of Chandragupta Maurya) - Observations: - Greek envoy sent by Antiochus I (Seleucid ruler) to Bindusara's court. - Descriptions of Indian society, but fewer records than Megasthenes. - Dionysius (Greek, c. 2nd century BCE) - Time Period: - Ptolemaic Dynasty's ambassador to Maurya or post-Maurya rulers. - Observations: - Sent by Ptolemy II Philadelphus (Egyptian-Greek ruler). - Limited records, but provided insights on trade and diplomacy. - Apollonius of Tyana (Greek, c. 1st century CE) - Time Period: - Kushan era or Indo-Parthian rule - Observations: - Greek philosopher and mystic, visited Taxila (Punjab). - Described Indian ascetics (yogis, sages) and their spiritual practices. - His journey recorded by Philostratus, but contains mystical elements. - Fa-Hien (Chinese, c. 399-414 CE) - Time Period: - Gupta Empire (Chandragupta II's reign) - Book: - Fo-Kuo-Ki (Account of Buddhist Kingdoms) - Observations: - Documented Buddhist practices, monasteries, and social conditions. - Described Sarnath, Nalanda, Pataliputra, and Bodh Gaya. - Noted a decline in Buddhist influence in some regions. - Hieun Tsang (Xuanzang) (Chinese, c. 629-645 CE) - Time Period: - Harsha's reign - Book: - Si-Yu-Ki (Records of the Western World) - Observations: - Most detailed account of early medieval India. - Described Nalanda University, Buddhism, and Hinduism. - Documented Harsha's rule, governance, and religious tolerance. - I-Tsing (Chinese, c. 671-695 CE) - Time Period: - Late Nalanda phase - Book: - A Record of Buddhist Practices - Observations: - Studied Buddhism in Nalanda and documented monastic traditions. - Provided linguistic notes on Sanskrit and its use in Buddhist texts. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Mauryan records (e.g., Q34 [1998]), Gupta culture (e.g., Q41 [1998]), or Buddhist sites (e.g., Q37 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - The correct sequence—Megasthanese (302 BCE), Fa-Hien (399 CE), Hieun-Tsang (629 CE), I-Tsing (671 CE)—spans India's ancient travelers from Greek to Chinese Buddhist perspectives. - Q43: Which one of the following was initially the most powerful city-state of India in the 6th century B.C.? - Options: (a) Gandhar (b) Kamboj (c) Kashi (d) Magadh - Answer: (d) Magadh - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Strategic Location: - Fertile Gangetic plains supported agriculture and population growth. - Rivers like the Ganga and Son facilitated trade and communication. - Military Strength: - Early rulers, including Bimbisara and Ajatashatru, expanded Magadh through conquests. - Use of war elephants and fortified capital cities gave it a military edge. - Political Expansion: - Magadh annexed Anga, Kashi, and Vajji, weakening its rivals. - Later, it formed the foundation for the Mauryan Empire. - Why Not Others? - (a) Gandhar: - Important for Indo-Greek trade and culture but not the most dominant state in the 6th century B.C. - (b) Kamboj: - A significant warrior tribe but remained semi-nomadic with less centralization. - (c) Kashi: - Initially powerful but later absorbed by Magadh. - Key Takeaway: - Magadh's early dominance in the 6th century B.C. laid the foundation for imperial unification under the Mauryas. - Q44: The Indo-Greek Kingdom set up in north Afghanistan in the beginning of the second century B.C. was: - Answer: (c) a speech group - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The term "Aryan" originates from the Sanskrit word Ārya, meaning "noble" or "honorable." - It was used in the Vedic texts to describe cultural and linguistic identity rather than racial or ethnic distinctions. - Why a Speech Group? - Linguistic Classification: - Aryans spoke an early form of Sanskrit, classified under the Indo-Iranian branch of the Indo-European language family. - Migration and Spread: - The Indo-Aryan language speakers migrated into the Indian subcontinent around 1500 BCE. - No Racial Connotation: - Modern studies confirm that Aryans were identified by language, not physical characteristics. - Why Not Others? - (a) an ethnic group: - Incorrect, as Aryans were linguistically diverse and not a homogenous ethnic group. - (b) a nomadic people: - Partially correct, as early Aryans were pastoralists, but the term refers primarily to language. - (d) a superior race: - Incorrect, as the "Aryan race" theory was a later European misinterpretation with no historical basis. - [2000] - Q47: Statements - Assertion (A): The Aham and Puram poems of the Padinen Kilukanakku group formed a continuation of the Sangam composition. - Reason (R): They were included under the post-Sangam works as against the Sangam works proper. - Explanation of Assertion (A): - The Aham (love) and Puram (war and ethics) poems belong to the Padinen Kilukanakku (Eighteen Lesser Texts) group. - These texts reflect Sangam-era themes but were written in the post-Sangam period (c. 300-600 CE). - Explanation of Reason (R): - While the Padinen Kilukanakku texts continue the themes of Sangam literature, they are not classified as Sangam works proper but as post-Sangam texts. - This distinction is why they are considered a continuation rather than part of the original corpus. -
