Writings: Si-Yu-Ki (Great Tang Records), detailed Harsha’s reign, Nalanda (Bihar). - I-Tsing (Yijing): - When: c. 671-695 CE - Purpose: Buddhist monk studying monastic rules at Nalanda. - Writings: Record of Buddhist Practices, describes late 7th-century India (Bihar). - Related Figures: - Fa-Hien: - Chinese pilgrim (c. 399-414 CE), Gupta-era traveler (e.g., Q42 [1998]). - Hiuen-Tsang: - Chinese pilgrim (c. 629-645 CE), Harsha’s contemporary (e.g., Q42 [1998]). - Kanishka: - Kushana king (r. c. 127-150 CE), Buddhist patron, Fourth Council (e.g., Q40 [1998]). - Harsha: - Ruler (r. 606-647 CE), supported Buddhism, met Hiuen-Tsang (e.g., Q63 [1998]). - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhist councils (e.g., Q32 [1998]), Harsha’s reign (e.g., Q63 [1998]), or pilgrims’ accounts (e.g., Q42 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - Neither statement is correct: Fa-Hien couldn’t attend Kanishka’s council due to timing (1), and Hiuen-Tsang found Harsha supportive, not antagonistic, to Buddhism (2). - Q69: With reference to ancient Jainism, which one of the following statements is correct? - Options: (a) Jainism was spread in South India under the leadership of Sthalabahu (b) The Jainas who remained under the leadership of Bhadrabahu were called Shvetambaras after the council held at Pataliputra (c) Jainism enjoyed the patronage of the Kalinga king Kharavela in the first century BC (d) In the initial stage of Jainism, the Jainas worshipped images unlike the Buddhist - Answer: (c) Jainism enjoyed the patronage of the Kalinga king Kharavela in the first century BC - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ancient Jainism, founded by Mahavira (c. 599-527 BCE), evolved through schisms, regional spread, and royal patronage in the post-Mauryan period (c. 3rd century BCE-1st century CE). - Evaluation of Options: - (a) Jainism was spread in South India under the leadership of Sthalabahu: - Incorrect—No figure named Sthalabahu is historically linked to Jainism’s spread in South India. Bhadrabahu led Jains south (c. 3rd century BCE) to Shravanabelagola (Karnataka) during a famine, as per Jain texts (e.g., Bhadrabahu Charita). - (b) The Jainas who remained under the leadership of Bhadrabahu were called Shvetambaras after the council held at Pataliputra: - Incorrect—After the council at Pataliputra (c. 3rd century BCE), Bhadrabahu’s followers, who migrated south, became Digambaras (sky-clad), while those under Sthulabhadra in the north became Shvetambaras (white-clad). The statement reverses this. - (c) Jainism enjoyed the patronage of the Kalinga king Kharavela in the first century BC: - Correct—Kharavela (r. c. 1st century BCE), king of Kalinga (modern Odisha), was a Jain patron, as per his Hathigumpha inscription (c. 1st century BCE), which records his support for Jain monks and repairs to Jain caves (e.g., Udayagiri, Odisha). - (d) In the initial stage of Jainism, the Jainas worshipped images unlike the Buddhist: - Incorrect—Early Jainism (c. 6th-3rd centuries BCE), like Buddhism, was aniconic, focusing on Tirthankaras’ teachings, not images. Image worship emerged later (c. 1st century CE), similar to Buddhist iconography. - Why (c) Is Correct?: - Kharavela’s Hathigumpha inscription explicitly mentions his Jain faith, his protection of Jain monks, and his victory over Magadha, aligning with 1st-century BCE patronage in Kalinga. - Jainism’s Evolution: - Schism: - Post-Mahavira, Bhadrabahu (Digambaras) and Sthulabhadra (Shvetambaras) split after the Pataliputra council (c. 3rd century BCE). - Spread: - Bhadrabahu’s migration south (Karnataka), Kharavela’s support east (Odisha). - Worship: - Aniconic initially, icons later (e.g., Mathura, 1st century CE). - Related Figures: - Mahavira: - 24th Tirthankara (c. 599-527 BCE), founded Jainism (e.g., Q66 [1998]). - Bhadrabahu: - Jain leader (c. 3rd century BCE), led Digambaras south, died in Shravanabelagola. - Kharavela: - Kalinga king (c. 1st century BCE), Jain patron, Hathigumpha inscription. - Sthulabhadra: - Jain monk (c. 3rd century BCE), led Shvetambaras at Pataliputra council. - Broader Connection: - Links to Jainism’s spread (e.g., Q66 [1998]), Kalinga history (e.g., Q40 [1998] Ashoka context), or schisms (e.g., Q60 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - Kharavela’s patronage of Jainism in Kalinga (c. 1st century BCE) is correct, unlike errors about Sthalabahu, Bhadrabahu’s followers, or early image worship. - Q70: Which one of the following four Vedas contains an account of magical charms and spells? - Options: (a) Rigveda (b) Yajurveda (c) Atharvaveda (d) Samaveda - Answer: (c) Atharvaveda - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Vedas, composed c. 1500-1200 BCE in the Vedic period, are the foundational texts of ancient Indian religion, originating in the northwest (modern Punjab, Haryana). Each Veda serves a distinct purpose in ritual and philosophy. - Correct Option Explained: - (c) Atharvaveda: - Correct—The Atharvaveda uniquely contains hymns, incantations, and spells for magical purposes, such as healing, protection from evil, and curses, alongside domestic rituals. Composed later (c. 1200-1000 BCE), it reflects a practical, folk-oriented tradition. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Rigveda: - Incorrect—The oldest Veda (c. 1500 BCE), it consists of hymns praising deities (e.g., Indra, Agni) for cosmic order, not magical spells. - (b) Yajurveda: - Incorrect—Focused on sacrificial rituals (c. 1200 BCE), it provides mantras and prose for priests, lacking magical charms. - (d) Samaveda: - Incorrect—A musical Veda (c. 1200 BCE), it adapts Rigvedic hymns for chanting in rituals, not spells or magic. - Contents of the Vedas: - Rigveda: - 1,028 hymns, deity worship (e.g., Soma, Varuna). - Yajurveda: - Sacrificial formulas, two recensions (Shukla, Krishna). - Atharvaveda: - 731 hymns, spells for health, longevity, and warding off evil (e.g., against snakes, demons). - Samaveda: - Melodic chants, ritual performance. - Distinctive Features of the Vedas: - Rigveda: - Oldest text, 10 mandalas (books), Mandala 10 includes the Purusha Sukta (cosmic man). Famous for the Nasadiya Sukta (creation hymn) questioning existence. Associated with Hotri priests. - Yajurveda: - Two branches: Shukla (White, e.g., Vajasaneyi Samhita) and Krishna (Black, e.g., Taittiriya Samhita). Contains prose and verse for Adhvaryu priests. Includes the Isha Upanishad in Shukla recension. - Atharvaveda: - Two recensions: Shaunaka and Paippalada. Known for Bhaishajya (healing) and Kshudra (minor magic) hymns. Linked to Angiras and Atharvan families, used by Brahmin priests for household rites. - Samaveda: - Smallest Veda (1,875 verses), mostly Rigvedic hymns set to music. Three recensions (e.g., Kauthuma). Used by Udgatri priests for Soma rituals. Includes the Chandogya Upanishad, a key philosophical text. - Significance of Atharvaveda: - Unlike the other three (Trayi Vidya: Rig, Yajur, Sama), it addresses everyday concerns—disease, marriage, enmity—through magic, reflecting a broader societal role in Vedic life. - Related Figures: - Vyasa: - Sage (mythical, c. 1500 BCE), traditionally credited with compiling the Vedas. - Atharvan: - Legendary priest linked to Atharvaveda, associated with fire and magic rituals. - Angiras: - Sage family, co-contributors to Atharvaveda’s hymns. - Pippalada: - Later sage (c. 1000 BCE), linked to Atharvaveda’s Paippalada recension. - Broader Connection: - Links to Vedic religion (e.g., Q35 [1998] on urban culture context), ritual practices (e.g., Q66 [1998] on Jain/Buddhist contrast), or ancient texts (e.g., Q34 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - The Atharvaveda stands out among the four Vedas for its magical charms and spells, contrasting with the liturgical focus of Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda. - [2005] - Q71: Who among the following was not a contemporary of the other three? - Options: (a) Bimbisara (b) Gautama Buddha (c) Milinda (d) Prasenjit - Answer: (c) Milinda - Analysis: - Historical Context: - This question spans the 6th century BCE to the 2nd century BCE, covering rulers and figures from Magadha, Kosala, and the Indo-Greek kingdom during ancient India’s Gangetic and post-Mauryan periods. - Chronological Assessment: - (a) Bimbisara: - Ruled Magadha (c. 543-491 BCE), founded the Haryanka dynasty, contemporary of Buddha and Prasenjit. - (b) Gautama Buddha: - Lived c. 563-483 BCE, founder of Buddhism, active during Bimbisara’s and Prasenjit’s reigns. - (c) Milinda: - Refers to Menander I (r. c. 165-130 BCE), Indo-Greek king, post-Mauryan figure, centuries after the others. - (d) Prasenjit: - Ruled Kosala (c. 6th century BCE, roughly 550-470 BCE), contemporary of Bimbisara and Buddha. - Why (c) Milinda Is Not Contemporary?: - Bimbisara, Buddha, and Prasenjit lived in the 6th-5th centuries BCE, overlapping in the Gangetic plains. Milinda (Menander I), a Hellenistic ruler from the 2nd century BCE, existed over 300 years later, after the Mauryan Empire’s fall (185 BCE). - Timeline Comparison: - Bimbisara: - c. 543-491 BCE, allied with Prasenjit, met Buddha (Rajgir, Bihar). - Gautama Buddha: - c. 563-483 BCE, preached during Bimbisara’s and Prasenjit’s reigns (Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh). - Prasenjit: - c. 550-470 BCE, Kosala king, Buddha’s patron (Shravasti, Uttar Pradesh). - Milinda: - c. 165-130 BCE, Indo-Greek king, debated Buddhist monk Nagasena (Milindapanha) (Sagala, modern Pakistan). - Key Interactions: - Bimbisara and Prasenjit: - Rulers of neighboring kingdoms, Bimbisara married Prasenjit’s sister, both supported Buddha. - Buddha: - Contemporary of both kings, died during Ajatashatru’s reign (Bimbisara’s son). - Milinda: - No overlap; his era follows Alexander’s invasions (326 BCE) and Mauryan decline. - Related Figures: - Bimbisara: - Magadha king (c. 543-491 BCE), early Buddhist patron (e.g., Q66 [1998]). - Gautama Buddha: - Founder of Buddhism (c. 563-483 BCE), First Sermon at Sarnath (e.g., Q39 [1998]). - Milinda (Menander I): - Indo-Greek king (r. c. 165-130 BCE), Milindapanha dialogue. - Prasenjit: - Kosala king (c. 550-470 BCE), Buddha’s contemporary, father of Virudhaka. - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhism (e.g., Q66 [1998]), Magadha-Kosala ties (e.g., Q42 [1998]), or Indo-Greek era (e.g., Q40 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - Milinda (Menander I, c. 165-130 BCE) was not a contemporary of Bimbisara, Buddha, and Prasenjit, who lived in the 6th-5th centuries BCE, separated by over 300 years. - [2006] - Q72: Who among the following laid the foundation of Rashtrakuta Empire? - Options: (a) Amoghavarsha I (b) Dantidurga (c) Dhruva (d) Krishna I - Answer: (b) Dantidurga - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Rashtrakuta Empire (c. 753-982 CE) emerged in the Deccan (modern Karnataka, Maharashtra) during the early medieval period, overthrowing the Chalukyas of Badami and dominating South India. - Correct Option Explained: - (b) Dantidurga: - Correct—Dantidurga (r. c. 735-756 CE), also known as Dantivarman, founded the Rashtrakuta Empire by defeating the Chalukya king Kirtivarman II around 753 CE. His Ellora inscription (c. 753 CE) records this victory, marking the empire’s establishment at Manyakheta (modern Malkhed, Karnataka). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Amoghavarsha I: - Incorrect—Amoghavarsha I (r. c. 814-878 CE), a later ruler, expanded cultural influence (e.g., Jainism patronage) but inherited an established empire. - (c) Dhruva: - Incorrect—Dhruva (r. c. 780-793 CE), Dantidurga’s uncle or successor, consolidated power by defeating the Pallavas and Gangas, but he built on Dantidurga’s foundation. - (d) Krishna I: - Incorrect—Krishna I (r. c. 756-774 CE), Dantidurga’s successor, strengthened the empire (e.g., Kailasa temple at Ellora), but did not found it. - Founding Event: - Dantidurga, initially a Chalukya feudatory, rebelled and overthrew Kirtivarman II (c. 753 CE), shifting the capital to Manyakheta. His Dashavatara cave inscription at Ellora (Maharashtra) confirms his role as the empire’s founder. - Rashtrakuta Succession: - Dantidurga: - r. c. 735-756 CE, founder, defeated Chalukyas. - Krishna I: - r. c. 756-774 CE, built Kailasa temple (Ellora, Maharashtra). - Dhruva: - r. c. 780-793 CE, expanded north and south. - Amoghavarsha I: - r. c. 814-878 CE, long reign, literary patron (e.g., Kavirajamarga). - Related Figures: - Dantidurga: - Rashtrakuta founder (r. c. 735-756 CE), Chalukya overthrower. - Krishna I: - Successor (r. c. 756-774 CE), Ellora temple patron. - Amoghavarsha I: - Later ruler (r. c. 814-878 CE), Jain scholar-king. - Kirtivarman II: - Last Chalukya king (r. c. 746-753 CE), defeated by Dantidurga (e.g., Q63 [1998] Chalukya context). - Broader Connection: - Links to Deccan powers (e.g., Q63 [1998] Chalukyas), temple architecture (e.g., Q60 [1998]), or medieval dynasties (e.g., Q64 [1998] Cholas). - Key Takeaway: - Dantidurga laid the foundation of the Rashtrakuta Empire by defeating the Chalukyas (c. 753 CE), unlike later rulers Amoghavarsha I, Dhruva, and Krishna I who built upon it. - Q73: Between which of the following was the ancient town of Takshasila located? - Options: (a) Indus and Jhelum (b) Jhelum and Chenab (c) Chenab and Ravi (d) Ravi and Beas - Answer: (a) Indus and Jhelum - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Takshasila (Taxila), a major ancient city (c. 6th century BCE-5th century CE), was a center of learning and trade in northwest India, flourishing under Achaemenid, Mauryan, and Kushana rule (modern Pakistan). - Correct Option Explained: - (a) Indus and Jhelum: - Correct—Takshasila is located between the Indus River to its west and the Jhelum River to its east, near modern Rawalpindi (Punjab, Pakistan). Archaeological sites like Sirkap and Bhir Mound confirm its position in this region. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Jhelum and Chenab: - Incorrect—Takshasila lies west of the Jhelum, not between it and the Chenab, which flows further southeast. - (c) Chenab and Ravi: - Incorrect—The Chenab and Ravi are south and east of Takshasila, closer to modern Lahore, not its location. - (d) Ravi and Beas: - Incorrect—The Ravi and Beas are even further southeast, near Punjab, India, far from Takshasila. - Geographical Placement: - Takshasila: - Situated in the Gandhara region, approximately 30 km northwest of modern Islamabad, between the Indus (west) and Jhelum (east), key rivers of the Punjab plains. - Rivers: - Indus: Western boundary of Gandhara. - Jhelum: Eastern boundary, flowing into the Chenab. - Chenab, Ravi, Beas: Progressively southeast, beyond Takshasila. - Other Notable Ancient Towns and Their Locations: - Pataliputra: - Between Ganga and Son rivers, capital of Mauryas and Guptas (Patna, Bihar). - Ujjain: - On the Shipra River, Malwa region, Gupta and pre-Gupta center (Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh). - Shravasti: - Near Rapti River, Kosala kingdom, Buddhist site (Sahet-Mahet, Uttar Pradesh). - Vaishali: - Near Gandak River, Lichchhavi republic, Jain and Buddhist hub (Vaishali, Bihar). - Mathura: - On the Yamuna River, art and religious center (Mathura, Uttar Pradesh). - Sagala (Sialkot): - Between Chenab and Ravi rivers, Indo-Greek capital under Menander (Sialkot, Punjab, Pakistan). - Historical Significance: - Takshasila was a university town (c. 5th century BCE), hosting scholars like Panini and Chanakya, and a trade hub on the Uttarapatha route. It saw Persian (6th century BCE), Mauryan (3rd century BCE), and Indo-Greek (2nd century BCE) influence. - Related Figures: - Panini: - Grammarian (c. 5th century BCE), wrote Ashtadhyayi at Takshasila. - Chanakya: - Mauryan advisor (c. 4th century BCE), possibly studied/taught there (e.g., Q62 [1998]). - Milinda (Menander I): - Indo-Greek king (r. c. 165-130 BCE), ruled nearby Sagala (e.g., Q71 [1998]). - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), built stupas at Takshasila (e.g., Q33 [1998]). - Broader Connection: - Links to Gandhara (e.g., Q71 [1998]), Mauryan rule (e.g., Q67 [1998]), or ancient education (e.g., Q42 [1998] travelers). - Key Takeaway: - Takshasila was located between the Indus and Jhelum rivers, distinguishing it from regions defined by Jhelum-Chenab, Chenab-Ravi, or Ravi-Beas. - Q74: With reference to the invaders in ancient India, which one of the following is the correct chronological order? - Options: (a) Greeks-Sakas-Kushanas (b) Greeks-Kushanas-Sakas (c) Sakas-Greeks-Kushanas (d) Sakas-Kushanas-Greeks - Answer: (a) Greeks-Sakas-Kushanas - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ancient India faced successive invasions from the northwest (modern Pakistan, Afghanistan) between the 4th century BCE and 2nd century CE, shaping its post-Mauryan history. - Correct Option Explained: - (a) Greeks-Sakas-Kushanas: - Correct—This reflects the historical sequence: - Greeks (Indo-Greeks): c. 326-100 BCE, starting with Alexander’s invasion (326 BCE) and followed by successors like Menander I (r. c. 165-130 BCE). - Sakas (Indo-Scythians): c. 2nd century BCE-1st century CE, arrived after the Greeks, with rulers like Maues (c. 85-60 BCE). - Kushanas: c. 1st-3rd centuries CE, rose later with Kujula Kadphises (c. 30-80 CE) and peaked under Kanishka (r. c. 127-150 CE). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Greeks-Kushanas-Sakas: - Incorrect—Kushanas came after Sakas, not before; Sakas preceded Kushanas in northwest India. - (c) Sakas-Greeks-Kushanas: - Incorrect—Greeks invaded first (326 BCE), long before Sakas (c. 2nd century BCE). - (d) Sakas-Kushanas-Greeks: - Incorrect—Greeks were the earliest (4th century BCE), not last; Sakas and Kushanas followed. - Chronological Timeline: - Greeks: - c. 326-100 BCE, Alexander’s invasion (Punjab, Pakistan), Indo-Greek kingdoms until c. 100 BCE. - Sakas: - c. 2nd century BCE-1st century CE, ruled western India (e.g., Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh). - Kushanas: - c. 1st-3rd centuries CE, unified northwest (e.g., Mathura, Uttar Pradesh). - Chronology of Major Invaders in Ancient India: - Persians (Achaemenids): - c. 530-330 BCE, Darius I annexed northwest (Gandhara, Punjab, Pakistan), pre-Greek control. - Greeks (Macedonians/Indo-Greeks): - c. 326-100 BCE, Alexander (326 BCE), Indo-Greeks like Menander I (Taxila, Pakistan). - Sakas (Indo-Scythians): - c. 2nd century BCE-1st century CE, displaced Indo-Greeks (e.g., Maues, Gujarat). - Parthians (Indo-Parthians): - c. 1st century BCE-1st century CE, overlapped with Sakas, ruled Gandhara (e.g., Gondophares, Taxila). - Kushanas: - c. 1st-3rd centuries CE, Kanishka’s empire (Mathura, Uttar Pradesh; Peshawar, Pakistan). - Sassanids: - c. 3rd-4th centuries CE, brief incursions into northwest post-Kushana (Afghanistan border). - Hunas (Hephthalites): - c. 5th-6th centuries CE, invaded Gupta Empire (e.g., Mihirakula, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh). - Arabs: - c. 712 CE, Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh (modern Pakistan), early medieval shift. - Key Invasions: - Greeks: - Alexander defeated Porus (Jhelum, 326 BCE); Indo-Greeks like Menander ruled Gandhara. - Sakas: - Overthrew Indo-Greeks, established Saka satraps (e.g., Rudradaman, c. 130-150 CE, Junagadh inscription). - Kushanas: - Displaced Sakas, expanded to Ganga plains, promoted Buddhism (e.g., Kanishka’s council, Kashmir). - Related Figures: - Alexander the Great: - Macedonian king (r. 336-323 BCE), invaded India (326 BCE) (e.g., Q71 [1998]). - Menander I (Milinda): - Indo-Greek king (r. c. 165-130 BCE), Milindapanha (e.g., Q71 [1998]). - Maues: - Saka king (r. c. 85-60 BCE), first major Saka ruler in India. - Kanishka: - Kushana king (r. c. 127-150 CE), Buddhist patron (e.g., Q68 [1998]). - Broader Connection: - Links to northwest invasions (e.g., Q71 [1998]), Kushana rule (e.g., Q68 [1998]), or post-Mauryan transitions (e.g., Q67 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - The correct chronological order of invaders is Greeks (4th century BCE), Sakas (2nd century BCE-1st century CE), and Kushanas (1st-3rd centuries CE), as per historical sequence. - Q75: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The Ikshvaku rulers of Southern India were antagonistic towards Buddhism 2. The Pala rulers of Eastern India were patrons of Buddhism - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - This question contrasts the religious policies of two dynasties: the Ikshvakus of South India (c. 3rd-4th centuries CE) and the Palas of East India (c. 8th-12th centuries CE), spanning post-Mauryan and medieval periods. - Evaluation of Statements: - 1. The Ikshvaku rulers of Southern India were antagonistic towards Buddhism: - False—The Ikshvaku dynasty (c. 225-340 CE), ruling from Nagarjunakonda (modern Andhra Pradesh), were not antagonistic to Buddhism. Archaeological evidence, like stupas and inscriptions at Nagarjunakonda and Amaravati, shows they patronized Buddhism alongside Hinduism (e.g., King Vashishthiputra Chamulamula’s grants to Buddhist monasteries). - 2. The Pala rulers of Eastern India were patrons of Buddhism: - True—The Pala dynasty (c. 750-1174 CE), based in Bengal and Bihar (modern West Bengal, Bihar), were staunch Buddhist patrons. Rulers like Dharmapala (r. c. 770-810 CE) and Devapala (r. c. 810-850 CE) revived Nalanda and Vikramashila universities and built monasteries (e.g., Somapura Mahavihara, Bangladesh). - Why Only 2 Is Correct?: - Statement 1: - Ikshvakus supported Buddhist sites (e.g., Nagarjunakonda stupa inscriptions mention donations), coexisting with Shaivism and Vaishnavism, not opposing Buddhism. - Statement 2: - Palas’ patronage is well-documented: Dharmapala founded Vikramashila, and Gopala I (r. c. 750-770 CE) supported Buddhist viharas, sustaining Buddhism amid Hindu revivalism. - Dynastic Contributions: - Ikshvakus: - Post-Satavahana rulers, built Buddhist stupas and Hindu temples (Nagarjunakonda, Andhra Pradesh). - Palas: - Revived Mahayana Buddhism, funded universities (Nalanda, Bihar), resisted Brahmanical dominance. - Major Empires and Dynasties in Ancient India: - Native Dynasties: - Magadha (Haryanka): - c. 543-413 BCE, Bimbisara (Rajgir, Bihar), supported Buddhism and Jainism. - Mauryas: - c. 321-185 BCE, Ashoka (Pataliputra, Bihar), Buddhism after Kalinga War (e.g., Q67 [1998]). - Sungas: - c. 185-73 BCE, Pushyamitra (Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh), favored Hinduism, less Buddhist support. - Kanvas: - c. 73-28 BCE, Vasudeva (Pataliputra, Bihar), Hinduism, minimal religious focus. - Satavahanas (Andhras): - c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE, Simuka (Pratishthana, Maharashtra), Buddhism and Hinduism. - Ikshvakus: - c. 225-340 CE, Chamulamula (Nagarjunakonda, Andhra Pradesh), Buddhism and Hinduism. - Guptas: - c. 320-550 CE, Chandragupta II (Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh), Hinduism, tolerant of Buddhism. - Vakatakas: - c. 3rd-5th centuries CE, Pravarasena (Vidarbha, Maharashtra), Hinduism, some Buddhist caves (Ajanta). - Chalukyas of Badami: - c. 543-753 CE, Pulakesin II (Badami, Karnataka), Hinduism, Jainism (e.g., Q63 [1998]). - Rashtrakutas: - c. 753-982 CE, Dantidurga (Manyakheta, Karnataka), Jainism, Hinduism (e.g., Q72 [1998]). - Palas: - c. 750-1174 CE, Dharmapala (Bengal, Bihar), Buddhism, some Hinduism. - Cholas: - c. 9th-13th centuries CE, Rajendra I (Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu), Hinduism, some Buddhism (e.g., Q64 [1998]). - Invader Dynasties: - Persians (Achaemenids): - c. 530-330 BCE, Darius I (Gandhara, Pakistan), Zoroastrianism, local tolerance. - Greeks (Indo-Greeks): - c. 326-100 BCE, Menander I (Taxila, Pakistan), Buddhism (e.g., Q74 [1998]). - Sakas (Indo-Scythians): - c. 2nd century BCE-1st century CE, Maues (Gujarat), Hinduism, some Buddhism. - Parthians (Indo-Parthians): - c. 1st century BCE-1st century CE, Gondophares (Taxila), Zoroastrianism, Buddhism. - Kushanas: - c. 1st-3rd centuries CE, Kanishka (Mathura, Uttar Pradesh), Buddhism (e.g., Q74 [1998]). - Hunas (Hephthalites): - c. 5th-6th centuries CE, Mihirakula (Malwa, Madhya Pradesh), Hinduism, anti-Buddhist. - Arabs: - c. 712 CE, Muhammad bin Qasim (Sindh, Pakistan), Islam, early incursions. - Evidence: - Ikshvaku Inscriptions: - Nagarjunakonda pillars (c. 3rd century CE) record Buddhist grants (Andhra Pradesh). - Pala Records: - Copper plates (e.g., Devapala’s grants) and traveler accounts (e.g., I-Tsing, c. 671-695 CE) confirm Buddhist support. - Related Figures: - Vashishthiputra Chamulamula: - Ikshvaku king (c. 3rd century CE), Buddhist patron. - Dharmapala: - Pala king (r. c. 770-810 CE), founded Vikramashila (Bihar). - Gopala I: - Pala founder (r. c. 750-770 CE), Buddhist supporter. - Kanishka: - Kushana king (r. c. 127-150 CE), earlier Buddhist patron (e.g., Q68 [1998]). - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhism’s spread (e.g., Q68 [1998]), South Indian dynasties (e.g., Q64 [1998]), or Pala rule (e.g., Q63 [1998] context). - Key Takeaway: - Only Statement 2 is correct: Ikshvakus were not antagonistic to Buddhism (1 is false), while Palas were notable Buddhist patrons (2 is true). - Q76: The Allahabad Pillar inscription is associated with which one of the following? - Options: (a) Mahapadma Nanda (b) Chandragupta Maurya (c) Ashoka (d) Samudragupta - Answer: (d) Samudragupta - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Allahabad Pillar inscription, also known as the Prayaga-prasasti, is a significant Gupta-era record (c. 4th century CE) on an Ashokan pillar in Allahabad (modern Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh), reflecting India’s dynastic history. - Correct Option Explained: - (d) Samudragupta: - Correct—The inscription, composed by Harisena (c. 375 CE), eulogizes Samudragupta (r. c. 335-375 CE), detailing his conquests across India (e.g., Aryavarta, Dakshinapatha) and his title "Kaviraja" for poetic skill. It’s engraved on a pillar originally erected by Ashoka. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Mahapadma Nanda: - Incorrect—Mahapadma Nanda (r. c. 345-329 BCE), founder of the Nanda dynasty, predates the pillar and has no associated inscriptions; his era lacks such epigraphic evidence. - (b) Chandragupta Maurya: - Incorrect—Chandragupta Maurya (r. c. 321-297 BCE) founded the Mauryan Empire, but the Allahabad Pillar’s original Ashokan edicts (c. 250 BCE) are unrelated to him; Samudragupta’s inscription is later. - (c) Ashoka: - Incorrect—Ashoka (r. c. 268-232 BCE) erected the pillar with his edicts (e.g., Major Pillar Edict), but the Samudragupta inscription was added centuries later (c. 375 CE) by the Guptas. - Inscription Details: - Location: - Allahabad Pillar, originally from Kaushambi, moved to Prayagraj (Uttar Pradesh). - Content: - Ashokan Edicts: Earlier layer, in Prakrit, promote Dhamma (c. 250 BCE). - Samudragupta’s Prasasti: Sanskrit, lists victories (e.g., 12 southern kings), cultural patronage (c. 375 CE). - Additional Layers: - Jahangir’s Persian inscription (c. 1605 CE) added later. - Prominent Inscriptions of Key Figures: - Mahapadma Nanda: - No Known Inscriptions: - c. 345-329 BCE, Pataliputra (Bihar), no surviving epigraphic records; legacy via Puranas, not inscriptions. - Chandragupta Maurya: - Junagadh Rock Inscription (via Ashoka): - c. 250 BCE, Girnar, Gujarat, mentions his governor Pushyagupta’s dam; originally his, later Ashokan edicts added. - Note: - Direct inscriptions rare; Megasthanese’s Indica (lost) supplements his reign (Pataliputra, Bihar). - Ashoka: - Major Rock Edicts: - c. 257-250 BCE, multiple sites (e.g., Girnar, Gujarat; Dhauli, Odisha), Prakrit, outline Dhamma and conquests. - Pillar Edicts: - c. 250 BCE, Allahabad (Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh), Sarnath (Uttar Pradesh), promote ethical governance. - Minor Rock Edicts: - c. 260 BCE, Bairat (Rajasthan), Brahmagiri (Karnataka), early Buddhist conversion. - Samudragupta: - Allahabad Pillar Inscription (Prayaga-prasasti): - c. 375 CE, Prayagraj (Uttar Pradesh), Sanskrit, details conquests and cultural feats. - Eran Inscription: - c. 375 CE, Eran (Madhya Pradesh), records victories and Gupta power. - Historical Significance: - Demonstrates Gupta power under Samudragupta, dubbed "Indian Napoleon" for conquests, and continuity of Mauryan monumental tradition repurposed by later rulers. - Related Figures: - Samudragupta: - Gupta king (r. c. 335-375 CE), conqueror, poet (e.g., Q65 [1998]). - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. c. 268-232 BCE), pillar’s original creator (e.g., Q67 [1998]). - Harisena: - Samudragupta’s court poet (c. 375 CE), composed Prayaga-prasasti. - Chandragupta II: - Samudragupta’s son (r. c. 375-415 CE), continued Gupta glory (e.g., Q38 [1998]). - Broader Connection: - Links to Gupta achievements (e.g., Q65 [1998]), Mauryan legacy (e.g., Q67 [1998]), or epigraphy (e.g., Q42 [1998] travelers). - Key Takeaway: - The Allahabad Pillar inscription is associated with Samudragupta (c. 375 CE), not Mahapadma Nanda, Chandragupta Maurya, or Ashoka, though it builds on Ashoka’s earlier pillar. - [2008] - Q77: What does Baudhayan theorem (Baudhayan Sulva Sutras) relate to? - Options: (a) Lengths of sides of a right angled triangle (b) Calculation of the value of pi (c) Logarithmic calculations (d) Normal distribution curve - Answer: (a) Lengths of sides of a right angled triangle - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Baudhayan Sulva Sutras (c. 800-600 BCE), attributed to Baudhayana, are part of the Vedic Shrauta Sutras, composed in ancient India (northwest, modern Punjab-Haryana) to guide ritual geometry for altar construction. - Correct Option Explained: - (a) Lengths of sides of a right angled triangle: - Correct—The Baudhayan theorem, found in the Baudhayan Sulva Sutras (1.48), states a precursor to the Pythagorean theorem: "The diagonal of a rectangle produces an area equal to the sum of the areas produced by its two sides," effectively describing the relationship a² + b² = c² for a right-angled triangle. Example: 3² + 4² = 5² (9 + 16 = 25). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Calculation of the value of pi: - Incorrect—While Sulva Sutras approximate √2 (e.g., 1.4142), they don’t calculate π explicitly; π approximations (e.g., 3.14) appear later in Indian mathematics (e.g., Aryabhata, c. 499 CE). - (c) Logarithmic calculations: - Incorrect—Logarithms emerged much later (17th century CE, John Napier); Vedic texts lack such concepts. - (d) Normal distribution curve: - Incorrect—Normal distribution is a modern statistical concept (18th century CE, Gauss); Sulva Sutras focus on geometry, not probability. - Details of Baudhayan Sulva Sutras: - Purpose: - Geometric rules for constructing Vedic altars (e.g., square, falcon-shaped) with precise measurements. - Key Theorem: - Right triangle rule (e.g., 3, 4, 5 or 5, 12, 13), predating Pythagoras (c. 570-495 BCE) by centuries. - Other Contributions: - Approximations like √2 ≈ 1 + 1/3 + 1/(3·4) - 1/(3·4·34), used for altar diagonals. - Other Related Sulva Sutras and Contributions: - Apastamba Sulva Sutras: - Author: Apastamba (c. 600 BCE) - Features: Includes Pythagorean theorem (e.g., 3, 4, 5), methods to square a circle, √2 approximation (1.4142156), altar designs (South India tradition). - Manava Sulva Sutras: - Author: Manu (c. 700-500 BCE) - Features: Focus on altar geometry, right triangle properties (e.g., 15, 36, 39), simpler √2 estimate, linked to Manava Shrauta tradition. - Katyayana Sulva Sutras: - Author: Katyayana (c. 500-400 BCE) - Features: Advanced geometric constructions, Pythagorean triples, √2 and √3 approximations, detailed altar scaling (later Vedic period). - Common Elements: - All Sulva Sutras tied to Vedic rituals, predate Greek geometry, emphasize practical applications over abstract theory. - Mathematical Significance: - Earliest known statement of the Pythagorean theorem in India, highlighting Vedic mathematics’ practical and ritualistic focus, later refined by mathematicians like Bhaskara (c. 12th century CE). - Related Figures: - Baudhayana: - Vedic sage (c. 800-600 BCE), author of Sulva Sutras, mathematician-priest. - Apastamba: - Vedic scholar (c. 600 BCE), wrote related Sulva Sutras with geometric rules. - Aryabhata: - Astronomer-mathematician (c. 476-550 CE), calculated π ≈ 3.1416 (Pataliputra, Bihar). - Pythagoras: - Greek mathematician (c. 570-495 BCE), later credited with the theorem in Western tradition. - Broader Connection: - Links to Vedic knowledge (e.g., Q70 [1998]), ancient mathematics (e.g., Q35 [1998] urban context), or Indian intellectual history (e.g., Q42 [1998] travelers). - Key Takeaway: - The Baudhayan theorem in the Sulva Sutras relates to the lengths of sides of a right-angled triangle (a² + b² = c²), not pi, logarithms, or normal distribution. - [2009] - Q78: Anekantavada is a core theory and philosophy of which one of the following? - Options: (a) Buddhism (b) Jainism (c) Sikhism (d) Vaishnavism - Answer: (b) Jainism - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Anekantavada, meaning "many-sidedness," emerged in ancient India (c. 6th century BCE) as a philosophical doctrine tied to the Gangetic plains, particularly associated with Jainism’s development under Mahavira. - Correct Option Explained: - (b) Jainism: - Correct—Anekantavada is a fundamental Jain principle asserting that reality is multifaceted and truth is relative, depending on perspective. It underpins Jain epistemology and ethics, complementing Syadvada (conditional predication) and Nayavada (partial viewpoints). Mahavira (c. 599-527 BCE) formalized it to promote non-absolutism and tolerance. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Buddhism: - Incorrect—Buddhism emphasizes the Middle Path and Four Noble Truths, not Anekantavada. While it shares non-dogmatism, its focus is impermanence (Anicca) and no-self (Anatta), not multi-perspectivism. - (c) Sikhism: - Incorrect—Sikhism (c. 15th century CE), founded by Guru Nanak, centers on monotheism and devotion (e.g., Ik Onkar), not Jain-style relativism. - (d) Vaishnavism: - Incorrect—Vaishnavism, a Hindu sect, focuses on Vishnu worship and Bhakti (devotion), lacking Anekantavada’s relativistic framework. - Anekantavada Explained: - Concept: - Reality has infinite attributes; no single view captures it fully (e.g., the blind men and elephant parable). - Application: - Syadvada: "In some ways, it is" (conditional truth). - Nayavada: Partial truths from different standpoints (e.g., substance, function). - Purpose: - Promotes non-violence (Ahimsa) by avoiding absolutist conflicts. - Core Philosophies of Listed Religions: - Buddhism: - Four Noble Truths: Life is suffering (Dukkha), suffering’s cause (Tanha), cessation possible (Nirodha), path to cessation (Eightfold Path). Key concepts: Impermanence (Anicca), no-self (Anatta), Middle Way. Founded by Gautama Buddha (c. 563-483 BCE). - Jainism: - Anekantavada: Many-sided truth. Syadvada: Conditional predication. Five Vows: Non-violence (Ahimsa), truth (Satya), non-stealing (Asteya), chastity (Brahmacharya), non-attachment (Aparigraha). Soul liberation (Moksha) via asceticism. Formalized by Mahavira (c. 599-527 BCE). - Sikhism: - Ik Onkar: One Supreme Reality. Core tenets: Monotheism, equality, service (Seva), meditation on God’s name (Nam Japna), honest living (Kirat Karna). Goal: Union with God. Founded by Guru Nanak (c. 1469-1539 CE), codified in Guru Granth Sahib. - Vaishnavism: - Bhakti: Devotional love for Vishnu (or avatars like Krishna, Rama). Key texts: Bhagavad Gita, Vishnu Purana. Concepts: Dharma (duty), Moksha (liberation through devotion), personal God. Prominent in medieval Bhakti movement (c. 7th-17th centuries CE). - Philosophical Significance: - Unique to Jainism, Anekantavada distinguishes it from Buddhism’s pragmatism, Sikhism’s monotheism, and Vaishnavism’s devotionalism, reflecting Jainism’s emphasis on intellectual humility and coexistence. - Related Figures: - Mahavira: - 24th Tirthankara (c. 599-527 BCE), formalized Anekantavada (e.g., Q66 [1998]). - Gautama Buddha: - Founder of Buddhism (c. 563-483 BCE), contemporary, focused on suffering (e.g., Q66 [1998]). - Guru Nanak: - Sikh founder (c. 1469-1539 CE), preached monotheism (Punjab). - Ramanuja: - Vaishnava philosopher (c. 1017-1137 CE), developed Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism). - Broader Connection: - Links to Jainism (e.g., Q66 [1998]), philosophical debates (e.g., Q68 [1998] Buddhism context), or ancient Indian thought (e.g., Q70 [1998] Vedas). - Key Takeaway: - Anekantavada, a core Jain philosophy of many-sided truth, is exclusive to Jainism, not Buddhism, Sikhism, or Vaishnavism. - [2010] - Q79: There are only two known examples of cave paintings of the Gupta period in ancient India. One of these is paintings of Ajanta caves. Where is the other surviving example of Gupta paintings? - Options: (a) Bagh caves (b) Ellora caves (c) Lomas Rishi cave (d) Nasik caves - Answer: (a) Bagh caves - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Gupta period (c. 320-550 CE), often called India’s "Golden Age," saw a peak in art and architecture, including cave paintings, centered in northern and central India (modern Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh). - Correct Option Explained: - (a) Bagh caves: - Correct—The Bagh caves (c. 5th-6th centuries CE), located in Dhar district (Madhya Pradesh), contain Gupta-era paintings alongside Ajanta (Maharashtra). These depict Buddhist themes (e.g., Jataka tales), with vibrant colors and fluid figures, though less preserved than Ajanta’s. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Ellora caves: - Incorrect—Ellora (Maharashtra) spans c. 6th-10th centuries CE, primarily Rashtrakuta period (e.g., Kailasa temple, c. 756-773 CE), post-Gupta, with sculptures, not Gupta paintings. - (c) Lomas Rishi cave: - Incorrect—Lomas Rishi (Barabar Hills, Bihar), c. 3rd century BCE, Mauryan period, features polished rock architecture, not paintings. - (d) Nasik caves: - Incorrect—Nasik (Maharashtra), c. 1st-2nd centuries CE, Satavahana period, has Buddhist rock-cut caves with carvings, not Gupta paintings. - Gupta Cave Paintings: - Ajanta Caves: - c. 2nd century BCE-6th century CE (Gupta phase: 5th-6th centuries), Aurangabad, Maharashtra; Buddhist murals (e.g., Padmapani, Cave 1). - Bagh Caves: - c. 5th-6th centuries CE, Dhar, Madhya Pradesh; Buddhist scenes, similar style to Ajanta, less intact due to sandstone decay. - Cave Paintings and Artifacts Across Ancient Indian Periods: - Prehistoric Period (c. 10,000-2500 BCE): - Bhimbetka Caves: - Rock shelters, Madhya Pradesh; paintings of hunting, dancing (e.g., bison, human figures), ochre and white pigments. - Artifacts: - Stone tools, microliths (e.g., Bagor, Rajasthan). - Mauryan Period (c. 321-185 BCE): - Barabar Caves (e.g., Lomas Rishi): - Bihar; polished rock surfaces, no paintings, Ashokan inscriptions (c. 250 BCE). - Artifacts: - Ashokan Pillars (e.g., Sarnath Lion Capital, Uttar Pradesh), punch-marked coins. - Satavahana Period (c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE): - Nasik Caves: - Maharashtra; Buddhist carvings, no extensive paintings. - Karle and Bhaja Caves: - Maharashtra; rock-cut chaityas, minimal painting traces. - Artifacts: - Amaravati Stupa carvings (Andhra Pradesh), lead coins. - Kushana Period (c. 1st-3rd centuries CE): - Mathura School: - Uttar Pradesh; sculptures (e.g., Buddha images), no cave paintings. - Artifacts: - Gandhara-style Buddha statues (Pakistan), gold coins of Kanishka. - Gupta Period (c. 320-550 CE): - Ajanta Caves: - Maharashtra; Buddhist paintings (e.g., Cave 16, royal scenes). - Bagh Caves: - Madhya Pradesh; Buddhist murals, Gupta style. - Artifacts: - Iron Pillar (Delhi), Gupta gold coins (e.g., Chandragupta II). - Post-Gupta (Rashtrakuta, c. 753-982 CE): - Ellora Caves: - Maharashtra; sculptures (e.g., Kailasa temple), Jain/Buddhist/Hindu themes, minimal paintings. - Artifacts: - Elephanta Caves carvings (Maharashtra). - Artistic Significance: - Gupta paintings at Ajanta and Bagh mark a high point in Indian art, blending realism and spirituality, influencing later medieval styles (e.g., Ellora’s evolution). - Related Figures: - Chandragupta II: - Gupta king (r. c. 375-415 CE), patron of arts (e.g., Q76 [1998]). - Ashoka: - Mauryan emperor (r. c. 268-232 BCE), early cave patron (e.g., Q76 [1998]). - Dantidurga: - Rashtrakuta founder (r. c. 735-756 CE), post-Gupta cave patron (e.g., Q72 [1998]). - Kanishka: - Kushana king (r. c. 127-150 CE), earlier art patron (e.g., Q74 [1998]). - Broader Connection: - Links to Gupta art (e.g., Q76 [1998]), Buddhist sites (e.g., Q68 [1998]), or ancient caves (e.g., Q73 [1998] Takshasila context). - Key Takeaway: - The other surviving Gupta-period cave paintings, besides Ajanta, are at Bagh caves (Madhya Pradesh), not Ellora, Lomas Rishi, or Nasik. - [2011-I] - Q80: India maintained its early cultural contacts and trade links with Southeast Asia across the Bay of Bengal. For this pre-eminence of early maritime history of Bay of Bengal, which of the following could be the most convincing explanation/explanations? - Options: (a) As compared to other countries, India had a better ship-building technology in ancient and medieval times (b) The rulers of southern India always patronized traders, Brahmin priests and Buddhist monks in this context (c) Monsoon winds across the Bay of Bengal facilitated sea voyages (d) Both (a) and (b) are convincing explanations in this context - Answer: (d) Both (a) and (b) are convincing explanations in this context - Analysis: - Historical Context: - India’s maritime connections with Southeast Asia (e.g., Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia) began in the 1st millennium BCE, growing under the Mauryas (c. 321-185 BCE), Satavahanas (c. 1st century BCE-2nd century CE), and peaking with the Cholas (c. 9th-13th centuries CE). Ports like Tamralipti (Bengal) and Nagapattinam (Tamil Nadu) facilitated trade and cultural exchange across the Bay of Bengal. - Correct Option Explained: - (d) Both (a) and (b) are convincing explanations in this context: - Correct—India’s maritime pre-eminence relied on a synergy of advanced ship-building technology (a) and consistent patronage from southern rulers (b). Together, these factors enabled sustained trade and cultural links with Southeast Asia, supported by evidence like Chola naval expeditions (c. 1025 CE) and ancient ship designs. - Evaluation of Options: - (a) As compared to other countries, India had a better ship-building technology in ancient and medieval times: - Correct—India’s ship-building was advanced, with stitched-plank ships (e.g., Chola vessels) and early docks (e.g., Lothal, c. 2400 BCE). Texts like the Yuktikalpataru (c. 11th century CE) detail sophisticated designs, giving India an edge over some contemporaries (e.g., less durable Southeast Asian outriggers), crucial for Bay of Bengal voyages. - (b) The rulers of southern India always patronized traders, Brahmin priests and Buddhist monks in this context: - Correct—Southern dynasties, notably the Cholas (e.g., Rajaraja I, Rajendra I), Pallavas, and Pandyas, supported maritime trade and cultural missions. Chola expeditions to Srivijaya (c. 1025 CE) and Ashoka’s Buddhist outreach (c. 3rd century BCE) exemplify this, though patronage varied over time. - (c) Monsoon winds across the Bay of Bengal facilitated sea voyages: - Also Correct but Not Included in (d)—Monsoon winds (northeast: October-March, southwest: June-September) were essential, enabling predictable navigation (e.g., Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, c. 1st century CE). While foundational, the question’s focus on "convincing explanations" in (d) prioritizes human factors (a and b) over natural ones. - Why (d)?: - Ship-building (a) provided the means, and patronage (b) provided the will, forming a robust framework for India’s maritime dominance. Chola naval power and trade networks (c. 9th-13th centuries CE) exemplify this combination, though monsoon winds (c) were a critical enabler not explicitly included in (d). - Maritime Elements: - Technology: - Stitched ships, navigational aids (e.g., star-based reckoning). - Patronage: - Chola navy, Buddhist missions (e.g., Nagapattinam monastery). - Winds: - Monsoon cycles shaped voyage timing. - Maritime Cultural Exchanges with Southeast Asia: - Religion: - Buddhism spread (e.g., Ashoka’s missions, c. 3rd century BCE); Hindu temples in Angkor Wat (c. 12th century CE). - Art: - Pallava-style architecture in Champa (Vietnam, c. 7th century CE). - Language: - Sanskrit inscriptions (e.g., Vo Canh stele, Vietnam, c. 3rd century CE). - Trade Goods: - Spices, textiles, pearls (e.g., Pandya pearls to Java). - Historical Significance: - The interplay of technology and patronage, amplified by monsoon winds, made India a maritime hub, influencing Southeast Asia’s culture and economy for centuries. - Related Figures: - Ashoka: - Mauryan king (r. c. 268-232 BCE), Buddhist missions (e.g., Q117 [1998]). - Rajaraja I: - Chola king (r. c. 985-1014 CE), naval patron (e.g., Q64 [1998]). - Rajendra I: - Chola king (r. c. 1014-1044 CE), Srivijaya conqueror. - Bhoja: - Paramara king (c. 11th century CE), Yuktikalpataru author. - Broader Connection: - Ties to trade networks (e.g., Q35 [1998]), Gupta economy (e.g., Q79 [1998]), or Buddhist diffusion (e.g., Q118 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - India’s maritime pre-eminence in the Bay of Bengal stemmed from superior ship-building (a) and southern ruler patronage (b), making (d) the book’s correct answer, though monsoon winds (c) were a vital underlying factor. - Q81: The Jain philosophy holds that the world is created and maintained by: - Options: (a) Universal Law (b) Universal Truth (c) Universal Faith (d) Universal Soul - Answer: (a) Universal Law ( The book is saying option d, but option A is most relevant) - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Jainism, originating in ancient India (c. 6th century BCE), was formalized by Mahavira (599-527 BCE), the 24th Tirthankara, in the Gangetic plains. It emerged alongside Buddhism, emphasizing non-violence (Ahimsa) and a rejection of Vedic rituals. Jain cosmology posits an eternal, uncreated universe governed by natural principles rather than a creator deity. - Correct Option Explained: - (a) Universal Law: - Correct—In Jain philosophy, the world is eternal, without beginning or end, and operates under Dravya (substances) and Tattvas (principles), collectively forming a "Universal Law." Key concepts include Karma (action and its consequences), Dharma (motion), and Adharma (rest), which govern the cosmos naturally. No supreme deity creates or maintains it; instead, it’s a self-sustaining system of cause and effect. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Universal Truth: - Incorrect—While Jainism values truth (Satya), "Universal Truth" implies an abstract, absolute principle (e.g., Buddhist Four Noble Truths). Jainism focuses on operational laws (Karma, Tattvas), not a singular truth creating the world. - (c) Universal Faith: - Incorrect—Faith (Shraddha) is a personal quality in Jainism, not a cosmic force. The universe’s functioning doesn’t depend on belief but on inherent laws. - (d) Universal Soul: - Incorrect—Jainism recognizes infinite individual souls (Jivas), each eternal and uncreated. There’s no singular "Universal Soul" (e.g., Brahman in Advaita Vedanta) responsible for creation or maintenance. - Jain Cosmology Explained: - Universe: - Eternal, uncreated, infinite; consists of Loka (cosmos) and Aloka (non-cosmic space). - Key Principles: - Dravya: Six substances (soul, matter, motion, rest, space, time). - Tattvas: Nine realities (e.g., soul, non-soul, karma, liberation). - Karma: Material particles binding to the soul, driving the cycle of birth and death. - Purpose: - Souls achieve liberation (Moksha) by shedding karma through asceticism, not through divine intervention. - Philosophies of Major Religions: - Jainism: - Core: Universal Law (Karma, Tattvas); eternal universe, no creator. Five vows: Ahimsa (non-violence), Satya (truth), Asteya (non-stealing), Brahmacharya (chastity), Aparigraha (non-attachment). Goal: Moksha via self-effort. Key figure: Mahavira (c. 599-527 BCE). - Buddhism: - Core: Four Noble Truths (suffering, cause, cessation, path); impermanence (Anicca), no-self (Anatta), dependent origination (Pratityasamutpada). Universe: Cyclical, no creator. Goal: Nirvana. Founder: Gautama Buddha (c. 563-483 BCE). - Hinduism: - Core: Diverse schools—Advaita (Brahman as Universal Soul), Dvaita (Vishnu as creator), Samkhya (dualism of Purusha-Prakriti). Texts: Vedas, Upanishads, Gita. Universe: Created/maintained by gods (e.g., Brahma, Vishnu) or eternal cycles (Yugas). Goal: Moksha. Key figures: Shankaracharya (c. 788-820 CE), Ramanuja (c. 1017-1137 CE). - Sikhism: - Core: Ik Onkar (One Supreme Reality); monotheism, equality, devotion. Universe: Created and sustained by Waheguru (God). Goal: Union with God via Nam Japna (meditation), Kirat Karna (honest work), Vand Chakna (sharing). Founder: Guru Nanak (c. 1469-1539 CE). - Vaishnavism (Hindu Sect): - Core: Bhakti (devotion to Vishnu/Krishna). Universe: Created/maintained by Vishnu. Texts: Bhagavad Gita, Vishnu Purana. Goal: Moksha through devotion. Key figure: Ramanuja (c. 1017-1137 CE). - Shaivism (Hindu Sect): - Core: Shiva as supreme deity; universe created/maintained by Shiva’s cosmic dance (Tandava). Goal: Liberation via devotion/knowledge. Key text: Shaiva Agamas. Key figure: Lakulisha (c. 2nd century CE). - Christianity: - Core: Monotheism; God as creator and sustainer. Universe: Created by God (Genesis). Goal: Salvation through faith in Jesus Christ. Founder: Jesus (c. 4 BCE-30 CE). - Islam: - Core: Tawhid (oneness of Allah); Allah creates and maintains the universe. Goal: Submission to Allah’s will, paradise. Text: Quran. Founder: Prophet Muhammad (c. 570-632 CE). - Philosophical Significance: - Jainism’s rejection of a creator deity and emphasis on natural laws (Karma, Dharma) distinguish it from theistic traditions (e.g., Sikhism, Islam) and truth-centric philosophies (e.g., Buddhism). Its cosmology aligns with a scientific-like view of a self-regulating universe. - Related Figures: - Mahavira: - 24th Tirthankara (c. 599-527 BCE); codified Jain philosophy, emphasized Universal Law. - Rishabhanatha: - 1st Tirthankara (mythical); early proponent of Jain teachings. - Gautama Buddha: - Contemporary (c. 563-483 BCE); focused on suffering, not cosmic laws. - Shankaracharya: - Hindu philosopher (c. 788-820 CE); proposed Brahman as Universal Soul. - Broader Connection: - Links to Jainism (e.g., Q66 [1998]), philosophical debates (e.g., Q68 [1998] Buddhism), or Indian thought (e.g., Q70 [1998] Vedas). - Key Takeaway: - Jain philosophy holds that the world is created and maintained by Universal Law (a), a system of natural principles (Karma, Tattvas), not truth, faith, or a universal soul. - Q82: Regarding the Indus Valley Civilization, consider the following statements: [Harappan-Related] - Statements: 1. It was predominantly a secular civilization and the religious element, though present, did not dominate the scene 2. During this period, cotton was used for manufacturing textiles in India - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (c) Both 1 and 2 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Indus Valley Civilization (IVC), also known as the Harappan Civilization (c. 3300-1300 BCE), flourished in the northwestern Indian subcontinent (modern Pakistan and northwest India). Major sites include Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro, Dholavira, and Lothal. It was a Bronze Age urban culture known for advanced city planning, trade, and craftsmanship. - Statement Analysis: - Statement 1: It was predominantly a secular civilization and the religious element, though present, did not dominate the scene: - Correct—Evidence suggests the IVC was largely secular in its public life. Unlike Mesopotamia or Egypt, there are no grand temples or monumental religious structures dominating city layouts. Artifacts like seals (e.g., Pashupati seal), terracotta figurines, and fire altars indicate religious practices (possibly proto-Shiva worship or fertility cults), but these appear secondary to urban infrastructure (e.g., Great Bath, granaries). The lack of priest-king palaces or elaborate burials further supports a less theocratic society. - Statement 2: During this period, cotton was used for manufacturing textiles in India: - Correct—Archaeological finds, such as cotton fragments from Mohenjo-Daro and spindle whorls, confirm cotton textile production. The IVC is credited with early cotton cultivation and weaving (c. 2500 BCE), evidenced by trade with Mesopotamia, where Harappan cotton was identified (e.g., Sumerian texts mention "Sindhu cloth"). This predates cotton use in other civilizations like Egypt. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is also true, as cotton textile production is archaeologically verified. - (b) 2 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is also true, given the secular emphasis in IVC urban planning and governance. - (d) Neither 1 nor 2: - Incorrect—Both statements are supported by evidence, making this option invalid. - Key Features of the Indus Valley Civilization: - Urban Planning: - Grid-patterned cities, standardized baked bricks, advanced drainage systems (e.g., Mohenjo-Daro’s covered sewers). - Economy: - Trade with Mesopotamia (e.g., carnelian beads, seals found in Ur), agriculture (wheat, barley, cotton), metallurgy (bronze, copper). - Technology: - Cotton textiles, standardized weights/measures, dockyard at Lothal (possibly world’s earliest). - Religion: - No dominant temples; possible worship of nature (trees, animals), proto-Shiva (Pashupati seal), mother goddess figurines. - Decline: - c. 1900-1300 BCE; theories include climate change (drying of Sarasvati River), Aryan migration, or trade collapse. - Other Ancient Civilizations: - Mesopotamian Civilization (c. 3500-539 BCE): - Region: Tigris-Euphrates (modern Iraq) - Features: City-states (Uruk, Ur), ziggurats (religious centers), cuneiform writing, theocracy (priest-kings), trade (barley, wool), laws (Hammurabi’s Code, c. 1750 BCE). - Religion: Polytheistic (Anu, Enlil, Ishtar); temples dominated cities. - Egyptian Civilization (c. 3100-30 BCE): - Region: Nile River (modern Egypt) - Features: Pyramids, hieroglyphs, centralized monarchy (pharaohs as gods), agriculture (wheat, papyrus), trade (gold, incense). - Religion: Polytheistic (Ra, Osiris); theocracy, afterlife focus (mummification). - Chinese Civilization (Yellow River, c. 2070 BCE onward): - Region: Huang He (Yellow River, modern China) - Features: Shang dynasty (bronze, oracle bones), Zhou dynasty (Mandate of Heaven), silk production, agriculture (rice, millet). - Religion: Ancestor worship, animism; less theocratic than Egypt/Mesopotamia. - Aegean Civilization (Minoan, c. 2700-1450 BCE): - Region: Crete (modern Greece) - Features: Palaces (Knossos), frescoes, maritime trade (pottery, saffron), Linear A script. - Religion: Polytheistic (snake goddess); palaces had ritual significance. - Mesoamerican Civilization (Olmec, c. 1200-400 BCE): - Region: Gulf of Mexico (modern Mexico) - Features: Colossal heads, jade work, agriculture (maize), early writing. - Religion: Polytheistic (jaguar gods); ritualistic, less urban than IVC. - Philosophical/Cultural Significance: - The IVC’s secular bent and technological advancements (e.g., cotton textiles) contrast with the temple-centric societies of Mesopotamia and Egypt, highlighting diverse paths of early urban development. Its trade networks (e.g., with Sumer) underscore its economic sophistication. - Related Evidence: - Seals: - Over 400 symbols (undeciphered script), depict animals, rituals (e.g., Pashupati seal). - Cotton: - Fragments at Mohenjo-Daro, trade links in Mesopotamian records. - Sites: - Mohenjo-Daro (Great Bath), Harappa (granaries), Dholavira (water reservoirs). - Broader Connection: - Links to ancient urbanism (e.g., Q35 [1998]), trade networks (e.g., Q79 [1998]), or Indian history (e.g., Q70 [1998] Vedas). - Key Takeaway: - Both statements are true: The IVC was predominantly secular with subdued religious dominance (1), and it pioneered cotton textile production (2), making (c) the correct answer. - Q83: The "Dharma" and "Rita" depict a central idea of ancient Vedic civilization of India. In this context, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Dharma was a conception of obligations and of the discharge of one's duties to oneself and to others 2. Rita was the fundamental moral law governing the functioning of the universe and all it contained - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (c) Both 1 and 2 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Vedic civilization (c. 1500-500 BCE) emerged in the northwest Indian subcontinent (modern Punjab, Haryana) during the composition of the Rigveda (c. 1500-1200 BCE). This Indo-Aryan culture, rooted in pastoralism and later urbanism, centered on rituals, hymns, and cosmological ideas preserved in the Vedas (Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda). - Statement Analysis: - Statement 1: Dharma was a conception of obligations and of the discharge of one's duties to oneself and to others: - Correct—In the Vedic context, Dharma (from dhri, "to hold") initially meant duties tied to rituals and social roles (e.g., Rta-guided sacrifices, familial obligations). The Rigveda (e.g., 10.90) links it to maintaining cosmic and social order through actions. Later, in texts like the Mahabharata and Manusmriti (post-Vedic), it evolved into a broader ethical framework, but in the Vedic period, it primarily denoted obligations to self (e.g., purity) and others (e.g., community). - Statement 2: Rita was the fundamental moral law governing the functioning of the universe and all it contained: - Correct—Rita (or Rta, "truth/order") is the cosmic principle in the Rigveda (e.g., 1.105, 10.85) that regulates the universe’s natural and moral order—seasons, celestial movements, and human conduct. Gods like Varuna and Mitra uphold Rita, ensuring harmony. It’s the precursor to later concepts like Dharma but is more universal and abstract, governing all existence. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is also true, as Rita is a well-documented Vedic concept of universal order. - (b) 2 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is also true, as Dharma reflects duty-based obligations in Vedic texts. - (d) Neither 1 nor 2: - Incorrect—Both statements align with Vedic philosophy, supported by textual and historical evidence. - Vedic Concepts Explained: - Dharma: - Duty and righteousness; context-specific (e.g., priest’s ritual duty, warrior’s protection). Rooted in Rita, it ensures societal stability. - Rita: - Cosmic order; regulates nature (e.g., dawn, seasons) and morality. Sacrifices (Yajna) align human actions with Rita. - Connection: - Rita is the universal law; Dharma is its human application. Together, they form the Vedic worldview of harmony between cosmos and society. - Similar Concepts in Other Ancient Cultures: - Ma’at (Egyptian Civilization, c. 3100-30 BCE): - Meaning: Truth, balance, order. - Role: Governs cosmic and social harmony; upheld by pharaohs and gods (e.g., Osiris). Judged in afterlife (heart vs. feather). - Text: Book of the Dead. - Tao (Chinese Civilization, c. 500 BCE onward): - Meaning: The "Way" or natural order. - Role: Universal principle in Taoism; guides nature and human life (e.g., yin-yang balance). Non-intervention (Wu Wei) aligns with it. - Text: Tao Te Ching (Laozi). - Asha (Zoroastrianism, Persian Civilization, c. 1200 BCE): - Meaning: Truth, righteousness, order. - Role: Cosmic law upheld by Ahura Mazda; opposes Druj (falsehood). Humans align via good thoughts, words, deeds. - Text: Avesta (Gathas). - Nomos (Greek Civilization, c. 1200-300 BCE): - Meaning: Law, custom, order. - Role: Social and natural laws in philosophy (e.g., Plato’s Laws); less cosmic than Rita but governs human conduct. - Context: Emerged in polis societies. - Dharma (Later Hinduism, post-Vedic): - Meaning: Evolved into universal duty/ethics (e.g., Bhagavad Gita, c. 200 BCE-200 CE). - Role: Personal and societal righteousness; caste-specific duties (Varna-Dharma). - Philosophical Significance: - Rita and Dharma reflect the Vedic emphasis on order at both cosmic and human levels, distinguishing it from theistic creation (e.g., Christianity) or chaos-accepting philosophies (e.g., early Buddhism). Rita’s universality parallels Ma’at and Asha, while Dharma’s duty focus is unique to Indian thought. - Related Evidence: - Rigveda: - Rita: “Varuna upholds Rita” (1.23); “The sun follows Rita” (1.50). - Dharma: “He who performs his duty” (10.90, Purusha Sukta). - Rituals: - Yajna aligns human actions with Rita (e.g., Agni as mediator). - Broader Connection: - Links to Vedic knowledge (e.g., Q70 [1998]), Indian philosophy (e.g., Q81 [Jainism]), or ancient thought (e.g., Q82 [IVC]). - Key Takeaway: - Both statements are true: Dharma as obligations to self and others (1) and Rita as the universal moral law (2) define Vedic ideology, making (c) the correct answer. - [2012-I] - Q84: With reference to the scientific progress of ancient India, which of the statements given below are correct? - Statements: 1. The concept of sine of an angle was known in 5th century AD 4. The concept of cyclic quadrilaterals was known in 7th century AD - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 and 4 only (c) 1, 3 and 4 only (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: (c) 1, 3 and 4 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ancient India made significant contributions to science, particularly in medicine, mathematics, and astronomy, from the Vedic period (c. 1500-500 BCE) through the classical age (c. 1st-12th centuries AD). Texts like the Sushruta Samhita, Charaka Samhita, Aryabhatiya, and Brahmasphutasiddhanta document these advancements, often linked to urban centers like Pataliputra, Taxila, and Ujjain. - Statement Analysis: - Statement 1: Different kinds of specialized surgical instruments were in common use by 1st century AD: - Correct—The Sushruta Samhita (c. 6th century BCE-1st century AD), attributed to Sushruta, describes over 120 surgical instruments (e.g., scalpels, forceps, probes) used for procedures like cataract surgery, rhinoplasty, and lithotomy. By the 1st century AD, these were refined and widely practiced, as evidenced by Taxila’s medical tradition and Greek accounts (e.g., Megasthenes, c. 300 BCE). - Statement 2: Transplant of internal organs in the human body had begun by the beginning of 3rd century AD: - Incorrect—No evidence exists of internal organ transplants (e.g., heart, liver) by the 3rd century AD (c. 201-300 AD).
