This statement overstates ancient Indian capabilities. - Statement 3: The concept of sine of an angle was known in 5th century AD: - Correct—Aryabhata (476-550 AD) introduced the sine concept in his Aryabhatiya (499 AD), calling it "jya" (chord half-angle). He provided a sine table for astronomical calculations (e.g., 3.1416 for pi), predating its formalization in Europe. This marks a key mathematical advancement by the 5th century AD. - Statement 4: The concept of cyclic quadrilaterals was known in 7th century AD: - Correct—Brahmagupta (598-668 AD) in his Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 AD) defined cyclic quadrilaterals (quadrilaterals inscribed in a circle) and gave the area formula: Area = √((s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)), where s is the semi-perimeter. This was a significant geometric insight by the 7th century AD. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is false; organ transplants were not performed by the 3rd century AD. - (b) 3 and 4 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is true; surgical instruments were in use by the 1st century AD. - (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is false, invalidating this option. - (c) 1, 3 and 4 only: - Correct—Statements 1, 3, and 4 are supported by historical evidence, while 2 is not. - Key Scientific Contributions: - Medicine: - Sushruta Samhita: Surgery (e.g., rhinoplasty, cataract removal), instruments, anatomy (c. 6th century BCE-1st century AD). - Charaka Samhita: Internal medicine, diagnostics (c. 2nd century BCE-2nd century AD). - Mathematics: - Aryabhata: Sine, zero as a placeholder, pi approximation (499 AD). - Brahmagupta: Cyclic quadrilaterals, zero operations, negative numbers (628 AD). - Astronomy: - Aryabhatiya: Earth’s rotation, eclipses; Siddhantas: planetary models. - Related Figures: - Sushruta: - Surgeon (c. 6th century BCE-1st century AD); pioneer of plastic surgery. - Aryabhata: - Mathematician-astronomer (476-550 AD); sine and pi contributions. - Brahmagupta: - Mathematician (598-668 AD); cyclic quadrilaterals, algebra. - Charaka: - Physician (c. 2nd century BCE-2nd century AD); holistic medicine. - Broader Connection: - Links to ancient Indian knowledge (e.g., Q70 [1998] Vedas), mathematics (e.g., Q77 [Baudhayan]), or intellectual history (e.g., Q81 [Jainism]). - Key Takeaway: - Statements 1 (surgical instruments by 1st century AD), 3 (sine by 5th century AD), and 4 (cyclic quadrilaterals by 7th century AD) are correct, while 2 (organ transplants by 3rd century AD) is not, making (c) the correct answer. - Q85: With reference to the history of ancient India, which of the following was/were common to both Buddhism and Jainism? - Statements: 1. Avoidance of extremities of penance and enjoyment 2. Indifference to the authority of the Vedas 3. Denial of efficacy of rituals - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Buddhism and Jainism emerged in ancient India (c. 6th-5th centuries BCE) in the Gangetic plains during the Second Urbanization, challenging Vedic orthodoxy. Buddhism was founded by Gautama Buddha (c. 563-483 BCE), while Jainism was formalized by Mahavira (c. 599-527 BCE), the 24th Tirthankara. Both arose as Shramana movements, emphasizing personal liberation over Vedic ritualism. - Statement Analysis: - Statement 1: Avoidance of extremities of penance and enjoyment: - Incorrect for both—Buddhism advocates the Middle Path, avoiding extremes of asceticism and indulgence (e.g., Buddha rejected severe penance after his early austerities). Jainism, however, embraces extreme penance (e.g., Mahavira’s 12 years of harsh asceticism, fasting in Digambara tradition). Thus, this is not common to both. - Statement 2: Indifference to the authority of the Vedas: - Correct—Both rejected Vedic authority. Buddhism dismissed the Vedas as irrelevant to liberation (e.g., Four Noble Truths focus on suffering, not scripture). Jainism also disregarded Vedic texts, emphasizing its own Agamas and Tattvas (e.g., karma, soul liberation) over Brahminical traditions. - Statement 3: Denial of efficacy of rituals: - Correct—Both opposed Vedic rituals’ efficacy. Buddhism criticized sacrificial rites (e.g., Dhammapada rejects external acts for salvation). Jainism denied rituals’ salvific power, focusing on internal purification (e.g., Ahimsa, asceticism) rather than Yajnas. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is not common; Jainism’s extreme penance contrasts with Buddhism’s Middle Path. - (c) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is not common, though 3 is true for both. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is not shared; only 2 and 3 align. - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Correct—Both Buddhism and Jainism share indifference to Vedic authority and denial of ritual efficacy. - Key Philosophical Differences and Commonalities: - Buddhism: - Core: Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, Anatta (no-self), Nirvana. - Approach: Middle Path, pragmatic rejection of extremes. - Texts: Pali Canon (e.g., Tripitaka). - Jainism: - Core: Anekantavada, Syadvada, Five Vows (e.g., Ahimsa), Moksha. - Approach: Extreme asceticism for karma removal. - Texts: Agamas. - Commonalities: - Rejection of Vedic authority and rituals; focus on personal effort for liberation; non-theistic; karma-driven cosmology. - Differences: - Buddhism’s moderation vs. Jainism’s ascetic rigor; Anatta vs. eternal Jivas (souls). - Historical Evidence: - Buddhism: - Buddha’s rejection of Vedic sacrifices (e.g., Sutta Pitaka); preached in Pali, not Sanskrit. - Jainism: - Mahavira’s nudity and fasting (e.g., Acaranga Sutra); Agamas over Vedas. - Context: - Both thrived in Magadha (e.g., Ashoka’s patronage of Buddhism, Jain presence in Bihar). - Broader Connection: - Links to Shramana traditions (e.g., Q81 [Jainism]), philosophical debates (e.g., Q68 [1998]), or Vedic critique (e.g., Q83 [Dharma/Rita]). - Key Takeaway: - Statements 2 (indifference to Vedas) and 3 (denial of rituals) were common to Buddhism and Jainism, while 1 (avoidance of extremes) was not, making (b) the correct answer. - Q86: The Nagara, the Dravida and the Vesara are the: - Options: (a) three main racial groups of the Indian subcontinent (b) three main linguistic divisions into which the languages of India can be classified (c) three main styles of Indian temple architecture (d) three main musical Gharanas prevalent in India - Answer: (c) three main styles of Indian temple architecture - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Indian temple architecture evolved from the Gupta period (c. 4th-6th centuries AD) onward, reflecting regional styles and religious traditions (Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism). The Nagara, Dravida, and Vesara styles emerged as distinct architectural forms between the 5th and 13th centuries AD, documented in texts like the Shilpa Shastras and visible in temples across India. - Correct Option Explained: - (c) three main styles of Indian temple architecture: - Correct—Nagara, Dravida, and Vesara are the three primary styles of Indian temple architecture. Nagara (northern India) features a curvilinear shikhara (tower), Dravida (southern India) has a pyramidal vimana (tower), and Vesara (central/deccan India) blends elements of both. These styles are defined by their superstructure, layout, and regional development. - Why Not Others?: - (a) three main racial groups of the Indian subcontinent: - Incorrect—Racial classifications (e.g., Australoid, Mongoloid, Caucasoid) exist in anthropology, but Nagara, Dravida, and Vesara are unrelated; they are architectural terms, not ethnic categories. - (b) three main linguistic divisions into which the languages of India can be classified: - Incorrect—Indian languages are grouped into families like Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, and Tibeto-Burman (per the Constitution and linguistic surveys), not Nagara, Dravida, and Vesara. Dravida overlaps with Dravidian languages, but the terms here denote architecture, not linguistics. - (d) three main musical Gharanas prevalent in India: - Incorrect—Gharanas (e.g., Gwalior, Agra, Kirana) are schools of Hindustani classical music, unrelated to Nagara, Dravida, or Vesara, which pertain to temple design. - Details of Temple Architecture Styles: - Nagara: - Region: Northern India (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan). - Features: Curved, beehive-like shikhara; square plan; examples include Kandariya Mahadeva Temple (Khajuraho, c. 11th century AD) and Sun Temple (Konark, c. 13th century AD). - Period: Dominant from Gupta period (5th century AD) onward. - Dravida: - Region: Southern India (e.g., Tamil Nadu, Karnataka). - Features: Pyramidal vimana, gopuram (tower gateway); rectangular plan; examples include Brihadeeswara Temple (Thanjavur, c. 1010 AD) and Shore Temple (Mamallapuram, c. 7th century AD). - Period: Pallava (6th-9th centuries AD) to Chola (9th-13th centuries AD). - Vesara: - Region: Deccan/Central India (e.g., Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh). - Features: Hybrid of Nagara and Dravida; shorter shikhara with Dravidian elements; examples include Hoysaleswara Temple (Halebidu, c. 12th century AD) and Chennakesava Temple (Belur, c. 12th century AD). - Period: Chalukya (6th-12th centuries AD) and Hoysala influence. - Architectural Significance: - These styles reflect regional diversity, technological skill (e.g., stone carving), and religious patronage (e.g., Chola temples for Shiva). Nagara emphasizes verticality, Dravida horizontal elaboration, and Vesara synthesis, showcasing India’s cultural adaptability. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Shilpa Shastras (e.g., Manasara) codify temple design rules. - Examples: - Nagara: Lingaraja Temple (Bhubaneswar), Dravida: Meenakshi Temple (Madurai), Vesara: Lad Khan Temple (Aihole). - Broader Connection: - Links to ancient Indian culture (e.g., Q80 [maritime trade]), Gupta legacy (e.g., Q84 [science]), or regional history (e.g., Q82 [IVC]). - Key Takeaway: - Nagara, Dravida, and Vesara are the three main styles of Indian temple architecture (c), not racial, linguistic, or musical categories, making (c) the correct answer. - Q87: Lord Buddha's image is sometimes shown with the hand gesture called 'Bhumisparsha Mudra'. It symbolizes: - Options: (a) Buddha's calling of the Earth to watch over Mara and to prevent Mara from disturbing his meditation (b) Buddha's calling of the Earth to witness his purity and chastity despite the temptations of Mara (c) Buddha's reminder to his followers that they all arise from the Earth and finally dissolve into the Earth, and thus this life is transitory (d) Both the statements (a) and (b) are correct in this context - Answer: (b) Buddha's calling of the Earth to witness his purity and chastity despite the temptations of Mara - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Bhumisparsha Mudra ("Earth-touching gesture") is tied to Gautama Buddha’s enlightenment under the Bodhi tree in Bodh Gaya (c. 5th century BCE). As per Buddhist texts (e.g., Nidana Katha, Lalitavistara), this gesture occurred during his confrontation with Mara, the demon of desire and death, just before attaining Nirvana. - Correct Option Explained: - (b) Buddha's calling of the Earth to witness his purity and chastity despite the temptations of Mara: - Correct—Bhumisparsha Mudra symbolizes Buddha touching the Earth with his right hand to call it as a witness to his past virtuous deeds (e.g., generosity, discipline) over countless lives, proving his worthiness for enlightenment. Mara challenged Buddha’s merit, tempting him with desire and fear. Buddha’s gesture signifies his triumph over Mara by invoking the Earth as testimony to his purity and moral steadfastness, not merely to "watch over" Mara. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Buddha's calling of the Earth to watch over Mara and to prevent Mara from disturbing his meditation: - Incorrect—The gesture isn’t about asking the Earth to guard against Mara but to affirm Buddha’s own merit. The Earth’s role is as a witness, not a protector, per texts like the Buddhacarita (c. 2nd century AD). - (c) Buddha's reminder to his followers that they all arise from the Earth and finally dissolve into the Earth, and thus this life is transitory: - Incorrect—While impermanence (Anicca) is a Buddhist teaching, Bhumisparsha Mudra specifically relates to the Mara episode, not a general lesson on transience. This interpretation lacks textual support in this context. - (d) Both the statements (a) and (b) are correct in this context: - Incorrect—Only (b) aligns with the traditional narrative; (a) misrepresents the gesture’s purpose. - Details of Bhumisparsha Mudra: - Gesture: - Right hand touches the ground, palm inward; left hand rests in lap, palm upward. - Event: - Mara’s daughters tempted Buddha with desire; Mara then demanded proof of his merit. Buddha’s Earth-touching gesture silenced Mara, leading to enlightenment. - Symbolism: - Victory over temptation, affirmation of resolve, connection to Earth as a universal witness. - Other Buddhist Mudras: - Dhyana Mudra: - Gesture: Both hands in lap, right over left, palms up, thumbs touching. - Meaning: Meditation, concentration; associated with Buddha’s ascetic phase. - Example: Meditating Buddha statues (e.g., Sarnath). - Abhaya Mudra: - Gesture: Right hand raised, palm outward; left hand down. - Meaning: Fearlessness, protection; linked to Buddha calming a mad elephant. - Example: Standing Buddha images. - Vitarka Mudra: - Gesture: Right hand raised, thumb and index finger forming a circle. - Meaning: Teaching, discussion; represents the First Sermon at Sarnath. - Example: Dharmachakra Buddha. - Anjali Mudra: - Gesture: Palms pressed together at chest level. - Meaning: Greeting, respect; common in Buddhist devotion. - Example: Worshipping monks. - Gestures of Other Important Figures: - Mahavira (Jainism): - Gesture: Standing upright (Kayotsarga), hands relaxed by sides. - Meaning: Renunciation, meditation; reflects Jain asceticism. - Example: Statues at Shravanabelagola. - Shiva (Hinduism): - Gesture: Abhaya (right hand up) or Nataraja pose (dance with raised leg). - Meaning: Protection or cosmic creation/destruction. - Example: Nataraja bronze (Chola art). - Vishnu (Hinduism): - Gesture: Varada Mudra (right hand down, palm open). - Meaning: Boon-giving, compassion. - Example: Vishnu icons with conch and discus. - Guru Nanak (Sikhism): - Gesture: Hand raised in blessing or holding mala. - Meaning: Divine guidance, devotion. - Example: Paintings in Sikh tradition. - Philosophical Significance: - Bhumisparsha Mudra underscores Buddhism’s emphasis on self-reliance and moral victory, distinguishing it from theistic reliance (e.g., Hinduism’s divine aid) or Jainism’s extreme penance. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Pali Canon (e.g., Digha Nikaya) narrates the Mara episode. - Art: - Buddha statues at Sarnath, Ajanta (c. 5th-6th centuries AD) depict this mudra. - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhism (e.g., Q85 [Buddhism/Jainism]), Indian art (e.g., Q86 [temple styles]), or philosophy (e.g., Q81 [Jainism]). - Key Takeaway: - Bhumisparsha Mudra symbolizes Buddha calling the Earth to witness his purity against Mara’s temptations (b), not protection or transience, making (b) the correct answer. - Q88: The religion of early Vedic Aryans was primarily of: - Options: (a) Bhakti (b) image worship and Yajnas (c) worship of nature and Yajnas (d) worship of nature and Bhakti - Answer: (c) worship of nature and Yajnas - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The early Vedic Aryans (c. 1500-1000 BCE) were Indo-Aryan pastoralists who migrated into northwest India (modern Punjab, Haryana) during the Rigvedic period. Their religion, preserved in the Rigveda (c. 1500-1200 BCE), revolved around oral hymns, rituals, and a pantheon of deities tied to natural forces, performed through sacrificial rites known as Yajnas. - Correct Option Explained: - (c) worship of nature and Yajnas: - Correct—The early Vedic religion centered on worshipping natural elements personified as gods (e.g., Indra for rain, Agni for fire, Surya for sun) and conducting Yajnas (fire sacrifices) to appease them. The Rigveda (e.g., 1.1 to Agni, 1.50 to Surya) reflects this nature-centric polytheism, with Yajnas (e.g., Agnihotra, Soma rituals) as the primary means of connecting with deities for prosperity and cosmic order (Rita). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Bhakti: - Incorrect—Bhakti (devotional worship) emerged later, during the post-Vedic period (c. 500 BCE-1000 CE), with texts like the Bhagavad Gita and the Bhakti movement (e.g., Alvars, Nayanars, 7th-12th centuries AD). Early Vedic religion lacked personal devotion, focusing instead on ritualistic offerings. - (b) image worship and Yajnas: - Incorrect—Image worship (e.g., idols, murtis) is absent in the early Vedic period. The Rigveda mentions no temples or icons; deities were invoked through hymns and fire altars. Image worship developed later, in the Puranic period (c. 300 BCE onward). - (d) worship of nature and Bhakti: - Incorrect—While nature worship was central, Bhakti was not part of early Vedic practice. This option mixes an early trait (nature worship) with a later development (Bhakti). - Key Features of Early Vedic Religion: - Nature Worship: - Deities: Indra (rain/thunder), Agni (fire), Surya (sun), Vayu (wind), Varuna (sky/water), Usha (dawn). - Purpose: Sought natural benefits (rain, cattle, health) and cosmic harmony (Rita). - Yajnas: - Types: Simple (e.g., daily Agnihotra) to complex (e.g., Ashvamedha, horse sacrifice). - Ritual: Offerings (ghee, soma) into consecrated fire, led by priests (e.g., Hotri, Adhvaryu). - Texts: Rigveda hymns chanted during sacrifices. - Belief: - Polytheistic, no supreme deity; gods anthropomorphized natural forces. - Evolution of Vedic Religion: - Later Vedic Period (c. 1000-500 BCE): - Shift to philosophical speculation (Upanishads), rituals grew elaborate (Shrauta Sutras). - Post-Vedic Period: - Bhakti and image worship emerged with Puranas and temple culture (e.g., Gupta period, 4th-6th centuries AD). - Related Evidence: - Rigveda: - "Agni, the chosen priest" (1.1); "Surya rises in the east" (1.50); "Indra slays Vritra" (1.32). - Artifacts: - Fire altars at sites like Kalibangan (c. 2000 BCE) suggest continuity with Harappan practices. - Broader Connection: - Links to Vedic concepts (e.g., Q83 [Dharma/Rita]), ancient India (e.g., Q82 [IVC]), or religious evolution (e.g., Q85 [Buddhism/Jainism]). - Key Takeaway: - The early Vedic Aryans’ religion was primarily worship of nature and Yajnas (c), focused on natural deities and sacrificial rites, not Bhakti or image worship, making (c) the correct answer. - Q89: With reference to the guilds (Shreni) of ancient India that played a very important role in the country's economy, which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. Every guild was registered with the central authority of the State and the king was the chief administrative authority on them 2. The wages, rules of work, standards and prices were fixed by the guild 3. The guild had judicial powers over its own members - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Guilds, known as Shrenis, were prominent in ancient India from the Mauryan period (c. 321-185 BCE) through the Gupta period (c. 4th-6th centuries AD). These were associations of artisans, traders, and craftsmen (e.g., weavers, potters, metalworkers) that regulated economic activities in urban centers like Pataliputra, Taxila, and Ujjain. Texts like the Arthashastra (c. 3rd century BCE), Jataka tales, and inscriptions (e.g., Nashik caves, c. 2nd century AD) highlight their role. - Statement Analysis: - Statement 1: Every guild was registered with the central authority of the State and the king was the chief administrative authority on them: - Incorrect—No definitive evidence shows mandatory registration of every guild with a central state authority or the king as their direct overseer. The Arthashastra (e.g., Book II) mentions state oversight of trade and taxes, but Shrenis operated semi-autonomously under their own leaders (Shreshthin or Jetthaka). Kings intervened only in disputes or taxation, not as chief administrators of all guilds. - Statement 2: The wages, rules of work, standards and prices were fixed by the guild: - Correct—Shrenis had internal autonomy to set wages, work conditions, quality standards, and prices. The Jataka tales and inscriptions (e.g., Mathura guild seals) describe guilds regulating apprenticeship, production norms (e.g., silk weaving), and market rates, ensuring economic stability and member welfare. - Statement 3: The guild had judicial powers over its own members: - Correct—Guilds exercised judicial authority over internal disputes (e.g., breaches of contract, misconduct). The Arthashastra (Book III) and Smritis (e.g., Yajnavalkya Smriti) recognize Shreni-dharma, allowing guilds to enforce rules and settle member conflicts, reducing state burden. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false; guilds weren’t centrally registered or directly administered by the king. - (b) 3 only: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is also true; guilds controlled wages and standards alongside judicial powers. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false, invalidating this option. - (c) 2 and 3 only: - Correct—Statements 2 and 3 accurately reflect the guilds’ economic and judicial autonomy. - Key Features of Shrenis: - Organization: - Led by a head (Shreshthin); included members of specific trades (e.g., carpenters, jewelers). - Economic Role: - Controlled production, trade (e.g., silk to Rome), banking (loans, deposits); issued seals/coins. - Autonomy: - Set rules, resolved disputes; paid taxes to the state but retained self-governance. - Examples: - Nashik inscription (c. 2nd century AD): Guilds donated to Buddhist caves; Mathura lion capital (c. 1st century AD): Guild seals. - Decline: - Weakened post-Gupta (c. 7th century AD) due to invasions, feudalism, and reduced urban trade. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Arthashastra: Guilds under Kautilya’s economic oversight; Jataka tales: Guild disputes and norms. - Archaeology: - Guild seals (e.g., Basarh, Vaishali); donations to stupas (e.g., Sanchi). - Broader Connection: - Links to ancient economy (e.g., Q80 [maritime trade]), urbanism (e.g., Q82 [IVC]), or governance (e.g., Q84 [science]). - Key Takeaway: - Shrenis fixed wages, rules, standards, and prices (2) and had judicial powers over members (3), but were not centrally registered under the king (1), making (c) the correct answer. - [2013-I] - Q90: Some Buddhist rock-cut caves are called Chaityas, while the others are called Viharas. What is the difference between the two? - Options: (a) Vihara is a place of worship, while Chaitya is the dwelling place of the monks (b) Chaitya is a place of worship, while Vihara is the dwelling place of the monks (c) Chaitya is the stupa at the far end of the cave, while Vihara is the hall axial to it (d) There is no material difference between the two - Answer: (b) Chaitya is a place of worship, while Vihara is the dwelling place of the monks - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Buddhist rock-cut caves emerged during the Mauryan period (c. 3rd century BCE) and flourished under the Satavahanas, Guptas, and later dynasties (c. 2nd century BCE-6th century AD). Found in sites like Ajanta, Ellora, Bhaja, and Karla (western India), these caves served the Buddhist monastic community (Sangha) and reflect early architectural innovation. - Correct Option Explained: - (b) Chaitya is a place of worship, while Vihara is the dwelling place of the monks: - Correct—Chaityas are prayer halls or shrines, typically containing a stupa (relic mound) for worship and meditation, designed with an apsidal (semicircular) end and vaulted roof (e.g., Karla Chaitya, c. 1st century BCE). Viharas are residential quarters for monks, featuring cells around a central hall for living and study (e.g., Ajanta Cave 1). The distinction lies in their function: Chaityas for devotion, Viharas for habitation. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Vihara is a place of worship, while Chaitya is the dwelling place of the monks: - Incorrect—This reverses the roles. Viharas were monastic residences, not worship spaces; Chaityas housed stupas for rituals. - (c) Chaitya is the stupa at the far end of the cave, while Vihara is the hall axial to it: - Incorrect—Chaitya refers to the entire cave structure (hall + stupa), not just the stupa. Vihara is a separate residential cave, not a hall within a Chaitya. - (d) There is no material difference between the two: - Incorrect—Chaityas and Viharas differ significantly in purpose and design: worship vs. living, apsidal vs. rectangular layout. - Details of Chaityas and Viharas: - Chaitya: - Structure: Apsidal hall, vaulted ceiling, stupa at the rear, often with pillars and a facade (e.g., rock-cut arches). - Purpose: Worship, circumambulation (pradakshina) around the stupa. - Examples: Bhaja (c. 2nd century BCE), Karla (c. 1st century BCE), Ajanta Cave 19 (c. 5th century AD). - Vihara: - Structure: Rectangular hall with small cells along the walls, sometimes with a shrine later added. - Purpose: Monks’ residence, meditation, study. - Examples: Ajanta Cave 1 (c. 5th century AD), Ellora Cave 5 (c. 6th century AD). - Evolution: - Early Chaityas (e.g., Lomas Rishi, 3rd century BCE) were simple; later ones (e.g., Ajanta) became ornate. Viharas grew complex with Gupta patronage. - Cultural Significance: - Chaityas reflect Buddhist devotion to the stupa (symbolizing Buddha’s presence), while Viharas highlight the Sangha’s communal life, supporting the spread of Buddhism across India and beyond (e.g., Ashokan edicts, 3rd century BCE). - Related Evidence: - Inscriptions: - Nashik caves (c. 2nd century AD) mention Chaitya donations by guilds; Ajanta inscriptions note Vihara use. - Archaeology: - Karla Chaitya’s wooden ribs; Ajanta Vihara’s painted cells. - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhist history (e.g., Q85 [Buddhism/Jainism]), Indian architecture (e.g., Q86 [temple styles]), or ancient economy (e.g., Q89 [guilds]). - Key Takeaway: - Chaityas are places of worship with stupas, while Viharas are monks’ dwellings, making (b) the correct answer, distinct in function and form. - Q91: With reference to the history of philosophical thought in India, consider the following statements regarding Sankhya school: - Statements: 1. Sankhya does not accept the theory of rebirth or transmigration of soul 2. Sankhya holds that it is the self-knowledge that leads to liberation and not any exterior influence or agent - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Sankhya (or Samkhya) school, one of the six orthodox (Astika) Indian philosophical systems, emerged around the 4th-3rd centuries BCE, attributed to sage Kapila. It is detailed in the Sankhya Karika by Ishvarakrishna (c. 4th century AD) and influenced texts like the Bhagavad Gita. Sankhya is a dualistic philosophy focusing on Purusha (consciousness) and Prakriti (matter). - Statement Analysis: - Statement 1: Sankhya does not accept the theory of rebirth or transmigration of soul: - Incorrect—Sankhya accepts rebirth and transmigration. It posits that the soul (Purusha) is eternal and bound to Prakriti through ignorance, undergoing cycles of birth and death until liberation (Kaivalya). The Sankhya Karika (e.g., verse 19) implies karma-driven transmigration, consistent with broader Indian thought (e.g., Upanishads). - Statement 2: Sankhya holds that it is the self-knowledge that leads to liberation and not any exterior influence or agent: - Correct—Sankhya emphasizes self-knowledge (Viveka) as the path to liberation. Realizing the distinction between Purusha (pure consciousness) and Prakriti (material nature) frees the soul from bondage. Unlike theistic schools (e.g., Nyaya, Yoga), Sankhya is atheistic, rejecting divine intervention or external agents for salvation (Sankhya Karika, verse 64). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false; Sankhya accepts rebirth. - (c) Both 1 and 2: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false, though 2 is true. - (d) Neither 1 nor 2: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is true, aligning with Sankhya’s core tenets. - (b) 2 only: - Correct—Only statement 2 reflects Sankhya’s focus on self-knowledge for liberation. - Key Features of Sankhya: - Dualism: - Purusha (conscious, inactive) vs. Prakriti (unconscious, active with three gunas: Sattva, Rajas, Tamas). - Cosmology: - Prakriti evolves into 23 tattvas (e.g., intellect, ego, senses, elements); Purusha is unchanging. - Liberation: - Kaivalya (isolation) via discriminative knowledge, ending rebirth cycle. - Atheism: - No God; liberation is self-realized, not granted. - Other Indian Philosophical Schools: - Nyaya: - Founder: Gautama (c. 2nd century BCE). - Core: Logic, epistemology; accepts God as efficient cause. Liberation via valid knowledge (pramana). - Text: Nyaya Sutras. - Vaisheshika: - Founder: Kanada (c. 2nd century BCE). - Core: Atomism, realism; categories (e.g., substance, quality). Liberation via understanding reality, later theistic. - Text: Vaisheshika Sutras. - Yoga: - Founder: Patanjali (c. 2nd century BCE-4th century AD). - Core: Sankhya-based dualism + theistic practice (Ishvara). Liberation via meditation (Ashtanga Yoga). - Text: Yoga Sutras. - Mimamsa: - Founder: Jaimini (c. 3rd-2nd century BCE). - Core: Vedic ritualism; duty (dharma) over liberation initially. Later (Kumarila Bhatta) includes Moksha. - Text: Mimamsa Sutras. - Vedanta: - Founder: Badarayana (Vyasa); key figures: Shankara (Advaita), Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita). - Core: Upanishadic monism/qualified monism; Brahman as ultimate reality. Liberation via knowledge/devotion. - Text: Brahma Sutras. - Charvaka (Nastika): - Core: Materialism, atheism; rejects afterlife, karma. Liberation as pleasure in this life. - Text: Lost; known via critiques (e.g., Madhavacharya’s Sarvadarshanasangraha). - Philosophical Significance: - Sankhya’s atheistic, knowledge-driven liberation contrasts with theistic schools (e.g., Yoga, Vedanta) and ritualistic Mimamsa, influencing later Indian thought (e.g., Gita’s Sankhya-Yoga synthesis). - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Sankhya Karika: “Knowledge of Purusha-Prakriti distinction ends suffering” (verse 64). - Influence: - Bhagavad Gita (Chapter 2) reflects Sankhya dualism. - Broader Connection: - Links to Indian philosophy (e.g., Q81 [Jainism]), Vedic thought (e.g., Q83 [Dharma/Rita]), or intellectual history (e.g., Q84 [science]). - Key Takeaway: - Sankhya accepts rebirth (1 is false) but holds self-knowledge as the path to liberation (2 is true), making (b) the correct answer. - Q92: Which one of the following describes best the concept of Nirvana in Buddhism? - Options: (a) The extinction of the flame of desire (b) The complete annihilation of self (c) A state of bliss and rest (d) A mental stage beyond all comprehension - Answer: (a) The extinction of the flame of desire - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Nirvana (or Nibbana in Pali) is the ultimate goal in Buddhism, articulated by Gautama Buddha (c. 563-483 BCE) in the Gangetic plains. Rooted in the Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path, it represents liberation from the cycle of birth and death (Samsara), as described in texts like the Pali Canon (e.g., Dhammapada, Sutta Pitaka). - Correct Option Explained: - (a) The extinction of the flame of desire: - Correct—Nirvana literally means "blowing out" or "extinction" (from Sanskrit nir + va, "to cease blowing"). In Buddhism, it signifies the extinguishing of the three fires—desire (raga), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha)—that fuel suffering (Dukkha). The Dhammapada (verse 87) and Samyutta Nikaya describe it as the cessation of craving (Tanha), leading to liberation. This is the most precise definition. - Why Not Others?: - (b) The complete annihilation of self: - Incorrect—Buddhism rejects a permanent self (Anatta), but Nirvana isn’t annihilation of an entity. It’s the end of clinging to a false notion of self, not a destruction of existence. The Milinda Panha (c. 100 BCE) clarifies Nirvana as freedom, not non-existence. - (c) A state of bliss and rest: - Partially Correct but Incomplete—Nirvana includes peace (Shanti) and freedom from suffering, often described as blissful (e.g., Theragatha). However, "bliss and rest" oversimplifies it, missing the core idea of extinguishing desire, which is more fundamental in Buddhist doctrine. - (d) A mental stage beyond all comprehension: - Incorrect—While Nirvana transcends ordinary understanding (e.g., Udana 8.1: "There is an unborn, unoriginated"), it’s not merely incomprehensible. Buddha taught it as an attainable state through the Path, with clear causes (e.g., cessation of craving), not an abstract mystery. - Details of Nirvana: - Types: - Nirvana with remainder (Sopadhishesha): Attained in life (e.g., Buddha at Bodh Gaya). - Nirvana without remainder (Parinirvana): After death, no rebirth (e.g., Buddha at Kushinagar). - Process: - Achieved via Eightfold Path, ending the Three Poisons (desire, hatred, delusion). - Symbolism: - Flame extinguished; coolness (Sita) replacing the heat of Samsara. - Similar Concepts in Other Religions and Philosophies: - Moksha (Hinduism): - Meaning: Liberation from Samsara. - Context: Union with Brahman (Advaita) or eternal service to God (Vaishnavism). Achieved via knowledge (Jnana), devotion (Bhakti), or action (Karma). - Text: Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita. - Kaivalya (Jainism): - Meaning: Isolation of soul (Jiva) from matter (Ajiva). - Context: End of karma through asceticism; eternal solitude of the soul. Non-theistic. - Text: Tattvartha Sutra. - Kaivalya (Sankhya/Yoga): - Meaning: Isolation of Purusha from Prakriti. - Context: Liberation via self-knowledge (Sankhya) or meditation (Yoga). Atheistic in Sankhya, theistic in Yoga. - Text: Sankhya Karika, Yoga Sutras. - Salvation (Christianity): - Meaning: Eternal life with God. - Context: Redemption from sin through faith in Jesus Christ. Theistic and afterlife-focused. - Text: New Testament (e.g., John 3:16). - Fana (Sufism, Islam): - Meaning: Annihilation of ego in Allah. - Context: Mystical union with the divine via love and devotion. Theistic. - Text: Poetry of Rumi, Attar. - Wu Wei (Taoism): - Meaning: Non-action, alignment with the Tao. - Context: Harmony with natural order, not liberation from rebirth. Non-theistic. - Text: Tao Te Ching. - Philosophical Significance: - Nirvana’s focus on extinguishing desire distinguishes it from Moksha’s union, Kaivalya’s isolation, or Salvation’s divine grace, reflecting Buddhism’s unique emphasis on psychological liberation over metaphysical states. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - “The fire of lust, hatred, delusion extinguished” (Samyutta Nikaya 35.28). - Events: - Buddha’s enlightenment (c. 528 BCE) exemplifies Nirvana in life. - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhism (e.g., Q85 [Buddhism/Jainism]), Indian philosophy (e.g., Q91 [Sankhya]), or spiritual goals (e.g., Q81 [Jainism]). - Key Takeaway: - Nirvana in Buddhism is best described as the extinction of the flame of desire (a), the cessation of craving leading to liberation, making (a) the correct answer. - Q93: Which of the following characterizes/characterize the people of Indus Civilization? [Harappan-Related] - Statements: 1. They possessed great palaces and temples 2. They worshipped both male and female deities 3. They employed horse-drawn chariots in warfare - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 only (c) 1, 2 and 3 (d) None of the statements given above is correct - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Indus Valley Civilization (IVC), or Harappan Civilization (c. 3300-1300 BCE), thrived in the northwestern Indian subcontinent (modern Pakistan, northwest India). Known for urban planning, trade, and craftsmanship, its major sites include Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro, Dholavira, and Lothal. It was a Bronze Age culture with a peak during the Mature Harappan phase (c. 2600-1900 BCE). - Statement Analysis: - Statement 1: They possessed great palaces and temples: - Incorrect—No definitive evidence exists of grand palaces or large temples in the IVC. Unlike Mesopotamia (e.g., ziggurats) or Egypt (e.g., pyramids), Harappan sites lack monumental religious or royal structures. The Great Bath (Mohenjo-Daro) may have had ritual use, but it’s not a temple. Citadels (e.g., Harappa) suggest administration, not palatial residences. - Statement 2: They worshipped both male and female deities: - Correct—Archaeological finds suggest worship of male and female deities. The Pashupati seal (Mohenjo-Daro) depicts a horned figure, possibly a male deity (proto-Shiva), surrounded by animals. Terracotta figurines of a Mother Goddess indicate female deity worship, linked to fertility cults. These imply a polytheistic or animistic tradition. - Statement 3: They employed horse-drawn chariots in warfare: - Incorrect—No evidence supports horse-drawn chariots in the IVC. Horses were rare; skeletal remains are absent or post-date the Mature phase (c. 1900 BCE onward). Chariots appear later with Indo-Aryans (c. 1500 BCE, Rigveda). IVC warfare, if any, likely used simpler means (e.g., copper weapons), with no chariot iconography. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false; no great palaces or temples are evident. - (c) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Statements 1 and 3 are false; only 2 is correct. - (d) None of the statements given above is correct: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is true, supported by archaeological evidence. - (b) 2 only: - Correct—Only statement 2 accurately characterizes IVC religious practices. - Key Features of IVC Religion and Culture: - Religion: - Polytheistic/animistic; Pashupati seal (male), Mother Goddess figurines (female), tree worship (e.g., pipal motifs). - No large temples; possible ritual sites (e.g., fire altars at Kalibangan). - Society: - Urban, egalitarian tendencies; no clear royal elite or palaces. - Technology: - Advanced drainage, standardized bricks, weights; no horse-drawn vehicles. - Characteristics of Other Ancient Civilizations: - Mesopotamian Civilization (c. 3500-539 BCE): - Region: Tigris-Euphrates (modern Iraq). - Traits: City-states (Uruk, Ur), ziggurats (temples), cuneiform writing, palaces (e.g., Mari), chariots (post-2000 BCE), polytheism (e.g., Anu, Ishtar). - Egyptian Civilization (c. 3100-30 BCE): - Region: Nile River (modern Egypt). - Traits: Pyramids (tombs), temples (e.g., Karnak), hieroglyphs, pharaohs’ palaces, chariots (New Kingdom, c. 1550 BCE), polytheism (e.g., Ra, Isis). - Chinese Civilization (Yellow River, c. 2070 BCE onward): - Region: Huang He (modern China). - Traits: Shang palaces (Anyang), oracle bones, bronze weapons, chariots (c. 1200 BCE), ancestor worship, no large temples initially. - Aegean Civilization (Minoan, c. 2700-1450 BCE): - Region: Crete (modern Greece). - Traits: Palaces (Knossos), no temples, frescoes, maritime trade, bull worship, no chariots evidenced. - Mesoamerican Civilization (Olmec, c. 1200-400 BCE): - Region: Gulf of Mexico (modern Mexico). - Traits: Ceremonial centers (La Venta), no palaces, colossal heads, jaguar deities, no chariots, maize-based economy. - Related Evidence: - Artifacts: - Seals (e.g., Pashupati, c. 2500 BCE), terracotta figurines (Mohenjo-Daro), fire altars (Lothal). - Absence: - No horse bones or chariot depictions in Mature Harappan phase; contrast with Vedic spoked wheels (c. 1500 BCE). - Broader Connection: - Links to IVC (e.g., Q82 [secular traits]), ancient India (e.g., Q88 [Vedic Aryans]), or trade (e.g., Q80 [maritime links]). - Key Takeaway: - The IVC people worshipped male and female deities (2) but lacked great palaces/temples (1) and horse-drawn chariots (3), making (b) the correct answer. - Q94: Which of the following statements is/are applicable to Jain doctrine? - Statements: 1. The surest way of annihilating Karma is to practice penance 2. Every object, even the smallest particle has a soul 3. Karma is the bane of the soul and must be ended - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Jainism, formalized by Mahavira (c. 599-527 BCE), the 24th Tirthankara, emerged in ancient India (Gangetic plains) as a Shramana tradition alongside Buddhism. Rooted in earlier Tirthankaras (e.g., Rishabhanatha), it emphasizes non-violence (Ahimsa), asceticism, and liberation (Moksha) through its scriptures, the Agamas, and texts like the Tattvartha Sutra (c. 2nd-5th centuries AD). - Statement Analysis: - Statement 1: The surest way of annihilating Karma is to practice penance: - Correct—Jain doctrine holds that penance (Tapas) is a primary means to burn off accumulated karma. Practices like fasting, meditation, and Sallekhana (voluntary death by fasting) purify the soul (Jiva) by shedding karmic matter (Acaranga Sutra, Tattvartha Sutra 9.19). Mahavira’s 12-year penance exemplifies this path to liberation. - Statement 2: Every object, even the smallest particle has a soul: - Correct—Jainism posits that all entities—living (plants, animals, humans) and elemental (earth, water, fire, air)—possess a soul (Jiva). Even the smallest particle (nigoda, microscopic life forms) has consciousness, reflecting Jainism’s animistic worldview and strict Ahimsa (Tattvartha Sutra 2.11-13). - Statement 3: Karma is the bane of the soul and must be ended: - Correct—Karma is seen as material particles that bind to the soul, obscuring its purity and causing rebirth (Samsara). Ending karma through ethical living (Five Vows) and asceticism leads to Moksha (liberation), a core tenet of Jainism (Tattvartha Sutra 10.1-3). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect—Statements 2 and 3 are also true, integral to Jain metaphysics and soteriology. - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is true; penance is a key method to annihilate karma in Jain practice. - (c) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is true; the universal presence of souls underpins Jain ethics. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Correct—All three statements accurately reflect Jain doctrine. - Key Elements of Jain Doctrine: - Karma: - Material substance binding the soul; eight types (e.g., knowledge-obscuring, feeling-producing). - Soul (Jiva): - Eternal, present in all matter; infinite souls exist, seeking liberation. - Penance (Tapas): - Internal (meditation) and external (fasting); burns karma, aids Moksha. - Five Vows: - Ahimsa (non-violence), Satya (truth), Asteya (non-stealing), Brahmacharya (chastity), Aparigraha (non-attachment). - Doctrines of Other Major Religions: - Buddhism: - Core: Four Noble Truths (suffering, cause, cessation, path); Anatta (no-self), Anicca (impermanence). - Karma: Action’s consequences, not material; ended via Eightfold Path, not penance alone. - Liberation: Nirvana (extinction of desire), not soul-based. - Text: Pali Canon (e.g., Dhammapada). - Hinduism (Vedanta): - Core: Brahman as ultimate reality; Atman (soul) unites with Brahman (Advaita) or serves God (Dvaita). - Karma: Influences rebirth; ended via Jnana (knowledge), Bhakti (devotion), or Karma Yoga. - Liberation: Moksha; soul eternal, not in all objects. - Text: Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita. - Sankhya: - Core: Dualism (Purusha vs. Prakriti); atheistic. - Karma: Binds Purusha to Prakriti; ended by self-knowledge (Viveka), not penance. - Liberation: Kaivalya; souls distinct, not universal in matter. - Text: Sankhya Karika. - Christianity: - Core: Monotheism; God as creator, Jesus as savior. - Karma: Sin, not rebirth; overcome by faith, not penance alone. - Liberation: Salvation (eternal life); soul eternal, not in objects. - Text: Bible (New Testament). - Islam: - Core: Tawhid (oneness of Allah); submission to God’s will. - Karma: Deeds judged on Day of Judgment, no rebirth. - Liberation: Paradise; soul eternal, not in all matter. - Text: Quran. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Acaranga Sutra: Mahavira’s penance; Tattvartha Sutra: “Souls render services to one another” (5.21). - Practices: - Monks’ austere lifestyle, Paryushana festival (penance). - Broader Connection: - Links to Jainism (e.g., Q81 [Anekantavada]), Shramana traditions (e.g., Q85 [Buddhism/Jainism]), or Indian philosophy (e.g., Q91 [Sankhya]). - Key Takeaway: - All statements—penance annihilating karma (1), souls in every object (2), and karma as the soul’s bane (3)—apply to Jain doctrine, making (d) the correct answer. - Q95: With reference to the history of Indian rock-cut architecture, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The caves at Badami are the oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India 2. The Barabar rock-cut caves were originally made for Ajivikas by Emperor Chandragupta Maurya 3. At Ellora, caves were made for different faiths - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Indian rock-cut architecture, spanning from c. 3rd century BCE to 10th century CE, reflects the evolution of religious and artistic traditions. It includes Buddhist viharas and chaityas, Jain temples, and Hindu shrines, showcasing advanced engineering and patronage from rulers like the Mauryas, Satavahanas, Chalukyas, and Rashtrakutas. Major sites include Barabar, Badami, Ellora, Ajanta, and Elephanta. - Statement Analysis: - Statement 1: The caves at Badami are the oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India: - Incorrect—The Badami caves (Karnataka), carved during the Chalukya dynasty (c. 6th century CE), are significant for Hindu (Vishnu, Shiva) and Jain iconography. However, they are not the oldest. The Barabar caves (Bihar), dated to the Mauryan period (c. 3rd century BCE under Ashoka), predate Badami by centuries, making them the earliest surviving rock-cut caves in India. - Statement 2: The Barabar rock-cut caves were originally made for Ajivikas by Emperor Chandragupta Maurya: - Incorrect—The Barabar caves (c. 3rd century BCE) were indeed carved for the Ajivikas, a heterodox sect contemporary with Jainism and Buddhism. Inscriptions (e.g., at Sudama and Lomas Rishi caves) attribute them to Emperor Ashoka (r. 268-232 BCE) and his grandson Dasharatha, not Chandragupta Maurya (r. 321-297 BCE), who was Ashoka’s grandfather. Chandragupta is linked to Jainism (e.g., his abdication and death at Shravanabelagola), not Ajivika patronage or cave construction. - Statement 3: At Ellora, caves were made for different faiths: - Correct—The Ellora caves (Maharashtra), carved between the 6th and 10th centuries CE under the Rashtrakutas, exemplify religious syncretism. Of the 34 caves, 17 are Hindu (e.g., Kailasa Temple, Cave 16), 12 are Buddhist (e.g., Cave 10, Vishvakarma), and 5 are Jain (e.g., Cave 32, Indra Sabha). This diversity reflects patronage across faiths, unlike Ajanta (primarily Buddhist). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false; Badami caves are not the oldest (Barabar predates them). - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is false (Chandragupta Maurya didn’t commission Barabar caves; Ashoka did), though 3 is true. - (c) 3 only: - Correct—Only statement 3 accurately describes Ellora’s multi-faith caves. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Statements 1 and 2 are false; only 3 is correct. - Key Features of Indian Rock-Cut Architecture: - Barabar Caves (c. 3rd century BCE): - Location: Bihar; Mauryan period. - Purpose: Ajivika ascetic shelters; polished interiors (e.g., Lomas Rishi’s arched facade). - Patron: Ashoka, not Chandragupta Maurya. - Badami Caves (c. 6th century CE): - Location: Karnataka; Chalukya period. - Purpose: Hindu (e.g., Cave 3, Vishnu) and Jain worship. - Features: Ornate carvings, structural pillars. - Ellora Caves (c. 6th-10th century CE): - Location: Maharashtra; Rashtrakuta period. - Purpose: Hindu, Buddhist, Jain worship. - Features: Monolithic Kailasa Temple, viharas, chaityas. - Other Notable Sites: - Ajanta (c. 2nd century BCE-6th century CE): Buddhist; paintings, chaityas (e.g., Cave 1). - Elephanta (c. 5th-8th century CE): Hindu (Shiva); Trimurti sculpture. - Comparative Timeline: - 3rd century BCE: Barabar (Mauryan, Ajivika). - 2nd century BCE onward: Ajanta, Udayagiri (early Buddhist, Hindu). - 6th century CE: Badami (Chalukya). - 6th-10th century CE: Ellora (Rashtrakuta). - Related Evidence: - Inscriptions: - Barabar: Ashoka’s edicts (e.g., “for Ajivikas”); no mention of Chandragupta. - Ellora: Rashtrakuta inscriptions (e.g., Cave 16). - Artifacts: - Badami: Vishnu reliefs; Ellora: Buddha statues, Jain Tirthankaras. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mauryan art (e.g., Q87 [Ashokan pillars]), Chalukya architecture (e.g., Q89 [temple styles]), or religious pluralism (e.g., Q92 [syncretism]). - Key Takeaway: - Only Ellora’s multi-faith caves (3) are correctly described; Badami isn’t the oldest (1), and Barabar wasn’t made by Chandragupta (2), making (c) the correct answer. - Q96: The Chinese traveller Yuan Chwang (Hiuen Tsang) who visited India recorded the general conditions and culture of India at that time. In this context, which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. The roads and river-routes were completely immune from robbery 2. As regards punishment for offences, ordeals by fire, water and poison were the instruments for determining the innocence or guilt of a person 3. The tradesmen had to pay duties at ferries and barrier stations - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Yuan Chwang (Hiuen Tsang), a Chinese Buddhist monk, traveled to India between 629-645 CE during Harsha’s reign (606-647 CE) of the Pushyabhuti dynasty. His work, Si-Yu-Ki (Buddhist Records of the Western World), details India’s socio-political conditions, culture, and Buddhist sites like Nalanda, Taxila, and Prayag, offering a 7th-century snapshot under Harsha’s rule and smaller kingdoms. - Statement Analysis: - Statement 1: The roads and river-routes were completely immune from robbery: - Incorrect—Hiuen Tsang notes relative safety due to Harsha’s strict governance, but not absolute immunity. He mentions occasional banditry in less-controlled areas, contradicting the claim of complete safety. - Statement 2: As regards punishment for offences, ordeals by fire, water and poison were the instruments for determining the innocence or guilt of a person: - Correct—Hiuen Tsang describes trials by ordeal (fire, water, poison) as judicial methods, consistent with Dharmashastras (e.g., Manu Smriti) and observed in Harsha’s era for divine judgment. - Statement 3: The tradesmen had to pay duties at ferries and barrier stations: - Correct—Hiuen Tsang records tolls and duties at ferries and checkpoints for tradesmen, reflecting Harsha’s taxation system, also supported by the Arthashastra and trade evidence. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false; robbery wasn’t entirely absent. - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Correct—Statements 2 and 3 align with Hiuen Tsang’s account; 1 does not. - (c) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false; only 3 holds among this pair. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Statement 1’s exaggeration rules this out. - Key Observations from Hiuen Tsang’s Account: - Governance: - Harsha’s rule: Efficient, centralized, but not robbery-free. - Judicial System: - Ordeals alongside fines; minimal imprisonment. - Economy: - Trade flourished; duties levied at crossings. - Accounts of Other Travelers: - Faxian (c. 399-414 CE): - Period: Gupta Empire. - Observations: Roads relatively safe under Gupta peace; no explicit mention of ordeals; trade duties lighter, reflecting prosperous economy (A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms). - Al-Biruni (c. 1030 CE): - Period: Ghaznavid invasions. - Observations: Roads less secure due to turmoil; judicial system varied (Islamic influence); trade duties persisted but disrupted (Kitab al-Hind). - Ibn Battuta (c. 1333-1345 CE): - Period: Tughlaq dynasty. - Observations: Roads often unsafe (bandits, rebellions); punishments included mutilation, not ordeals; heavy taxation on trade (Rihla). - Marco Polo (c. 1292 CE): - Period: Pandya/Chola trade peak (South India). - Observations: Coastal routes busy, some piracy; no judicial ordeal mention; trade regulated with tolls. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Si-Yu-Ki: Ordeals (Book II), duties (Book IV). - Inscriptions: - Harsha’s Banskhera inscription: Administrative efficiency, not absolute safety. - Archaeological: - Nalanda seals, coins: Taxed trade under Harsha. - Broader Connection: - Links to Harsha’s reign (e.g., Q90 [administration]), Buddhist sites (e.g., Q84 [Nalanda]), or trade networks (e.g., Q80 [Silk Road]). - Key Takeaway: - Hiuen Tsang confirms ordeals (2) and trade duties (3), but roads weren’t robbery-free (1), making (b) correct. - Q97: In the context of cultural history of India, a pose in dance and dramatics called ‘Tribhanga' has been a favourite of Indian artists from ancient times till today. Which one of the following statements best describes this pose? - Options: (a) One leg is bent and the body is slightly but oppositely curved at waist and neck (b) Facial expressions, hand gestures and make-up are combined to symbolize certain epic or historic characters (c) Movements of body, face and hands are used to express oneself or to tell a story (d) A little smile, slightly curved waist and certain hand gestures are emphasized to express the feelings of love or eroticism - Answer: (a) One leg is bent and the body is slightly but oppositely curved at waist and neck - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Tribhanga (Sanskrit: "three bends") is a classical pose in Indian art, dance, and sculpture, prominent since ancient times (c. 2nd century BCE onward). It features in temple sculptures (e.g., Khajuraho, Konark), classical dance forms (e.g., Odissi, Bharatanatyam), and medieval paintings. Rooted in the Natyashastra (c. 200 BCE-200 CE) by Bharata Muni, it symbolizes grace, fluidity, and aesthetic balance, often depicting deities (Krishna, Vishnu) or apsaras. - Option Analysis: - (a) One leg is bent and the body is slightly but oppositely curved at waist and neck: - Correct—Tribhanga is defined by three distinct bends: one leg bent at the knee, the torso curved oppositely at the waist, and the neck tilted in the opposite direction. This S-shaped posture creates a dynamic, harmonious form, as seen in Odissi’s iconic stance or sculptures like Krishna playing the flute (e.g., Chola bronzes, c. 10th century CE). - (b) Facial expressions, hand gestures and make-up are combined to symbolize certain epic or historic characters: - Incorrect—This describes Abhinaya (expression) in Indian dance/drama (Natyashastra, Ch. 8-13), not Tribhanga. Abhinaya uses mudras (hand gestures), bhavas (emotions), and makeup, but Tribhanga is a specific physical pose, not an expressive technique. - (c) Movements of body, face and hands are used to express oneself or to tell a story: - Incorrect—This broadly describes Nritya (expressive dance) in Indian tradition, not Tribhanga specifically. Tribhanga is a static pose, not a narrative movement sequence. - (d) A little smile, slightly curved waist and certain hand gestures are emphasized to express the feelings of love or eroticism: - Incorrect—While Tribhanga can convey sensuality (e.g., in Radha-Krishna depictions), it’s not defined by a smile, gestures, or eroticism. The pose’s essence lies in its triple curvature, not specific emotions or mudras. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b): Refers to Abhinaya, not a pose like Tribhanga. - (c): Too general; describes dance storytelling, not a specific stance. - (d): Partially overlaps (curved waist), but adds unrelated elements (smile, love), missing Tribhanga’s full definition. - Key Features of Tribhanga: - Structure: - Three bends: leg (knee), waist (torso), neck (head). - Usage: - Dance: Odissi (e.g., Batu Nritya), Bharatanatyam (subtle variations). - Sculpture: Gupta era (e.g., Sarnath Buddha), Chola bronzes, Khajuraho figures. - Symbolism: - Grace, balance; often divine or feminine figures (Krishna, Gopis). - Related Concepts in Indian Art: - Bhanga Poses (Natyashastra): - Samabhanga: Straight, symmetrical (e.g., standing deities). - Abhanga: Single bend (slight tilt). - Tribhanga: Triple bend (most dynamic). - Atibhanga: Extreme bend (rare, e.g., cosmic dance). - Mudras: - Hand gestures (e.g., Abhaya, Varada) complement poses but aren’t Tribhanga. - Related Evidence: - Texts: - Natyashastra: Defines poses like Tribhanga (Ch. 4, sculptural context). - Artifacts: - Didarganj Yakshi (c. 3rd century BCE): Early Tribhanga prototype. - Khajuraho (c. 10th century CE): Apsaras in Tribhanga. - Broader Connection: - Links to Indian dance (e.g., Q83 [classical forms]), temple art (e.g., Q89 [Chola bronzes]), or aesthetics (e.g., Q91 [Rasa theory]). - Key Takeaway: - Tribhanga is best described as a pose with one bent leg and opposite curves at waist and neck (a), distinguishing it from expressive or narrative elements in other options. - Q98: Consider the following historical places: - Places: 1. Sanchi Stupa - Question: Which of the above places is/are also known for mural paintings? - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 and 2 only (c) 1, 2 and 3 (d) None - Answer: (b) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Mural paintings in India, created with natural pigments on walls or rock surfaces, span ancient to medieval periods, reflecting Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain themes. Ajanta, Lepakshi, and Sanchi highlight diverse artistic traditions. - Place Analysis: - 1. Ajanta Caves: - Correct—In Maharashtra, Ajanta (c. 2nd century BCE-6th century CE) is a Buddhist site famous for murals depicting Jataka tales and Buddha’s life, painted in caves like 1 and 2. - 2. Lepakshi Temple: - Correct—In Andhra Pradesh, Lepakshi (c. 16th century CE), a Vijayanagara-era temple, features ceiling murals of Ramayana and Shiva stories. - 3. Sanchi Stupa: - Incorrect—In Madhya Pradesh, Sanchi (c. 3rd century BCE, expanded under Guptas) is known for stone carvings on its gateways, not murals. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Excludes Lepakshi’s murals. - (b) 1 and 2 only: - Correct—Captures both mural sites. - (c) 1, 2 and 3: - Sanchi lacks murals. - (d) None: - Ajanta and Lepakshi disprove this. - Key Features: - Ajanta: Buddhist narratives, tempera style. - Lepakshi: Hindu epics, fresco-secco technique. - Sanchi: Sculptural reliefs, no paintings. - Related Figures: - Vakataka Rulers (Ajanta): - Patrons like Harishena (c. 5th century CE) supported Ajanta’s murals. - Hiuen Tsang (Ajanta context): - Traveler (c. 629-645 CE); notes Buddhist cave art, likely Ajanta’s painted figures. - Vijayanagara Kings (Lepakshi): - Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509-1529 CE) or governors funded Lepakshi’s art. - Ashoka (Sanchi): - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE); Sanchi patron, tied to carvings. - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhist art (Q95 [Ellora]), Vijayanagara style (Q89), or painting traditions. - Key Takeaway: - Ajanta (1) and Lepakshi (2) are mural sites, Sanchi (3) is not, making (b) correct. - [2014-I] - Q99: With reference to the Indian history of art and culture, consider the following pairs: - Pairs (Famous work of sculpture : Site): 1. A huge image of Varaha Avatar (boar incarnation) of Vishnu, as he rescues Goddess Earth from the deep and chaotic waters, sculpted on rock: Mount Abu 3. “Arjuna's Penance”/“Descent of Ganga” sculpted on the surface of huge boulders: Mamallapuram - Question: Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched? - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 1 and 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Indian sculptural art, spanning ancient to medieval periods, reflects religious and cultural narratives through rock-cut and free-standing works, often patronized by dynasties like the Vakatakas, Pallavas, and others. A grand image of Buddha's Mahaparinirvana with numerous celestial musicians above and the sorrowful figures of his followers below: Ajanta: - Correct—At Ajanta Caves (Maharashtra, c. 2nd century BCE-6th century CE), Cave 26 features a large reclining Buddha sculpture (c. 5th century CE) depicting his Mahaparinirvana (final nirvana at death). The described Varaha sculpture is at Udayagiri Caves (Madhya Pradesh, c. 5th century CE, Gupta period), a rock-cut relief showing Vishnu lifting Goddess Earth (Prithvi). - 3. “Arjuna's Penance”/“Descent of Ganga” sculpted on the surface of huge boulders: Mamallapuram: - Correct—Mamallapuram (Tamil Nadu, c. 7th-8th century CE), a Pallava-era site, features the massive rock relief known as “Arjuna’s Penance” or “Descent of Ganga.” Carved on two boulders, it depicts either Arjuna’s austerity or the Ganga’s descent, with gods, sages, and animals. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect—Pair 2 mismatches; Varaha is at Udayagiri, not Mount Abu. - (b) 3 only: - Incorrect—Pair 1 is also correct (Ajanta’s Mahaparinirvana). - (c) 1 and 3 only: - Correct—Pairs 1 (Ajanta) and 3 (Mamallapuram) match; 2 does not. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Pair 2 is wrong. - Key Features: - Ajanta (Pair 1): Buddhist rock-cut, Mahaparinirvana scene. - Mount Abu (Pair 2): Jain marble work, not Varaha; correct site is Udayagiri. - Mamallapuram (Pair 3): Hindu rock relief, narrative complexity. - Related Figures: - Vakataka Rulers (Ajanta): - Patrons like Harishena (c. 5th century CE) oversaw Ajanta’s art, including the Mahaparinirvana sculpture. - Hiuen Tsang (Ajanta context): - Traveler (c. 629-645 CE); describes Buddhist caves with sculptures, likely Ajanta’s. - Gupta Rulers (Varaha context): - Patrons (c. 5th century CE) of Udayagiri’s Varaha relief, not Mount Abu. - Pallava Kings (Mamallapuram): - Narasimhavarman I (r. 630-668 CE) commissioned Mamallapuram’s rock art, including “Arjuna’s Penance.” - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhist art (Q95 [Ellora]), Gupta sculpture (Q88), or Pallava style (Q89). - Key Takeaway: - Pairs 1 (Ajanta) and 3 (Mamallapuram) are correctly matched, but 2 (Varaha at Mount Abu) is not, making (c) correct. - Q100: With reference to Buddhist history, tradition and culture in India, consider the following pairs: - Pairs (Famous shrine : Location): 1. Tabo monastery and temple complex: Spiti Valley 2. Lhotsava Lhakhang temple, Nako: Zanskar Valley 3. Alchi temple complex: Ladakh - Question: Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched? - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 1 and 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Buddhist shrines in India, particularly in the Himalayan region, reflect the spread of Buddhism from the Mauryan period (c. 3rd century BCE) onward, flourishing under various patrons. - Options: (a) Mimamsa and Vedanta (b) Nyaya and Vaisheshika (c) Lokayata and Kapalika (d) Sankhya and Yoga - Answer: (c) Lokayata and Kapalika - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The six systems of Indian philosophy, known as Shad-Darshanas, are orthodox (Astika) schools that accept Vedic authority: Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Sankhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, and Vedanta. Emerging between c. 1000 BCE and 500 CE, they offer frameworks for understanding reality, ethics, and liberation (Moksha). - Pair Analysis: - (a) Mimamsa and Vedanta: - Correct Pair—Both are Shad-Darshanas. Mimamsa (Purva Mimamsa) focuses on Vedic rituals and karma, while Vedanta (Uttara Mimamsa) interprets the Upanishads for metaphysical liberation. - (b) Nyaya and Vaisheshika: - Correct Pair—Both belong to the six systems. Nyaya emphasizes logic and epistemology, while Vaisheshika focuses on atomistic metaphysics; they often complement each other. - (c) Lokayata and Kapalika: - Incorrect Pair—Lokayata (Charvaka), a materialist, heterodox (Nastika) school rejecting Vedic authority, is not part of the Shad-Darshanas. Kapalika, a Shaivite tantric sect, is a religious tradition, not a philosophical system, and also falls outside the six. - (d) Sankhya and Yoga: - Correct Pair—Both are Shad-Darshanas. Sankhya provides a dualistic metaphysics (Purusha-Prakriti), while Yoga offers practical methods (e.g., Patanjali’s eight limbs) for liberation based on Sankhya. - Why (c) Is the Answer?: - Lokayata and Kapalika don’t align with the six orthodox systems. Lokayata denies the Vedas, and Kapalika is a ritualistic sect, not a Darshana. - The Six Systems (Shad-Darshanas): - Nyaya: Logic, epistemology (Gautama). - Vaisheshika: Atomism, categories (Kanada). - Sankhya: Dualism, enumeration (Kapila). - Yoga: Practice, meditation (Patanjali). - Mimamsa: Ritual, duty (Jaimini). - Vedanta: Metaphysics, unity (Badarayana). - Related Figures: - Gautama (Nyaya): - Founder (c. 2nd century CE), authored Nyaya Sutras. - Kanada (Vaisheshika): - Founder (c. 6th century BCE), Vaisheshika Sutras. - Kapila (Sankhya): - Sage (c. 6th century BCE), Sankhya philosophy. - Patanjali (Yoga): - Codifier (c. 2nd century CE), Yoga Sutras. - Jaimini (Mimamsa): - Founder (c. 4th century BCE), Mimamsa Sutras. - Badarayana (Vedanta): - Author (c. 4th century BCE), Brahma Sutras. - Brihaspati (Lokayata): - Attributed founder (pre-6th century BCE), materialist school. - Broader Connection: - Ties to Indian philosophy (Q94 [Jainism]), Vedic traditions (Q88), or heterodox schools (Q85). - Key Takeaway: - Lokayata and Kapalika (c) don’t belong to the six systems, unlike the orthodox pairs in (a), (b), and (d). - Q102: The national motto of India, ‘Satyameva Jayate' inscribed below the Emblem of India is taken from: - Options: (a) Katha Upanishad (b) Chandogya Upanishad (c) Aitareya Upanishad (d) Mundaka Upanishad - Answer: (d) Mundaka Upanishad - Analysis: - Historical Context: - ‘Satyameva Jayate’ ("Truth Alone Triumphs") became India’s national motto on January 26, 1950, inscribed below the Emblem of India. The Upanishads, philosophical texts from the Vedic period (c. 1200-600 BCE), influenced India’s cultural and national identity. - Option Analysis: - (a) Katha Upanishad: - Incorrect—Focuses on Nachiketa’s dialogue with Yama about the soul and liberation, not ‘Satyameva Jayate.’ - (b) Chandogya Upanishad: - Incorrect—Known for ‘Tat Tvam Asi,’ not the motto. - (c) Aitareya Upanishad: - Incorrect—Covers creation and consciousness, no mention of the phrase. - (d) Mundaka Upanishad: - Correct—Mundaka Upanishad (3.1.6) states "Satyameva jayate nanritam" ("Truth alone triumphs, not falsehood"), the source of the motto. - Why (d) Is Correct?: - The Mundaka Upanishad’s emphasis on truth reflects India’s constitutional ethos, chosen by the Constituent Assembly. - Key Features of Mundaka Upanishad: - Part of Atharva Veda; distinguishes higher (Para) and lower (Apara) knowledge, advocating truth as supreme. - Related Figures: - Badarayana: - Compiler of Brahma Sutras (c. 4th century BCE), systematized Upanishadic philosophy. - Shankaracharya: - Philosopher (c. 8th century CE), commented on Mundaka, enhancing its legacy. - B.R. Ambedkar: - Key figure in India’s Constitution (1950), linked to motto adoption. - Other National Symbols from Ancient India: - Ashoka’s Lion Capital: - From Sarnath (c. 250 BCE), adopted as the Emblem of India (1950), symbolizing righteousness and unity. - ‘Satyameva Jayate’: - From Mundaka Upanishad, inscribed below the Emblem, reflects Vedic truth. - Dharma Chakra: - Ashokan wheel on the Lion Capital, featured in the National Flag, signifies law and progress. - Jana Gana Mana: - National Anthem by Rabindranath Tagore (1911), inspired by ancient cultural unity, not directly Vedic but rooted in heritage. - Lotus: - National Flower, symbol of purity in ancient texts (e.g., Bhagavad Gita). - Broader Connection: - Links to Vedic thought (Q101 [Darshanas]), national symbols (Q87 [Ashoka]), or philosophy (Q94). - Key Takeaway: - ‘Satyameva Jayate’ is from Mundaka Upanishad (d), a Vedic root of India’s identity. - Q103: Which of the following Kingdoms were associated with the life of the Buddha? - Kingdoms: 1. Avanti 2. Gandhara 3. Kosala 4. Magadha - Options: (a) 1, 2 and 3 (b) 2 and 4 (c) 3 and 4 only (d) 1, 3 and 4 - Answer: (c) 3 and 4 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Gautama Buddha (c. 563-483 BCE) lived during the Mahajanapada era (c. 6th-4th centuries BCE) in northern India. His life events—birth, enlightenment, teaching, and death—occurred in specific kingdoms, as documented in Buddhist texts like the Pali Canon. - Kingdom Analysis: - 1. Avanti: - Incorrect—Avanti (modern Madhya Pradesh, capital: Ujjain) was a major kingdom but not directly tied to Buddha’s core life events. His disciples (e.g., Mahakaccana) later preached there. - 2. Gandhara: - Incorrect—Gandhara (modern northwest Pakistan/Afghanistan) became a Buddhist hub post-Buddha (e.g., Kushan period, c. 1st century CE), not during his lifetime. - 3. Kosala: - Correct—Kosala (modern Uttar Pradesh, capital: Shravasti) hosted Buddha’s birth (Lumbini, then part of Kosala) and much of his teaching (Shravasti), supported by King Prasenajit. - 4. Magadha: - Correct—Magadha (modern Bihar, capitals: Rajgir, Pataliputra) was central: enlightenment (Bodh Gaya), first sermon (Sarnath), and death (Kushinagar, under Magadha’s influence), backed by Kings Bimbisara and Ajatashatru. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1, 2 and 3: - Avanti (1) and Gandhara (2) lack direct association. - (b) 2 and 4: - Misses Kosala (3); Gandhara (2) is unrelated. - (c) 3 and 4 only: - Correct—Kosala and Magadha were key. - (d) 1, 3 and 4: - Avanti (1) isn’t directly linked. - Key Associations: - Kosala: Birth, teaching hub. - Magadha: Enlightenment, preaching, death. - Related Figures: - Gautama Buddha: - Lived and taught in Kosala and Magadha (c. 563-483 BCE). - Bimbisara: - Magadha king (r. c. 543-491 BCE), early patron. - Prasenajit: - Kosala king (c. 6th century BCE), contemporary supporter. - Ajatashatru: - Magadha king (r. c. 491-459 BCE), post-death council host. - Other Significant Places in Buddhist and Jain Contexts: - Lumbini (Kosala): - Buddha’s birthplace (c. 563 BCE), now Nepal. - Bodh Gaya (Magadha): - Buddha’s enlightenment (c. 528 BCE). - Sarnath (Magadha): - First sermon (c. 528 BCE), Dhamek Stupa. - Kushinagar (Magadha): - Buddha’s death (c. 483 BCE), Parinirvana site. - Shravasti (Kosala): - Teaching center, Jetavana Monastery. - Rajgir (Magadha): - Early teachings, Gridhrakuta Hill. - Vaishali (Vajji): - Second Buddhist Council (c. 383 BCE), Jainism link (Mahavira’s death). - Pataliputra (Magadha): - Third Buddhist Council (c. 250 BCE), Jain council (c. 3rd century BCE). - Shravanabelagola (South India): - Jain site, Bhadrabahu’s death (c. 3rd century BCE). - Udayagiri-Khandagiri (Kalinga): - Jain caves, Kharavela’s patronage (c. 1st century BCE). - Broader Connection: - Ties to Buddhist history (Q100 [shrines]), Ashokan legacy (Q87), or Mahajanapadas (Q88). - Key Takeaway: - Kosala (3) and Magadha (4) were directly associated with Buddha’s life, making (c) correct. - Q104: With reference to the art and archaeological history of India, which one among the following was made earliest? - Options: (a) Lingaraja Temple at Bhubaneswar (b) Rock-cut Elephant at Dhauli (c) Rock-cut Monuments at Mahabalipuram (d) Varaha Image at Udayagiri - Answer: (b) Rock-cut Elephant at Dhauli - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Indian art and archaeology span millennia, from Mauryan rock-cut works (c. 3rd century BCE) to medieval temple architecture (c. 11th century CE), reflecting diverse patronage and styles across dynasties. - Option Analysis: - (a) Lingaraja Temple at Bhubaneswar: - Incorrect—Built c. 11th century CE (Somavamshi dynasty) in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, this Hindu temple is a late example of Kalinga architecture, featuring a towering deul (spire). - (b) Rock-cut Elephant at Dhauli: - Correct—Carved c. 3rd century BCE (Mauryan period) near Dhauli, Odisha, this rock-cut elephant is part of Ashoka’s edict site, post-Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE), making it the earliest. - (c) Rock-cut Monuments at Mahabalipuram: - Incorrect—Created c. 7th-8th centuries CE (Pallava dynasty) in Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu, these include the “Descent of Ganga” relief and rathas, much later than Dhauli. - (d) Varaha Image at Udayagiri: - Incorrect—Sculpted c. 5th century CE (Gupta period) at Udayagiri Caves, Madhya Pradesh, this rock-cut Varaha (Vishnu’s boar avatar) rescuing Earth is early but postdates Dhauli. - Why (b) Is Correct?: - The Dhauli Elephant (c. 3rd century BCE) predates the others by centuries, tied to Ashoka’s reign and the Mauryan era’s earliest surviving rock art. - Timeline: - Rock-cut Elephant, Dhauli: c. 3rd century BCE. - Varaha Image, Udayagiri: c. 5th century CE. - Rock-cut Monuments, Mahabalipuram: c. 7th-8th centuries CE. - Lingaraja Temple, Bhubaneswar: c. 11th century CE. - Other Important Ancient Indian Artworks: - Sanchi Stupa (Madhya Pradesh): - c. 3rd century BCE, Mauryan carvings, gateways added later. - Ajanta Caves (Maharashtra): - c. 2nd century BCE-6th century CE, Buddhist murals and sculptures. - Didarganj Yakshi (Bihar): - c. 3rd century BCE, Mauryan polished stone statue. - Ellora Caves (Maharashtra): - c. 6th-10th centuries CE, multi-faith rock-cut temples. - Khajuraho Temples (Madhya Pradesh): - c. 9th-11th centuries CE, Chandela dynasty, erotic sculptures. - Related Figures: - Ashoka (Dhauli): - Mauryan emperor (r. 268-232 BCE), commissioned Dhauli’s elephant and edicts. - Gupta Rulers (Udayagiri): - Patrons like Chandragupta II (r. c. 375-415 CE), oversaw Varaha sculpture. - Narasimhavarman I (Mahabalipuram): - Pallava king (r. 630-668 CE), key figure in Mahabalipuram’s rock art. - Somavamshi Kings (Bhubaneswar): - Rulers (c. 9th-11th centuries CE), built Lingaraja Temple. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mauryan art (Q87 [Ashoka]), Gupta sculpture (Q99), or Pallava style (Q95). - Key Takeaway: - The Rock-cut Elephant at Dhauli (b), from c. 3rd century BCE, is the earliest among the options. - [2015-I] - Q105: Which one of the following books of ancient India has the love story of the son of the founder of Sunga dynasty? - Options: (a) Swapnavasavadatta (b) Malavikagnimitra (c) Meghadoota (d) Ratnavali - Answer: (b) Malavikagnimitra - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Sunga dynasty (c. 185-73 BCE) succeeded the Mauryas in northern India (Magadha, modern Bihar), founded by Pushyamitra Sunga (r. c. 185-149 BCE). Ancient Indian literature, especially Sanskrit plays, often wove historical figures into romantic narratives. - Correct Option Explained: - (b) Malavikagnimitra: - Correct—Malavikagnimitra, a Sanskrit play by Kalidasa (c. 4th-5th century CE, Gupta period), narrates the love story of Agnimitra, son of Pushyamitra Sunga, and Malavika, a princess. Set in the Sunga court (Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh), it blends romance with court intrigue. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Swapnavasavadatta: - Incorrect—Swapnavasavadatta by Bhasa (c. 2nd century BCE) tells the love story of King Udayana (pre-Mauryan) and Vasavadatta, unrelated to the Sungas. - (c) Meghadoota: - Incorrect—Meghadoota by Kalidasa (c. 4th-5th century CE) is a lyrical poem about a Yaksha’s longing for his wife, not a Sunga narrative. - (d) Ratnavali: - Incorrect—Ratnavali by Harsha (c. 7th century CE) depicts the romance of King Udayana and Princess Ratnavali, post-Sunga, unrelated to Pushyamitra’s lineage. - Plot Summary: - Malavikagnimitra: - Agnimitra, a Sunga prince, falls for Malavika, a disguised princess. Despite queenly opposition, their love triumphs, reflecting Gupta-era romantic drama (Prakarana genre). - Other Relevant Ancient Indian Books and Plays: - Mrichchhakatika: - Author: Shudraka (c. 4th-5th century CE, Gupta period) - Theme: Love between Charudatta (merchant) and Vasantasena (courtesan), social drama (e.g., Q65 [1998]). - Location: Ujjain (Madhya Pradesh). - Mudrarakshasa: - Author: Vishakhadatta (c. 4th-5th century CE, Gupta period) - Theme: Political intrigue, Chanakya’s alliance with Chandragupta Maurya, not romance (e.g., Q62 [1998]). - Location: Pataliputra (Bihar). - Abhijnanashakuntalam: - Author: Kalidasa (c. 4th-5th century CE, Gupta period) - Theme: Love between King Dushyanta and Shakuntala, mythological romance. - Location: Hastinapura (Uttar Pradesh context). - Priyadarshika: - Author: Harsha (c. 7th century CE) - Theme: Love story of King Udayana and Priyadarshika, romantic drama. - Location: Kaushambi (Uttar Pradesh). - Uttararamacharita: - Author: Bhavabhuti (c. 8th century CE) - Theme: Rama’s later life and love for Sita, post-Ramayana narrative. - Location: Ayodhya (Uttar Pradesh context). - Literary Significance: - Malavikagnimitra reflects Gupta-era idealization of Sunga history, blending historical figures with poetic license, a hallmark of Kalidasa’s dramatic style. - Related Figures: - Pushyamitra Sunga: - Sunga founder (r. c. 185-149 BCE), overthrew Mauryas (e.g., Q67 [1998]). - Agnimitra: - Sunga prince (r. c. 149-141 BCE), son of Pushyamitra, Malavikagnimitra’s hero. - Kalidasa: - Gupta poet (c. 4th-5th century CE), authored Malavikagnimitra (e.g., Q65 [1998]). - Bhasa: - Playwright (c. 2nd century BCE), wrote Swapnavasavadatta. - Broader Connection: - Links to Sunga history (e.g., Q67 [1998]), Gupta literature (e.g., Q65 [1998]), or ancient plays (e.g., Q62 [1998] Mudrarakshasa). -
