Jaugada (Odisha, not Madhya Pradesh) and Kalsi (Uttarakhand, not Karnataka) are mismatched, aligning with option (b). - Site Details: - Dhauli: - Location: Odisha, near Bhubaneswar. - Features: Edicts I-IX, XI-XIV, Kalinga Edict; elephant sculpture. - Erragudi: - Location: Andhra Pradesh, Kurnool district. - Features: Full set of 14 edicts, boulder inscriptions. - Jaugada: - Location: Odisha, Ganjam district. - Features: Edicts I-IX, XI-XIV, Kalinga Edict; fort ruins. - Kalsi: - Location: Uttarakhand, Dehradun district. - Features: Full set of 14 edicts, riverside rock. - Other Related Ashokan Sites: - Girnar: - Location: Gujarat, Junagadh. - Context: 14 Major Rock Edicts (e.g., Q128 [Girinagar]). - Shahbazgarhi: - Location: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. - Context: 14 edicts in Kharoshthi script. - Sopara: - Location: Maharashtra, near Mumbai. - Context: Edict fragments, coastal trade link. - Maski: - Location: Karnataka, Raichur district. - Context: Minor Rock Edict naming Ashoka. - Sannathi: - Location: Karnataka, Gulbarga district. - Context: Edict site, Buddhist remains. - Historical Significance: - Ashoka’s edicts, including those at Dhauli and Erragudi, reflect his governance through Dhamma, promoting ethics and unity across diverse regions, with accurate locations critical to understanding Mauryan reach (e.g., Q127 [Ashoka’s tolerance]). - Related Evidence: - Inscriptions: - Dhauli: Kalinga Edict (ASI, 19th century). - Erragudi: Full edict set (Hultzsch, 1925). - Texts: - Divyavadana (c. 2nd century CE): Ashoka’s reign context. - Archaeology: - Kalsi rock: Cunningham’s documentation. - Related Figures: - Ashoka: - Mauryan king (r. c. 268-232 BCE); edict issuer. - Alexander Cunningham: - ASI founder (1861); mapped edict sites. - E. Hultzsch: - Epigraphist (1925); deciphered edicts. - Broader Connection: - Links to Mauryan policy (e.g., Q127 [edict quote]), sites (e.g., Q132 [Sanchi]), or trade (e.g., Q129 [ports]). - Key Takeaway: - Only two pairs—Dhauli (Odisha) and Erragudi (Andhra Pradesh)—are correctly matched, making (b) the correct answer. - Ashoka's rock edicts already discussed in detail in previous PYQ's - [2022-I] - Q139: Which one of the following statements about Sangam literature in ancient South India is correct? - Options: (a) Sangam poems are devoid of any reference to material culture (b) The social classification of Varna was known to Sangam poets (c) Sangam poems have no reference to warrior ethic (d) Sangam literature refers to magical forces as irrational - Answer: (b) The social classification of Varna was known to Sangam poets - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Sangam literature, composed in Tamil between c. 300 BCE and 300 CE, represents the earliest secular poetry of South India, compiled during the Sangam Age by poets in academies (Sangams) in Madurai, Tamil Nadu. Preserved in anthologies like Ettuthokai and Pattuppattu, and the Tolkappiyam (grammar text), it reflects the culture of the Pandya, Chola, and Chera kingdoms, blending Dravidian traditions with northern influences. - Evaluation of Statements: - (a) Sangam poems are devoid of any reference to material culture: - Incorrect—Sangam poems are rich with material culture references, detailing agriculture (e.g., Purananuru 18 on rice fields), trade (e.g., Pattinappalai on Kaveripattinam port), jewelry, and weapons (e.g., Akananuru 73 on iron swords), showcasing a vibrant society. - (b) The social classification of Varna was known to Sangam poets: - Correct—While Sangam society was primarily tribal and occupation-based (e.g., Kuravar hunters, Velalar farmers), Varna (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) appears in poems, indicating Aryan influence. For example, Purananuru 166 mentions Brahmins (Andanar) and kings (Kshatriya-like), and Tolkappiyam references Vedic rituals, showing familiarity with the system. - (c) Sangam poems have no reference to warrior ethic: - Incorrect—Warrior ethic is central to Sangam poetry, especially in Purananuru, which glorifies bravery, honor, and death in battle (e.g., Poem 74 on a warrior’s valor). Kings and chieftains (e.g., Chera’s Neduncheralathan) are celebrated for martial prowess. - (d) Sangam literature refers to magical forces as irrational: - Incorrect—Sangam poems embrace magical forces as part of life, not irrational. Akananuru 59 describes omens and spirits (e.g., Anangu), and Tolkappiyam integrates supernatural elements into cosmology, reflecting a worldview where magic coexists with reality. - Why (b) only?: - Option (a): False—Material culture abounds (e.g., trade goods in Silappadikaram). - Option (b): True—Varna is evident (e.g., Brahmin priests in Purananuru 15). - Option (c): False—Warrior ethic is pervasive (e.g., Purananuru 278). - Option (d): False—Magic is revered, not dismissed (e.g., Akananuru 149). - Sangam Literature Details: - Period: c. 300 BCE-300 CE. - Texts: Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies), Pattuppattu (Ten Songs), Tolkappiyam. - Themes: Love (Akam), war (Puram), kingship, nature. - Language: Old Tamil, preserved by Tamil Sangams. - Other Related Sangam Concepts: - Tinai: - Meaning: Ecological zones (e.g., Kurinji hills, Marudam plains). - Context: Framework for Akam poetry (e.g., Akananuru). - Akam and Puram: - Meaning: Inner (love) and outer (war) themes. - Context: Dual structure of Sangam poetry. - Velir: - Meaning: Chieftains or minor kings. - Context: Warrior patrons (e.g., Purananuru 201). - Anangu: - Meaning: Sacred forces or spirits. - Context: Supernatural beliefs (e.g., Akananuru 59). - Kaveripattinam: - Meaning: Port city (Puhar). - Context: Trade hub in Pattinappalai. - Other period literature basics -
Period Key Literature Language Themes

Harsha Period (606–647 CE) Harshacharita (Banabhatta), Ratnavali Sanskrit Biography, drama, political history
Chalukya-Pallava Period (6th–8th Century CE) Natyashastra (Bharata), Kiratarjuniya (Bharavi) Sanskrit Drama, epic poetry

If a son born to a female slave was fathered by her master, the son was entitled to the legal status of the master's son: - Correct—Arthashastra (Book 3, Chapter 13) states that a son born to a female slave by her master was considered free and could inherit the legal status of the master’s legitimate son, ensuring his rights within the household. - [2023-I] - Q143: With reference to ancient South India, Korkai, Poompuhar and Muchiri were well known as: - Options: (a) capital cities (b) ports (c) centres of iron-and-steel making (d) shrines of Jain Tirthankaras - Answer: (b) ports - Analysis: - Historical Context: - During the Sangam period (c. 3rd century BCE-3rd century CE), South India under the Chola, Chera, and Pandya dynasties was a maritime powerhouse, with ports like Korkai, Poompuhar, and Muchiri facilitating trade with Rome, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East, as evidenced by Sangam literature, Roman texts, and archaeology. - Options: (a) Buddhism (b) Jainism (c) Shaivism (d) Vaishnavism - Answer: (b) Jainism - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ancient Indian religious sects (c. 6th century BCE onward) like Buddhism, Jainism, Shaivism, and Vaishnavism developed distinct metaphysical views. Jainism uniquely emphasizes the omnipresence of souls (jiva) across all existence, influencing its ethical practices. - Option Analysis: - (a) Buddhism: - Incorrect—Buddhism (c. 5th century BCE) denies a permanent soul (anatta), focusing on consciousness and rebirth without attributing souls to inanimate objects like rocks or water. - (b) Jainism: - Correct—Jainism (c. 6th century BCE, Mahavira’s era) holds that all entities—animals, plants, and even inanimate objects like rocks, water, air, and fire—possess souls (jiva). This animistic belief, detailed in texts like Tattvartha Sutra, underpins its strict non-violence (ahimsa) toward all forms. - (c) Shaivism: - Incorrect—Shaivism (c. 5th century BCE onward), a Hindu sect, worships Shiva and views the soul (atman) as eternal but limits it to living beings, not rocks or water, aligning with Vedic distinctions between sentient and insentient. - (d) Vaishnavism: - Incorrect—Vaishnavism (c. 4th century BCE onward), another Hindu sect, venerates Vishnu and similarly restricts the soul (atman) to living entities, not extending it to natural objects like Jainism does. - Why (b) Is Correct?: - Jainism’s core doctrine of jivastikaya posits souls in five elements (earth, water, fire, air, space), distinguishing it from Buddhism’s soul-less view and Hinduism’s living-only soul concept, perfectly matching the statement. - Key Features: - Jainism: Souls in all matter, basis for ahimsa and asceticism. - Related Figures: - Mahavira: - 24th Tirthankara (c. 599-527 BCE), formalized Jain soul doctrine. - Umasvati: - Jain scholar (c. 2nd-5th century CE), wrote Tattvartha Sutra on jiva. - Gautama Buddha: - Founder (c. 563-483 BCE), rejected permanent souls in Buddhism. - Shankaracharya (Shaivism/Vaishnavism context): - c. 8th century CE, unified Hindu atman concepts, distinct from Jainism. - Other Core Beliefs of Major Ancient Indian Sects: - Buddhism: - Anatta (no soul), Nirvana (cessation), Four Noble Truths. - Jainism: - Ahimsa (non-violence), Anekantavada (many-sided truth), souls in all. - Shaivism: - Shiva as supreme, Pashupati (lord of souls), liberation via devotion. - Vaishnavism: - Vishnu as supreme, Bhakti (devotion), Moksha via grace. - Broader Connection: - Links to Jainism (Q141 [scholars]), Buddhism (Q145 [Dhanyakataka]), or Hindu sects (Q102 [Upanishads]). - Key Takeaway: - The belief in souls in rocks, water, and all objects reflects Jainism (b), not Buddhism, Shaivism, or Vaishnavism. - Q149: Consider the following pairs: - Pairs (Site : Well known for): 1. Besnagar: Shaiva cave shrine: - Incorrect—Besnagar (modern Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh) is famous for the Heliodorus Pillar (c. 2nd century BCE), a Vaishnava monument linked to Vishnu worship, not a Shaiva cave shrine. No significant Shaiva caves are noted here. - 2. Bhaja: Buddhist cave shrine: - Correct—Bhaja (Maharashtra, c. 2nd century BCE) is a Buddhist rock-cut cave complex, part of the early Hinayana phase, known for its stupas, chaityas, and viharas, similar to nearby Karle. - 3. Sittanavasal: Jain cave shrine: - Correct—Sittanavasal (Tamil Nadu, c. 7th-9th century CE) is a Jain cave shrine, renowned for its rock-cut monastery and frescoes depicting Jain monks and deities, linked to Pandya patronage. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: - Incorrect—Two pairs (2 and 3) are correct. - (b) Only two: - Correct—Bhaja (2) and Sittanavasal (3) match; Besnagar (1) does not. - (c) All three: - Incorrect—Besnagar (1) is mismatched. - (d) None: - Incorrect—Pairs 2 and 3 are accurate. - Key Features: - Besnagar: Heliodorus Pillar, Vaishnava site. - Bhaja: Buddhist chaitya hall, early rock art. - Sittanavasal: Jain frescoes, monastic caves. - Related Figures: - Heliodorus (Besnagar): - Indo-Greek ambassador (c. 2nd century BCE), erected Vishnu pillar. - Satavahana Kings (Bhaja): - Rulers (c. 2nd century BCE-3rd century CE), patronized Bhaja caves. - Pandya Kings (Sittanavasal): - Rulers (c. 7th-9th century CE), supported Jain caves. - Mahavira (Jain context): - 24th Tirthankara (c. 599-527 BCE), inspired Sittanavasal’s tradition. - Other Notable Cave Shrines in Ancient India: - Ajanta (Maharashtra): - c. 2nd century BCE-6th century CE, Buddhist, murals and stupas. - Ellora (Maharashtra): - c. 6th-10th century CE, Buddhist, Jain, and Shaiva caves (e.g., Kailasa). - Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh): - c. 5th century CE, Gupta-era, Vaishnava and Shaiva caves. - Elephanta (Maharashtra): - c. 5th-7th century CE, Shaiva, Trimurti sculpture. - Karle (Maharashtra): - c. 2nd century BCE, Buddhist, grand chaitya hall. - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhist art (Q145 [Dhanyakataka]), Jain sites (Q148), or Gupta architecture (Q104 [Udayagiri]). - Key Takeaway: - Only two pairs—Bhaja (Buddhist) and Sittanavasal (Jain)—are correctly matched; Besnagar is Vaishnava, not Shaiva, making (b) the answer. - [2024-I] - Q150: Which one of the following is a work attributed to playwright Bhasa? - Options: (a) Kavyalankara (b) Natyashastra (c) Madhyama-vyayoga (d) Mahabhashya - Answer: (c) Madhyama-vyayoga - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Ancient Indian drama flourished between c. 2nd century BCE and 5th century CE, with playwrights like Bhasa contributing to Sanskrit theater. Bhasa, active around c. 2nd century BCE-2nd century CE, is known for plays based on epics like the Mahabharata and Ramayana, predating Kalidasa. - Option Analysis: - (a) Kavyalankara: - Incorrect—Kavyalankara is a treatise on poetics by Bhamaha (c. 7th century CE), not a play or by Bhasa. - (b) Natyashastra: - Incorrect—Natyashastra, the foundational text on dramaturgy, is attributed to Bharata Muni (c. 2nd century BCE-2nd century CE), not Bhasa, though it influenced his works. - (c) Madhyama-vyayoga: - Correct—Madhyama-vyayoga is a one-act play attributed to Bhasa, based on the Mahabharata, depicting Bhima’s quest for his son Ghatotkacha. It’s one of 13 plays discovered in 1912, linked to Bhasa’s style. - (d) Mahabhashya: - Incorrect—Mahabhashya is a grammatical commentary on Panini’s Ashtadhyayi by Patanjali (c. 2nd century BCE), not a dramatic work or by Bhasa. - Why (c) Is Correct?: - Madhyama-vyayoga matches Bhasa’s known corpus of Sanskrit plays, characterized by simple language and epic themes, distinct from poetics, dramaturgy, or grammar in the other options. - Key Features: - Madhyama-vyayoga: Short play, Mahabharata-based, Bhasa’s direct style. - Related Figures: - Bhasa: - Playwright (c. 2nd century BCE-2nd century CE), authored Madhyama-vyayoga, Svapnavasavadatta. - Bharata Muni: - Sage (c. 2nd century BCE-2nd century CE), wrote Natyashastra. - Bhamaha: - Poet (c. 7th century CE), authored Kavyalankara. - Patanjali: - Grammarian (c. 2nd century BCE), wrote Mahabhashya. - Other Notable Works by Ancient Indian Playwrights: - Svapnavasavadatta (Bhasa): - c. 2nd century BCE-2nd century CE, romantic play on Udayana. - Abhijnanashakuntala (Kalidasa): - c. 5th century CE, love story of Shakuntala and Dushyanta. - Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta): - c. 6th century CE, political drama on Chandragupta Maurya. - Mrichchhakatika (Shudraka): - c. 3rd-5th century CE, social play on Charudatta’s love. - Ratnavali (Harsha): - c. 7th century CE, romantic drama by King Harsha. - Broader Connection: - Links to Sanskrit literature (Q147 [literary works]), ancient theater (Q142 [Arthashastra context]), or epic traditions (Q104). - Key Takeaway: - Madhyama-vyayoga (c) is a work by Bhasa, unlike the others, which are not plays or his creations. - Q151: Sanghabhuti, an Indian Buddhist monk, who travelled to China at the end of the fourth century AD, was the author of a commentary on: - Options: (a) Prajnaparamita Sutra (b) Visuddhimagga (c) Sarvastivada Vinaya (d) Lalitavistara - Answer: (c) Sarvastivada Vinaya - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In the late 4th century CE (c. 380-400 CE), Indian Buddhist monks like Sanghabhuti traveled to China, contributing to the spread of Buddhism during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This period saw translations and commentaries on key texts, facilitated by monks and Chinese patrons. - Option Analysis: - (a) Prajnaparamita Sutra: - Incorrect—The Prajnaparamita Sutra, a Mahayana text on "Perfection of Wisdom" (c. 1st century BCE-1st century CE), was translated by figures like Kumarajiva (c. 401 CE), not commented on by Sanghabhuti. - (b) Visuddhimagga: - Incorrect—The Visuddhimagga, a Theravada meditation manual (c. 5th century CE), was authored by Buddhaghosa in Sri Lanka, not linked to Sanghabhuti or China. - (c) Sarvastivada Vinaya: - Correct—The Sarvastivada Vinaya, the monastic code of the Sarvastivada school (c. 2nd century BCE), was commented on by Sanghabhuti. He arrived in China c. 381 CE and worked on this text, which was translated into Chinese around 404-405 CE under supervision of Faxian and Buddhabhadra. - (d) Lalitavistara: - Incorrect—The Lalitavistara, a Mahayana biography of the Buddha (c. 3rd century CE), was translated later (e.g., by Divakara, 7th century CE), not associated with Sanghabhuti’s work. - Why (c) Is Correct?: - Historical records (e.g., Chinese Buddhist chronicles like the Gaoseng Zhuan) confirm Sanghabhuti’s commentary on the Sarvastivada Vinaya, a key disciplinary text, aligning with his mission to propagate monastic rules in China. - Key Features: - Sarvastivada Vinaya: Monastic regulations, Sarvastivada sect, translated into Chinese. - Related Figures: - Sanghabhuti: - Indian monk (fl. c. 381-405 CE), authored Sarvastivada Vinaya commentary. - Faxian: - Chinese monk (c. 337-422 CE), collaborated on Sarvastivada Vinaya translation. - Buddhabhadra: - Indian monk (c. 359-429 CE), co-translated with Sanghabhuti. - Kumarajiva: - Monk (344-413 CE), translated Prajnaparamita, contemporary context. - Other Notable Buddhist Texts Translated or Commented in China: - Lotus Sutra: - Mahayana, translated by Kumarajiva (c. 406 CE). - Heart Sutra: - Part of Prajnaparamita, translated by Xuanzang (c. 649 CE). - Diamond Sutra: - Mahayana, translated by Kumarajiva (c. 402 CE). - Abhidharma-kosa: - Sarvastivada, translated by Xuanzang (c. 651-654 CE). - Vinaya Pitaka (Dharmaguptaka): - Translated by Buddhayashas (c. 408 CE). - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhist texts (Q147 [Milinda-Panha]), travel accounts (Q96 [Hiuen Tsang]), or sects (Q145 [Mahasanghikas]). - Key Takeaway: - Sanghabhuti’s commentary was on the Sarvastivada Vinaya (c), not the other listed texts. - Q152: With reference to ancient India, Gautama Buddha was generally known by which of the following epithets? - Epithets: 1. Nayaputta 2. Shakyamuni 3. Tathagata - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1, 2 and 3 (d) None of the above are epithets of Gautama Buddha - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In ancient India (c. 6th century BCE onward), epithets were used to denote identity, lineage, or spiritual status for religious leaders and rulers, as seen in Buddhist, Jain, and royal traditions. Gautama Buddha (c. 563-483 BCE) earned titles reflecting his enlightenment and origins. - Epithet Analysis: - 1. Nayaputta: - Incorrect—"Nayaputta" (or Jnatiputra), meaning "son of the Naya clan," is an epithet for Mahavira, the Jain Tirthankara (c. 599-527 BCE), not Buddha. - 2. Shakyamuni: - Correct—"Shakyamuni" ("Sage of the Shakya clan") refers to Buddha’s birth in the Shakya tribe, widely used in Pali Canon (e.g., Digha Nikaya) and Mahayana texts. - 3. Tathagata: - Correct—"Tathagata" ("Thus Gone/Come") is a title Buddha used for himself in scriptures (e.g., Majjhima Nikaya), denoting an enlightened being, common across traditions. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect—Nayaputta is Mahavira’s, not Buddha’s. - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Correct—Shakyamuni and Tathagata are Buddha’s epithets; Nayaputta is not. - (c) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Nayaputta is misapplied. - (d) None of the above are epithets of Gautama Buddha: - Incorrect—Shakyamuni and Tathagata are accurate. - Key Features: - Shakyamuni: Lineage-based, historical. - Tathagata: Spiritual, self-referential. - Related Figures: - Gautama Buddha: - Founder (c. 563-483 BCE), known as Shakyamuni, Tathagata. - Mahavira: - Jain Tirthankara (c. 599-527 BCE), called Nayaputta. - Ananda: - Disciple (c. 5th century BCE), preserved Buddha’s epithets in teachings. - Ashoka: - Mauryan king (r. 268-232 BCE), used Buddha’s titles in edicts. - Other Notable Epithets of Gautama Buddha: - Bhagavan: - "Blessed One," reverential title in sutras. - Siddhartha: - Birth name, "He who achieves his goal." - Sasta Devamanusyanam: - "Teacher of Gods and Men," Pali Canon. - Samyak Sambuddha: - "Perfectly Enlightened One," Mahayana. - Lokavidu: - "Knower of the World," Theravada. - Notable Epithets of Other Ancient Indian Figures: - Ashoka: Devanampiya Piyadasi: - "Beloved of the Gods, He Who Looks with Kindness," Mauryan king (r. 268-232 BCE), from edicts. - Chandragupta Maurya: Sandrocottus: - Greek name (c. 321-297 BCE), from Megasthenes’ Indica. - Mahavira: Vardhamana: - "One Who Grows," Jain Tirthankara (c. 599-527 BCE), birth name. - Ajatashatru: Kunika: - Magadha king (r. c. 491-459 BCE), from Buddhist texts. - Harsha: Shiladitya: - "Lord of Virtue," king (r. 606-647 CE), from Hiuen Tsang. - Broader Connection: - Links to Buddhist history (Q145 [Dhanyakataka]), Jainism (Q148 [souls]), or rulers (Q103 [kingdoms]). - Key Takeaway: - Gautama Buddha was known as Shakyamuni (2) and Tathagata (3), but not Nayaputta, making (b) the answer. - Q153: Consider the following information: - Rows (Archaelogical site : State : Description): 1. There are no parables in Upanishads 2. Upanishads were composed earlier than the Puranas - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Hindu literature in ancient India spans the Vedic period (c. 1500-500 BCE) to the medieval era (c. 3rd century CE onward). The Upanishads, as philosophical Vedic texts (c. 1200-600 BCE), predate the narrative-heavy Puranas (c. 3rd century CE-10th century CE), reflecting an evolution from abstract inquiry to mythological synthesis. - Statement Analysis: - 1. There are no parables in Upanishads: - Incorrect—Parables are present in several Upanishads to illustrate complex ideas. Examples include Nachiketa’s dialogue with Yama on death and the soul in Katha Upanishad (c. 5th century BCE), Svetaketu’s salt-water analogy for Brahman in Chandogya Upanishad (c. 8th century BCE), and Prajapati’s teaching on the self via birds in Chandogya. - 2. Upanishads were composed earlier than the Puranas: - Correct—The Upanishads, as end portions (Vedanta) of the Vedas, date to c. 1200-600 BCE, while the Puranas, compiled later (c. 3rd century CE onward, e.g., Gupta period), draw from earlier oral traditions but postdate the Vedic corpus, focusing on cosmology and devotion. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false due to parables. - (b) 2 only: - Correct—Statement 2 is true; 1 is not. - (c) Both 1 and 2: - Incorrect—Only 2 is correct. - (d) Neither 1 nor 2: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is valid. - Key Features: - Upanishads: - Philosophical core of Vedanta, exploring Atman (soul) and Brahman (universal reality). - Composed in Sanskrit, often as dialogues (e.g., Yajnavalkya-Maitreyi in Brihadaranyaka). - Contain parables, metaphors (e.g., two birds in Mundaka Upanishad), and meditative practices (e.g., Om in Mandukya). - Number over 100, with 13 principal ones (e.g., Isha, Kena, Katha). - Puranas: - 18 major texts (e.g., Vishnu, Shiva, Bhagavata), blending mythology, history, and theology. - Focus on five topics (Pancha Lakshana): creation, dissolution, genealogies, Manvantaras, and dynasties. - Devotional narratives (e.g., Krishna in Bhagavata Purana), often linked to temple traditions. - Later compilations, reflecting Gupta and post-Gupta Bhakti movements. - Related Figures: - Yajnavalkya: - Sage (c. 8th century BCE), Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, taught Atman-Brahman unity. - Nachiketa: - Katha Upanishad (c. 5th century BCE), parable figure on mortality. - Vyasa: - Legendary sage (c. 3rd century CE), credited with compiling Puranas. - Badarayana: - Sage (c. 4th century BCE), Brahma Sutras, systematized Upanishadic thought. - Other Notable Hindu Texts in Ancient India: - Rig Veda: - c. 1500-1200 BCE, hymns to deities (e.g., Indra, Agni), earliest Vedic text. - Brahmanas: - c. 1000-800 BCE, ritual explanations attached to Vedas (e.g., Shatapatha Brahmana). - Aranyakas: - c. 1000-700 BCE, forest treatises bridging rituals and philosophy. - Bhagavad Gita: - c. 5th-2nd century BCE, part of Mahabharata, Krishna’s teachings on duty and yoga. - Manusmriti: - c. 2nd century BCE-3rd century CE, legal and social code by Manu. - Ramayana (Valmiki): - c. 5th century BCE, epic of Rama, moral and devotional narrative. - Broader Connection: - Links to Vedic literature (Q102 [Mundaka]), philosophy (Q101 [Darshanas]), or texts (Q147 [literary works]). - Key Takeaway: - Statement 2 (Upanishads predate Puranas) is correct, but 1 (no parables) is false, making (b) the answer.
